description: Double displacement reaction. Purpose: Production of a weaker acid and an insoluble salt. Key transformation: Exchange of cations and anions between HCl and silver acetate to form acetic acid and silver chloride precipitate. Conditions: Room temperature, aqueous solution. No catalyst required.

Oximation (condensation) of glyoxal with hydroxylamine to form glyoxime and water; each aldehyde carbonyl undergoes nucleophilic addition of NH₂OH followed by dehydration to generate the corresponding oxime (glyoxime). Conducted in an aqueous or alcoholic solution (often 1 M NH₂OH·HCl) at 0–25 °C, adjusting pH to about 5–6 with a buffer; the reaction proceeds readily without additional catalyst.

Free‑radical bromination of an alkane (secondary carbon substitution); purpose is to generate a brominated isomer; key transformation is abstraction of a hydrogen at C‑2 of 3‑ethylpentane and recombination with Br· to afford 2‑bromo‑3‑ethylpentane and HBr; typical conditions are similar to other radical brominations: Br2, UV light or heat, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride; no additional catalyst needed.

Redox reaction. Purpose: Oxidation of Fe²⁺ and reduction of Mn⁴⁺. Key transformations: Manganese dioxide (MnO₂) oxidizes FeSO₄ (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺), itself reduced to Mn²⁺. Sulfuric acid provides H⁺ for acidic medium. Conditions: Hot concentrated sulfuric acid solution.

Oxidation reaction. Purpose: Oxidation of hydrogen selenide (H₂Se) to selenium trioxide (SeO₃). Key transformation: Ozone oxidizes H₂Se (Se²⁻ → Se⁶⁺ in SeO₃). Conditions: Cold aqueous or gaseous phase. Ozone acts as a strong oxidizing agent.

Oxidation-reduction reaction. Purpose: Selective oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Key transformation: TEMPO catalyzes sodium hypochlorite-mediated oxidation of 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol. Conditions: Aqueous buffered solution (~pH 6-7), room temperature. Solvent: Water. Catalyst: TEMPO (nitroxide radical).

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; purpose is ion exchange to form more soluble salts; key transformation: K⁺ swaps with Ba²⁺ giving potassium bromide and barium hydroxide; typical conditions: dissolve potassium hydroxide and barium bromide in water, stir at room temperature; common solvent is water, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt reversal); protonation of potassium asparaginate with HCl regenerates L‑asparagine and produces KCl; performed in water, usually at 0‑25 °C with excess HCl to ensure complete conversion; no catalyst.

Double displacement reaction. Purpose: Precipitation of silver iodate (AgIO₃). Key transformation: Silver nitrate and lithium iodate exchange ions; AgIO₃ may precipitate if insoluble. Conditions: Aqueous solution, room temperature. No catalyst required.

Redox (disproportionation) reaction; purpose is to reduce iodic acid to elemental iodine while oxidizing bisulfite to sulfate; key transformation: HIO3 is reduced to I2 and NaHSO3 is oxidized to Na2SO4 with formation of water; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation); purpose is to prepare the fatty acid methyl ester methyl oleate; key transformation: oleic acid reacts with methanol to give methyl oleate and water; conducted with excess methanol and a strong acid catalyst such as concentrated H2SO4 or p‑TsOH, refluxing for several hours; common solvent is methanol itself, reaction driven by removal of water (Dean–Stark or azeotropic distillation).

Neutral methyl esterification using diazomethane; purpose is to convert the carboxyl group of L‑histidine into a methyl ester without affecting the side‑chain; key transformation: L‑histidine reacts with CH2N2 to give L‑histidine methyl ester and release N2 gas; performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane, with careful addition of freshly prepared diazomethane solution; no additional catalyst required.

Peracid oxidation of thioether: S‑methylcysteine reacts with m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (1.1 equiv) in dichloromethane, 0 °C → rt, converting the thioether to the sulfoxide (2‑amino‑3‑methanesulfinylpropanoic acid) while generating m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Inert atmosphere, DCM solvent.

Halogen‑azide substitution (formation of iodine azide); purpose is to generate the highly reactive iodine azide reagent; key transformation: I2 reacts with trimethylsilyl azide (TMSN3) to give IN3 (iodine azide) and trimethylsilyl iodide (TMSI); carried out at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous, non‑protic solvents like dry dichloromethane or chloroform under inert atmosphere; reaction mixture is protected from light and moisture.

Fischer esterification of an amino acid. Isoleucine is esterified with methanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid, producing methyl 2‑amino‑3‑methylpentanoate (the methyl ester of isoleucine) and water. The mixture is refluxed in methanol; the acid catalyst protonates the carbonyl to facilitate nucleophilic attack by methanol. Excess methanol can serve as solvent and reactant.

Chlorination of sucrose (nucleophilic substitution with thionyl chloride) to produce sucralose; purpose is to replace three hydroxyl groups of sucrose with chlorine atoms, yielding the high‑intensity sweetener sucralose; key transformation: sucrose reacts with SOCl2 in the presence of pyridine, which acts as base and HCl scavenger, generating HCl, SO2 gas, and the trichlorinated product; typical conditions involve cooling sucrose and pyridine to 0–5 °C, slow addition of thionyl chloride, then stirring at room temperature under nitrogen; pyridine serves both as solvent and catalyst, and the reaction is performed in anhydrous, inert atmosphere.

Hydroboration‑oxidation (anti‑Markovnikov hydration); provides 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol (isobutanol) from isobutylene; syn‑addition of BH3 (from diborane or BH3·THF) to the less substituted carbon of the double bond forms a C–B bond, which is oxidized with aqueous H2O2 in the presence of NaOH to give a primary alcohol; hydroboration is carried out in THF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere, followed by oxidation at 0 °C to rt in aqueous alkaline medium.

Esterification. Synthesis of the preservative butylparaben from p-hydroxybenzoic acid and n-butanol. Forms water as a byproduct. Typically conducted under acidic conditions (e.g., sulfuric acid as catalyst) with excess alcohol or azeotropic distillation to remove water. Solvents include organic alcohols or toluene. Reaction proceeds via Fischer esterification mechanism.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2): sodium methoxide attacks chloromethyl methyl ether, displacing chloride to form dimethoxymethane and NaCl. Conducted in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF at 0–25 °C; methoxide serves as both nucleophile and base.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation of 2,1,3‑benzothiadiazole. Fuming sulfuric acid (conc. H2SO4 containing excess SO₃) acts as the sulfonating agent, installing a sulfonic acid group at the 5‑position of the heteroaromatic ring. Purpose: to introduce a strongly acidic, water‑soluble functionality for further derivatization or to modify electronic properties. Typical conditions: reaction carried out neat or in excess H₂SO₄ at 80–150 °C for 1–4 h under anhydrous conditions; no additional solvent required.

Redox oxidation of copper metal by hydrogen peroxide in acidic medium; hydrogen peroxide acts as the oxidant, sulfuric acid provides Cu²⁺ solubility and proton balance; copper is converted to copper(II) sulfate while peroxide is reduced to water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating, no additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of samarium hexaboride (SmB₆) via carbothermic reduction; samarium(III) oxide and elemental carbon are reduced while boron incorporates into the lattice, yielding SmB₆ and carbon monoxide as the only gaseous by‑product; performed in a sealed ampoule or furnace at >1500 °C under inert (argon) atmosphere; no solvents or catalysts.

Oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde using Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate) as a mild, stoichiometric oxidant; the primary alcohol is selectively oxidized to the aldehyde with water as the sole reduced product; generally conducted in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., acetone‑water) at 0 °C to room temperature; no metal catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of tert‑butyl 2‑phenylacetate; aqueous NaOH attacks the ester carbonyl, forming the sodium salt of 2‑phenylacetic acid, which upon acid work‑up yields the free acid, while the tert‑butyl group departs as tert‑butyl alcohol; reflux in water or water/ethanol mixture is typical; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (elimination) of 1‑pentadecanol to 1‑pentadecene; reaction type is E1 elimination; purpose is to convert a primary alcohol into the corresponding terminal alkene; key transformation: removal of water from the alcohol, forming a C=C bond; typical conditions: excess concentrated H₂SO₄, heating to 130‑150 °C, the sulfuric acid acts as both reagent and solvent; no other catalyst required.

Chlorination (oxidative halogenation) of magnesium antimonide to give antimony trichloride and magnesium chloride; chlorine gas reacts with the intermetallic compound, cleaving Mg–Sb bonds and forming the corresponding chlorides; typically performed in a sealed quartz tube or flow reactor at elevated temperature (≈300‑500 °C) under anhydrous conditions; no additional catalyst.

Radical metal‑mediated C–H trifluoromethylation (silver‑catalyzed). Purpose: install a CF₃ group at the C5 position of 2′‑deoxyuridine to give the antiviral nucleoside trifluridine. Key transformation: formation of a C–CF₃ bond on the uracil base, with loss of tert‑butyl hydroperoxide reduced to t‑BuOH and silver carbonate acting as base/oxidant. Typical conditions: reaction in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, under inert atmosphere, heated to 50–80 °C; Ag₂CO₃ (1–2 equiv) and t‑BuOOH (1–2 equiv) are used, CF₃I (1–1.5 equiv) as the CF₃ source.

Acid‑amine condensation (direct amidation). Purpose: prepare isobutyramide from isobutyric acid and ammonia. Key transformation: conversion of the carboxylic acid carbonyl into an amide carbonyl with loss of one molecule of water. Typical conditions: gaseous or aqueous NH₃ passed over neat isobutyric acid or a melt of the acid at 150–200 °C; sometimes a metal oxide catalyst (e.g., MgO, Al₂O₃) or a coupling agent is employed to improve yield. No external solvent is required; the acid can act as the reaction medium.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrazone hydrolysis (deprotection). Purpose: regenerate cyclohexanone and recover phenylhydrazine from its phenylhydrazone derivative. Key transformation: cleavage of the C=N bond of the hydrazone by addition of water, producing the ketone and free phenylhydrazine. Typical conditions: aqueous phosphoric acid (≈5–10 % w/w) heated to reflux (≈100 °C) for 1–2 h; the reaction is performed in water or a water‑ethanol mixture. No additional catalyst is required beyond the acid.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction generating chlorite. Purpose: prepare sodium chlorite from chloric acid and sodium bisulfite, useful as a bleaching or disinfecting agent. Key transformation: reduction of Cl⁺⁵ in HClO₃ to Cl⁺³ (ClO₂⁻) and oxidation of S⁺⁴ in HSO₃⁻ to S⁺⁶ (SO₄²⁻), with concomitant formation of H₂O and H₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, temperature kept below 30 °C to control exotherm; reagents are mixed slowly with stirring. No organic solvent or catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; sodium phosphate reacts with barium chloride forming insoluble barium phosphate and soluble sodium chloride; the reaction is performed in water, often with pH adjustment to keep phosphate available, at ambient temperature; barium phosphate precipitate is filtered; no catalyst required.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation). Purpose: synthesize ethyl oleate, a biodiesel component, from oleic acid and ethanol. Key transformation: condensation of the carboxylic acid and alcohol to form an ester bond, releasing one molecule of water. Typical conditions: excess ethanol as both reactant and solvent, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid 0.5–1 % v/v), reflux at 78 °C for several hours; removal of water (e.g., by azeotropic distillation or molecular sieves) drives the equilibrium to completion.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to isolate insoluble silver cyanide while forming soluble potassium sulfate; aqueous solution of KCN and Ag2SO4 mixed at room temperature; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Nitration (esterification of alcohols with nitric acid). Purpose: produce propylene glycol dinitrate, a high‑energy nitrate ester used as a propellant. Key transformation: conversion of two hydroxyl groups of 1,2‑propanediol into nitrate esters (–ONO₂) with elimination of two water molecules. Typical conditions: cold (0–5 °C) addition of the diol to concentrated HNO₃ (often mixed with concentrated H₂SO₄ as a dehydrating catalyst), followed by gradual warming to 30–40 °C under stirring; reaction is performed in the nitric acid medium itself, in a glass vessel resistant to oxidation.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Sodium hydroxide attacks the phenyl ester of furan‑2‑carboxylic acid, cleaving the C–O bond. The phenyl group is liberated as phenol, while the carboxylate portion becomes sodium furan‑2‑carboxylate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–2 h; solvent often water or water/ethanol mixture; reaction is run under ambient pressure.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. In aqueous solution potassium phosphate exchanges anions with iron(II) nitrate, producing soluble potassium nitrate and sparingly soluble iron(II) phosphate, which precipitates out. Conducted at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required. Common solvent: distilled water.

Base‑catalyzed aldol condensation followed by dehydration (self‑condensation of acetone with formaldehyde). Sodium hydroxide generates the acetone enolate, which attacks formaldehyde to give a β‑hydroxy ketone; subsequent base‑promoted elimination of water yields the α,β‑unsaturated ketone methyl vinyl ketone. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (0.1–1 M), temperature 0 °C to 25 °C for the addition step, then heating (60–80 °C) to promote dehydration; solvent can be water or a water‑alcohol mixture (e.g., methanol).

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of polysulfide; the S₄²⁻ anion attacks methyl bromide to produce dimethyl tetrasulfide and sodium bromide. Typically performed in dry polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO under inert atmosphere, at room temperature or mild heating.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkylation of a carboxylate). Potassium trifluoroacetate acts as nucleophile, displacing bromide from ethyl bromide to afford ethyl trifluoroacetate, while potassium bromide is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; no catalyst required.

Acetic‑anhydride esterification; cyclohexylmethanol reacts with acetic anhydride to give cyclohexylmethyl acetate and acetic acid. Purpose is to prepare the ester while generating a less aggressive by‑product. Key transformation: alcohol attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride, opening the anhydride ring. Typical conditions: catalysis by a nucleophilic base or acyl transfer catalyst (DMAP, pyridine) in a solvent like dichloromethane or chloroform, often at room temperature or gentle heating.

Oxidation of 1,10‑phenanthroline to 4,7‑phenanthroline‑5,6‑dione using potassium permanganate; reaction type is permanganate oxidation; purpose is to convert the heterocycle into a quinone‑type dione; key transformation: two adjacent carbon atoms are oxidized to carbonyl groups while the nitrogen atoms remain unchanged; typical conditions: aqueous KMnO₄ (often alkaline with NaOH), reflux for 1‑2 h, water (or water/MeCN) as solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

N‑alkylation (or O‑alkylation) of morphine via deprotonation with sodium hydride. NaH abstracts a proton from the phenolic or secondary amine site of morphine, releasing H₂ gas and generating the sodium alkoxide/amide. The resulting nucleophile attacks ethyl iodide in an SN2 step, producing ethyl‑morphine and sodium iodide. Conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (THF or DMF), inert atmosphere (N₂), 0 °C to room temperature; NaH is used in slight excess to ensure complete deprotonation.

Hydrolysis/condensation (sol‑gel process) of a metal alkoxide; purpose is to generate TiO₂ as a precipitate or gel and recycle methanol. Ti(OMe)₄ reacts with water, each MeO⁻ group is replaced by –OH, releasing MeOH; subsequent condensation of Ti–OH groups forms Ti–O–Ti networks (TiO₂). Conditions: often performed in an alcoholic or mixed solvent (e.g., isopropanol/water) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; acidic or basic catalysts may be added to control rate.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction between strontium sulfate and barium hydroxide; reaction type is metathesis with precipitation; purpose is to exchange the anion and precipitate insoluble barium sulfate; key transformation: SrSO₄ + Ba(OH)₂ → BaSO₄↓ + Sr(OH)₂; typical conditions: aqueous solutions of the reactants mixed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Type: combustion (oxidative oxidation). Purpose: complete oxidation of bicyclohexyl to CO₂ and H₂O, releasing energy. Key transformation: C–H and C–C bonds are oxidized by O₂, yielding carbon dioxide and water. Typical conditions: high temperature flame or furnace, excess O₂ or air, often in open air; no solvent or catalyst required.

Free‑radical bromination (radical substitution) of 1,2‑dibromoethane to give 1,1,2,2‑tetrabromoethane; reaction type is radical halogenation; purpose is to replace the remaining hydrogen atoms with bromine atoms; key transformation: each CH₂Br group is converted to CHBr₂ by addition of Br₂; typical conditions: excess Br₂, initiation by UV light or heat (sometimes with a peroxide), solvent such as carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) or chloroform; no metal catalyst is employed.

Redox disproportionation of hydrogen sulfide with chlorine; Cl₂ gas reacts with H₂S (gas or aqueous solution) at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, oxidizing sulfide to elemental sulfur (precipitate) and reducing chlorine to hydrogen chloride, which remains in solution as HCl; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis/acid‑base reaction. Samarium(III) oxide reacts with water to give samarium(III) hydroxide: Sm2O3 + 3 H2O → 2 Sm(OH)3. Usually performed in aqueous media at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of thioxanthene to thioxanthone via sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid; strong acidic oxidizing conditions with chromium(VI) serving as the oxidant, producing chromium(III) sulfate and water as byproducts.

Double displacement precipitation; silver nitrate reacts with sodium chromate to precipitate red insoluble Ag2CrO4 while forming soluble NaNO3; conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature, water as solvent, no additional reagents.

Reductive amination of a ketone; 1‑(4‑methylphenyl)propan‑2‑one is condensed with pyrrolidine to form an imine, which is subsequently reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to give 4′‑methyl‑α‑pyrrolidinopropiophenone; generally run in methanol or dichloromethane with a mild acid (e.g., AcOH) to promote imine formation, at 0 °C to rt; NaBH3CN is the reducing agent, no metal catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolysis of a methyl ester); water attacks methyl palmitate, yielding palmitic acid and methanol; usually performed under reflux in a mixture of water and a polar organic solvent (e.g., THF) with a catalytic amount of strong acid such as HCl or H2SO4; reaction temperature around 80–120 °C; no special catalyst beyond the acid.

Lewis‑acid–alcohol exchange (formation of aluminum alkoxide); anhydrous AlCl3 reacts with ethanol, replacing chloride ligands with ethoxy groups to generate aluminum triethoxide and liberating HCl gas; carried out under dry, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), often at 0 °C to rt, with excess ethanol as both reagent and solvent; no additional catalyst, HCl is removed to drive the reaction.

Oxidation of a terminal propargyl alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane; a mild, selective primary‑alcohol → aldehyde oxidation. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane under nitrogen; DMP generates acetic acid and 2‑iodobenzoic acid as by‑products.

Knoevenagel condensation between benzaldehyde and malononitrile to afford 2‑benzylidene‑propanedinitrile (an α,β‑unsaturated dinitrile) with loss of water. The reaction proceeds via base‑catalyzed deprotonation of malononitrile, nucleophilic addition to the aldehyde, and elimination of water. Typical conditions: 10–20 mol % piperidine or ammonium acetate as catalyst, ethanol or methanol as solvent, reflux 1–4 h; alternatively, solvent‑free heating or microwave irradiation can be used.

Halide metathesis (halogen exchange) between antimony(III) bromide and potassium fluoride producing antimony(III) fluoride and potassium bromide. Usually carried out by grinding the solids together or heating the mixture in a sealed tube; anhydrous conditions are preferred and no solvent is required.

Nucleophilic S_N2 substitution of iodoacetic acid by tetradecanethiol, forming tetradecyl thioacetic acid (R‑S‑CH₂‑COOH) and releasing hydrogen iodide. The thiol is usually deprotonated with a mild base (e.g., triethylamine or NaH) to generate the thiolate nucleophile. Typical conditions: DCM or acetonitrile solvent, 0 °C to rt, 1–2 equiv base, 1 equiv iodoacetic acid, reaction time 2–6 h; the liberated HI is scavenged by the base.

Acidolysis of a metal alkoxide (acid–base reaction) in aqueous sulfuric acid; converts titanium tetramethoxide to titanium(IV) sulfate and liberates methanol; key transformation: Ti(OCH₃)₄ + 2 H₂SO₄ → Ti(SO₄)₂ + 4 CH₃OH; typically performed at 0‑5 °C to control exotherm, then warmed to reflux; solvent is water or a mixture of water and methanol; no additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation (neutralization) of zirconium(IV) sulfate with calcium hydroxide to afford insoluble calcium sulfate and zirconium hydroxide. Conducted in aqueous medium, the reagents are mixed at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; the CaSO₄ precipitates and is filtered, while Zr(OH)₄ remains in suspension or can be isolated by further drying. No special catalyst is required.

Multi‑component synthesis of cyclophosphamide from 2‑chloroethylamine hydrochloride, phosphorus oxychloride, aqueous ammonia and sodium carbonate. The process involves nucleophilic substitution of POCl₃ by the amine to give a bis‑(2‑chloroethyl)phosphorodichloridate intermediate, which, after reaction with excess ammonia (generated in situ from NH₃/Na₂CO₃), cyclizes to the phosphoramide ring, releasing NaCl, CO₂ and water. Typical industrial conditions:  POCl₃ added dropwise to a chilled aqueous solution of Na₂CO₃ and NH₃ (0–5 °C), then 2‑chloroethylamine·HCl is added; the mixture is warmed to 50–80 °C for several hours, pH controlled around 7–8, and the product is isolated by precipitation and recrystallization. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑base (proton transfer) neutralization; strong sulfuric acid protonates acetate ion to give acetic acid and forms sodium bisulfate; generally performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; molecular oxygen acts as the oxidant, usually in the presence of a metal‑based catalyst (e.g., Co‑Mn‑Br, copper, or platinum) in aqueous or alcoholic media; carried out at elevated temperature (≈80–120 °C) and often under O₂ pressure; purpose is conversion of 1‑hexadecanol to palmitic acid; common solvents include water or water/tert‑butanol mixtures.

Formation of a Grignard reagent via halogen exchange (metathesis); n‑propyl lithium reacts with magnesium bromide to produce n‑propylmagnesium bromide and lithium bromide; conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry ether or THF, typically 0 °C to reflux; no catalyst needed; anhydrous ether/THF is the solvent.

Acid‑base reaction (oxide dissolution); purpose: preparation of soluble gallium nitrate; key transformation: Ga2O3 reacts with HNO3, oxide O2‑ is protonated to water and Ga3+ forms Ga(NO3)3; typical conditions: reflux in concentrated aqueous nitric acid, water as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Type: precipitation double‑displacement (metathesis). Purpose: exchange of anions to isolate silver bromide. Key transformation: Ag⁺ reacts with Br⁻ from KBr, precipitating yellow AgBr, while K⁺ associates with ClO₄⁻ to produce KClO₄ in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature; often performed in the dark or low‑light to prevent photodecomposition of AgBr. No catalyst required.

SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution); phenylsodium attacks allyl chloride yielding allylbenzene and NaCl; provides a route to allyl‑substituted aromatics; carried out in dry ether or THF, under nitrogen or argon, at 0 °C to rt, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑bromopentane by ammonia to give pentylamine, which is immediately protonated by HCl to its hydrochloride salt; hydrogen bromide is released as a by‑product; usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia with excess HCl, heated to reflux; purpose is synthesis of pentylamine hydrochloride; water/ethanol are typical solvents.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; phenylboronic acid couples with 4‑iodopyrazole in the presence of a palladium catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(dppf)) and a base (K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃) to afford 4‑phenylpyrazole, with boric acid generated as by‑product; performed in mixed organic/aqueous solvents such as toluene/water or dioxane/ethanol at 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere; purpose is construction of a C–C bond between phenyl and pyrazole rings.

SN2 alcoholysis of a primary alkyl mesylate; methanol attacks n‑propyl methanesulfonate, displacing the propyl group to give n‑propyl alcohol and methyl methanesulfonate; typically done by refluxing the sulfonate in excess methanol, optionally with a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaOMe) to accelerate the reaction; solvent is methanol; purpose is interchange of the alkyl groups on the sulfonate leaving group.

Carbodiimide-mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); purpose is to synthesize phenyl hexanoate from phenol and hexanoic acid; key transformation is activation of the carboxylic acid by DCC to form an O‑acylurea intermediate that reacts with phenol, yielding the ester and precipitating dicyclohexylurea; typically performed at room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, often with catalytic DMAP as a nucleophilic catalyst.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) between potassium metavanadate and ammonium chloride in aqueous solution. General type: ion‑exchange precipitation. Purpose: preparation of ammonium metavanadate. Key transformation: K⁺ exchanges with NH4⁺, forming NH4VO3 solid and KCl soluble. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature, stirring until precipitation, filtration of the ammonium metavanadate. Common solvent: water; no additional catalyst required.

Metal‑hydride reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol; purpose is to convert 3‑heptanone into 3‑heptanol; NaBH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl while Cu(II) is reduced to Cu(I), generating NaCl and CuCl as by‑products; usually carried out in protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt; reaction is quenched with water, producing additional water.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfoxide using Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate); purpose is to obtain tert‑butyl methyl sulfoxide from the corresponding sulfide; the peroxide oxidizes the sulfur atom, giving potassium bisulfate and water as by‑products; commonly performed in aqueous acetone or acetonitrile at ambient temperature, often under mild stirring.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination); purpose is to form the vinyl pyridine moiety from 2‑(2‑bromoethyl)pyridine; ethoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen, eliminating HBr and generating 2‑vinylpyridine, while the ethoxide picks up the proton to give ethanol; sodium bromide remains as the inorganic salt; typical conditions involve anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or DMF, heated to 80–120 °C.

Aqueous carbonation/precipitation of stannate; purpose is to convert soluble sodium stannate into insoluble cassiterite (SnO₂) while generating sodium carbonate; CO₂ dissolves in water to form carbonate, which reacts with stannate to precipitate SnO₂ and leave Na₂CO₃ in solution; carried out in aqueous solution at elevated temperature (60–90 °C) under a CO₂ atmosphere, often with stirring to promote precipitation.

Acid‑base reaction of cesium carbonate with hydrobromic acid; gives cesium bromide and carbonic acid which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O; typically performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to evolve CO₂; water is the solvent.

Base‑induced β‑elimination (E2) of an α‑bromo ketone. Treatment of 4‑bromobutan‑2‑one with potassium tert‑butoxide in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMSO at 0 °C to rt removes HBr to form methyl vinyl ketone (CH2=CH‑CO‑CH3) and KBr. The strong, non‑nucleophilic base abstracts the β‑hydrogen, effecting dehydrohalogenation.

Transesterification of a phosphonate ester; purpose is to replace the methyl groups on dimethyl methylphosphonate with isopropyl groups, yielding diisopropyl methylphosphonate; isopropanol attacks the phosphorus center, displacing methanol; typically catalyzed by an acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or a base (e.g., pyridine) and performed under reflux in a solvent such as toluene or xylene, with continuous removal of methanol to drive the equilibrium.

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using sodium borohydride; NaBH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of myrtenal, converting the aldehyde functional group into the corresponding allylic alcohol (myrtenol). Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol or THF; reaction is mild, inexpensive, and yields the alcohol with high chemoselectivity.

Diazomethane methylation (esterification) of a carboxylic acid; purpose: convert the acid to its methyl ester; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of diazomethane on the carbonyl, loss of N₂, formation of methyl 2‑methylpentanoate; typical conditions: solution of diazomethane in ether (or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; solvent: ether; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative conversion of a primary alkyl iodide to a carboxylic acid with potassium permanganate; KMnO₄ oxidizes 1‑iododecane in aqueous medium, cleaving the C–I bond and further oxidizing the resulting primary carbon to decanoic acid while reducing Mn(VII) to MnO₂ (insoluble) and producing KI. Conducted in water or dilute alkaline solution, heated under reflux; excess KMnO₄ is usually used, and the solid MnO₂ precipitate is filtered off after the reaction.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (O‑demethylation) of an aryl methyl ether; concentrated HCl protonates the methoxy oxygen of 2,5‑dichloroanisole, facilitating cleavage of the C–O bond and generating 2,5‑dichlorophenol and methanol. Performed in aqueous HCl, heated under reflux (often 80–100 °C); the reaction is driven to completion by using excess acid and removal of methanol.
Base‑promoted deprotonation; sodium hydroxide deprotonates 2‑chlorophenol to form sodium 2‑chlorophenoxide and water; conducted in aqueous NaOH solution at room temperature.

Acidic hydrolysis of an aromatic acetate ester; sulfuric acid (often concentrated) protonates the carbonyl of 3‑ethyl phenyl acetate, allowing water to attack the carbonyl carbon, leading to cleavage of the ester bond and formation of 3‑ethyl phenol and acetic acid. Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid under reflux; the reaction mixture is typically cooled and the phenol is extracted after neutralization.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; ZnBr2 reacts with KOH in water to form soluble KBr and insoluble Zn(OH)2 precipitate. Carried out at room temperature in aqueous solution; the zinc hydroxide can be filtered off. No catalyst needed.

Halogen addition of bromine (electrophilic addition of Br2); generates a vicinal dibromide for subsequent elimination or substitution; anti‑addition of Br2 across the double bond affords 1,2‑dibromo‑2‑methylpropane; carried out in carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, protected from light; no catalyst needed.
precipitation/double displacement; purpose: produce cerium(III) hydroxide; transformation: exchange of ammonium and cerium ions; aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst

nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether synthesis); forms benzyl methyl ether via ether bond; sodium methoxide acts as nucleophile displacing chloride from benzyl chloride; protic solvent (e.g., methanol) or aprotic solvent (e.g., THF), ambient or moderate heat.

Metal‑halogen exchange followed by carboxylation (lithiation–CO₂) of a dibromo heteroaromatic; n‑butyllithium in dry THF at –78 °C effects lithium‑bromine exchange at the 2‑ and 5‑positions of 2,5‑dibromothiophene, producing a dilithiated intermediate which reacts with gaseous CO₂ to afford thiophene‑2,5‑dicarboxylic acid. Lithium bromide precipitates as a by‑product. After CO₂ addition, the reaction is quenched with aqueous acid, and the dicarboxylic acid is isolated by filtration or extraction.

Oxidation of benzaldehyde to benzoic acid using concentrated nitric acid; aldehyde is converted to a carboxylic acid with release of nitrogen dioxide (brown gas) and water; typically performed by heating benzaldehyde with HNO₃ (70–100 °C) where nitric acid serves as both oxidant and solvent.

Double displacement (ligand exchange) reaction; used to replace thiocyanate ligands on mercury with cyanide, producing mercuric cyanide and potassium thiocyanate; key transformation: Hg(SCN)2 + KCN → Hg(CN)2 + KSCN; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient to reflux temperature; common solvent is water or aqueous ethanol; no catalyst required.

Reductive conversion of a nitro phenol to an aniline salt using zinc and hydrochloric acid; Zn metal in excess HCl reduces the nitro group of 4‑nitrophenol to an amine, which is immediately protonated to give 4‑aminophenol hydrochloride. The process also generates ZnCl₂ and water. Conducted in aqueous HCl at reflux or elevated temperature; the solid zinc is filtered off, and the product is isolated by evaporation or crystallization from the acidic solution.

Type: Rearrangement reaction (likely acid-catalyzed). Purpose: Conversion of bicyclic sesquiterpene to a tricyclic hydrocarbon. Key transformation: Ring-opening followed by recyclization via carbocation shifts. Conditions: Acidic environment (e.g., H2SO4), heat. Solvent: Non-polar or inert solvent.

Type: Electrophilic hydration. Purpose: Alcohol production from alkenes. Key transformation: Addition of H2O across the alkene. Conditions: Acidic catalyst (e.g., H2SO4), aqueous solution. Product follows Markovnikov's rule. Solvent: Water.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution/amidation. Purpose: Synthesis of sulfamide and ammonium salts. Key transformation: Ammonia replacing the chlorine in chlorosulfonic acid. Conditions: Reaction in aqueous ammonia solution. Catalyst: No additional catalyst required.

Type: Acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis. Purpose: Cleavage of ester to carboxylic acid and alcohol. Key transformation: Hydration of the ester group with acid. Conditions: Dilute hydrochloric acid, heat. Solvent: Water.

Type: Ligand protonolysis. Purpose: Release of free dithiocarbamic acid. Key transformation: Protonation of dithiocarbamate groups by acetic acid. Conditions: Mildly acidic environment. Solvent: Acetic acid.

Type: Radical hydrobromination. Purpose: Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr to an alkene. Key transformation: Bromine addition opposite to hydrogen. Conditions: Presence of peroxides or UV light. Catalyst: Light or peroxide initiators. Solvent: Inert organic solvent (e.g., CCl4).

Oxidation (re‑oxidation) of titanium(II) oxide to titanium dioxide; purpose is to restore Ti⁴⁺ oxidation state or to produce TiO₂ from TiO; TiO reacts with O₂ gas to give TiO₂; usually carried out at moderate temperatures (≈400‑600 °C) in an oxygen or air atmosphere; solid‑gas reaction, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization; sodium bicarbonate (a weak base) reacts with L‑ascorbic acid (a weak acid) in water to afford the sodium salt of ascorbic acid (sodium ascorbate) and carbonic acid, which readily decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O. Typically carried out at room temperature in aqueous solution; no catalyst required; gentle heating may be applied to drive off CO₂.

Nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) of an alkyl halide with aqueous ammonia (ammonolysis). n‑Butyl chloride reacts with excess ammonia to afford n‑butylamine and ammonium chloride. The process usually requires heating (reflux) of the chloride in concentrated aqueous ammonia, often in a sealed tube at 100‑130 °C; no additional catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane (DMP). 1‑Nonanol is converted to 1‑nonanal with DMP as a stoichiometric oxidant. Reaction is mild, chemoselective for aldehydes, usually performed in dry dichloromethane (0 °C to rt) under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst; by‑products are iodobenzene diacetate and acetic acid.
Hydrolysis of tin(IV) fluoride; water reacts with SnF4 to give solid SnO₂ and aqueous HF. Usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating; no catalyst required.

Peracid epoxidation; m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) transfers an oxygen atom to the C=C bond of allyl alcohol, forming the epoxide glycidol while being reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen. Stoichiometric m‑CPBA is required; no metal catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration (cyclization) of butane‑1,2‑diol to give 1,2‑epoxybutane. Concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as both acid catalyst and dehydrating agent, promoting loss of water and ring closure. Typical conditions: reflux (80–120 °C) in the absence of added solvent or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., toluene); water is formed as the only by‑product.

Nucleophilic substitution/alkoxylation followed by epoxide formation to synthesize triglycidyl glycerol. Glycerol reacts with epichlorohydrin in the presence of KOH (base) and the ionic liquid 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium chloride (phase‑transfer catalyst). The alkoxide of glycerol attacks epichlorohydrin, displacing chloride; subsequent intramolecular ring closure yields three glycidyl (epoxy) groups. Performed at 50–80 °C, often solvent‑free or with minimal epichlorohydrin serving as solvent; by‑products are KCl and water.

Diazonium salt hydrolysis (Sandmeyer‑type) of p‑bromobenzenediazonium chloride to give 4‑bromophenol. The diazonium ion undergoes nucleophilic substitution by water, releasing N₂ gas and forming the phenol; HCl is generated from the diazonium counter‑ion. Reaction is carried out in aqueous acidic medium, usually at 0–5 °C initially then warmed to room temperature; no metal catalyst is required.

Paal–Knorr pyrrole synthesis; condensation of β‑amino acid with a 1,4‑diketone to form a pyrrole ring bearing a carboxylic acid substituent. The amino group attacks a carbonyl, followed by dehydration and cyclization, releasing water. Typically performed by heating the reactants in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, acetic acid) often under acidic catalysis (p‑TsOH) at reflux.

Hydrolysis of indium tribromide in water to generate indium(III) hydroxide precipitate and hydrobromic acid; proceeds readily at room temperature in aqueous medium, solution becomes acidic due to HBr formation.

Primary‑alcohol oxidation; NaOCl oxidizes benzyl alcohol to the benzoate anion. The benzylic CH2OH group is converted to a carboxylate, producing water and NaCl as by‑products. Conducted in aqueous bleach solution, usually buffered (NaHCO3) and stirred at ambient temperature or mild heating; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of phenol with ethyl chloroformate to form ethyl phenyl carbonate; reaction type is carbonate (or mixed carbonate) formation. Hydrogen chloride generated is scavenged by a base (commonly pyridine or triethylamine). Typical conditions: phenol (1‑equiv) and ethyl chloroformate (1‑equiv) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with catalytic/stoichiometric pyridine (or Et₃N) to neutralize HCl.

Ester aminolysis (ammonolysis); ammonia attacks methyl lactate, cleaving the ester to give methanol and the ammonium salt of lactic acid. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic acyl substitution with loss of methanol. Carried out in aqueous ammonia, often refluxing in water or a water‑ethanol mixture.

Acidic oxidation of a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon; potassium dichromate in concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidizes acenaphthene to acenaphthene‑quinone (a dione). Two benzylic C–H bonds are converted to carbonyl groups, producing water and K₂SO₄. Reaction conditions involve refluxing the substrate in hot conc. H₂SO₄ with stoichiometric K₂Cr₂O₇ under an inert atmosphere.

Ketone reduction; NaBH₄ reduces methyl isobutyl ketone (4‑methyl‑2‑pentanone) to the corresponding secondary alcohol, 4‑methyl‑2‑pentanol. Hydride transfer to the carbonyl carbon yields the alkoxide, which is protonated on work‑up. Performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, with NaBH₄ added portionwise.

Acid–base (salt metathesis) reaction; protonates the carboxylate to liberate hexanoic acid and forms potassium chloride; typically performed in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C by adding dilute HCl to a solution of potassium hexanoate with stirring; water or aqueous ethanol is the common solvent.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of alkyl bromide); hydroxide ion displaces bromide on 2‑(bromomethyl)tetrahydrofuran to form tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol and NaBr. Reaction proceeds via backside attack, inverting configuration at the carbon. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol co‑solvent) at room temperature or under reflux.

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using sodium borohydride; purpose is to convert 4,4,4‑trifluorobutanal to the corresponding alcohol; key transformation is hydride delivery to the carbonyl carbon, turning C=O into C‑OH; typically performed with 1–2 equiv NaBH4 in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl iodide by sulfide ion; purpose is synthesis of 3‑mercaptopropan‑1‑ol; key transformation is replacement of I⁻ with S²⁻ to form a C‑S bond, producing NaI; carried out with Na₂S in aqueous ethanol or DMF, heated 50–100 °C, often under nitrogen, no catalyst.

Electrophilic methylation of a secondary amine with dimethyl sulfate; purpose is to install an additional methyl on N‑methylputrescine yielding N,N′‑dimethylputrescine; key transformation is transfer of a methyl group to nitrogen with formation of methyl hydrogen sulfate; conducted in pyridine or aqueous base (e.g., NaOH) in acetone or DMF, 0 °C to room temperature, no catalyst.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution where acetate ion displaces iodide on ethyl iodide to afford ethyl acetate; used to alkylate a carboxylate and form an ester. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF) at reflux or elevated temperature with excess sodium acetate; sodium iodide precipitates out as a by‑product.

Acid–base neutralization of mercury(II) hydroxide with acetic acid to give mercury(II) acetate and water; conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring, water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of cyclohexanone using performic acid; purpose is to convert the cyclic ketone to ε‑caprolactone; key transformation is insertion of an oxygen adjacent to the carbonyl and migration to give a lactone, releasing formic acid; performed by generating performic acid in situ from H₂O₂ and formic acid and adding it to cyclohexanone in CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN at 0 °C to rt, reaction time 1–2 h, no catalyst.

Radical dehalogenation of 2‑bromo‑1,1,1‑trifluoroethane with tributyltin hydride; purpose is to replace bromine with hydrogen to afford 1,1,1‑trifluoroethane; key transformation is hydrogen atom transfer from Bu₃SnH to the carbon radical after bromine abstraction, forming Bu₃SnBr; carried out with 2–3 equiv Bu₃SnH and a radical initiator (e.g., AIBN) in toluene or benzene under reflux (80–110 °C) under nitrogen, no additional catalyst.

Reductive amination of acetone with ethylamine using sodium cyanoborohydride; purpose is to produce N‑ethyl‑2‑propanamine (a secondary amine); key steps are imine formation between acetone and ethylamine followed by reduction to the amine, generating water; typically done in methanol or ethanol with catalytic AcOH (pH ≈ 5–6) at 0 °C then rt, NaBH₃CN (1–1.5 equiv) added, inert atmosphere optional.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an α‑halo ketone; 4‑phenylpiperidine attacks the carbon bearing chlorine in chloroacetone to give the β‑keto‑amine Ketobemidone while HCl is released; carried out under basic conditions (e.g., triethylamine or NaH) in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature to avoid side‑reactions.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of sec‑butyl formate with ethanol to afford sec‑butanol and ethyl formate. Catalyzed by an acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a base (e.g., NaOEt) and refluxed in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene, or performed under solvent‑free conditions; removal of the volatile ethanol drives the equilibrium.

Acid‑catalyzed ether interchange (transetherification) of dipropyl ether with methanol; protonation of the ether oxygen permits methanol attack on one propyl group, yielding methyl propyl ether and 1‑propanol; performed in refluxing methanol with a strong acid such as 5–10 % H₂SO₄, often under Dean‑Stark removal of the liberated 1‑propanol, at 60–80 °C.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction of a metal carbonate with a carboxylic acid; zinc carbonate reacts with lactic acid to give zinc dilactate, releasing CO₂ and water. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient to mildly elevated temperature; excess lactic acid drives the reaction, no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine; reduces cyclooctanecarbonitrile to cyclooctylamine. Typically performed under H₂ pressure (1–10 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C, or Pt in an alcoholic solvent (EtOH, MeOH) at elevated temperature.

Catalytic partial hydrogenation of an aromatic system; H₂ adds across the 9,10‑double bond of anthracene to give 9,10‑dihydroanthracene; carried out with Pt/C (5–10 % metal) in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate under 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, at room temperature to 50 °C, with stirring until uptake ceases.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation (acid‑base neutralization); hydroxide ions convert insoluble lead arsenite into soluble sodium arsenite while lead(II) hydroxide precipitates; performed in water at ambient temperature, typically with stoichiometric NaOH added dropwise to a suspension of lead arsenite, followed by filtration of the Pb(OH)₂ solid.

Precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction; purpose is to prepare insoluble manganese(II) hydroxide; key transformation: Mn(NO3)2(aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Mn(OH)2(s) + 2 NaNO3(aq); performed in water at 0–25 °C to avoid oxidation of Mn(II); water is the reaction medium; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of bromoacetic acid by hydroxylamine; the nitrogen of hydroxylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon of the bromide, displacing Br⁻ to form aminooxyacetic acid (HO‑NH‑CH₂‑COOH) and HBr; usually conducted in an aqueous or mixed aqueous‑methanol medium, pH adjusted to ~7–8 with a weak base (e.g., NaHCO₃) and kept at 0–25 °C to minimize side reactions.

Transesterification between isopropyl alcohol and isoamyl acetate yielding isopropyl acetate and isoamyl alcohol. Commonly acid‑catalyzed (H₂SO₄, TsOH) or catalyzed by immobilized lipases; reaction run at reflux in a solvent like toluene or under solvent‑free heating, with removal of the more volatile isopropyl acetate to shift equilibrium.

Catalytic reductive amination of cyclohexanol (or in situ formed cyclohexanone) with ammonia under hydrogen to produce cyclohexylamine and water; hydrogenation using a metal catalyst (Raney Ni, Pd/C, PtO₂) at elevated H₂ pressure (10–50 atm) and moderate temperature (80–150 °C); solvent commonly ethanol, isopropanol or THF; ammonia supplied as gas or aqueous solution.

Reduction of trifluoroacetic acid to 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol using lithium aluminium hydride; strong hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid; carried out in dry ether solvents (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; reaction quenched carefully with water or a protic work‑up to afford the primary alcohol.

Acid–base reaction (salt formation); purpose is to convert solid uranyl hydroxide into a soluble uranyl nitrate salt. The dihydroxy(dioxo)uranium (UO2(OH)2) reacts with aqueous nitric acid, exchanging the hydroxide for nitrate ions and releasing water. Typically performed in water at ambient temperature or mild heating (≤50 °C) using dilute HNO₃; no catalyst required.

Synthesis of phosphorus oxybromide (POBr₃) by reaction of phosphorus pentabromide with phosphorus pentoxide; a halogen‑oxygen exchange forming an oxybromide; performed in a dry, inert atmosphere at elevated temperature (often 80–120 °C); no solvent or uses dry carbon tetrachloride; produces POBr₃ as a liquid or gas and is used as a brominating reagent.

Formation of bis(cyclopentadienyl)hafnium dichloride (hafnocene dichloride) by ligand exchange between cyclopentadiene and hafnium tetrachloride; a metathesis/complexation reaction producing HCl as a by‑product; carried out under nitrogen or argon, in non‑protic solvents such as THF or dichloromethane, often at 0 °C to room temperature; HCl gas is removed or trapped.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of 1‑methyl‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline to 1‑methylisoquinoline using manganese dioxide as a solid oxidant; MnO₂ abstracts hydrogen to aromatize the heterocycle; typically reflux in an inert organic solvent (toluene, chlorobenzene, or dichloromethane) under ambient pressure; the reaction yields the aromatic isoquinoline and reduced manganese species (Mn₂O₃).

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); NaCN acts as a source of cyanide ion which attacks the primary carbon bearing iodine in 1‑iododecane, displacing iodide and forming decanenitrile; generally performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at modest heating (50‑80 °C) under anhydrous conditions; sodium iodide is generated as the by‑product.

Halide metathesis/precipitation (double displacement); Ytterbium(III) chloride exchanges chloride ligands for fluoride from silver fluoride, producing insoluble silver chloride that precipitates and soluble ytterbium fluoride; typically carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the driving force is the formation of AgCl solid.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (formation of a sulfonate ester); ethanol acts as nucleophile toward the sulfonic acid group of benzenesulfonic acid, yielding ethyl benzenesulfonate and water; the reaction proceeds under reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or xylene, often with removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) to drive equilibrium forward; benzenesulfonic acid itself serves as both reagent and acid catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a benzylic chloride with sodium azide; introduces an azide group on the methyl side chain. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0–50 °C (often reflux) under anhydrous conditions; NaCl precipitates out. The azide product can be reduced to an amine or used in click chemistry.

Thermal decomposition of a metal nitrate; solid nickel(II) nitrate is heated strongly (≈300‑400 °C) in the absence of solvent, decomposing to NiO solid, gaseous NO2 and O2; furnace or muffle oven used, inert or air atmosphere, no additional catalyst.

Fischer esterification; conversion of a primary alcohol and a carboxylic acid into an ester. Key transformation is condensation of 1‑propanol with acetic acid to give propyl acetate with loss of water. Typically performed by refluxing the mixture in an inert organic solvent (toluene or benzene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid such as concentrated H2SO4 or p‑TsOH; removal of water by a Dean–Stark trap drives the equilibrium to product.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary tosylate; iodide ion from sodium iodide attacks the carbon bearing the p‑toluenesulfonate leaving group in pentyl p‑toluenesulfonate, displacing the tosylate and forming 1‑iodopentane; commonly performed in acetone (a polar aprotic solvent) at reflux, exploiting the poor solubility of NaOTs to shift equilibrium; sodium p‑toluenesulfonate precipitates.

Double‑displacement (halide metathesis) to exchange bromide for iodide; used to prepare gadolinium(III) iodide. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution where GdBr₃ and KI are dissolved, the mixture is heated under reflux, and the insoluble GdI₃ precipitates and is filtered; KBr remains in solution. No special catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds by simple ion exchange.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride (chlorination) using phosphorus pentachloride; the carbonyl oxygen of nicotinic acid attacks PCl₅, generating nicotinoyl chloride, POCl₃ and HCl as by‑products; the reaction is conducted under anhydrous conditions in a dry chlorinated solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, typically at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; POCl₃ and HCl are evolved and removed.

Selective reduction of an aldose to a polyol (hydride reduction); sodium borohydride delivers hydride to the aldehyde carbonyl of erythrose, converting it to a primary alcohol and giving butane‑1,2,3,4‑tetrol (erythritol); performed in a mixture of methanol and water (or aqueous THF) at 0 °C to room temperature; the by‑product sodium metaborate (or sodium borate) is formed and the reaction is quenched with acid after completion.

SN2 cyanation of a primary alkyl chloride; cyanide ion replaces chloride to form 2‑methylheptanenitrile. Conducted with NaCN in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, usually at 60–80 °C (reflux). The reaction proceeds via an SN2 mechanism; no metal catalyst is required.

Isomerization (skeletal rearrangement) of a branched C7 alkane to a less branched isomer; used to adjust fuel octane or physical properties; involves migration of a methyl group via carbocation intermediates; typically performed at 200‑400 °C over solid acid catalysts such as zeolites or acidic alumina; no stoichiometric reagents needed.

Selenium dioxide oxidation of heteroaromatic amine (oxidative formylation). Pyridine is oxidized by SeO₂ in the presence of water to afford pyridine‑2‑carboxaldehyde (2‑formylpyridine); selenium dioxide is reduced to elemental selenium and water is regenerated. Commonly carried out by refluxing pyridine with a catalytic amount of SeO₂ in aqueous acetic acid or a mixed water/organic solvent (e.g., dioxane) at 80–100 °C.

Direct combination of potassium metal with elemental tellurium to give potassium telluride (K₂Te); a metal–nonmetal solid‑state synthesis; carried out in a dry, oxygen‑free environment, often in a sealed tube or under inert gas and heated (≈150‑250 °C) until the tellurium dissolves; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic hydride reduction of a carbonyl; sodium borohydride reduces acetone to isopropanol; typically performed in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or isopropanol at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is mild, stoichiometric NaBH₄ provides hydride; by‑product is sodium metaborate; no additional catalyst.

Redox metathesis between phosphorus pentachloride and aluminum; aluminum reduces PCl₅ to phosphorus trichloride while being oxidized to aluminum chloride; useful for generating AlCl₃ (a strong Lewis acid) and PCl₃ (a chlorinating reagent); conducted by grinding the solids together and heating to 150‑250 °C in an inert atmosphere; no solvent is used.

SN1 nucleophilic substitution of a secondary alcohol with HBr to give 2‑bromooctane; purpose is conversion of the alcohol to an alkyl bromide; key transformation is replacement of the OH group by Br via a carbocation intermediate; typical conditions use excess HBr, reflux temperature, often neat HBr or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane; no additional catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between barium chloride and potassium selenate in aqueous solution; forms insoluble barium selenate and soluble potassium chloride; performed at room temperature with stirring; the precipitate is isolated by filtration and washing with water.

Acid–base neutralization forming an ammonium phosphate salt; purpose is to generate ethylammonium dihydrogen phosphate from ethylamine and phosphoric acid; key transformation is proton transfer to give EtNH₃⁺·H₂PO₄⁻; typically done in aqueous medium at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis: deprotonation of benzyl alcohol by sodium hydride to give benzyl alkoxide, which undergoes SN2 attack on ethyl iodide to afford benzyl ethyl ether; by‑product is sodium iodide; carried out in dry aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to ambient temperature under nitrogen; the reaction mixture is quenched and the ether purified by standard work‑up.

Direct amidation of pent‑4‑ynoic acid with ammonia to afford pent‑4‑ynamide; purpose is formation of a primary amide; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ammonia on the activated carboxyl group with loss of water; typically achieved by first converting the acid to a more reactive intermediate (acid chloride using SOCl₂ or using a coupling reagent such as EDC/HOBt) and then treating with excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃; reactions are performed in an aprotic solvent (THF, DMF) at 0‑25 °C to 80 °C, often under pressure for gaseous NH₃; no additional catalyst beyond the activation step is needed.

Carbothermic reduction of plutonium dioxide by carbon; high‑temperature solid‑state redox to produce metallic plutonium and carbon dioxide; performed in a furnace at ≈1500–2000 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Aqueous redox reaction where potassium iodate is reduced to iodide and sodium bisulfite is oxidized to sulfate, yielding water as by‑product; carried out in water at ambient temperature or mild heating, usually under slightly acidic conditions; no catalyst needed.

This is a reduction reaction, used to extract scandium metal from its oxide. Key transformation: Reduction of scandium oxide to scandium metal using hydrogen gas, producing water as a byproduct. Typical reaction conditions: High temperatures around 1000-1500°C in a hydrogen atmosphere, with no specific catalysts required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 2,2,2‑tribromoethyl acetate to give acetic acid and 2,2,2‑tribromoethanol; reaction performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., HCl or H₂SO₄) with reflux; solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture; no external catalyst beyond the acid.

Hydride reduction (dehalogenation) of a tertiary alkyl chloride; purpose: replace the chlorine with hydrogen to generate the corresponding alkane; key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers a hydride to the carbon bearing Cl, yielding 2‑methylpentane and forming LiCl/AlCl3 (as complexes) as by‑products; typical conditions: LiAlH4 (1–2 equiv) in dry THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen, 0 °C to room temperature followed by reflux, careful aqueous work‑up; no additional catalyst.

Selective reduction of the 6‑ketone of oxymorphone to the corresponding secondary alcohol (hydromorphone) using sodium borohydride; typically conducted in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; aqueous NaBH₄ provides hydride donor; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of trans‑1,4‑dichloro‑2‑butene with aqueous sodium hydroxide to afford but‑2‑ene‑1,4‑diol; converts allylic chlorides to the corresponding diol; each chloride is displaced by hydroxide via SN2 (or SN2′) pathway; typically performed with refluxing NaOH solution (often 5‑10 % NaOH) in water or water/ethanol mixture at 80‑100 °C; water (or water/ethanol) is the solvent, no catalyst.

Reaction type: Friedländer quinoline synthesis (condensation). Purpose: build the quinoline core with a methyl group at C‑2. Key transformation: condensation of the aldehyde‑group of 2‑aminobenzaldehyde with a keto‑group of 2,4‑pentanedione, followed by cyclodehydration to give 2‑methylquinoline and water. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or glacial acetic acid with an acid catalyst (p‑TsOH, HCl) or ZnCl₂, 80‑120 °C, 2‑6 h.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (chlorination) of aniline. Chlorine reacts with aniline in aqueous medium, substituting a hydrogen ortho to the amino group to give 2‑chloroaniline and generating hydrogen chloride as a by‑product. The reaction is usually performed at 0–5 °C in dilute HCl or water to control mono‑chlorination and minimize over‑chlorination; no additional catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 3,4‑methylenedioxyphenylacetonitrile to the corresponding carboxylic acid (3,4‑methylenedioxyphenylacetic acid); reflux in aqueous NaOH followed by acidification; water is the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of the secondary amine nortriptyline with methyl iodide using potassium carbonate as a base; converts the secondary amine to the tertiary amitriptyline, producing KI, CO₂ and H₂O as by‑products. Typical conditions: reflux in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetone, DMF or acetonitrile; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis reaction; phosphorus trichloride reacts with water to form phosphorous acid (H3PO3) and hydrochloric acid; a common method for preparing phosphorous acid and generating HCl gas; performed by slowly adding PCl3 to cold water with vigorous stirring, temperature kept below 25 °C to control exotherm; aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Electrophilic epoxidation of 2‑pentene with the peracid m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (mCPBA). The peracid transfers an oxygen atom to the C=C bond to give 2‑pentyloxirane, while the acid is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Usually performed in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst needed.

N‑methylation of the secondary amine N‑methyltryptamine using methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (methyl triflate), a very strong methylating agent. The reaction affords N,N‑dimethyltryptamine (DMT) and triflic acid as the acidic by‑product. Conducted at low temperature (‑20 °C to 0 °C) in a dry aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; no additional catalyst.

Disulfur reacts with hydrogen gas in a hydrogenation/reduction (disproportionation) reaction to produce hydrogen sulfide and sulfur; carried out in the gas phase at elevated temperatures (≈400‑500 °C), often with a metal catalyst and no solvent.

Decarboxylative methyl esterification of pivalic acid with dimethyl carbonate. The carboxylic acid is methylated to give methyl pivalate while dimethyl carbonate is converted to methanol and carbon dioxide. The reaction proceeds under heating (140–180 °C) either neat or with a solid base/catalyst such as K₂CO₃, ZnO or TiO₂; dimethyl carbonate can serve as both reagent and solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the carbamate felbamate with aqueous HCl. The carbamate group is cleaved, releasing carbon dioxide and ammonia (which forms NH₄Cl) and furnishing 2‑phenyl‑1,3‑propanediol. Typical procedure: reflux in aqueous hydrochloric acid; no additional catalyst.

Eschweiler–Clarke methylation of 5‑hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) using formic acid and formaldehyde. The primary amine is sequentially methylated to the N,N‑dimethyl product bufotenine, with carbon dioxide and water generated as the only stoichiometric by‑products. Reaction conditions: reflux in a mixture of formic acid and aqueous formaldehyde (or formalin); no catalyst needed.

Redox fluorination: elemental fluorine oxidizes solid lead dioxide to lead tetrafluoride while reducing oxygen atoms to molecular O₂. Used to prepare PbF₄, a high‑oxidation‑state fluoride. Conducted by passing F₂ gas over PbO₂ at elevated temperatures (≈300‑500 °C) under dry, inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

Acid–base salt metathesis (protonation of pyrophosphate); calcium pyrophosphate reacts with aqueous HCl to form soluble calcium chloride and pyrophosphoric acid (H₄P₂O₇); typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating, using excess HCl to drive the reaction to completion; no special catalyst required.

Free‑radical halogenation (chlorination) of 2‑methylhexane. A tertiary C–H bond is abstracted and replaced by chlorine, yielding 2‑chloro‑2‑methylhexane and HCl. Typical conditions: UV irradiation or thermal initiation, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, ambient to reflux temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of 3‑methyl phenyl acetate; purpose is de‑protection to regenerate the phenol; key transformation: acetate ester cleaved by water to give 3‑methyl phenol and acetic acid; typical conditions: aqueous HCl or dilute acid reflux in MeOH/H2O or aqueous NaOH followed by acid work‑up; temperature 60–100 °C.

Reduction of a phosphine halide; transforms chlorodiphenylphosphine into diphenylphosphine by replacing the P–Cl bond with a P–H bond. LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to phosphorus, reducing the chloride to chloride ion (forming LiCl) and producing diphenylphosphine. Reaction is performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at low temperature (0 °C) progressing to reflux, under nitrogen; LiAlH₄ is the key reducing agent.

Selective reduction of dimethylarsinic acid with sodium borohydride. NaBH₄ reduces arsenic(V) to arsenic(III), converting (CH₃)₂AsO(OH) to dimethylarsine oxide while producing water and sodium metaborate. Performed in a water/ethanol mixture, °C to reflux, with NaBH₄ added portionwise; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (acyl transfer) between benzyl alcohol and 1‑adamantyl acetate. The acetate group migrates to benzyl alcohol, forming benzyl acetate and 1‑adamantyl alcohol. Usually carried out with catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH in toluene or dichloromethane, often under reflux with azeotropic removal of the liberated alcohol.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of ethyl chloroformate by ammonia to give ethyl carbamate (urethane) and HCl. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0‑5 °C to room temperature, typically in the presence of a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl. Provides a route to carbamate protecting groups.

Raney‑nickel desulfurization of 2‑benzyl‑2‑methyl‑1,3‑dithiane to give phenylacetone; the 1,3‑dithiane protecting group is removed, revealing the carbonyl. Reaction carried out in ethanol or THF with Raney Ni under H₂ (1 atm) at 25–80 °C. Alternative reagents: HgCl₂/CuCl in aqueous acetone.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution: lead chromate reacts with ammonium carbonate, exchanging anions to precipitate lead(II) carbonate and form soluble ammonium chromate. Performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the insoluble PbCO₃ is filtered off. No catalyst required.

Double‑dis (metathesis) reaction in aqueous medium; dipotassium malate exchanges its potassium ions with magnesium sulfate’s magnesium ions, giving magnesium malate and potassium sulfate. Usually performed in water with stirring; reaction proceeds at room temperature; precipitation is not required but may be used to isolate one product.

Acid–base neutralization; preparation of praseodymium(III) chloride from the hydroxide; key transformation: Pr(OH)₃ + 3 HCl → PrCl₃ + 3 H₂O; conducted in aqueous HCl solution at room temperature or mild heating with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to cleave the acetate and give the alcohol together with sodium acetate. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl of the ester, yielding 2‑(2‑ethoxyethoxy)ethanol and acetate anion, which is protonated by water to give sodium acetate. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux or 60–80 °C, solvent water or water/MeOH.

Salt formation (acid–base reaction); used to generate the pharmaceutically useful detomidine hydrochloride salt. Detomidine, a basic heterocycle, is protonated by one equivalent of HCl, producing detomidine·HCl. Conditions: dissolve detomidine in a polar solvent (e.g., ethanol, isopropanol, or water), add aqueous or gaseous HCl, stir at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required; water/ethanol mixture commonly employed.

Oxidation (redox) of tungsten metal by ozone; yields tungsten trioxide (WO₃) and releases oxygen gas. The reaction proceeds in the gas phase, often at elevated temperature to initiate the oxidation of the metal surface. Typical conditions: pass ozone (generated in situ or from an O₃ generator) over tungsten at 300–500 °C; no solvent, no catalyst other than the metal itself.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange in aqueous solution; swaps the carbonate and sulfite anions to give sodium sulfite and ammonium carbonate. Reaction is carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of Na₂CO₃ and (NH₄)₂SO₃, usually at room temperature. No catalyst required; water is the reaction medium.

Catalytic hydrogenation; Pd/C reduces the exocyclic double bond of α‑pinene to give saturated pinane. The reaction is carried out under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to reflux, with a catalytic amount of palladium on carbon.

Direct oxidation (combustion) synthesis; purpose is to produce germanium dioxide from elemental germanium. Key transformation: Ge is oxidized by O₂ to form GeO₂. Conducted by heating germanium metal in a flow of air or pure oxygen at elevated temperatures (typically >400 °C). No solvent; reaction proceeds in the gas/solid phase, no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis/precipitation) reaction; purpose is to exchange iodide for nitrate and isolate insoluble silver iodide; aqueous LuI₃ solution is mixed with AgNO₃ solution, AgI precipitates as a yellow solid while Lu(NO₃)₃ remains in solution; performed at room temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization to liberate 2‑butoxyacetic acid from its sodium salt. Sodium 2‑butoxyacetate reacts with one equivalent of HCl, forming the free acid and NaCl. Conditions: aqueous solution or mixed water/organic solvent (e.g., ethanol), temperature at 0 °C to reflux as needed; no catalyst needed.

Acidic hydrolysis of 2‑mercaptoethyl acetate to 2‑mercaptoethanol and acetic acid; conducted in aqueous HCl (or other strong acid) under reflux; water acts as solvent, and the reaction proceeds via ester cleavage.

N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of 1H‑indazole‑3‑carboxylic acid by 2,4‑dichlorobenzyl chloride, forming a benzyl‑substituted indazole derivative and HCl as by‑product. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO with a base (e.g., triethylamine, DIPEA, or K₂CO₃) to scavenge the released HCl. Reaction is heated (50–100 °C) under inert atmosphere; no metal catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition (halogenation) of Cl₂ across the C=C bond of cyclopropene; purpose is to synthesize 1,2‑dichlorocyclopropane. The reaction adds two chlorine atoms vicinally, preserving the three‑membered ring. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, often under exclusion of light; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of 4‑acetoxybenzoic acid; purpose is to deprotect the phenolic acetate and obtain p‑hydroxybenzoic acid. The acetoxy group is protonated, water attacks, and the C–O bond is broken to give the phenol and acetic acid. Conducted in aqueous HCl (often 1–6 M) with heating (reflux) or at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is needed.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis (saponification) of acetic anhydride; purpose is to convert the anhydride into equimolar amounts of acetic acid and sodium acetate. Hydroxide attacks one carbonyl, opening the anhydride and yielding acetate ion which is protonated. Performed in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (phosphorylation) of 3‑methyl‑4‑nitrophenol with O,O‑diethyl phosphorochloridothioate in the presence of pyridine; purpose is the synthesis of the organophosphate insecticide dioxathion. The phenoxide attacks the phosphorus, displacing chloride which is trapped by pyridine to form pyridinium chloride. Reaction is run under anhydrous conditions in pyridine (which acts as both solvent and base) or in dry dichloromethane, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen.

Amide coupling via acid‑chloride activation: thionyl chloride converts 5‑chloro‑2‑hydroxybenzoic acid to its acid chloride, which then reacts with 2‑chloro‑4‑nitroaniline to afford niclosamide. By‑products are HCl and SO₂ gas. The reaction is performed in anhydrous solvent (e.g., pyridine, dichloromethane, or toluene) at 0 °C to reflux, with pyridine often serving as HCl scavenger; inert atmosphere is preferred.

Type: Combustion (oxidation) of deuterium gas. Purpose: Generate heavy water (D₂O) from elemental gases. Key transformation: D₂ reacts with O₂ under ignition (spark or flame) to form D₂O, analogous to the H₂ + O₂ → H₂O reaction. Typical conditions: Equimolar mixture of D₂ and O₂ ignited by spark or heated flame; reaction is highly exothermic and proceeds without catalyst.

Intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation (Kostanecki/Dieckmann‑type cyclization) of 2‑hydroxyacetophenone using acetic anhydride as both reagent and solvent, promoted by sodium acetate; purpose is the synthesis of chromone (1‑benzopyran‑4‑one). The acetate ion activates acetic anhydride, facilitating acyl transfer onto the aromatic ring followed by cyclization and dehydration to give the chromone core. Conducted by refluxing the mixture in excess acetic anhydride (≈150 °C) with catalytic NaOAc; no additional catalyst is required.

Selective reduction of α‑keto‑aldehyde to diol (carbonyl reduction) using sodium borohydride. NaBH₄ reduces both the aldehyde and the adjacent ketone of phenylglyoxal to give phenylglycol (2‑phenyl‑1,2‑ethanediol). Conducted in a polar protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol (or a mixed THF/MeOH system) at 0 °C to room temperature, typically under inert atmosphere; reaction quenched with water.

Acid anhydride exchange (dehydration) used to prepare triflic anhydride; acetyl groups are transferred from acetic anhydride to triflic acid, releasing two equivalents of acetic acid and forming one equivalent of trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride; typically carried out at 0–5 °C in a dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane under nitrogen, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑metal salt metathesis (acid dissolution) converting solid calcium aluminate into soluble metal chlorides; protonation of oxide ligands produces water while chloride ions replace oxide to give aluminum chloride and calcium chloride; usually performed by adding excess concentrated aqueous HCl to the solid and heating to 60–100 °C with stirring until dissolution is complete.

General type: metallurgical reduction (metal‑oxide redox). Purpose: reduces V₂O₃ to V O (vanadium(II) oxide) while generating calcium oxide as a by‑product; useful in preparation of low‑valent vanadium compounds. Key transformation: V³⁺O + Ca⁰ → V²⁺O + CaO. Typical conditions: intimate mixture of finely divided V₂O₃ and calcium metal is heated under inert atmosphere (argon) at 800–1000 °C for several hours. Reaction occurs in a sealed crucible or high‑temperature tube furnace; no solvent.

Electrophilic epoxidation (peracid oxidation) of cycloheptene to cycloheptene oxide; peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom across the C=C bond, forming the three‑membered epoxide and generating acetic acid; carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane, often with a buffering base to neutralize the acid by‑product.

Bis‑epoxidation of vinylcyclohexene using m‑chloroperbenzoic acid; two equivalents of the peracid each deliver an oxygen atom to one of the double bonds, yielding vinyl cyclohexene dioxide (a diepoxide) and two equivalents of m‑chlorobenzoic acid; reaction is performed at 0–25 °C in dichloromethane with slow addition of mCPBA and quenched with aqueous sodium thiosulfate.

Redox/decomposition of nitric acid by barium peroxide generating oxygen; BaO2 oxidizes HNO3, reducing the peroxide to water while nitric acid is converted to nitrate, releasing O₂ gas and forming solid barium nitrate; typically heated gently (≈80 °C) in a closed system or gas‑collection apparatus with concentrated HNO3, allowing precipitation of Ba(NO₃)₂.

N‑acetylation (acyl chloride amidation) of DL‑aspartic acid using acetyl chloride in pyridine; the amine attacks acetyl chloride to form N‑acetyl‑DL‑aspartic acid, while the liberated HCl is scavenged by pyridine to give pyridinium chloride; carried out in pyridine as solvent/base at 0 °C to room temperature, with dropwise addition of acetyl chloride and subsequent aqueous work‑up.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride to a conjugated diene; hydrohalogenation of 1,3‑butadiene to give the allylic chloride 3‑chlorobut‑1‑ene. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or ether; the reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate following Markovnikov addition.

Double‑replacement (acid‑base) reaction between selenic acid and lead(II) acetate; the strong acid displaces acetate, forming lead(II) selenate as an insoluble salt and acetic acid as the by‑product. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution of a tertiary alkyl iodide with aqueous ammonium hydroxide; an SN1 substitution that converts 2‑iodo‑2‑methylbutane to the corresponding tertiary amine (2‑methyl‑2‑butylamine) while generating ammonium iodide and water. Conducted in aqueous ammonia, usually under reflux to promote ionization of the iodide.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine: diethylamine reacts with isoamyl nitrite to give N‑nitroso‑diethylamine and isoamyl alcohol.
