This is a nitrosation reaction; typically performed in a cold, aprotic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to avoid side reactions. No added catalyst is required.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) between aqueous hydrochloric acid and thallium(I) nitrate; the chloride ion pairs with thallium(I) to give thallium(I) chloride, while nitrate pairs with proton to form nitric acid. Carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

N‑alkylation of hexahydro‑1,4‑diazepine with methyl iodide; a nucleophilic substitution (likely SN2) on the nitrogen atom giving N‑methylhexahydro‑1,4‑diazepine and hydrogen iodide. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF with a mild base (e.g., triethylamine) to scavenge HI, at 0–25 °C.

Redox synthesis of sodium selenide using sodium amalgam; purpose is to prepare Na2Se from elemental selenium; key transformation is reduction of Se^0 to Se^2‑ with concurrent oxidation of Na to Na^+ and release of elemental mercury from the amalgam; typically carried out under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in dry ether or THF at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst required, the mercury of the amalgam acts as the medium.

Decomposition (denitrosation); nitrosocyanamide thermally or photolytically breaks the N–NO bond, yielding cyanamide and nitric oxide gas; usually carried out neat or in an inert solvent at elevated temperature; no catalyst required.

Strong hydride reduction of an ester (methyl 2‑phenoxypropanoate) with lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert the ester to the corresponding primary alcohols; the carbonyl carbon is reduced to a methanol fragment while the alkoxy methyl group is liberated as methanol, giving 2‑phenoxypropanol; performed in anhydrous diethyl ether or THF, cooled to 0 °C then allowed to warm to reflux under nitrogen; LiAlH4 is used stoichiometrically, no further catalyst needed.

Redox halogenation reaction of nitrosyl chloride with aluminum metal; purpose is to generate aluminum chloride and nitric oxide gas; aluminum is oxidized from 0 to +3, while nitrosyl chloride is reduced, releasing NO; usually conducted in a dry, sealed vessel, often at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to control gas evolution; no solvent is essential, and the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Alcoholysis (protonolysis) of trimethylborane with methanol; purpose is to exchange a methyl group on boron for a methoxy group, liberating methane; one B–CH₃ bond is cleaved by proton transfer from methanol, producing CH₄ and forming methoxy‑trimethylborane (or a related methoxyborane species); carried out under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, typically at 0–25 °C under nitrogen; no catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis/neutralization of boron trichloride with aqueous sodium hydroxide; purpose is to produce sodium borate (e.g., sodium tetraborate) and sodium chloride while consuming acid chloride; BCl₃ reacts with OH⁻ to form BO₃³⁻ (which precipitates as sodium borate) and releases Cl⁻ as NaCl, with water generated; performed in aqueous solution, usually cooled initially to control the exotherm then allowed to warm; water acts as the solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Double dehydrohalogenation of 3,4‑dibromohexane with sodium amide; purpose is to synthesize the internal alkyne 3‑hexyne; NaNH₂ abstracts two equivalents of HBr from adjacent carbon–bromine bonds, forming a carbon–carbon triple bond; reaction is carried out in liquid ammonia (or THF) at –33 °C to reflux with excess NaNH₂, followed by aqueous work‑up; sodium amide serves both as base and nucleophile, no extra catalyst required.

Type: Acid–base (salt metathesis). Purpose: Convert the sodium salt of 2‑bromoacetate to the free acid. Key: Protonation of the carboxylate anion and replacement of Na⁺ by H⁺, yielding 2‑bromoacetic acid and NaCl. Typical conditions: Aqueous or ethanolic solution of hydrochloric acid (1 equiv), ambient temperature, stirring. No catalyst required; common solvent is water or a water/organic mixture (e.g., EtOH/H₂O).

Acid–base reaction (carbonate dissolution); HF protonates the carbonate anion of indium carbonate, releasing CO2 gas and water while forming indium(III) fluoride; typically performed in aqueous hydrofluoric acid at room temperature or mild heating; no additional solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of acetylcarnitine back to carnitine and acetic acid; cleavage of the acetate ester; carried out in aqueous HCl or dilute H₂SO₄ at 50‑80 °C, often in a water‑ethanol mixture.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis (double displacement); calcium oxide exchanges anions with zinc sulfide to give zinc oxide and calcium sulfide; carried out in a furnace at 800–1000 °C in the solid state; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Aminolysis of ethyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑phenylacetate with ammonia to give mandelamide; purpose is conversion of the ester into the corresponding amide; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of NH₃ on the carbonyl, displacement of ethanol; conditions: excess aqueous or gaseous NH₃, reflux 80‑120 °C, often in ethanol or isopropanol as co‑solvent, 4‑12 h.

Hydrolysis and condensation of a metal alkoxide (sol‑gel route) to a perovskite oxide; water hydrolyzes titanium isopropoxide, producing isopropanol and Ti–OH species that condense with strontium hydroxide to form SrTiO₃; performed in aqueous or mixed water/alcohol media at 0–80 °C, often under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

Coordination complex formation via ligand substitution; palladium(II) chloride coordinates two acetonitrile molecules to give PdCl2(MeCN)2; usually performed by refluxing PdCl2 in dry acetonitrile under nitrogen; inert atmosphere may be used; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage (hydrohalogenolysis); concentrated HCl protonates ethyl isopropyl ether, leading to cleavage into ethanol and isopropyl chloride via an SN1/SN2 pathway; reflux in aqueous or alcoholic HCl solution at 60–80 °C; HCl itself acts as the catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); basic lead carbonate reacts with barium chloride to precipitate insoluble barium carbonate while soluble lead(II) chloride remains in solution, with water as by‑product; carried out in water at ambient temperature; no additional reagents required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction of a metal with a halogen; chromium metal reacts with fluorine gas to form chromium tetrafluoride, an oxidation of Cr⁰ to Cr⁴⁺; performed in a fluorine‑resistant reactor at 200–400 °C under an inert carrier gas; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Oxidation reaction; sodium hypochlorite oxidizes tris(dimethylamino)phosphine (P(III)) to hexamethylphosphoramide (HMPA, P(V)) while generating water and NaCl. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no special catalyst required. Used for preparation of HMPA, a polar aprotic solvent.

Aerobic oxidative dehydrogenation (aromatization); molecular oxygen oxidizes 2‑acetyl‑1,4,5,6‑tetrahydropyridine to the aromatic 2‑acetylpyridine, releasing water. Usually performed with a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu, Pd, or Fe) in a solvent such as acetonitrile or toluene under mild heating (40–80 °C) and an oxygen atmosphere.

Strong oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate. The aldehyde carbonyl is oxidized to the corresponding carboxylate, which is isolated after acid work‑up as 2‑methylbutanoic acid. Conducted in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH or KOH), usually at reflux; excess KMnO4 is filtered off as MnO2.

Free‑radical benzylic bromination; bromine reacts with toluene under radical initiation (UV light or peroxide) to substitute a benzylic hydrogen, forming benzyl bromide and hydrogen bromide as by‑product. Conducted in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at reflux or with controlled temperature; radical initiator may be added.

Nucleophilic substitution (phosphorothioate formation); phenoxide generated from 4‑hydroxybenzonitrile by NaOH attacks dimethyl phosphorochloridothioate, displacing chloride to give the O‑aryl phosphorothioate insecticide Cyanophos, with NaCl and water as side products. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH and an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF), low to ambient temperature, with vigorous stirring.

Oxidative dissolution (acid digestion); concentrated nitric acid oxidizes palladium sulfide, converting PdS to palladium(II) nitrate, while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas and sulfide is converted to sulfuric acid. Carried out by refluxing PdS in hot concentrated HNO₃; nitrogen dioxide evolves as a brown gas and excess acid is removed by evaporation.

Acid chloride formation and esterification (Schotten‑Bauman type); oxalyl chloride activates p‑hydroxybenzoic acid to its acyl chloride, releasing CO and CO₂ gases. Pyridine scavenges the generated HCl, and subsequent addition of benzyl alcohol yields benzyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate (benzyl ester) and pyridinium chloride. Reaction is performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acid-catalyzed decomposition of iron(III) ferrocyanide; purpose is to liberate hydrogen cyanide and convert iron to soluble iron(III) sulfate. Key transformation: protonation of cyanide ligands releases HCN gas; Fe(III) ferrocyanide is converted to Fe₂(SO₄)₃. Typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄, temperature 0–25 °C to control HCN evolution, aqueous medium. No additional catalyst; water is the solvent.

Esterification via acyl chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); converts hexan‑1‑ol to hexyl benzoate by replacing the chloride of benzoyl chloride with the alkoxy group; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, using a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the released HCl.

Fischer esterification of 4‑methylpentanoic acid with methanol to give the methyl ester; reflux the acid‑methanol mixture in the presence of a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) and remove the generated water (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) to drive the equilibrium toward methyl 4‑methylpentanoate.

Oxidation of a phosphite (P(III)) to the corresponding phosphate (P(V)); m‑chloroperbenzoic acid acts as the oxidant, converting tributyl phosphite to tributyl phosphate while being reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid; usually carried out in dichloromethane at 0 °C → rt; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange (salt swap). Nickel(II) thiocyanate reacts with two equivalents of hydrochloric acid in aqueous solution, exchanging the thiocyanate ligands for chloride to give nickel(II) chloride and two equivalents of hydrogen thiocyanate (HSCN). Typically carried out at room temperature in water; the mixture is often heated gently to ensure complete conversion and the products are isolated by evaporation or precipitation.

Oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfone (S(II) → S(VI)); two equivalents of m‑chloroperbenzoic acid oxidize diphenyl sulfide first to diphenyl sulfoxide and then to diphenyl sulfone, with m‑chlorobenzoic acid as the by‑product; reaction typically run in dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required beyond the peracid.

Base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation (E2): treatment of 2‑chloro‑2‑methylheptane with aqueous or alcoholic NaOH at elevated temperature induces elimination of HCl to afford the more substituted alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑heptene, with sodium chloride and water as by‑products; the reaction proceeds via a concerted anti‑periplanar transition state.

Proton transfer (acid–base reaction) between sulfuric acid and sodium metaperiodate; yields metaperiodic (periodic) acid (HIO₄) and sodium bisulfate; performed in aqueous medium, often at 0 °C to control exotherm; straightforward stoichiometric conversion, no catalyst.

Conversion of a secondary allylic alcohol to the chloride; 2,3‑dihydro‑1H‑inden‑1‑ol is treated with thionyl chloride (SOCl2) to afford 1‑chloro‑2,3‑dihydro‑1H‑indene. Typical conditions: reflux of the alcohol in excess SOCl2 (often with a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMF) for 1–2 h, removal of excess SOCl2 under reduced pressure, and purification of the chloride product.

Amidation via acyl chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); the amino group of β‑alanine attacks 4‑fluorobenzoyl chloride, forming N‑(4‑fluorobenzoyl)‑β‑alanine and releasing HCl; carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF with a base (triethylamine, NaHCO₃) to neutralize HCl, typically at 0 °C to room temperature.

Hydrolytic deamination of guanosine to xanthosine; a nucleobase transformation where the exocyclic amino group is replaced by a carbonyl oxygen, releasing ammonia. Typically performed in aqueous solution, often under mild acidic or basic conditions and gentle heating (50‑80 °C) to promote the deamination; no special solvent beyond water is required.

Direct combination (halogenation) synthesis of rhenium tetrachloride; elemental rhenium reacts with chlorine gas to form ReCl₄. Conducted in a dry, inert atmosphere at elevated temperature (≈300‑400 °C) with a flow of Cl₂; no solvent is used, and quartz or stainless‑steel reactors are common.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of benzanilide to N‑phenylbenzylamine; an amide functional group is reduced to a secondary amine. Reaction carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, typically refluxing or at 0‑25 °C for addition of LAH followed by stirring at reflux for 1‑3 h; excess LAH is used, and the mixture is quenched with water or dilute acid after completion.

Catalytic isomerization of p‑xylene to o‑xylene; a positional isomerization of dimethylbenzene often employed to adjust xylene feedstocks. Performed in the gas phase at 300‑400 °C over solid acid catalysts such as zeolites (e.g., H‑ZSM‑5) or metal chloride catalysts (AlCl₃, PtCl₂); carrier gas (N₂ or H₂) may be used, and no liquid solvent is involved.

N‑alkylation of 2‑pyrrolidone with methyl iodide to give N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone; a SN2 substitution where the lactam nitrogen attacks methyl iodide, generating HI as a by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent (acetone, DMF, or MeCN) at 0‑25 °C to room temperature, often in the presence of a base such as Na₂CO₃, K₂CO₃, or triethylamine to neutralize the formed HI and drive the reaction to completion.

Reductive halogen exchange between hydrogen gas and titanium(IV) iodide yielding titanium(II) iodide and hydrogen iodide; a redox reduction of Ti(IV) to Ti(II) by H₂. Typically carried out in a sealed tube or high‑pressure reactor at elevated temperature (200‑300 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is required, and the generated HI may be removed by a cold trap or dissolved in a suitable liquid for collection.

Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride. Water attacks theyl carbon of 2‑acetoxyacetyl chloride, cleaving the acid‑chloride bond to afford aceburic acid (the corresponding carboxylic acid) and hydrogen chloride. Performed in aqueous solution, usually at low to moderate temperature to control HCl evolution; no catalyst needed.

General reaction type: Hydrolysis. Purpose: Decomposition of acetic anhydride into acetic acid. Key transformation: Acetic anhydride reacts with water to yield two molecules of acetic acid. Conditions: Occurs under mild conditions with water at room temperature or slightly elevated temperatures. No catalyst typically required, though acidic or basic conditions may accelerate the reaction.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reduction) of an alkyl iodide; replaces the C–I bond with hydrogen to give the corresponding alkane and HI as a by‑product. Typically carried out under hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt, or Raney Ni in an alcohol (e.g., ethanol) or ether solvent at 25–80 °C.

Halogen‑lithium exchange at phosphorus (metal‑halogen exchange). n‑Butyllithium reacts with chlorodiphenylphosphine, replacing the P–Cl bond with a P–Li bond to generate lithium diphenylphosphide while forming n‑butyl chloride as the by‑product. Conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry THF or diethyl ether at –78 °C to 0 °C; organolithium reagent serves as both reagent and base.

General reaction type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Purpose: Synthesis of esters via alkylation of carboxylic acid salts. Key transformation: Potassium acetate displaces chloride in isopropyl chloride to form isopropyl acetate, with potassium chloride as a byproduct. Conditions: Proceeds in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., acetone, DMF) at moderate temperatures (e.g., 50-100°C).

General reaction type: Cyclization/dehydration. Purpose: Formation of lactams from hydroxyamides. Key transformation: The hydroxyl group bonds with the carbonyl carbon of the amide, eliminating water and forming the cyclic 2-pyrrolidone. Conditions: Typically requires heat under acidic conditions (e.g., catalytic H2SO4) or high-boiling solvents (e.g., xylene, reflux).

General reaction type: Phosphorylation/esterification. Purpose: Synthesis of phosphate esters. Key transformation: 1-Naphthol undergoes ester bond formation with phosphoric acid, releasing water. Conditions: Conducted at elevated temperatures in the presence of acidic catalysts (e.g., concentrated H2SO4, p-toluenesulfonic acid) or in organic solvents (e.g., pyridine) to drive condensation.

Grignard carboxylation; purpose is to convert an aryl halide into the corresponding benzoic acid. The phenylmagnesium bromide adds to carbon dioxide to form the magnesium carboxylate, which upon aqueous acidic work‑up yields benzoic acid and MgBr2. Typically performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; work‑up with dilute HCl or water.

Double‑displacement precipitation; aqueous solutions of barium selenite and potassium carbonate exchange ions, forming insoluble barium carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium selenite; carried out at room temperature with stirring; solid BaCO3 is filtered off, leaving K2SeO3 in solution.

Carbamate hydrolysis; purpose is to decompose a protected amine back to ammonia and the corresponding alcohol while releasing CO2. Water attacks the carbonyl of propyl carbamate, leading to cleavage of the C–N bond and formation of carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO2) and propanol; ammonia is liberated. Conducted in aqueous medium, usually heated, under either acidic (e.g., dilute HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions.

Selective ester reduction with DIBAL‑H; purpose is to reduce a tert‑butyl ester to the aldehyde while preserving the aromatic ring. At –78 °C, diisobutylaluminium hydride adds a hydride to the carbonyl carbon of tert‑butyl 2,4,6‑trimethylbenzoate, giving an alkoxide that on work‑up furnishes 2,4,6‑trimethylbenzaldehyde and tert‑butanol as the by‑product. Reaction is carried out in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere; quench with dilute acid or water at low temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed alkene hydration (mercury(II) sulfate catalysis); purpose is to convert 2‑methylpropene into the corresponding tertiary alcohol (2‑methyl‑2‑propanol) via Markovnikov addition of water. Mercuric sulfate forms a mercurinium ion intermediate that is attacked by water; subsequent deprotonation yields the alcohol. Typically performed in aqueous dilute acid (e.g., H2SO4) at 60–80 °C with HgSO4 as catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution forming a diacylhydrazide; purpose is to prepare 1,2‑hydrazine‑dicarboxamide (oxalyl dihydrazide) from oxalyl chloride and hydrazine. Each acyl chloride reacts with a hydrazine nitrogen, releasing HCl and forming the bis‑acylated product. Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Reaction type: phosphorylation (nucleophilic substitution) of phenol with a chlorophosphate ester. Purpose: synthesis of dimethyl phenyl phosphate, a protected phosphate ester. Key transformation: phenolic oxygen attacks the phosphorus atom of dimethyl chlorophosphate, displacing chloride and forming the P–O–aryl bond; HCl is generated as a by‑product. Typical conditions: dissolve phenol and dimethyl chlorophosphate in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C, add a base such as triethylamine or pyridine (1‑2 equiv) to capture HCl, then allow the mixture to warm to room temperature and stir for 1‑2 h. Reaction is usually performed under nitrogen; work‑up includes aqueous wash to remove inorganic salts and purification by column chromatography or distillation.

Hydrolysis of a dialkylzinc reagent. Water reacts with dimethylzinc, protonating the Zn‑C bonds to release methane gas and produce zinc hydroxide precipitate. Performed by careful addition of dimethylzinc to cold water (0 °C) under stirring; no catalyst required, but the reaction must be controlled to avoid vigorous gas evolution.
Reduction reaction; reduces phosphorus tribromide to phosphine; uses hydrogen gas; typically requires high temperature and pressure; catalyst optional but may involve transition metals.

Acid–base displacement; generates hydrogen bromide gas while forming ammonium hydrogen sulfate; proton transfer from H2SO4 to NH4+; carried out in aqueous solution, often under reflux with cooling to condense HBr; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Decomposition (hydrolysis) of sodium percarbonate; solid Na₂CO₃·1.5 H₂O₂ dissolves in water, yielding sodium carbonate and hydrogen peroxide; used as a solid, stable source of H₂O₂ in cleaning and laundry; occurs at room temperature upon dissolution in water; water is the only solvent.
Neutralization (acid–base) of phenol; produces sodium phenoxide and water; deprotonation of phenol by NaOH; performed in water at room temperature; aqueous NaOH solution, no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (acidic bromination); installs three bromine atoms at the 2,4,6 positions of 3‑methylphenol to give 2,4,6‑tribromo‑3‑methylphenol; bromine generated in situ from NaBr/NaBrO3 in conc. H2SO4; reaction run in concentrated sulfuric acid (also serves as solvent) at 0 °C to 50 °C; no external catalyst.

Redox acid‑metal reaction (single‑displacement). Thallium metal reduces hydroiodic acid, generating hydrogen gas and forming thallium(I) iodide salt. Carried out in aqueous HI, often at ambient temperature or with mild heating to increase rate; no additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation; aqueous bismuth nitrate reacts with sodium hydroxide to precipitate bismuth hydroxide (Bi(OH)₃) and form soluble sodium nitrate. Conducted at room temperature in water; stirring ensures complete precipitation.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of 1,2‑diphenylethanol to give the more stable trans‑alkene, trans‑1,2‑diphenylethene. Conducted with concentrated H₂SO₄, heating to 60–80 °C; the acid acts both as catalyst and solvent, water is eliminated.

Nitrosyl ester formation (nitrosation of an alcohol); isopropyl alcohol reacts with nitrous acid to give isopropyl nitrite and water; generated by adding NaNO₂ to a dilute acid at 0–5 °C; performed in cold aqueous/acetone mixture; nitrous acid is generated in situ, no catalyst.

Reductive amination; ketone (3‑methoxyphenylacetone) condenses with methylamine, then NaBH₃CN reduces the imine to afford 3‑methoxymethcathinone; key steps: imine formation followed by selective hydride reduction; typically conducted in methanol or ethanol with a weakly acidic buffer (pH 5–6) at ambient temperature; sodium cyanoborohydride is the reducing agent.

Transmetallation (organometallic synthesis); preparation of a butyl‑mercury reagent by nucleophilic attack of n‑butyllithium on mercuric chloride; key transformation is LiCl formation and formation of n‑butylmercuric chloride; typically performed under inert atmosphere at –78 °C to 0 °C in dry ether or THF; anhydrous conditions required, no additional catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization (metathesis); the proton from hydrochloric acid transfers to the formate anion, generating formic acid and rubidium chloride. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water serves as the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of dinitrogen pentoxide; purpose is to generate nitric acid from its anhydride; key transformation is N2O5 + H2O → 2 HNO3; typically done by dissolving liquid N2O5 in water or passing N2O5 gas into water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Diazomethyl esterification (methylation of a carboxylic acid); diazomethane reacts with nicotinic acid to give methyl nicotinate with evolution of nitrogen gas; key transformation is formation of the methyl ester and loss of N₂; usually conducted in dry diethyl ether or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature, protected from light; excess diazomethane quenched with acetic acid.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchange of cations between magnesium chloride and potassium stearate yields insoluble magnesium stearate and soluble potassium chloride; typically carried out in hot water or ethanol where potassium stearate is soluble, then cooling to precipitate magnesium stearate; no catalyst, aqueous or alcoholic medium.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (halogenation) using sulfuryl chloride; chlorine is transferred to phenol to give chlorophenol while sulfuryl chloride decomposes to HCl and SO₂; key transformation is substitution of a hydrogen on the aromatic ring by chlorine; performed in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or dichloromethane, often at 0 °C to reflux; light or a small amount of radical initiator can accelerate the reaction.

Neutralization/precipitation (acid–base reaction) forming an insoluble metal arsenate; arsenic acid reacts with iron(III) oxide to give iron(III) arsenate and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution with heating to dissolve the arsenic acid, then cooling to precipitate the iron(III) arsenate; no special catalyst, water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of furfuryl chloride with aqueous ammonia, converting the alkyl chloride to furfurylamine and releasing hydrogen chloride. Typically carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution under reflux; excess ammonia or a base is often used to neutralize the generated HCl.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation of codeine to dihydrocodeine using palladium on carbon and ammonium formate as the hydrogen donor. The Pd/C catalyst reduces the 7,8‑double bond, giving the saturated dihydro analogue. Conducted in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol at 25‑80 °C under an inert atmosphere; no external H₂ gas is required.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of cyclohexanone to 2‑cyclohexen‑1‑one using palladium on carbon and molecular oxygen. The Pd/C catalyst abstracts two hydrogen atoms, forming the α,β‑unsaturated ketone and water. Usually performed in a non‑polar solvent (toluene, xylene) under O₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 80‑120 °C.

Nucleophilic alkylation of an H‑phosphonate; methyl iodide attacks the P–H of dimethyl phosphite to give dimethyl methylphosphonate while forming hydrogen iodide; used to prepare methyl‑phosphonate esters for agrochemical or nerve‑agent precursors; carried out in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or THF with a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to capture HI; reaction is typically refluxed for several hours under inert atmosphere.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) where elemental fluorine displaces chlorine from antimony trichloride, producing antimony trifluoride and chlorine gas. The reaction proceeds in the gas phase or in an inert solvent (e.g., CCl₄) at low temperature to control the highly exothermic process; no catalyst is required.

Gas‑phase fluorination/acid‑base reaction of calcium carbonate; produces calcium fluoride while liberating CO2 and O2; key transformation: CaCO3 + F2 → CaF2 + CO2 + 1/2 O2; performed at ambient to slightly elevated temperature with excess fluorine gas; dry, solid‑state, highly exothermic, no solvent or catalyst.

Reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol; NaBH4 selectively reduces the carbonyl of phenylacetone to give 1‑phenyl‑2‑propanol. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in protic solvents such as methanol, ethanol, or isopropanol (often with a small amount of THF); reaction quenched with water or dilute acid.

Double‑displacement acid–base precipitation: sodium hydroxide neutralizes beryllium nitrate to give soluble sodium nitrate and insoluble beryllium hydroxide, which precipitates. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a secondary amine; H2O2 in dilute H2SO4 oxidizes diethylamine to N,N‑diethylhydroxylamine. Typically carried out in aqueous acidic medium at 0–5 °C with slow addition of H2O2 to control exotherm; water serves as solvent and the reaction yields water as by‑product.

Fischer esterification; heptafluorobutyric acid reacts with methanol to give methyl heptafluorobutyrate and water. Conducted under reflux with excess methanol, often catalyzed by a strong acid such as H2SO4 or p‑TsOH; removal of water drives the equilibrium, solvent is generally methanol (or toluene for azeotropic removal).

Oxidation of nitrosobenzene to nitrobenzene; H2O2 acts as the oxidant, converting the –N=O functionality to –NO2 with water as the only by‑product. Usually performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile/water) at ambient temperature, sometimes under mildly acidic conditions to enhance rate.

Aluminothermic (thermite) reduction of zinc oxide; metallic aluminum reduces ZnO to elemental zinc while being oxidized to Al2O3. Requires high temperature (≈1000 °C) in a furnace, often under inert atmosphere; no solvent, solid‑state redox reaction.

Acid–base exchange generating peroxymonosulfuric acid (Caro’s acid); aqueous potassium peroxymonosulfate (KHSO5) reacts with sulfuric acid to give potassium bisulfate (KHSO4) and H2SO5. Performed at low to ambient temperature in water; the mixture is used as a strong oxidizing solution.

Dehydrative chlorination of a carboxylate to an acyl chloride; thionyl chloride converts potassium 2‑fluoroacetate into 2‑fluoroacetyl chloride, releasing SO2 and HCl (which combine with K⁺ to give KCl). Conducted in anhydrous organic solvent such as dichloromethane or CHCl3, often with a catalytic amount of DMF, under inert atmosphere and reflux.

Fischer esterification; condensation of pentanoic acid with pentanol yields pentyl pentanoate (an ester) and water. Acid‑catalyzed (H2SO4, p‑TsOH) reflux in an excess of the alcohol or in a Dean–Stark apparatus (toluene, benzene, or xylenes) to continuously remove water. Commonly used to prepare medium‑chain esters.

Redox oxidation of tetramethyllead by concentrated nitric acid; the organic lead compound is oxidized, producing lead(II) nitrate, carbon dioxide, water, and nitrogen dioxide gas. The reaction is carried out by heating the mixture of lead tetra‑methyl and fuming HNO₃, often in a refluxing glass apparatus; no additional catalyst is needed.

Reductive denitrosation; ascorbic acid reduces N‑nitrosomorpholine to the parent amine (morpholine) and releases nitric oxide, while ascorbic acid is oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid; carried out in aqueous or mixed solvent at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, no catalyst required.

Staudinger reduction of an acyl azide using triphenylphosphine and water; the azide loses N2, forming an iminophosphorane that hydrolyzes to the corresponding amide (acetamide) and triphenylphosphine oxide; conducted in an aprotic solvent such as THF or CH2Cl2 at 0 °C to room temperature, with water added for the hydrolysis step.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of 2‑fluoropropane by aqueous sodium hydroxide; fluoride displaced by hydroxide to give isopropanol and NaF; typically heated aqueous NaOH, often in water or ethanol.

Oxidative coupling of thiols; molecular iodine oxidizes allyl mercaptan to the corresponding disulfide (diallyl disulfide) while generating hydrogen iodide; performed at room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, iodine acts as the oxidant, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization; potassium hydroxide neutralizes vanadic (metavanadic) acid to form potassium metavanadate (KVO₃) and water; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, straightforward stoichiometric neutralization, no catalyst.

Salt hydrolysis/neutralization; aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes the hydrochloride salt of para‑toluidine, liberating the free amine, water, and NaCl; performed in water at room temperature or with gentle heating, simple acid‑base reaction, no catalyst.

Halogen displacement/redox exchange reaction where elemental chlorine oxidizes bromide in bismuth(III) bromide, replacing it with chloride to give bismuth(III) chloride and liberating bromine. Usually conducted in a sealed vessel or refluxing inert solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or carbon tetrachloride) at elevated temperature; chlorine gas is the reagent, no catalyst needed.

Disproportionation/Oxidation‑reduction; industrial preparation of bleach; chlorine is reduced to chloride and oxidized to hypochlorite while NaOH supplies hydroxide; performed in aqueous NaOH solution at 0–5 °C to suppress side reactions; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Salt metathesis/anion exchange; generation of nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate (NO⁺ BF₄⁻) by transferring fluorine from NOF to Ag⁺ forming AgF precipitate; carried out in dry, aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or nitrobenzene under inert atmosphere at 0–25 °C; no catalyst.

Redox disproportionation; cesium permanganate oxidizes hydrogen peroxide, the permanganate is reduced to manganese dioxide while peroxide is oxidized to oxygen, yielding cesium hydroxide, water and O₂; typically carried out in aqueous basic solution (pH > 7) at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent.

Carbothermic reduction (high‑temperature solid‑state); carbon reduces barium niobate to metallic niobium and barium oxide while producing CO₂; conducted in a graphite furnace at >1300 °C (often ~1500 °C) in an inert (Ar) or vacuum atmosphere; solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization; converts calcium hydroxide into calcium tellurate. Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is added to an aqueous solution of telluric acid, yielding calcium tellurate (CaTeO₄) and water. Conducted in water at room temperature or with slight warming; no catalyst needed.

Redox oxidation; ozone oxidizes bromate (BrO₃⁻) to perbromate (BrO₄⁻) while being reduced to O₂; reaction carried out in aqueous solution, typically neutral to alkaline, with ozone bubbled through potassium bromate solution at 0–25 °C; water solvent, no catalyst.

Acid‑base double displacement; tetrafluoroboric acid protonates potassium silicate to give silicic acid (H₂SiO₃) and forms potassium tetrafluoroborate (KBF₄) as the salt; performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

Reduction of an azide to an amine; methyl 3‑azidopropanoate is treated with LiAlH₄ in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to reflux, yielding methyl 3‑aminopropanoate with evolution of N₂; work‑up with aqueous acid quenches excess hydride.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation); HBr adds across the C=C bond of ethoxyethene (vinyl ether) in a Markovnikov fashion to afford 2‑bromoethyl ethyl ether; reaction run in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or ether at 0 °C to room temperature, using gaseous or aqueous HBr; no catalyst.

Free‑radical halogenation (substitution); purpose is to convert an alkane into a primary alkyl chloride. Initiated by UV light or heat, often in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; chlorine gas acts as both reagent and radical source. Key transformation is abstraction of a hydrogen atom from 2‑methylpropane followed by recombination with chlorine to give 1‑chloro‑2‑methylpropane and HCl.

Negishi cross‑coupling (palladium‑catalyzed C–C bond formation); used to install an ethyl group onto a bromopyridine ring. Typical conditions employ a Pd(0) source such as Pd(PPh₃)₄ (or Pd(dba)₂ with phosphine ligands) and a polar aprotic solvent like THF or DMF, often at 50–80 °C under nitrogen. The organozinc reagent (ethylzinc chloride) transmetallates to palladium, which then undergoes reductive elimination to afford 5‑ethyl‑2‑methylpyridine.

Acid‑driven metathesis (salt attack); concentrated hydrochloric acid reacts with solid calcium fluoride (fluorspar) to liberate hydrogen fluoride gas and form soluble calcium chloride; typically carried out at 200–300 °C in a sealed furnace or reactor, often with excess HCl; no solvent other than the acid itself, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of alkyl halides) under basic conditions; purpose is to replace the two chloro groups of bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfone with hydroxyl groups, yielding bis(2‑hydroxyethyl) sulfone. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, typically heated to reflux (50–100 °C). Each Cl is displaced by OH⁻ via an SN2 pathway, producing NaCl as by‑product.

Acid‑chloride formation with phosphorus pentachloride; phenoxyacetic acid is transformed into phenoxyacetyl chloride while generating POCl₃ and HCl. Conducted in a dry, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to reflux. Stoichiometric PCl₅ is added portion‑wise; the reaction mixture is usually filtered to remove solid POCl₃ and then the acid chloride is isolated.

Sandmeyer cyanation; conversion of the diazonium salt to benzonitrile; provides a route to aryl nitriles; key transformation: Ar‑N₂⁺ BF₄⁻ + CuCN → ArCN + N₂↑; typically performed in aqueous acidic medium (HBF₄) at 0–25 °C, copper(I) cyanide added as solid; solvent water or a water‑organic mixture; copper(I) cyanide acts as both catalyst and cyanide source.

Reductive amination of a ketone; employed to form the secondary amine 3‑methylamphetamine from 3‑methylphenylacetone and methylamine. The reaction requires a mild reducing agent such as NaCNBH₃ or catalytic hydrogenation (H₂, Pd/C) in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., AcOH) and a solvent like methanol or ethanol, usually at 0 °C to room temperature. The ketone is first converted to an imine with methylamine, which is then reduced to the amine, releasing water.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to exchange cations to isolate insoluble barium oxalate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; mixing aqueous sodium oxalate with aqueous barium perchlorate precipitates barium oxalate, while sodium perchlorate remains dissolved. No special catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) of a phenoxide; used to produce para‑chlorophenol (4‑chlorophenol); the phenoxide ion activates the aromatic ring and directs Cl₂ (or generated HOCl) to the para position; NaCl is formed as by‑product; typically done in aqueous NaOH solution, chlorine gas or NaOCl added at 0–25 °C, with continuous stirring.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed polyene cyclization; BF₃·OEt₂ activates geranylgeraniol to undergo intramolecular cyclization forming the bicyclic diterpene sclareol. Typical conditions involve low to moderate temperature (0 °C to 25 °C) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane under inert atmosphere. The BF₃ coordinates to the allylic alcohol, facilitating carbocation formation and cascade cyclization; work‑up with aqueous base quenches the reaction.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation). Primary amine of 2‑aminofluorene attacks acetyl chloride, giving 2‑acetylaminofluorene; triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

General type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification with an acyl chloride); purpose: introduce an acryloyloxy group onto hydroxyethyl methacrylate to form a di‑functional monomer; key transformation: the hydroxyl of 2‑hydroxyethyl methacrylate attacks acryloyl chloride, producing 2‑(acryloyloxy)ethyl methacrylate and HCl; typical conditions: 0–5 °C in dry dichloromethane or chloroform, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge HCl; common solvent/catalyst: dry CH2Cl2, base as HCl trap.

Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of a cyclic ketone. m‑Chloroperbenzoic acid transfers an oxygen to cyclohexanone, rearranging to the seven‑membered lactone ε‑caprolactone while producing m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often with a catalytic amount of acid to accelerate the rearrangement.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling of 3‑bromopyridine with phenylboronic acid; forms the C‑C bond to give 3‑phenylpyridine, with KBr and boric acid as by‑products. Typical protocol uses Pd(OAc)₂ (5 mol %), tri‑o‑tolylphosphine (10–20 mol %), K₂CO₃ (2 equiv) in a toluene/water (or dioxane/water) mixture, heated to reflux (≈110 °C) for 12–24 h under inert atmosphere.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of phenothiazine. Methyl iodide alkylates the nitrogen of phenothiazine to give N‑methylphenothiazine, usually in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃ or NaH) to deprotonate the nitrogen and trap HI.

Acid–base neutralization (formation of a sodium salt). Oxamic acid is deprotonated by aqueous NaOH, yielding water and sodium oxamate. Reaction proceeds in water at ambient temperature; excess base may be used to ensure complete conversion.

Salt formation (protonation) of N,N,N',N'-tetramethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine with hydrochloric acid to afford the dihydrochloride salt; the diamine is dissolved in ethanol or water and treated with aqueous HCl (or HCl gas) at ambient temperature; ethanol/water mixture is common; no catalyst is required.

Transesterification; converts a methyl ester into an isopropyl ester; purpose is to exchange the alcohol moiety; key transformation: methyl 3‑methylbutanoate + isopropanol ⇌ isopropyl 3‑methylbutanoate + methanol; typically acid‑catalyzed (e.g., catalytic H2SO4 or p‑TsOH) or base‑catalyzed (NaOEt) under reflux; common solvents: toluene or excess isopropanol; removal of methanol drives equilibrium.

Acid‑base neutralization forming chromium(III) perchlorate from chromium(III) hydroxide and perchloric acid. General type: salt formation (neutralization). The hydroxide is suspended in water and treated with aqueous perchloric acid (excess) at ambient temperature, producing soluble Cr(ClO₄)₃ and water. The reaction is exothermic; stirring ensures complete dissolution of the solid. No special catalysts are required; the resulting solution can be evaporated to isolate the perchlorate salt.

Exhaustive N‑methylation of a diamine (double SN2). Two equivalents of methyl iodide alkylate the two primary amine groups of hexamethylenediamine, producing N,N‑dimethyl‑hexane‑1,6‑diamine and generating HI. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) with an excess base such as NaH, K₂CO₃ or triethylamine to neutralize the formed HI and drive the reaction to completion.

High‑temperature oxidation of a metal selenide. Elemental oxygen oxidizes barium selenide to barium selenite (2 BaSe + 3 O₂ → 2 BaSeO₃). Typically performed in a furnace under a flowing O₂ atmosphere at several hundred °C; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Chan‑Lam C–N cross‑coupling; copper(II) acetate with 1,10‑phenanthroline ligates Cu(II) to promote arylation of the secondary amine piperazine with 4‑chlorophenylboronic acid, affording 1‑(4‑chlorophenyl)piperazine. Typically performed in a polar protic or alcoholic solvent (e.g., MeOH/H2O or EtOH) at ambient to moderate temperature under air or O2; a base such as pyridine may be added to assist transmetalation.

Sandmeyer halogenation; in situ generation of the diazonium salt from 4‑chloroaniline (nitrosyl chloride provides NO⁺/Cl⁻) followed by copper(I) chloride mediated replacement of the diazo group with chloride to give 1,4‑dichlorobenzene, releasing HCl and N₂. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium (HCl) at 0 °C to room temperature, with CuCl as catalyst.

Type: Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride (rapid nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: Generate the free carboxylic acid from the more reactive acyl chloride. Key transformation: Water attacks the carbonyl carbon of dodecanoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming dodecanoic acid; HCl is released as a by‑product. Typical conditions: Addition of the acyl chloride to ice‑cold water or dilute aqueous NaHCO₃ at 0 °C to rt, stirring for minutes. No additional catalyst required; the reaction is exothermic.

Acidic decomposition of copper(II) sulfide; purpose: generate soluble CuSO₄ and evolve hydrogen sulfide gas; key transformation: CuS + 2 H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂S ↑ + H₂O; typical conditions: dilute H₂SO₄, room temperature or mild heating, aqueous medium; no catalyst.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) of vinyl chloride with potassium hydroxide; chloride is abstracted along with a β‑hydrogen, acetylene, potassium chloride, and water. The reaction requires strong KOH under high temperature (≈200 °C) in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or water; no catalyst is employed.

Alkaline oxidative conversion of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; sinapaldehyde is oxidized by excess KMnO₄ in aqueous alkaline solution to sinapic acid, with MnO₂ precipitating and KOH regenerated. Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO₄, pH ~10, heating under reflux until the purple MnO₄⁻ is consumed.

Type: halogen exchange (Finkelstein reaction). Purpose: convert the chloride to a more reactive iodide. Key transformation: I⁻ displaces Cl⁻ via SN2, producing cyclopentyl iodide and precipitating KCl. Typical conditions: excess KI in dry acetone, reflux under inert atmosphere; KCl precipitates and is removed by filtration.

High‑temperature solid‑state reduction of a metal oxide by silicon; MnO (Mn²⁺) reacts with elemental Si at ≥1000 °C in an inert atmosphere, yielding silicon monoxide gas and forming manganese silicide (MnSi). No solvent; the reaction is carried out in a sealed tube or furnace under argon or vacuum.

Hydrogen reduction of a high‑valent metal halide; H₂ gas reduces NbCl₅ to NbCl₃, producing HCl as the gaseous by‑product. Performed at elevated temperatures (≈300–400 °C) in a flow of hydrogen or under static H₂ pressure, often in a quartz tube to avoid moisture.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of naphthalene; acetyl chloride reacts with naphthalene in the presence of the Lewis acid AlCl₃ to install an acetyl group at the 1‑position, giving 1‑acetylnaphthalene and releasing HCl. Conducted in anhydrous, non‑protic solvents such as dry CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂ at 0–50  under inert atmosphere; AlCl₃ is used in stoichiometric excess and the reaction mixture is quenched with ice‑water work‑up.

Synthesis (direct combination) reaction; chlorine oxidizes elemental antimony to antimony pentachloride, a Lewis‑acidic halide. Usually carried out by passing dry Cl2 over heated Sb (≈200–300 °C) in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent, inert atmosphere often used.

Redox (disproportionation) reaction; bromate ion is reduced to bromide while hydrogen peroxide is oxidized to water and molecular oxygen. Conducted in aqueous acidic solution (often dilute H₂SO₄) at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; may be assisted by a catalytic amount of transition‑metal oxide (e.g., MnO₂) to accelerate O₂ evolution.

Trans‑nitrosation (nitrosamine exchange) reaction; the nitroso group transfers from N‑nitrosodimethylamine to N,N‑dipropylamine, yielding dimethylamine and N‑nitrosodipropylamine. Performed in a polar protic solvent (water or alcoholic medium) at 0–25 °C, sometimes under mildly acidic conditions to promote nitrosyl transfer; no additional catalyst is required.

hydrohalogenation addition reaction; converts alkene to alkyl halide via electrophilic addition; hydrogen chloride adds across the double bond of cyclopentene following Markovnikov's rule; typically conducted in polar protic solvents (e.g., ethanol) or excess HCl without additional catalysts.

Acid-base neutralization reaction. Copper(II) oxide base reacts with hydrochloric acid to form copper(II) chloride and water. Transformation involves proton transfer from acid to oxide. Often requires gentle heating to accelerate the reaction. Aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alcohol by hydrobromic acid to give 2‑fluoroethyl bromide and water. Reaction is carried out by refluxing 2‑fluoroethanol with excess aqueous or conc. HBr (or generated HBr gas) at 80–100 °C; the acidic medium protonates the alcohol, facilitating bromide attack. No external catalyst is needed.
Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the acetal 1,2‑dimethoxyethane; dilute HCl in water protonates the ethers, water attacks, yielding ethylene glycol and methanol; carried out under reflux in aqueous HCl.

Azo coupling (oxidative coupling) between N,N-dimethylaniline and nitrosobenzene to form 4-(phenylazo)-N,N-dimethylaniline and water; used for synthesis of azo dyes. Key transformation: formation of an N=N linker between the aromatic rings with concomitant loss of water. Typically carried out in a mildly acidic aqueous medium (e.g., dilute HCl) at 0‑5 °C, often using water or water/ethanol as solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose is to generate arsenic acid and soluble calcium chloride from calcium arsenate; aqueous HCl reacts with calcium arsenate, protonating the arsenate anion to H₃AsO₄ and forming CaCl₂ (usually remaining in solution); typically conducted in water at ambient temperature; no special catalyst, just excess HCl if needed.

Oxidation; combustion of gallium metal in oxygen to form gallium(III) oxide; Ga metal is heated in air or O2 atmosphere, typically 300–500 °C, giving Ga2O3 solid; simple gas‑solid oxidation, no catalyst.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution/peroxide formation; purpose: synthesis of benzoyl peroxide as a radical initiator; key transformation: two benzoyl chloride molecules react with sodium peroxide, chloride ions are displaced as NaCl and a peroxide linkage (Bz‑O‑O‑Bz) is formed; typical conditions: dry ether or THF solvent, 0‑5 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); no additional catalyst, sodium peroxide serves as base/oxidant.

Reaction type: oxidative dissolution (redox) of a metal sulfide by concentrated nitric acid; purpose: convert insoluble silver sulfide to soluble silver nitrate while oxidizing sulfur to sulfate; key transformation: nitrate ions are reduced to nitrogen dioxide, sulfur is oxidized to sulfuric acid, and silver is released as AgNO₃; typical conditions: hot concentrated HNO₃ (≥68 %) with reflux, apparatus vented to capture NO₂ gas; no extra catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation); sodium hydroxide deprotonates allyl alcohol to give the allyloxide which attacks methyl iodide, forming allyl methyl ether and sodium iodide; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature, often under inert atmosphere.

Reaction type: high‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of a metal sulfide; purpose: obtain zirconium dioxide and gaseous sulfur dioxide; key transformation: ZrS₂ + 3 O₂ → ZrO₂ + 2 SO₂; typical conditions: furnace heating at 1000‑1300 °C in a flow of O₂ or air, solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Reaction type: halogen exchange (halide metathesis) on silicon; purpose: replace bromide with chloride to give chlorotriethylsilane; key transformation: Si–Br bond is substituted by Si–Cl while HCl protonates bromide to form HBr; typical conditions: dry organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or toluene), 0‑25 °C under inert atmosphere, excess HCl gas may be used; no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage (SN1/SN2); purpose: convert isobutyl methyl ether into isobutyl chloride and methanol; key transformation: protonation of the ether oxygen followed by C–O bond cleavage, methanol departs and Cl⁻ attacks the isobutyl carbon; typical conditions: aqueous HCl (6 M), reflux at 60‑80 °C, water as solvent; no extra catalyst.

Combustion of dimethyl sulfide; oxidation of (CH3)2S yields sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide and water; a complete oxidation that requires a flame or high temperature with excess O2; performed in the gas phase at temperatures above 500 °C, no solvent or catalyst.

Reaction type: free‑radical emulsion terpolymerization; purpose: produce acrylonitrile‑butadiene‑styrene (ABS) polymer; key transformation: persulfate initiator generates radicals that polymerize acrylonitrile, 1,3‑butadiene, and styrene within micelles stabilized by sodium lauryl sulfate; typical conditions: aqueous slurry with Na lauryl sulfate, 70‑85 °C, initiator (K₂S₂O₈) ~0.2 wt % of monomers, often under nitrogen; water is the medium, no organic solvent needed.

Sonogashira cross‑coupling of 4‑bromoanisole with acetylene using a palladium catalyst (often Pd(PPh3)2Cl2) together with CuI and a tertiary‑amine base (Et3N). Forms the aryl‑acetylene 4‑ethynylanisole by oxidative addition of the aryl bromide to Pd(0), transmetallation with the copper acetylide, and reductive elimination. Conducted under inert atmosphere at 50–80 °C in THF or DMF.

General type: aqueous hydrolysis of an amide. Purpose: convert the amide to the corresponding carboxylic acid and liberate ammonia. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon of 2‑bromoacetamide, followed by proton transfers to give bromoacetic acid and NH₃. Typical conditions: reflux in water or aqueous buffer, neutral to slightly acidic pH; reaction time 1–12 h. No special solvent beyond water; catalyst (acid or base) can be used to accelerate but is not required for the net conversion.

Halogen‑azide exchange (metathesis) between tributyltin chloride and trimethylsilyl azide. Produces trimethylsilyl chloride and tributyltin azide. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene at 0 °C to rt, without added catalyst, under nitrogen.

High‑temperature hydrogen reduction of niobium pentaiodide. Five equivalents of H2 reduce two equivalents of NbI5 to metallic niobium and generate hydrogen iodide gas. Carried out in a sealed tube or flow reactor at 500–800 °C under a stream of H2; no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (deoxygenative reduction) of 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol to isopentane. Hydrogen and the primary alcohol are passed over a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C or Pt at 100–200 °C and 30–50 atm H2. The C‑O bond is cleaved, yielding water and the corresponding alkane.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of pyrrole‑2‑carbonyl chloride with ammonia to give pyrrole‑2‑carboxamide. Reaction is typically carried out in a low‑temperature (0 °C to rt) organic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) with an excess of NH3 or in aqueous NH3; a base such as pyridine may be added to trap the liberated HCl.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of tert‑butyl acetate with aqueous NaOH. Under reflux in water or water/ethanol mixture, the ester is cleaved to tert‑butanol (2‑methyl‑2‑propanol) and sodium acetate. Reaction proceeds at 80–100 °C; neutralization after completion gives the free alcohol.

Double displacement/acid‑base reaction; lead(II) carbonate reacts with arsenious acid to form carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂ + H₂O) and lead arsenite precipitate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst, water as solvent.

Aromatic O‑demethylation with BBr₃: 4‑methoxypyridine reacts with boron tribromide to cleave the aryl‑OCH₃ bond, producing 4‑hydroxypyridine and methyl bromide. Conducted in dry CH₂Cl₂ at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen; after addition of BBr₃ the mixture is stirred, then quenched with methanol or water to release MeBr and afford the phenolic product.

Simple metathesis (double‑replacement) in water; magnesium formate exchanges anions with calcium chloride to give calcium formate and magnesium chloride; performed at room temperature in aqueous medium; no catalyst required.

Formation of a Grignard reagent (magnesium insertion); magnesium metal inserts into the C–Br bond of 2‑bromopyridine to generate 2‑pyridylmagnesium bromide; carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, under nitrogen or argon, often with a small amount of iodine or dibromoethane to activate Mg; reflux or gentle warming may be used.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification followed by salt formation (Fischer esterification); 4‑(butylamino)benzoic acid reacts with 2‑diethylaminoethanol in the presence of hydrochloric acid under microwave heating to produce the ester tetracaine, which is immediately protonated to tetracaine hydrochloride; typical conditions: excess alcohol, catalytic HCl, microwave or reflux, solvent often absent or methanol; product isolated as HCl salt.

Double‑replacement/precipitation reaction; arsenic acid reacts with barium chloride in aqueous solution, yielding insoluble barium arsenate precipitate and releasing hydrochloric acid into the solution; generally performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base (salt formation) reaction; combines ammonium fluoride with excess hydrofluoric acid to give ammonium bifluoride (NH4HF2), a useful etchant for glass and metal cleaning. Performed in aqueous solution, often at 0–25 °C to control HF evolution; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of sulfide to sulfone; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes 4,4′‑diaminodiphenyl sulfide to 4,4′‑diaminodiphenyl sulfone; commonly carried out in aqueous or mixed organic/aqueous solvent (e.g., acetonitrile/water) at 0–25 °C or under reflux, sometimes under acidic conditions (acetic acid); no metal catalyst is required, though tungstate or molybdate can be used to accelerate.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of primary amine to nitrile; benzylamine is oxidized by sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid, converting the –CH₂NH₂ group to a –C≡N group to give benzonitrile; reaction is performed under reflux in hot H₂SO₄, producing water, sodium sulfate and chromium(III) sulfate as by‑products; water‑free acidic medium is essential, no additional catalyst needed.

Direct combination oxidation of tin metal by oxygen to give tin(II) oxide; a synthesis (combustion) reaction performed by heating tin in air or oxygen at elevated temperatures (≈500‑600 °C); no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement precipitation; silver nitrate provides Ag⁺ which combines with sulfide from BaS to form black silver sulfide precipitate while barium nitrate remains dissolved; conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature, Ag₂S precipitates instantly and is filtered.

Acid‑base metathesis/precipitation where aqueous sulfuric acid reacts with lead(II) molybdate, producing insoluble lead(II) sulfate precipitate and soluble molybdic acid; carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst.

Ionic exchange (acid‑base) reaction between tetrafluoroboric acid and sodium perchlorate in aqueous solution, yielding perchloric acid and sodium tetrafluoroborate; typically performed at low to moderate temperature (0‑25 °C) in water; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation of potassium oxalate with magnesium chloride in water, forming precipitated magnesium oxalate and soluble potassium chloride; conducted at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst.

Organometallic alkylation (transmetallation) of indium(III) iodide with ethyl‑lithium to afford triethylindium and lithium iodide; performed in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C); no additional catalyst.

Acyl‑substitution esterification of 2,5‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride with methanol, producing methyl 2,5‑dichlorobenzoate and HCl; carried out in pyridine or with a base such as triethylamine to scavenge HCl, typically at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst required.

Conjugate (Michael) addition of cyanide to acrolein forming 3‑cyanopropanal, a β‑cyano aldehyde useful for further functionalization. Usually performed with NaCN or KCN (or HCN gas) in aqueous or alcoholic solution, often in the presence of a Lewis acid (ZnCl₂) or a phase‑transfer catalyst, at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of hexamethylenetetramine. The tetramine cage is cleaved in aqueous HCl to give formaldehyde and ammonium chloride. Used to generate formaldehyde in situ. Typically performed in water or aqueous HCl at ambient or reflux temperature; no special catalyst required.

Swern oxidation of codeine. Dimethyl sulfoxide is activated with oxalyl chloride at –78 °C, then triethylamine oxidizes the 6‑hydroxy group of codeine to a ketone, affording hydrocodone. Provides a mild, non‑metal oxidation that preserves sensitive functionalities. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane under inert atmosphere, low temperature, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Thermal solid‑state amidation (condensation). Benzoic acid and aniline are ground together and heated (≈200–250 °C) in the absence of solvent, allowing formation of benzanilide with loss of water. No catalyst is needed; high temperature drives the dehydration.

Formation of a Grignard reagent; magnesium turnings react with 1‑bromo‑2‑methoxyethane to afford 2‑methoxyethylmagnesium bromide. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at reflux or reflux‑temperature (≈ 70‑80 °C) under nitrogen or argon. Activation of Mg (e.g., iodine or a small amount of alkyl bromide) may be employed. Purpose is to generate an organomagnesium nucleophile for subsequent carbon‑carbon bond‑forming reactions.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling. Para‑chlorobenzoyl chloride, para‑chlorophenylboronic acid and CO undergo Pd(0)‑catalyzed CO insertion and transmetalation to give 4,4′‑dichlorobenzophenone. Typical conditions: Pd(PPh3)4 (≈5 mol %), base such as K2CO3, solvent dioxane or DMF, CO pressure 1–5 atm, temperature 80–120 °C.

Copper(II)‑mediated oxidation with tert‑butyl hydroperoxide. Cu(OAc)₂ catalyzes oxidation of 3‑methylcyclohexan‑1‑ol by TBHP, converting the secondary alcohol to the corresponding ketone while producing acetic acid and tert‑butanol as by‑products. Usually performed in acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to reflux, under ambient pressure.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction. Ammonium hydroxide reacts with mercuric sulfate to form soluble ammonium sulfate and insoluble mercury(II) hydroxide precipitate. Carried out in water at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Fischer esterification of salicylic acid with 2‑ethylhexanol to give 2‑ethylhexyl salicylate; purpose is to form a UV‑absorbing ester (sunscreen agent). Key transformation is condensation of a carboxylic acid and a primary alcohol with loss of water. Typical conditions: reflux in an inert organic solvent (toluene or xylene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) and removal of water by azeotropic distillation or Dean‑Stark trap.

Fischer esterification of tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol with acetic acid to afford tetrahydrofurfuryl acetate; used to protect the alcohol or to produce a flavor/fragrance ester. The reaction couples a carboxylic acid and a primary alcohol, eliminating water. Standard conditions: reflux in a solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane with a catalytic acid (typically sulfuric acid, p‑TsOH, or a solid acid resin) and removal of water by azeotropic distillation or using molecular sieves.

Acid–base reaction of triethylamine with phosphorus pentachloride producing triethylammonium chloride and phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃). This serves as a convenient method to generate POCl₃ in situ for subsequent chlorination or activation steps. The transformation involves nucleophilic attack of the amine on PCl₅, forming an ammonium salt and releasing POCl₃. Usually performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Jones oxidation (chromic acid oxidation) of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Purpose: convert 3‑phenylpropyl alcohol into 3‑phenylpropanoic acid. Key transformation: the CH₂OH group is oxidized first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid using Cr(VI). Typical conditions: CrO₃ (1.5 equiv) and concentrated H₂SO₄ are dissolved in acetone at 0 °C, the alcohol is added, and the mixture is stirred at room temperature for 1–2 h. The reaction is quenched with isopropanol or dilute acid, and the product is extracted.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; protonation of the carbonyl of 3‑methoxybenzamide followed by nucleophilic attack of water, yielding 3‑methoxybenzoic acid and ammonium bisulfate (NH₄HSO₄). Performed with concentrated H₂SO₄, heated (≈100–150 °C); water is the solvent or present as hydrate.

Acid‑base (double displacement) reaction; used to generate hydrofluoric acid from a fluoride salt. Calcium fluoride reacts with concentrated aqueous nitric acid to give calcium nitrate in solution and volatile hydrogen fluoride gas. Typical conditions: excess 68–70 % HNO₃, low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) to control HF evolution; aqueous medium.

Periodate oxidation of a primary alcohol: sodium periodate oxidizes 2,4‑dichlorobenzyl alcohol to 2,4‑dichlorobenzaldehyde while NaIO4 is reduced to NaIO3; reaction is done in a biphasic acetone/water or aqueous medium at 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric periodate, no additional catalyst.

Retro‑aldol / thermal decomposition of indole‑3‑carbinol; cleavage of the C‑C bond releases indole and formaldehyde. Key transformation: the benzylic C–C bond breaks, forming indole and gaseous formaldehyde. Typically induced by heating (≈150 °C) or by strong acid/base catalysis in a sealed vessel. No additional reagents are required; the reaction proceeds in the substrate itself.

Hydrolysis reaction; reversibly converts pyrazinamide and water to pyrazine-2-carboxylic acid and ammonia; amide bond cleavage under acidic or basic conditions; catalyzed by heat or enzymes in aqueous environment.

Salt formation (acid–base neutralization) of alprenolol with hydrochloric acid to give alprenolol hydrochloride. The purpose is to convert the free base into a pharmaceutically stable, water‑soluble salt. The primary transformation is protonation of the secondary amine of alprenolol. Conducted by dissolving alprenolol in a suitable solvent (e.g., ethanol, ethyl acetate, or isopropanol) and adding aqueous or gaseous HCl at 0 °C to room temperature; the salt precipitates upon evaporation of the solvent. No catalyst needed.

Strong‑base mediated dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination); converts a primary alkyl chloride to the corresponding terminal alkene. 1‑Chloropentane is treated with potassium tert‑butoxide in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or THF, typically at 50–80 °C, yielding 1‑pentene and KCl. The bulky base favors elimination over substitution.

Acid-carbonate reaction; generates RbI while releasing CO₂. Involves protonation of carbonate by HI, forming unstable carbonic acid which decomposes. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature.

Conversion of methacrylic acid to methacryloyl chloride using thionyl chloride; a classic acid‑chloride formation (chlorination) reaction. The key transformation replaces the hydroxyl of the carboxylic acid with a chloride, releasing gaseous HCl and SO₂. Typical conditions: reflux or gentle heating of methacrylic acid in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to accelerate the reaction; the gaseous by‑products are swept out. No additional solvent or catalyst beyond the solvent and optional DMF is required.

Cyclocondensation of ortho‑phenylenediamine with carbon disulfide in the presence of sodium hydroxide to generate 2‑mercaptobenzothiazole, with formation of water and sodium carbonate as by‑products. This reaction introduces a thiazole ring and a mercapto substituent, useful in rubber vulcanization accelerators. Carried out in aqueous NaOH solution, heated (typically 80–120 °C) to promote the formation of the dithiocarbamate intermediate, which then cyclizes. After completion the mixture is acidified, and the product is isolated by filtration or extraction. No special catalyst is required.

Redox fluorination where elemental fluorine oxidizes bromic acid (HBrO3) to perbromic acid (HBrO4) while being reduced to hydrogen fluoride; performed in the gas phase or inert solvent at low temperature, often in fluorinated media.

Acid‑base (salt metathesis) reaction: hydrochloric acid protonates ammonium phosphomolybdate, displacing ammonium chloride and forming phosphomolybdic acid. Carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with mild heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification): 2-(acryloyloxy)ethyl methacrylate reacts with water to give acrylic acid and 2‑hydroxyethyl methacrylate. Typically performed under acidic (e.g., 1 M HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions, with heating (50‑80 °C) in aqueous medium; the acid or base acts as catalyst, no additional reagents required.

Catalytic oxidative hydroxylation of 3,4‑dichlorobenzene to 3,4‑dichlorophenol using molecular oxygen in the presence of sodium hydroxide. This oxidative aromatic substitution inserts an OH group onto the ring, replacing a hydrogen atom. Typical conditions involve aqueous NaOH, elevated O₂ pressure, a copper or other transition‑metal catalyst, and temperatures of 150‑200 °C in an autoclave; water is the solvent.

Quaternization of tri‑n‑butylamine with iodomethane to form methyltributylammonium iodide, a quaternary ammonium salt. The reaction proceeds via SN2 under reflux or at rt in a polar solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or neat iodomethane); no catalyst is required.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (elimination): calcium hydroxide reacts with 1,1,1‑trichloroethane to produce 1,1‑dichloroethene, water and calcium chloride. Conducted as a dry distillation or reflux with solid Ca(OH)2 at 200‑250 °C; the solid base serves both as dehydrohalogenating agent and chloride scavenger, no additional catalyst required.

Halide metathesis (ion exchange); used to generate tetramethylammonium fluoride as a soluble fluoride source. The chloride anion of tetramethylammonium chloride exchanges with fluoride from silver fluoride, precipitating insoluble AgCl. Typically carried out in water or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at room temperature; the mixture is filtered to remove AgCl, yielding tetramethylammonium fluoride in solution.

Catalytic reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an amine; nickel(II) chloride activates sodium borohydride for transfer hydrogenation of 2,3-dimethyl nitrobenzene to 2,3-dimethylaniline. Reaction proceeds via hydride delivery to the nitro group, forming nitroso, hydroxylamino, and finally amine intermediates. Commonly performed in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to reflux, with catalytic amounts of NiCl₂ (often generated in situ from NiCl₂·6H₂O) and portionwise addition of NaBH₄ under inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a cis‑butene‑1,4‑diol using Raney nickel; H₂ adds across the C=C bond converting the unsaturated diol to 1,4‑butanediol; carried out under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 50–100 °C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or water.

Acid-catalyzed protolysis of a metal alkoxide; zirconium tetrapropoxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to give zirconium sulfate and propanol. The strong acid protonates the alkoxide ligands, liberating n‑propyl alcohol and forming the inorganic salt. Typically run in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (20–60 °C) with excess H₂SO₄ to drive complete conversion; no additional catalyst required.

Benzylic chloride hydrolysis (SN1 substitution); diphenylmethyl chloride reacts with water to form diphenylmethanol. The tertiary benzylic carbocation is generated in the aqueous medium and captured by a water molecule, followed by deprotonation to give the alcohol. Usually performed in a mixed water/acetone or water/ethanol solvent at reflux or under mild heating; acid or base can be added to accelerate the rate, but simple aqueous conditions are sufficient.

Transesterification (carbonate exchange); glycerol reacts with diphenyl carbonate to afford glycerol carbonate (a five‑membered cyclic carbonate) and phenol as the by‑product. The primary hydroxyl of glycerol attacks the carbonyl carbon of the carbonate, displacing phenoxide which abstracts a proton to give phenol. Conducted at 120–150 °C under reduced pressure or continuous removal of phenol to shift equilibrium, often with a basic catalyst such as zinc acetate, potassium carbonate, or an organometallic catalyst; glycerol itself serves as the reaction medium.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction); peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to hept‑2‑ene, converting the C=C double bond into a 2,3‑epoxyheptane epoxide and generating acetic acid as a by‑product. The reaction proceeds via a concerted pericyclic mechanism forming a three‑membered oxirane ring. Conducted in an inert, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0–25 °C to control exotherm; stoichiometric peracetic acid is used, and no metal catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed Knoevenagel condensation; purpose is to create the α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde 4‑(dimethylamino)cinnamaldehyde from 4‑(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde and acetaldehyde; key transformation is formation of a C=C double bond between the carbonyl carbon of the benzaldehyde and the α‑carbon of acetaldehyde with loss of water; typically performed in ethanol as solvent with catalytic piperidine (a secondary amine) at reflux (≈60–80 °C) under inert atmosphere.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) precipitation; dysprosium(III) chloride reacts with ammonium dihydrogen phosphate in aqueous solution to produce dysprosium(III) phosphate precipitate and ammonium chloride in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature or with slight warming; water is the reaction medium. No catalyst is needed; the product is collected by filtration and washed.

Metal‑mediated reduction (single‑electron transfer) of ZrCl4 by magnesium; purpose is to generate low‑valent zirconium(II) chloride; key transformation is transfer of two electrons from Mg to ZrCl4, yielding ZrCl2 and MgCl2; commonly carried out by heating a mixture of dry Mg turnings and ZrCl4 in anhydrous ether or THF under nitrogen or argon, often with gentle reflux; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aromatic amine to a nitro group using potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid; purpose is to replace the –NH2 substituent with –NO2 on the benzene ring. Key transformation: the aniline moiety is oxidized to a nitro group, while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) forming chromium(III) sulfate. Typical conditions: concentrated H2SO4 as solvent, K2Cr2O7 (1–1.5 equiv), temperature 50–100 °C under stirring; reaction is acid‑catalyzed and generates water as a by‑product.

Acid‑base proton transfer (neutralization) between phenol and sodium t‑butoxide; purpose is to form the phenoxide salt and regenerate t‑butanol; key transformation is deprotonation of phenol by the strong t‑butoxide base, producing NaOPh and t‑BuOH; performed at ambient temperature in aprotic polar solvents such as THF, DMF or MeCN; no catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution at sulfur (SuFEx chemistry) of a sulfamoyl fluoride with NaOMe; purpose is to prepare methyl sulfamate; key transformation is replacement of the fluorine atom on the sulfonyl fluoride group by a methoxy group, giving CH3OSO2NH2 and NaF; usually conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or DMF) at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction); peracetic acid adds an oxygen across the C=C of but‑2‑ene to form 2,3‑epoxybutane; carried out at 0‑25 °C in a non‑polar organic solvent such as dichloromethane, using a slight excess of peracetic acid.

Alkaline hydrolysis/oxidation of selenium disulfide with aqueous NaOH; purpose is to convert SeS2 into sulfide and selenite ions; key transformations include cleavage of Se–S bonds and oxidation of selenium to selenite while sulfur is reduced to sulfide, with water formed as a by‑product; performed in excess aqueous NaOH (typically 6 mol NaOH per mol SeS2) under heating (50–80 °C); reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Catalytic reductive amination of phenylacetaldehyde with pyrrolidine using hydrogen and Raney nickel; purpose is to synthesize the secondary amine 1‑(2‑phenylethyl)pyrrolidine; key transformations are condensation of the aldehyde with pyrrolidine to form an imine, followed by hydrogenation of the imine to the amine, releasing water; carried out in a protic solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–80 °C with Raney Ni as the heterogeneous catalyst; water is the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Sonogashira coupling (Pd‑catalyzed C‑C bond formation); replaces the iodine on a nucleoside with a terminal alkyne to give an ethynyl‑substituted deoxyuridine; typically performed with Pd(0) (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4) and CuI as co‑catalyst, a tertiary amine base (triethylamine or diisopropylethylamine) in THF or DMF under inert atmosphere at 50‑80 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; cleaves the C–N bond of 4‑chlorobenzamide to afford 4‑chlorobenzoic acid and ammonium chloride; carried out by refluxing the amide in aqueous HCl (6 M or conc.) for several hours, often in water or dilute HCl as solvent.

Acid–base neutralization (salt hydrolysis) of pyridine·HCl with potassium hydroxide; deprotonates the pyridinium ion to liberate free pyridine while forming potassium chloride and water; usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; simple stoichiometric mix of solid base and pyridinium salt.

Maillard-type condensation; thermal reaction of a reducing sugar (glucose) with an amino acid (lysine) that generates a heterocyclic pyrazine flavor compound. Key transformation: dehydration cyclization of sugar‐derived carbonyls with lysine’s ε‑amino group to form 2‑methylpyrazine plus water. Typical conditions: heating 120–180 °C under dry or low‑moisture conditions, often in the solid state or in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., DMSO); no added catalyst required, though mild acidity can accelerate.

Acidic hydrolysis of an isocyanate; phenyl isocyanate reacts with aqueous hydrobromic acid, water adds across the N=C=O group, releasing CO₂ and generating aniline which is protonated to anilinium bromide; conducted by heating the mixture in concentrated HBr (often 48 % aq.) at reflux.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; thallium(I) sulfate exchanges anions with barium bromide, precipitating insoluble barium sulfate and forming soluble thallium bromide; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Metallothermic reduction; sodium metal reduces V(II) chloride to elemental vanadium, forming NaCl. Key transformation: VCl2 → V (metal), Na → NaCl. Usually carried out in molten Na or in sealed ampoule at 400–600 °C under inert atmosphere; anhydrous conditions are essential, no solvent.

Acid–base displacement (proton transfer) reaction; employed for preparation of ammonium nitrate and HCl gas. Key transformation: nitric acid protonates NH4Cl, yielding NH4NO3 and HCl. Conducted in aqueous solution with cold (0‑5 °C) concentrated HNO3 to limit side reactions; reaction mixture is often diluted with water; no catalyst needed.
