Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; concentrated nitric acid oxidizes selenium dioxide to selenic acid while nitrogen dioxide gas is liberated; typically carried out by adding SeO₂ to hot conc. HNO₃, often under reflux, with careful gas handling for NO₂.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation); the alkoxide derived from 2‑methylpropan‑1‑ol attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide to give 1‑methoxy‑2‑methylpropane and sodium iodide; reaction is run in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to rt, without additional catalyst.

Metathesis/acid–base exchange converting scandium nitrate to scandium triflate while generating nitric acid; typically performed in aqueous or non‑aqueous solvent at ambient to mild temperature, no catalyst required.

Phosgenation of 2,2,2‑trichloroethanol to give the corresponding carbonate ester; a carbonyl chloride (phosgene) reacts with two equivalents of alcohol forming 2,2,2‑trichloroethyl carbonate and releasing HCl; carried out in dry inert solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0–5 °C to room temperature, often with a base (triethylamine) to absorb HCl.

Redox reaction of praseodymium metal with acetic acid; the metal is oxidized to Pr(III) acetate while acetic acid is reduced, liberating H₂ gas; performed in glacial acetic acid as both reagent and solvent, reflux under inert atmosphere; no catalyst.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative hydroxylation of 4‑tert‑butylphenol using H₂O₂ in basic aqueous medium; Cu(II) sulfate activates hydrogen peroxide (Fenton‑like) to generate •OH radicals, converting the phenol to 4‑tert‑butylcatechol (1,2‑diol) with water as by‑product; performed at ambient temperature, pH≈10, water as solvent.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification between ethanol and 2‑ethoxyethyl acetate; ethanol attacks the acetate carbonyl, swapping alkoxy groups to produce 2‑ethoxyethanol and ethyl acetate; typically run with catalytic NaOEt or acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) under reflux, using excess ethanol as solvent.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) forming thulium(III) oxalate from thulium sulfate and ammonium oxalate; the insoluble thulium oxalate precipitates while ammonium sulfate remains in solution; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst.

Esterification of propargyl alcohol with acetyl chloride producing propargyl acetate; HCl is liberated as by‑product. Conducted in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) at 0 °C to room temperature, using a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; useful for synthesizing alkynyl esters or protecting the alcohol.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of dimethyl phthalate with 2‑ethylhexanol to afford di(2‑ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) and methanol. Performed neat or with excess 2‑ethylhexanol at 180–220 °C in the presence of a solid acid resin (e.g., sulfonated polystyrene); methanol is continuously removed to drive the equilibrium. Provides the commercial plasticizer DEHP.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of barium silicate (BaSiO3) from barium carbonate and silica. Mixed powders are heated above ~1000 °C in air; CO2 evolves, leaving the ceramic BaSiO3. No solvent or catalyst required; employed in ceramic and refractory material production.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of cyclohexyl methanesulfonate with sulfide ion to give cyclohexyl thiol and sodium methanesulfonate. Typically carried out in aqueous or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO) at 50–80 °C; sulfide anion acts as nucleophile. Provides a method for thiol preparation from alkyl sulfonates.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; the purpose is to exchange anions and cations to form silver sulfate and potassium nitrate. Key transformation: Ag⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to give Ag₂SO₄, while K⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to give KNO₃. Typically carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of AgNO₃ and K₂SO₄ at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of N‑methoxyacetamide to acetic acid and methoxyamine. Conducted in water under acidic (e.g., 1 M HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions, heating to 80–120 °C. Cleavage of the amide bond releases the carboxylic acid and the O‑methoxy hydroxylamine; useful for generating methoxyamine as a nucleophilic reagent.

Nucleophilic substitution of 3‑chloro‑1‑butene with cyanide ion to yield 3‑cyanobut‑1‑ene and sodium chloride. Performed in aqueous or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., water/acetone) at ambient to reflux temperature; NaCN supplies CN⁻ as nucleophile. Generates an allylic nitrile useful for further functionalization.

Transesterification reaction; swaps the alkoxy groups of methanol and ethyl acrylate to give ethanol and methyl acrylate. Typically acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOEt) catalyzed; carried out under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene or methanol itself, with removal of the volatile ethanol to drive equilibrium forward.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; sodium sulfate reacts with praseodymium(III) chloride in aqueous solution to form insoluble calcium‑like? (actually praseodymium(III) sulfate) and soluble sodium chloride. Conducted in water at ambient or mildly elevated temperature with stirring; the solid Pr2(SO4)3 precipitates and is isolated by filtration.

Alkali‑mediated elimination with lithium hydroxide; aqueous LiOH (≈1 M) heated to 60–80 °C removes HCl from 1‑chloro‑1,1‑difluoroethane, affording 1,1‑difluoroethene, lithium chloride and water. The reaction is performed in water or water/acetone mixture under stirring.

Grignard acyl substitution with acetic anhydride; one equivalent of ethylmagnesium bromide attacks an anhydride carbonyl, displaces acetate and forms a magnesium alkoxide that on workup affords 2‑butanone; the expelled acetate gives acetic acid and MgBr₂. Performed in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen.

Oxidation of 5‑(hydroxymethyl)furfural to 5‑(hydroxymethyl)furan‑2‑carboxylic acid (HMFCA): hydrogen peroxide acts as the oxidant, converting the aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid while leaving the primary alcohol intact. The reaction is typically catalyzed by a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Fe, Mn, or heteropolyacid) in water or aqueous organic solvent, at ambient to 60 °C, often under mildly acidic to neutral pH.

Double displacement precipitation; used to synthesize lead azide, a primary explosive. Aqueous solutions of potassium azide and lead nitrate are mixed, leading to precipitation of insoluble lead azide while potassium nitrate remains in solution. Typically performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using silver(I) oxide as the oxidant; 2‑ethoxybenzaldehyde is converted to 2‑ethoxybenzoic acid while elemental silver precipitates. Usually performed in a basic aqueous medium (e.g., NaOH) at reflux; the reaction proceeds with gradual addition of Ag2O and filtration to remove silver.

Acid‑base neutralization and salt metathesis; sulfuric acid reacts with calcium acetate in water to produce acetic acid (distilled off) and insoluble calcium sulfate precipitate. The mixture is heated to facilitate acetic acid evolution; the CaSO4 solid is filtered and washed.

Copper‑catalyzed Kumada cross‑coupling (Negishi‑type) of the bromide with phenylmagnesium bromide; CuI (5–10 mol %) mediates transmetallation in THF or Et₂O at 0–25 °C, affording 1‑phenyl‑2,3‑dihydro‑1H‑indene after aqueous work‑up.

Sandmeyer cyanation (diazotization‑cyanation): Aniline (m‑chloro) is treated with NaNO2 and HCl at 0–5 °C to form the diazonium salt, which is displaced by CuCN, yielding m‑chlorobenzonitrile. Acidic aqueous medium; CuCN added at low temperature; water as solvent.

Electrophilic α‑bromination of a ketone under acidic conditions; 2‑butanone reacts with molecular bromine in the presence of a mild acid (often acetic acid or HBr) to give 3‑bromo‑2‑butanone. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature, typically in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane, and quenched with water after completion.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation/cyclization to form xanthone; phthalic anhydride and diphenyl ether undergo acyl transfer in the presence of anhydrous aluminum chloride, yielding xanthone (9H‑xanthen‑9‑one) and HCl as a by‑product. Performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent like nitrobenzene or dichloromethane at low temperature, then warmed to reflux; the mixture is worked up with aqueous acid to remove AlCl3 and isolate the crystalline product.

Gas‑phase chlorination of boron carbide; high‑temperature reaction of solid B4C with Cl2 to produce volatile carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) and boron trichloride (BCl3). Purpose: conversion of B4C to gaseous chlorides for analysis or purification. Key transformation: substitution of B–C bonds by B–Cl and C–Cl bonds. Typical conditions: dry Cl2 flow over B4C at 400–600 °C, often under nitrogen or argon carrier gas. No solvent; catalyst generally not required.

Acid–base/precipitation reaction; dysprosium(III) oxide reacts with aqueous phosphoric acid to form dysprosium(III) phosphate as an insoluble solid and water. Usually performed by heating the oxide in dilute H3PO4 (often 1–5 M) under reflux; the mixture is then cooled, and the phosphate precipitate is filtered and washed. No special catalyst is needed; water is the solvent.

Enzymatic hydrolysis (arginase‑catalyzed) of homoarginine in water to yield homocitrulline and urea. The reaction cleaves the guanidino C‑N bond, producing urea as a by‑product. Performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑9) at ~37 °C with Mg²⁺ as a cofactor; the medium is purely aqueous.
Acid–base neutralization; solid or suspended Cr(OH)3 dissolves in aqueous HCl to give CrCl3 and water. Typically done in dilute HCl solution, often with mild heating to aid dissolution; no catalyst.

Acid‑base salt metathesis; protonation of ammonium nitrite by HCl produces nitrous acid (HNO2) and ammonium chloride. Purpose: in‑situ generation of HNO2 for diazotisation or other nitrosation reactions. Key transformation: exchange of anions (Cl⁻ for NO2⁻). Conditions: aqueous solution, 0–5 °C to minimise decomposition of HNO2, often in dilute HCl (1 M). No special catalyst.

Acid leaching/oxidative decomposition of barium niobate with concentrated nitric acid. Purpose: to dissolve the solid and isolate niobium as Nb2O5 while converting Ba to soluble Ba(NO3)2. Key transformation: protonation and oxidation of the niobate lattice, releasing water and forming Ba(NO3)2 and Nb2O5. Conditions: reflux of BaNb2O5 (or related stoichiometry) in concentrated HNO3 (≈ 68 %) at 80–120 °C for several hours. No catalyst; water acts as solvent.

Oxidative digestion of silicon carbide with hot concentrated nitric acid. Purpose: to oxidize SiC to SiO2 and CO2 while reducing nitrate to nitrogen dioxide. Key transformation: oxidation of carbon to CO2 and silicon to SiO2, coupled with reduction of HNO3 to NO2. Conditions: excess conc. HNO3 (≈ 68 %) heated to 150–180 °C, often in a sealed Teflon vessel; reaction proceeds vigorously with evolution of gases. No catalyst; water from acid serves as medium.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 3‑fluoropropyl azide to 3‑fluoropropan‑1‑amine with release of N2. Purpose: preparation of primary amine from azide precursor. Key transformation: reduction of the azide functional group (–N3) to –NH2, nitrogen gas as by‑product. Conditions: H2 pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5 % on carbon) or Raney Ni catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Acid‑catalyzed ether hydrolysis; water attacks the diethylene glycol monopropyl ether cleaving the C–O bond to give diethylene glycol and 1‑propanol; typically performed by refluxing the ether in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 5–10 % H₂SO₄) or strong base; water is both reactant and solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization of a carbonate; oxalic acid protonates rubidium carbonate, producing carbon dioxide gas, water, and rubidium oxalate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Oxidation–redox reaction; hot concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes phosphorous acid to phosphoric acid while being reduced to sulfur dioxide gas; transformation: H3PO3 → H3PO4 and H2SO4 → SO2 + H2O; performed by heating a mixture of phosphorous acid and concentrated H2SO4 (≈150‑200 °C); reaction conducted in a sealed or vented tube; no solvent besides the sulfuric acid itself.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl bromide by isopropylamine to give N‑isopropylbenzylamine and hydrobromic acid (often neutralized by excess amine). Forms a new C‑N bond while breaking the C‑Br bond. Conducted in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to reflux; no additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis/oxidation of a metal dichalcogenide; water reacts with germanium diselenide to generate volatile hydrogen selenide and insoluble germanium dioxide; performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., dilute HCl) under reflux; gas evolved is captured in a basic trap; no catalyst needed.

Reverse water‑gas shift reaction: CO₂ is reduced by H₂ to give CO and H₂O. Provides CO for synthesis gas streams. Conducted in the gas phase at 600‑1000 °C, commonly over metal oxides (Cu/ZnO, Fe‑Cr, Ni) as catalysts; no solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a difluoro‑acetylene; H₂ adds across the C≡C triple bond to give 1,1‑difluoroethane; requires a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni) at 1–5 atm H₂ and temperatures 25–80 °C; solvent often methanol or ethanol.

Peracid oxidation (oxidative transformation); peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the azo bond of azobenzene, forming azoxybenzene and acetic acid; reaction is usually performed in a non‑protic solvent like dichloromethane or chloroform at 0–5 °C to avoid over‑oxidation; stoichiometric amount of peracetic acid is used, and the mixture is often kept mildly acidic.

N‑methylation of serotonin via phase‑transfer catalysis; methyl chloride reacts with the primary amine of serotonin in the presence of a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) and aqueous base, yielding N‑methylserotonin and HCl; performed in a biphasic system (water/CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) at 0–25 °C; base (NaOH or K₂CO₃) neutralizes the generated HCl.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of an N‑chloroamino acid; 2‑(chloroamino)acetic acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give glycine, sodium hypochlorite and water; carried out in water at 0–25 °C, typically under stirring, no catalyst required.

Oxidative fluorination (redox) of titanium(III) fluoride to the higher oxidation state; TiF3 + ½ F2 → TiF4; used to obtain titanium(IV) fluoride; carried out by passing fluorine gas over TiF3 solid at 200–300 °C, often in a flowing inert carrier gas (Ar); no solvent; reaction may be performed in fluorine‑compatible reactors, no additional catalyst.

Chlorination (halogenation) of isocyanuric acid to form trichloroisocyanuric acid; purpose is to install three chlorine atoms on the triazine ring, generating a strong oxidizing/bleaching agent while releasing HCl. Typically carried out by bubbling Cl₂ gas through a suspension of isocyanuric acid in water or glacial acetic acid at 0–25 °C; excess chlorine is vented, and the product precipitates upon cooling. No catalyst required; aqueous or acidic medium is common.

Acid‑base salt formation converting hydrazoic acid into caesium azide; the two equivalents of HN₃ neutralize caesium oxide, yielding CsN₃ and water. Performed under strictly anhydrous, low‑temperature conditions (0–5 °C) in a dry, inert solvent such as dry ethanol, methanol, or liquid ammonia to avoid explosive decomposition. No additional catalyst is used; the reaction is driven by stoichiometric neutralization.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of methyl 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxycinnamate (an ester) to the corresponding cinnamic acid and methanol. The transformation cleaves the ester C–O bond, converting the methyl ester into a carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in a mixture of water with a small amount of ethanol or methanol, using 1 M HCl (acidic hydrolysis) or NaOH (basic saponification) followed by acidification to isolate the free acid. No special catalyst beyond the acid/base is required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between hydrobromic acid and barium nitrate, producing soluble barium bromide and nitric acid. The purpose is the exchange of anions, often used to generate HNO₃ in situ. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; both reactants are dissolved, and the products remain in solution. No catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide with hydrogen sulfide (or HS⁻) to afford 2‑mercaptoethanol. Reaction carried out in aqueous basic medium (NaOH or KOH) to generate HS⁻, at 50‑100 °C, usually in water or water/ethanol solvent.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification between ethanol and isoamyl acetate, swapping alkoxy groups to give ethyl acetate and isoamyl alcohol. Used to modify ester profiles or recover alcohols. Typical conditions: reflux in excess ethanol with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid (≈1 % w/w) or sodium methoxide; removal of the more volatile product (ethyl acetate) drives the equilibrium. Solvent can be the reactants themselves; no metal catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑nitronaphthalene to 2‑naphthylamine; the nitro group is reduced to an amine while the aromatic ring remains intact. Conducted under hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) with 5–10 % palladium on carbon (Pd/C) as the catalyst, in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at 25–60 °C. The reaction provides a straightforward route to aromatic amines from nitro precursors.

Hydrolysis of an alkoxysilane; converts diphenyl dimethoxysilane to diphenylsilanediol while releasing methanol. Typically acid- or base‑catalyzed in aqueous media (e.g., dilute HCl or NaOH) at ambient to reflux temperature. Common solvents: THF, methanol, or water‑toluene mixtures.

Oxidative cleavage of a glycol ether using hot acidic potassium permanganate; breaks the C–C bonds adjacent to oxygen to give butoxyacetic acid, carbon dioxide, water and MnO2 precipitate. Conducted in aqueous H2SO4 with excess KMnO4, heated to reflux. No additional catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative cross‑coupling (carbonylation) of 3‑iodopyridine with methylmagnesium bromide in the presence of CO. Forms 3‑acetylpyridine via insertion of CO between the aryl‑Pd bond and the methyl nucleophile. Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)2 (5 mol %), PPh3 (10–20 mol %), CO pressure 1–5 atm, THF solvent, 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere.

SN2 cyanation of methyl iodide with trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN). Nucleophilic attack of the cyanide (from TMSCN) on the methyl carbon yields acetonitrile and trimethylsilyl iodide as by‑product. Performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base double‑displacement precipitation; cobalt(II) chloride reacts with oxalic acid in aqueous solution, forming cobalt(II) oxalate precipitate and releasing hydrochloric acid into the medium. Conducted at room temperature or with mild heating; the cobalt oxalate is collected by filtration.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl 2‑phenyl‑2‑(piperidin‑2‑yl)acetate with ethanol to give the corresponding ethyl ester and methanol. Usually reflux in excess ethanol with catalytic H2SO4, p‑TsOH, or NaOEt; removal of methanol (e.g., Dean‑Stark) drives the equilibrium.

Alkylation (SN2) of a secondary amine with a primary alkyl halide to form a tertiary amine; purpose is to increase basicity and steric bulk. The nucleophilic nitrogen attacks the electrophilic carbon of 1‑iodobutane, displacing iodide and yielding tributylamine and HI. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dimethylformamide at reflux; a base (e.g., NaHCO₃ or triethylamine) is often added to scavenge the generated HI.

Acid‑catalyzed ring‑opening hydrolysis; purpose is to produce ethylene glycol from ethylene oxide; the protonated ethylene oxide is attacked by water, yielding ethylene glycol; typically carried out in aqueous sulfuric acid (10–20 % H₂SO₄) at 50–100 °C under reflux; water is the solvent and the acid acts as both catalyst and source of protons.

Oxidative conversion of alkyl substituents to carboxylic acids; purpose is to transform 3,5‑dimethylpyridine into 3,5‑pyridinedicarboxylic acid; KMnO₄ oxidizes each methyl group to a carboxylate, producing MnO₂ precipitate and KOH; generally performed in aqueous solution with excess KMnO₄, heated to reflux (80–100 °C) until the purple color disappears; water is the solvent; the reaction is carried out under neutral to basic pH.

E2 elimination (base‑induced dehydrohalogenation); purpose: synthesize the alkene cyclohexene from the bromide; key transformation: potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen while Br− leaves, forming the C=C bond, and generating KBr and tert‑butanol; typical conditions: excess KOtBu in tert‑butanol or THF, reflux or 50–80 °C; no additional catalyst.

Reduction of a secondary alkyl bromide to an alcohol with LiAlH4; LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbon bearing bromine, replacing Br with H and giving 1‑propanol; carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, usually reflux.

Double displacement (acid-base reaction). Converts chromium(III) oxide to chromium(III) chloride in an acidic environment. Hydrochloric acid acts as the proton donor. Reaction occurs in aqueous solution under heating to accelerate dissolution. Water is a byproduct.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; converts soluble lead(II) acetate and sulfuric acid in aqueous solution into insoluble lead(II) sulfate precipitate and acetic acid; typically performed by mixing aqueous solutions at room temperature, water as solvent, filtration to isolate PbSO4.

Halide metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation; purpose is to exchange bromide for fluoride to obtain holmium fluoride; HoBr₃ reacts with KF yielding insoluble HoF₃ (or HoF) and soluble KBr; usually conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent; the solid HoFₓ precipitates and is filtered off.

Double‑displacement/base‑addition precipitation; used to prepare holmium(III) hydroxide; NH₄OH provides OH⁻ which replaces Cl⁻, yielding solid Ho(OH)₃ and soluble NH₄Cl; reaction carried out by adding aqueous ammonium hydroxide dropwise to a holmium chloride solution, maintaining pH around 8–9, with stirring at ambient temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ester; purpose is to saturate the C=C bond while leaving the ester unchanged. The reaction reduces the C=C of tert‑butyl (E)-but‑2‑enoate to give tert‑butyl butanoate. Typical conditions are H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, at 25–80 °C.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; purpose is to install a tert‑butyl group onto benzene to give tert‑butylbenzene; isobutylene forms a tert‑butyl carbocation in the presence of AlCl₃, which then attacks the aromatic ring; performed under anhydrous conditions, typically in a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, at 0–50 °C; AlCl₃ is the Lewis‑acid catalyst, and the reaction is quenched with ice‑water work‑up.

Ester reduction with lithium aluminium hydride: ethyl (E)‑2‑methylbut‑2‑enoate is reduced to the allylic alcohol 3‑methylbut‑2‑en‑1‑ol (ethanol is liberated from the ethoxy group). LAH delivers a hydride to the carbonyl, converting the ester to a primary alcohol. Typical conditions: 1 equiv LAH (70 % in mineral oil) added portionwise to a solution of the ester in dry diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C, then stirred at rt for 2–4 h. Reaction is quenched carefully with water, then dilute acid. No catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); purpose is to convert dimethylamine into N,N‑dimethylacetamide using acetyl nitrate as the acyl donor; the amine attacks the carbonyl of acetyl nitrate, displacing nitrate to give the amide and releasing nitric acid; usually carried out at 0–25 °C in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; the reaction is moisture‑sensitive and may require a base to neutralize the generated HNO₃.

Acidification of sodium pertechnetate with sulfuric acid; an acid‑base conversion yielding pertechnetic acid (HTcO4) and sodium sulfate; carried out in aqueous medium, often with concentrated H2SO4 and mild heating; no catalyst required.

Oxidative fluorination of silica; purpose is to produce silicon tetrafluoride gas and release oxygen; oxygen difluoride (OF₂) fluoridates SiO₂, reducing the oxygen to O₂ while forming volatile SiF₄; the reaction is highly exothermic and is performed at temperatures (often >200 °C) in a flow of OF₂ gas over quartz or powdered silica; no solvent is used; the gaseous products are collected downstream.

Base‑induced deprotonation of 2‑aminoethanol hydrobromide with sodium hydroxide, producing free 2‑aminoethanol, sodium bromide and water; aqueous medium, ambient temperature; common method for liberating the amine from its bromide salt.

Potassium‑metal reduction; similar to the lithium route, Nd2O3 is reduced by molten potassium to give neodymium metal and K2O. Carried out at elevated temperature (≈350–450 °C) in a dry, inert environment; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidative roasting of nickel sulfide; purpose is to convert sulfide ore to a metal oxide and release sulfur as SO₂ for further processing; O₂ oxidizes Ni₃S₂ to NiO while S is oxidized to SO₂; typically carried out at 600–900 °C in a flowing stream of air or pure O₂; no solvent, catalyst not required.

Oxidation of triphenylphosphine to triphenylphosphine oxide; used to generate the phosphine oxide or to detoxify phosphine reagents; hypofluorous acid transfers an O atom to PPh₃ forming Ph₃P=O and HF; conventionally performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or CHCl₃ at 0 °C to rt; no catalyst needed, reaction is stoichiometric.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑chloro‑1‑ethoxyethane by hydroxide; purpose is to synthesize 2‑ethoxyethanol from the corresponding halide; OH⁻ displaces Cl⁻ giving the alcohol and NaCl; carried out in aqueous NaOH solution, usually at ambient temperature or gentle heating; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Conversion of succinic acid to succinyl chloride using oxalyl chloride; a common method to prepare acid chlorides for further acylation chemistry; oxalyl chloride reacts with the di‑carboxylic acid, releasing CO₂, CO and HCl while forming the mono‑acid chloride; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform under reflux; a catalytic amount of DMF or pyridine is often added to accelerate the reaction and scavenge HCl.

Base‑catalyated transesterification of propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate with sodium methoxide; purpose is to exchange the acetoxy group for a methoxy group, yielding methyl acetate and propylene glycol monomethyl ether; NaOMe attacks the carbonyl, forming the new ester and releasing the alcohol; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or methanol at reflux; sodium methoxide serves as both nucleophile and catalyst.

Synthesis (direct combination) reaction. Fluorine gas reacts with magnesium metal to form magnesium fluoride (MgF2). Magnesium is oxidized to Mg2+ and fluorine is reduced to F−, producing a white solid. The reaction is conducted in anhydrous, fluorine‑compatible equipment (e.g., nickel tubes) at moderate temperatures (often 200–400 °C) to ensure complete conversion. No solvent is required; the MgF2 product is collected as a powder and can be washed with dry HF if necessary.

Metal‑alcohol acid–base reaction forming sodium propoxide and hydrogen gas; used to generate alkoxide reagents for later synthesis; sodium metal inserts into the O–H bond of propanol, producing NaOPr and H₂; performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry ether or THF, often with gentle heating; no additional catalyst; hydrogen is evolved as a gas.

Ester hydrolysis of methyl 2-(hydroxyamino)acetate to 2-(hydroxyamino)acetic acid, producing methanol; typically carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., dilute HCl) at reflux, often using water or a water/ethanol mixture as solvent.

Acidic redox oxidation of hydroxylamine sulfate by potassium permanganate, generating nitrogen gas, water, potassium sulfate and manganese(II) sulfate; performed in dilute H₂SO₄ at elevated temperature with no additional catalyst.

Condensation/cyclization of 2‑aminobiphenyl with glyoxal in the presence of ammonium acetate to afford acridine via multiple Schiff‑base formations and intramolecular aromatic ring closure; usually conducted in glacial acetic acid under reflux, with ammonium acetate serving as a nitrogen source and buffer.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of the ester, generating methyl acetate and liberating 2‑fluoroethanol; methanol acts as both reactant and solvent, protonation of the carbonyl facilitates nucleophilic attack by methanol, forming methyl acetate and the fluorinated alcohol; commonly carried out with 5–10 % mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or HCl) at reflux (~65 °C) for 1–4 h; solvent: excess methanol.

Type: free‑radical halogenation (substitution) using bromine; Purpose: form a bromo‑isobutane derivative; Key transformation: (CH₃)₂CH‑CH₃ + Br₂ → (CH₃)₂CH‑CH₂Br + HBr; Typical conditions: UV irradiation or gentle heating, inert solvent (e.g., typical solvent CCl₄ or C₆H₆); No catalyst.

Double‑displacement/precipitation (acid‑base metathesis); calcium hydroxide reacts with ammonium valerate to form sparingly soluble calcium valerate (precipitates) and ammonium hydroxide; performed in water with excess Ca(OH)₂ and mild heating; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between chlorine gas and antimony tribromide to give bromine gas and antimony trichloride; carried out in a sealed or heated vessel, often under inert atmosphere, without solvent or catalyst.

Reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine with lithium aluminium hydride. Purpose: convert 3‑phenylpropanenitrile into 3‑phenylpropylamine. Key transformation: the C≡N group is reduced to –CH₂NH₂ while LiAlH4 is converted to aluminum oxide. Typical conditions: LiAlH4 (2–3 equiv) is dissolved in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen, added to the nitrile at 0 °C, then the mixture is warmed to reflux for 2–4 h. The reaction is quenched with aqueous acid and the amine is isolated.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction of sodium carbonate with potassium selenate in aqueous solution, exchanging cations to form potassium carbonate and sodium selenate; performed at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed condensation/cyclodehydration of anthranilic acid with formic acid in the presence of ZnCl2 to construct the tricyclic acridine nucleus; ZnCl2 acts as a Friedel‑Crafts‑type catalyst, and formic acid provides the carbon atom for ring closure. Reflux temperatures of 200–250 °C are common; the reaction is a one‑pot heterocyclic synthesis.

Carbodiimide‑mediated phosphorylation of Fluconazole with phosphoric acid using dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) and 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) to produce Fosfluconazole, with dicyclohexylurea as by‑product; carried out in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, DMAP acting as acyl‑transfer catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive nitrene removal); purpose is to convert a para‑toluenesulfonyl azide into the corresponding sulfonamide while releasing inert nitrogen gas. Key transformation is reduction of the azide (–N3) to a sulfonamide (–SO2NH2) with evolution of N2. Typical conditions use H2 gas (1–5 atm) over 5–10 % Pd/C in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol, at room temperature to reflux, often under an inert atmosphere.

Aerobic oxidation of aldehyde; purpose is to oxidize furfural to 2‑furancarboxylic acid (furoic acid). The aldehyde carbonyl is transformed into a carboxylic acid with O2 as the terminal oxidant. Typical conditions employ a metal catalyst (e.g., Au, Pt, or Cu–based) in aqueous or alcoholic solution, oxygen pressure (1 atm or higher), temperature 80–120 °C. In the absence of a catalyst, strong base or high‑temperature air oxidation can be used.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); purpose is to remove the iodine atom from 3‑iodoheptane, yielding the corresponding alkane and hydrogen iodide. The C–I bond is reduced to C–H. Standard conditions use H2 gas (1–3 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C in ethanol or methanol, at ambient temperature to reflux, often for several hours under inert gas.

Hydrolysis of a thioester; purpose is to cleave S‑phenyl ethanethioate to give acetic acid and thiophenol. The thioester bond (C=O‑SPh) is attacked by water, yielding the carboxylic acid and liberating the thiol. Typical conditions are aqueous acidic or basic media (e.g., 1 M HCl or NaOH) at reflux for 1–4 h, followed by extraction. Neutral hydrolysis can be performed in aqueous methanol at elevated temperature.

Hydrolysis (decomposition) of peracetic acid. Peracetic acid reacts with water, yielding acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide. The reaction proceeds readily at room temperature in aqueous solution and can be accelerated by acid or base, but generally occurs without added catalyst.

Thermal dehydration (solid‑state condensation) of sodium dihydrogen phosphate; purpose is to generate the more basic disodium hydrogen phosphate while releasing water. Upon heating, NaH2PO4 loses a water molecule to form Na2HPO4. Typical conditions involve heating the solid to 180–210 °C for 1–2 h in a dry crucible, often under a nitrogen stream to avoid moisture uptake.

Selective reduction of a lactone carbonyl by LiAlH4; purpose is to convert chromone to 4‑hydroxychroman by reducing the carbonyl at the 4‑position. The cyclic α‑β‑unsaturated carbonyl is reduced to a secondary alcohol, preserving the aromatic system. Standard procedure uses LiAlH4 (1–2 equiv) in dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by careful quench with aqueous acid and work‑up.

Hydride reduction (dehalogenation); LiAlH4 reduces the carbon‑iodine bond to give the corresponding alkane (hexane); purpose is removal of the halogen to afford a saturated hydrocarbon; key transformation is insertion of a hydride and loss of I−; reaction is run in anhydrous ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up that yields LiI and Al(OH)3 residues.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). The free‑base tiletamine reacts with hydrochloric acid, transferring a proton to the amine nitrogen to give tiletamine·HCl. This improves the drug’s water solubility and stability. Typically performed at 0–25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, or neat, with stirring until gas evolution (if any) ceases; no catalyst is required.

Palladium‑catalyzed transfer‑hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation). Formic acid serves as a hydrogen donor, decomposing on Pd/C to generate hydrogen (or a hydride) that reduces the C–Br bond of pentafluorophenyl bromide, yielding pentafluorobenzene, hydrogen bromide and carbon dioxide. Conducted under reflux (80–120 °C) in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile, DMF or dioxane, using 1–5 % Pd/C; the reaction is carried out under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar).

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion exchange. Silver nitrate and hydrazinium acetate exchange anions, forming insoluble (or less soluble) silver acetate and soluble hydrazinium nitrate. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the precipitated silver acetate is filtered off and washed. No catalyst is needed.

Fischer esterification of 3‑sulfanylpropanoic acid with ethanol; acid‑catalyzed (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) reflux in excess ethanol, often with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water; forms ethyl 3‑sulfanylpropanoate and water while retaining the thiol group, a common method to protect a carboxylic acid as an ethyl ester.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of a cyclic ether – ring opening of tetrahydrofuran (THF) to the diol 1,4‑butanediol. Copper chromite catalyzes cleavage of the C–O bond under high pressure hydrogen (5–10 atm) at elevated temperature (150–200 °C). The reaction is typically carried out in a high‑boiling inert solvent such as decalin or dodecane, or under solvent‑free conditions with excess THF.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (ester exchange). Ethyl acetate reacts with 3‑methylbutanoic acid in the presence of a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) to give ethyl 3‑methylbutanoate and acetic acid. The mixture is refluxed (≈78 °C) to reach equilibrium, and removal of acetic acid (by distillation or excess acid) drives the reaction toward product. The reactants themselves serve as solvent; no additional solvent or catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Hydroxide ions from strontium hydroxide neutralize iodic acid, producing water and the salt strontium diiodate (Sr(IO₃)₂). The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating with stirring. The resulting solid can be isolated by evaporation. No catalyst is required.

Oxidation (permanganate oxidation) – converts acridine to acridine‑9‑carboxylic acid by cleaving the C‑9 position; KMnO4 acts as the oxidant, MnO2 precipitates as by‑product and water is formed. Typical conditions: aqueous or acetic‑acid medium, often heated under reflux; acid or neutral pH, with KMnO4 in stoichiometric excess.

Hydrolysis of alkyl nitrite – tert‑butyl nitrite reacts with water to give tert‑butanol and nitrous acid. Generally acid‑catalyzed (e.g., dilute HCl) or performed in aqueous buffer at ambient temperature; solvent is water or water‑mixed organic (e.g., MeOH).

Oxime formation from 4‑methylbenzaldehyde using free hydroxylamine (no HCl). Same transformation as above; usually performed in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to reflux, optionally with a catalytic amount of acetic acid or base to facilitate condensation.

Copper‑catalyzed C‑N coupling (Ullmann‑type or Chan–Lam) – nucleophilic substitution of the iodine on 3‑iodophenol by morpholine to afford 3‑(morpholin‑4‑yl)phenol. Common conditions: CuI (5–10 mol %), a nitrogen base (e.g., K₂CO₃), ligand such as 1,10‑phenanthroline, in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere.

Double neutralization (acid–base reaction) forming sodium ammonium tartrate from tartaric acid, NaOH, and NH4OH. The carboxylic acids are deprotonated by the bases, producing the mixed salt and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, with stoichiometric amounts of NaOH and NH4OH to achieve the desired salt ratio; the mixture is often stirred until pH reaches neutral to slightly basic, then the salt may be crystallized upon cooling.

Acid‑base protonation (salt metathesis). Hydrogen fluoride protonates the carboxylate anion of sodium fluoroacetate, producing fluoroacetic acid and sodium fluoride. Conducted in aqueous solution (or aqueous ethanol) at ambient temperature; HF is added dropwise to a suspension of the sodium salt under stirring. No special catalyst required.

Amide‑bond formation (DCC coupling, Steglich esterification) – activation of 4‑methoxyphenylacetic acid by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) enables nucleophilic attack by 2,6‑dimethylaniline to afford Nefiracetam; dicyclohexylurea precipitates as by‑product. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or DMF, 0 °C then room temperature, with catalytic DMAP or other nucleophilic catalyst; reaction under nitrogen atmosphere.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (phenol acetylation) to form an aromatic ester. Purpose: introduce an acetyl group onto the phenolic oxygen, generating 2,4,6‑trichlorophenyl acetate and releasing HCl. Key transformation: the phenolic OH attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride and producing the ester. Typical conditions: performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to trap the generated HCl. No metal catalyst is required.

Reaction type: ligand substitution/coordination complex formation (complexation of Pt(II)). Purpose: replace potassium counter‑ions with pyridine ligands to obtain dichlorobis(pyridine)platinum. Key transformation: two pyridine molecules coordinate to the Pt center, displacing potassium chloride as a by‑product. Typical conditions: carried out in refluxing ethanol or aqueous ethanol under nitrogen; the mixture is stirred until KCl precipitates, then the platinum complex is isolated by filtration or crystallization. No external catalyst is needed.

Reaction type: solid‑state redox/synthesis of a metal chalcogenide (direct selenization). Purpose: convert elemental nickel into nickel selenide while liberating hydrogen gas. Key transformation: hydrogen selenide acts as a reducing agent, delivering Se to Ni and being reduced to H2. Typical conditions: sealed‑tube or tube‑furnace reaction at 300–600 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) to avoid oxidation; excess H2Se drives the reaction to completion.

Reaction type: carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification). Purpose: couple salicylic acid with isopropyl alcohol to form isopropyl salicylate. Key transformation: DCC activates the carboxyl group of salicylic acid, forming an O‑acyl‑urea intermediate that is attacked by the alcohol; DMAP catalyzes the acyl transfer. By‑product dicyclohexylurea precipitates. Typical conditions: room temperature, dry dichloromethane (or THF) under nitrogen, with catalytic DMAP (≈0.1 eq). Reaction is monitored until complete, then filtered to remove dicyclohexylurea and purified by chromatography.

Reaction type: trans‑nitrosation (thiol‑NO exchange). Purpose: transfer the nitroso group from S‑nitroso‑N‑acetylpenicillamine to reduced glutathione, generating S‑nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) and free N‑acetylpenicillamine. Key transformation: the thiolate of glutathione attacks the nitroso sulfur, forming GS‑NO and releasing the amine. Typical conditions: aqueous buffered solution (phosphate buffer, pH 7–8), ambient temperature, inert atmosphere to prevent NO oxidation. No additional catalyst is required; reaction proceeds rapidly (minutes to hours).

Reaction type: Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: introduce a sixth methyl group onto pentamethylbenzene, yielding hexamethylbenzene. Key transformation: AlCl3 complexes with methyl chloride to generate a CH3⁺ electrophile, which attacks the aromatic ring; subsequent deprotonation restores aromaticity. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl3 (1–2 eq) in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon disulfide or dichloromethane, low temperature (0 °C) to control poly‑alkylation, then gradual warming to reflux. Reaction is quenched with ice‑water, and the product is isolated by extraction and recrystallization.

Acetylation of the amino group of 4‑nitroaniline; purpose is to protect or modify the aniline nitrogen; key transformation: 4‑nitroaniline + (CH₃CO)₂O → N‑acetyl‑4‑nitroaniline + CH₃COOH; conditions: stir at 80–120 °C neat with excess acetic anhydride, optionally pyridine or triethylamine as base; solvent is the acetic anhydride itself; no external catalyst required.

Condensation (Mannich-type polycondensation) used to synthesize the chelating polyamine triethylenetetramine; formaldehyde reacts with ammonia and ethylenediamine to generate methylene‑bridged nitrogen atoms, releasing water; typically performed in aqueous solution at 50‑80 °C under mildly basic conditions; water is the solvent and the reaction may be buffered with sodium carbonate or similar base.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution; purpose is to prepare a thioester. Methanethiolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetyl chloride, forming a tetra‑tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release chloride and afford methyl thioacetate. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; the sodium ion already neutralizes HCl, so no additional base or catalyst is required.
Decomposition (acid dissociation) of carbonic acid into water and carbon dioxide; occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution at room temperature, no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

SN2 substitution; forms a primary ether (1‑methoxyhexane) from the alkyl iodide and methoxide; purpose is ether formation; key transformation is I− displaced by OCH3−; usually carried out in methanol using sodium methoxide (or NaOMe) at room temperature or gentle reflux; polar protic solvent (methanol) facilitates the reaction; sodium iodide is generated as a by‑product.

Jones oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Hexadecan‑1‑ol is oxidized by the Jones reagent (chromic acid generated from CrO₃ in dilute H₂SO₄) to hexadecanoic acid, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) (often isolated as Cr₂(SO₄)₃ or Cr₂O₃). Reaction is performed in acetone as solvent, typically at 0 °C initially then warmed to room temperature, under anhydrous conditions, and the mixture is quenched with isopropanol or a reducing agent to destroy excess oxidant.

Elimination (E2 dehydrohalogenation) of ethyl bromide to give ethylene and hydrogen bromide; a strong base such as KOH or NaOH abstracts a β‑hydrogen while the C–Br bond leaves, forming the alkene; carried out under reflux in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol) at elevated temperature (≈80‑100 °C).

Double displacement precipitation. Aqueous sodium sulfide reacts with aqueous cadmium iodide, producing insoluble cadmium sulfide precipitate and soluble sodium iodide. Typically performed at ambient or mildly heated conditions; water solvent; no catalyst.

Carbamate formation via activation with carbonyl diimidazole (CDI); CDI converts 3‑chloroaniline into an imidazolyl carbamoyl intermediate which then reacts with isopropanol to afford chlorpropham (isopropyl N‑(3‑chlorophenyl)carbamate) while releasing two equivalents of imidazole; the reaction is conducted anhydrously in THF or DMF at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen.

Nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether synthesis, SN2) where sodium 4‑nitrophenolate attacks ethyl bromide to form 4‑nitrophenyl ethyl ether (4‑nitrophenetole) and sodium bromide; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 0 °C to reflux; inert atmosphere often employed to avoid side reactions.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) between aqueous zinc sulfate and silver nitrate; the anions exchange to give soluble zinc nitrate and sparingly soluble silver sulfate, which precipitates; performed at room temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization; solid calcium oxide reacts vigorously with aqueous hydrochloric acid to yield calcium chloride solution and water; performed at ambient temperature; the reaction is exothermic; water is both solvent and product; no catalyst required; used for preparation of CaCl₂ or acid neutralization.

Formation of potassium tetrachloroaurate(III); coordination complexation reaction where excess chloride converts AuCl3 into the chloroaurate anion [AuCl4]−. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with excess KCl; the mixture is stirred at room temperature or mild heating, yielding KAuCl4 precipitate or solution. No special catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction between potassium iodide and terbium nitrate in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange anions, producing soluble potassium nitrate and terbium(III) iodide which can be isolated by evaporation or precipitation; typically performed at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Reaction type: single‑displacement redox. Purpose: reduce mercuric chloride to elemental mercury, useful in mercury removal or amalgamation processes. Key transformation: Zn(s) + HgCl2(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + Hg(l). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient to slightly elevated temperature; zinc metal added to HgCl2 solution. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Double‑replacement precipitation reaction between magnesium chloride and sodium carbonate; magnesium carbonate precipitates out of solution while sodium chloride remains dissolved. Conducted in aqueous medium, usually at room temperature with stirring; the insoluble MgCO₃ is filtered off, and the filtrate contains NaCl. No catalyst is needed.

Carbothermic chlorination (high‑temperature halogenation) of thorium dioxide with chlorine gas using carbon as reducing agent; converts ThO2 to thorium tetrachloride while carbon is oxidized to CO; conducted in a furnace at >700 °C under a flow of dry Cl2, solid‑state gas‑phase reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization / deprotonation of 3,5‑dimethylpyrazole with sodium hydroxide; generates sodium 3,5‑dimethylpyrazolate and water; typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic NaOH solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 4‑(chloromethyl)pyridinium chloride by ammonia; ammonia displaces the chloride to give 4‑(aminomethyl)pyridine with formation of ammonium chloride; performed in excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia, often under reflux; no catalyst required.

Free radical chlorination of a saturated alkane; purpose is to introduce a chlorine atom at a secondary carbon. A hydrogen atom on heptane is replaced by chlorine producing 3‑chloroheptane and HCl. Typical conditions: Cl2 gas, UV light or heat to generate radicals, often performed in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform.

Acid‑catalyzed conversion of methanol to methyl chloride (halogenation of an alcohol); protonation of methanol by HCl followed by chloride substitution yields CH3Cl and water; typically carried out by passing dry HCl gas through refluxing methanol or using concentrated aqueous HCl with ZnCl2 (Lucas reagent) at 60–80 °C; solvent is methanol itself, ZnCl2 can act as catalyst.

Type: Double‑replacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution. Purpose: Prepare ammonium pyrophosphate while liberating sodium hydroxide. Key transformation: Na2P2O7 + 2 NH4OH → (NH4)2P2O7 + 2 NaOH; the pyrophosphate anion exchanges its sodium counter‑ions for ammonium ions. Typical conditions: Dissolve disodium pyrophosphate in water, add excess ammonium hydroxide at room temperature; the reaction proceeds readily, and the aqueous NaOH remains in solution. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Double displacement precipitation between barium chloride and triammonium arsenate in water; forms insoluble barium arsenate and soluble ammonium chloride; reaction is carried out at room temperature in aqueous solution with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); purpose is to fully brominate the aromatic ring of toluene to give pentabromotoluene; key transformation replaces five ring hydrogens with bromine atoms, generating HBr as by‑product; typically performed with excess Br2 and a Lewis acid catalyst AlCl3 under anhydrous conditions, often at 0 °C to reflux in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification using an acyl chloride); purpose is to synthesize benzyl benzoate; key transformation converts the hydroxyl of benzyl alcohol into an ester linkage with the benzoyl group, releasing HCl; usually carried out in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate insoluble barium fluoride; key transformation swaps nitrate and fluoride ions, forming soluble ammonium nitrate and solid BaF2; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required; the precipitate is isolated by filtration.

Oxidative side‑chain oxidation; converts 4‑chlorophenylacetone to 4‑chlorobenzoic acid by oxidizing the methyl group of the aromatic ketone to a carboxyl group. Typically carried out with potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH) under reflux; MnO2 precipitates and is filtered off, then the acid is acidified and extracted. Common solvent: water or aqueous NaOH.

Acid–base neutralization (proton transfer) between a strong Brønsted acid and a strong non‑nucleophilic base; purpose is to generate bis(trimethylsilyl)amine and sodium triflate; key transformation transfers a proton from TfOH to the bis(trimethylsilyl)amide anion, yielding the neutral amine and NaOTf; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acyl‑transfer (esterification) of an alcohol with acetic anhydride; purpose is to produce methyl acetate; key transformation transfers an acetyl group from acetic anhydride to methanol, forming methyl acetate and acetic acid; often carried out neat or in a low‑boiling solvent (e.g., toluene) at room temperature, sometimes with a catalytic amount of pyridine or a base to absorb the generated acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an aldehyde; purpose is to reduce pentanal to pentan‑1‑ol; key transformation adds H2 across the carbonyl, converting the aldehyde to a primary alcohol; performed with Pd/C (5–10 % Pd on carbon) under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at 20–50 °C.

Ester to acid chloride conversion via thionyl chloride; nucleophilic substitution of the alkoxy group by chloride generates butyryl chloride and methyl chloride while releasing SO₂; used to prepare acid chlorides for further acylation; typically performed under reflux in a dry aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane with pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl, under inert atmosphere.

Ligand exchange of titanium tetraphenoxide with acetic acid; formation of titanium(IV) acetate and phenol. Purpose: obtain Ti(OAc)4, a useful precursor for acetate‑mediated syntheses. Key transformation: protonation of phenoxide and coordination of acetate to Ti, yielding Ti(OAc)4 and phenol. Typical conditions: reflux acetic acid (often excess) under nitrogen; sometimes gentle heating (60‑80 °C); no external catalyst.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of an internal alkene; purpose is to fragment (E)-oct‑2‑ene into aldehyde fragments. Ozone adds across the C=C bond, forming a molozonide that rearranges to an ozonide; reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide) cleaves the ozonide to give acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) from the terminal fragment and hexanal (CH₃(CH₂)₄CHO) from the other side. Typical conditions: O₃ bubbled through a solution of the alkene in dichloromethane at –78 °C, followed by the reductive work‑up at low temperature, then gradual warming to room temperature.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Finkelstein reaction) of ethyl p‑toluenesulfonate with sodium iodide; iodide displaces the tosylate to give iodoethane and sodium p‑toluenesulfonate; carried out in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF) at reflux; excess NaI drives the reaction; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (dehydration) of a metal hydroxide; used to obtain NiO as a precursor for catalysts, ceramics, and batteries; Ni(OH)2 loses one molecule of water to give NiO; typically carried out by heating the hydroxide solid at 300‑400 °C in air; no solvent or catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed decarboxylative arylation (Ullmann‑type C–C coupling) of picolinic acid with iodobenzene; loss of CO₂ and formation of a new C(sp²)–C(sp²) bond affords 2‑phenylpyridine; typically uses CuI or Cu(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %) with a nitrogen ligand such as 1,10‑phenanthroline, a base (K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃), DMF or DMSO as solvent, and heating to 100–130 °C under inert atmosphere.

Redox halogenation of lanthanum nitride with chlorine gas; chlorine oxidizes the nitride to lanthanum chloride while nitrogen gas is liberated; solid‑state reaction performed at elevated temperature (≈300–500 °C) in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent or catalyst required, stoichiometric Cl₂.

Oxidation of 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene (tetralin) to 1‑tetralone using sodium dichromate in acidic medium (Jones oxidation); Na₂Cr₂O₇ provides Cr(VI) oxidant that converts the benzylic C–H to a ketone, with acetic acid often serving as solvent/co‑solvent; reaction conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in aqueous H₂SO₄ or AcOH/H₂O, with stirring; Cr(III) salts are formed as by‑products.

Acid–base double displacement between oxalic acid and cobalt(II) perchlorate in aqueous solution; cobalt(II) precipitates as cobalt oxalate while perchloric acid remains in solution; performed at ambient temperature in water; the cobalt oxalate precipitate is isolated by filtration.

Nucleophilic substitution (PBr3 conversion of an alcohol to an alkyl bromide). Purpose: replace the hydroxyl group of diphenhydramine with bromine to generate a more reactive alkyl halide for further derivatization. Key transformation: ROH → RBr, with formation of H3PO3. Typical conditions: add PBr3 dropwise to a solution of diphenhydramine in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; stir until gas evolution ceases. No additional catalyst required.

Acid-catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination); converts tertiary alcohol to the corresponding alkene (isobutylene) and water; used to generate a gaseous alkene for polymerization or alkylation; typically performed by heating tert‑butanol with dry benzenesulfonic acid (≈80–150 °C) under anhydrous conditions, no solvent or excess acid acts as medium.

Phosgenation (conversion of an aniline to an isocyanate). 2,4,6‑Trichloroaniline reacts with phosgene (Cl–CO–Cl) to give the corresponding isocyanate and HCl. The reaction proceeds via formation of a carbamoyl chloride intermediate that loses HCl. Performed at 0–5 °C under inert atmosphere (N₂) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride; a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) is commonly added to trap the liberated HCl, though the stoichiometry shown includes HCl as product. No metal catalyst required.

High‑temperature oxidation (direct combination of iron metal with oxygen). Purpose: synthesis of magnetite (Fe3O4) as a pigment or magnetic material. Key transformation: elemental Fe is oxidized, yielding Fe(II) and Fe(III) in the mixed oxide Fe3O4. Typical conditions: heat finely divided iron in a stream of dry O2 at 700–900 °C; reaction performed in the gas phase, no solvent.

Acid‑base deprotonation of a carboxylic acid by an organolithium reagent. Purpose: generate the lithium formate salt and liberate methane gas. Key transformation: HCOOH + CH3Li → HCOOLi + CH4. Typical conditions: dissolve formic acid in anhydrous THF, cool to –78 °C, add methyllithium dropwise under inert atmosphere; allow mixture to warm to 0 °C before quench. No catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Thallium(I) hydroxide reacts with nitric acid to give thallium(I) nitrate and water. Normally carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; dilute HNO₃ is added slowly to a stirred TlOH solution to control the exotherm. No catalyst is needed; water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration; concentrated sulfuric acid protonates ethylene glycol, facilitating loss of water and cyclization to ethylene oxide; usually carried out at 180–200 °C with excess acid; water is formed as the by‑product; no additional solvent or catalyst, although side polymerization can occur.

Acid‑base salt formation (protonation). DABCO (1,4‑diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane) reacts with gaseous or aqueous HCl, forming the stable DABCO·HCl hydrochloride salt. Usually carried out in anhydrous ether, ethanol, or water at ambient temperature with stirring.

Selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H). Purpose: convert heptanal to heptanol without over‑reduction. Key transformation: R‑CHO → R‑CH2OH. Typical conditions: stir heptanal in dry THF at –78 °C, add 1 equiv DIBAL‑H dropwise under nitrogen; monitor by TLC, then quench with dilute aqueous acid and extract. No additional catalyst.

Fischer esterification of trifluoroacetic acid with ethanol; TFA and ethanol are refluxed in the presence of a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) to form ethyl trifluoroacetate and water; water is removed (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) to drive the equilibrium; excess ethanol acts as solvent.

Redox fluorination/oxidation of aluminum oxide by oxygen difluoride. Purpose: produce aluminum fluoride and release elemental oxygen. Key transformation: Al2O3 + 3 OF2 → 2 AlF3 + 3 O2. Typical conditions: expose solid Al2O3 to gaseous OF2 at elevated temperature (≈200–300 °C) in a dry, inert apparatus; reaction proceeds spontaneously, no solvent or catalyst.

Reductive amination; purpose is to methylate the amino group of β‑alanine forming 3-(methylamino)propanoic acid; key steps: condensation of β‑alanine with formaldehyde to give an imine, followed by catalytic hydrogenation of the imine to a secondary amine with loss of water; typical conditions: hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) with 10 % Pd/C catalyst in methanol or ethanol at room temperature to 50 °C; water is generated as by‑product.

Alkaline oxidative conversion of a benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate. Purpose: oxidize toluene to benzoic acid. Key transformation: C6H5‑CH3 → C6H5‑CO2H; MnO4⁻ is reduced to MnO2, K⁺ becomes KOH. Typical conditions: reflux toluene with aqueous KMnO4 in the presence of NaOH or KOH (basic medium) at 80–100 °C; after completion, filter off MnO2 and acidify to isolate benzoic acid. No organic solvent necessary, water serves as reaction medium.

Acid‑catalyzed O‑methylation of catechol using trimethyl orthoformate; converts both phenolic OH groups into methoxy groups to afford veratrole with methanol as a by‑product; typically performed with catalytic H₂SO₄ in anhydrous toluene or dichloromethane under reflux, removing water or methanol to drive the reaction.

Chlorination (acyl‑chloride formation) of a carboxylic acid using phosphorus pentachloride; 2‑ethoxyacetic acid reacts with PCl₅ to afford 2‑ethoxyacetyl chloride, with POCl₃ and HCl as by‑products. Performed under anhydrous conditions, usually in CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂, at 0 °C to rt; the reaction is exothermic and generates gaseous HCl.

Peracid epoxidation (oxidation) of 1‑octene with meta‑chloroperoxybenzoic acid; delivers 1,2‑epoxyoctane by transfer of an oxygen atom to the C=C bond; carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often followed by a basic work‑up (e.g., NaHCO₃) to neutralize benzoic acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a hexachlorinated alkene; purpose is to saturate the C=C bond and obtain the fully saturated hexachloropropane. Key transformation is addition of H2 across the double bond, converting the vinyl carbon to a single bond. Typical conditions use a metal hydrogenation catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2, or Raney Ni under 1–5 atm hydrogen pressure at room temperature to 80 °C, in solvents like ethanol, ethyl acetate or THF.

Diazomethane methyl‑esterification of pentafluoropropionic acid; diazomethane reacts with the carboxylic acid to form methyl pentafluoropropionate while liberating N₂ gas; conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in ether or THF under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (Fischer ether synthesis) of two hexan‑1‑ol molecules to give di‑n‑hexyl ether and water; uses concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH at 140–180 °C, with continuous removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) to shift equilibrium toward ether formation.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride; 2‑furancarbonyl chloride reacts with water to afford furan‑2‑carboxylic acid and HCl; carried out at 0–25 °C in aqueous medium, often in a biphasic ether/water system or with a mild base (NaHCO₃) to capture HCl and prevent side reactions.

Nucleophilic substitution (alkyl sulfide formation) of ethyl bromide with hydrogen sulfide to afford ethyl mercaptan (ethyl sulfide) and HBr. Conducted in a sealed vessel or refluxing solvent (e.g., ethanol or water) containing H2S gas; mild heating is sufficient because bromide is a good leaving group.

Reductive amination of indole‑3‑acetaldehyde with ammonia; formation of an imine followed by reduction with sodium triacetoxyborohydride affords tryptamine; typically performed in dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to facilitate imine formation.

Alpha‑bromination (electrophilic halogenation) of phenylacetic acid; phosphorus tribromide activates Br₂ to generate the bromonium electrophile that substitutes the α‑hydrogen of the carboxylic acid, yielding α‑bromo phenylacetic acid and HBr; carried out in carbon tetrachloride or chloroform under reflux; catalytic PBr₃ (sub‑stoichiometric) and excess Br₂ are used.

Protonation/salt formation of 1‑(3‑chlorophenyl)piperazine with hydrochloric acid to give the corresponding hydrochloride salt; carried out by treating the free base with aqueous or gaseous HCl in a suitable solvent (e.g., ethyl acetate, methanol) at room temperature, followed by isolation of the solid salt.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester hydrolysis); purpose is to regenerate the parent acid and alcohol. Key transformation: cleavage of the ester C–O bond to give 2‑hydroxybutanoic acid and 1‑propanol. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl or H₂SO₄) or in aqueous acetic acid; excess water shifts equilibrium to the products. No special solvent is required beyond the aqueous medium.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); transforms cyclopentanol into cyclopentanone with water as by‑product. Typically carried out in dry dichloromethane at ambient temperature; PCC serves as the oxidant, no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an organic azide to a primary amine; H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with Pd/C catalyst in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, usually at room temperature to reflux; the azide (‑N₃) is reduced to an amine (‑NH₂), producing 3‑amino‑1‑propanol and nitrogen gas.

Condensation/phosphorylation synthesis of pamidronic acid (a bis‑phosphonate); phosphorus trichloride activates 2‑amino‑1,3‑propanediol which reacts with phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃), releasing HCl; performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media (often water, 0 °C to reflux) under inert atmosphere; yields pamidronic acid after work‑up.

Preparation of copper(I) hydride hexamer [(CuH)(PPh₃)]₆; copper(I) bromide and triphenylphosphine are reduced by sodium triethylborohydride (NaHB(C₂H₅)₃) in anhydrous THF under nitrogen/argon, addition kept cold (0 °C) then warmed to rt; isolates the CuH(PPh₃)₆ cluster.

Aerobic oxidation of ferrous sulfate in basic solution; FeSO₄ in aqueous NaOH is oxidized by dissolved O₂ (air) from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, which hydrolyzes to Fe(OH)₃ precipitate while sulfate pairs with Na⁺ to give Na₂SO₄; carried out at ambient temperature with stirring and air sparging.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of benzyl fluoride with azide ion; NaN₃ provides N₃⁻ which attacks the benzylic carbon displacing fluoride; reaction run in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, typically 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere; yields benzyl azide and NaF.

Formation of peroxynitrous acid from hydrogen peroxide and nitrous acid; H₂O₂ reacts with HNO₂ in aqueous acidic medium (pH ≈ 2–3) at 0–5 °C to give HOONO and water; low temperature is used to minimize decomposition of the unstable peroxynitrous acid.
Acid‑base neutralization; proton transfer from carbonic acid to carbonate yielding sodium bicarbonate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water as solvent, no catalyst required.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; potassium and cadmium ions exchange anions to give soluble potassium nitrate and insoluble cadmium sulfite precipitate; carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; solid cadmium sulfite isolated by filtration.

Silicon + chlorine → silicon tetrachloride: Direct combination (halogenation) synthesis. Purpose is to produce SiCl₄, a volatile liquid used as a precursor for silicone polymers and glass etching. Key transformation is Si(s) + 2 Cl₂(g) → SiCl₄(l). Typically carried out in a dry, inert‑gas furnace at 300–500 °C; moisture must be excluded to avoid HCl formation. No solvent; reaction performed in the gas phase.

Kinase‑catalyzed phosphorylation of glycerol by ATP (glycerol kinase). Purpose: metabolic activation of glycerol for entry into glycolysis or lipid biosynthesis. Key transformation: transfer of the terminal phosphate from ATP to the primary hydroxyl of glycerol, forming L‑α‑glycerophosphate (glycerol‑3‑phosphate) and ADP. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 7.5), Mg²⁺ as cofactor, presence of glycerol kinase enzyme, temperature around 37 °C (physiological). No organic solvent; reaction is enzymatic.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; hydrolysis of bismuth trichloride in aqueous NaOH to form insoluble bismuth oxychloride precipitate and NaCl; typically performed in water at ambient temperature, stirring; no special catalyst required.
LAH reduction of hexanamide to hexylamine; performed in anhydrous diethyl ether or THF under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to reflux, with lithium aluminium hydride added slowly.

Halide‑exchange metathesis in aqueous medium; silver bromide reacts with sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate to form soluble silver trifluoromethanesulfonate and sodium bromide; typically performed in water or a water‑organic mixture at mild temperature; no catalyst required.

Gas‑phase atmospheric oxidation. Ozone reacts with bromine chloride (BrCl) to yield molecular oxygen, chlorine monoxide (ClO·) and bromine monoxide (BrO·). This radical‑mediated reaction contributes to stratospheric ozone depletion and occurs under low‑pressure, sunlight‑driven conditions in the upper atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Free‑radical benzylic bromination; N‑bromosuccinimide provides bromine radicals that substitute the benzylic hydrogens of o‑xylene, giving o‑bis(bromomethyl)benzene; benzoyl peroxide initiates the radical chain; usually refluxed in an inert halogenated solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform (80–100 °C); by‑products are succinimide and hydrogen bromide.

Gas‑phase halogenation/oxidation; used to prepare cyanogen chloride (a chemical intermediate and warfare agent). Hydrogen cyanide reacts with chlorine gas to replace H by Cl, yielding ClCN and HCl. Typically carried out at ambient to moderate temperatures in the gas phase without solvent; often in a flow reactor with excess Cl2.

Oxidation of a Si–H bond by tert‑butyl hydroperoxide; the hydroperoxide transfers an oxygen atom to diphenylsilane forming diphenylsilanediol while being reduced to tert‑butanol; conducted in an inert organic solvent (e.g., THF) at 0–25 °C or with gentle warming; often catalyzed by a transition‑metal (Cu, Fe) complex but can proceed thermally; no additional reagents required.

Solid‑state high‑temperature synthesis; combines a basic oxide (MgO) with an acidic oxide (SiO₂) to form a magnesium silicate lattice (e.g., Mg₂SiO₄ or MgSiO₃). Typically performed by intimately grinding the powders together and heating in a furnace at 1200–1500 °C in air; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular Friedel‑Crafts alkylation/dehydration; purpose is to cyclize a phenyl‑propyl alcohol to the fused aromatic system tetralin. Key transformation is loss of water and formation of a new C‑C bond between the aromatic ring and the side chain, converting the primary alcohol into a benzylic carbocation that attacks the ring. Typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄ (or another strong protic acid), heating to 150–200 °C, often the acid acts as solvent; water is removed in situ.

Copper‑mediated oxidation of a hydroxylamine to a nitroxyl radical (TEMPO) using NaOCl; purpose is to generate the stable radical oxidant TEMPO while reducing Cu(II) to Cu(I). Key transformation: conversion of the secondary amine (4‑hydroxy‑2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine) to its N‑oxyl radical and concomitant reduction of CuCl₂ to CuCl, with NaOCl being reduced to NaCl and water formed. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOCl (bleach) buffered to pH 8–9 (often with NaHCO₃), 0 °C to room temperature, CuCl₂ used catalytically (0.1–5 mol %). Solvent is water; no additional organic solvent is required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of valproic acid with pivaloyloxymethyl chloride in the presence of pyridine; purpose is to prepare the pro‑drug valproate pivoxil (pivaloyloxymethyl ester). Key transformation: the carboxylate attacks the electrophilic carbon of the chloromethyl pivalate, displacing chloride which is captured by pyridine to give pyridinium chloride. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to ambient temperature, inert atmosphere; stoichiometric pyridine acts as base and HCl scavenger.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert 2‑butoxyacetic acid into 2‑butoxyethanol. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming an aldehyde intermediate that is further reduced to the alcohol; Al‑O and Li‑O bonds are hydrolyzed on work‑up. Typical conditions: dry ether solvent (diethyl ether or THF), low temperature (0 °C) during addition followed by reflux or room temperature for completion; excess LiAlH₄ is common. Quench with careful addition of aqueous NaOH or water, then extract.

E2 β‑elimination of a secondary alkyl bromide by ethoxide ion; purpose is to generate the more substituted alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑butene while consuming the base. Key transformation: ethoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 2‑methyl‑2‑bromobutane, the C–Br bond breaks concurrently, forming the double bond; ethoxide becomes ethanol, and NaBr is formed as the salt. Typical conditions: polar protic solvent (ethanol) or a mixed solvent, reflux temperature (≈78 °C) or 50–80 °C, stoichiometric sodium ethoxide; reaction proceeds quickly under these basic conditions.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of heptyl acetate with propanol. Purpose: produce propyl acetate and heptanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of propanol on the ester carbonyl, displacing the heptyl alkoxy group. Typical conditions: acid catalyst (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base catalyst (e.g., NaOPr) at 60–90 °C, using excess propanol as solvent/reagent. Common solvent: excess 1‑propanol.

Thermal decomposition of lutetium nitride to metallic lutetium and nitrogen gas; performed at very high temperature (often >1500 °C) under inert atmosphere or vacuum; no solvent or catalyst required; used to recover lutetium metal.

Esterification (acid‑catalyzed); forms a mono‑ester of glycerol with palmitic acid. Key transformation: hydroxyl of glycerol reacts with carboxyl of palmitic acid, releasing water. Typical conditions: reflux 120–150 °C with catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark). Solvent often toluene or the reaction may be run neat as bulk glycerol.

Peracid oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; acetic acid and H₂O₂ generate peracetic acid in situ, which oxidizes 4‑chlorobutanal to 4‑chlorobutanoic acid. Key transformation: aldehydic C=O is further oxidized to a carboxyl group. Typical conditions: aqueous/acetone mixture, 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric H₂O₂ (1.2 eq). No additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); converts 2-(1H-imidazol-2-yl)ethanol to the corresponding aldehyde with CrCl3 and water as by‑products. Reaction is performed in dry dichloromethane at room temperature under inert atmosphere; purpose is selective formation of an aldehyde without over‑oxidation.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acyl chloride to ester). The carbonyl chloride reacts with methanol to give methyl pyrrole‑2‑carboxylate while releasing HCl. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, using a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Metal‑hydride metathesis (salt metathesis). Lithium hydride transfers a hydride to triethylborane, generating lithium triethylborohydride (Superhydride) and H2 gas is not formed. Performed under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) in dry THF at 0 °C to rt; LiH is added to a THF solution of Et3B, stirred until the suspension clears.

Radical halogenationfree‑radical substitution). Chlorine replaces a hydrogen atom of pentane at the secondary (3) carbon, giving 3‑chloropentane and HCl as the only by‑product. Typically carried out under UV irradiation or thermal initiation in an inert, non‑participating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds via a chlorine radical chain mechanism.

Methylation using dimethyl sulfate; the phenoxide of 2,4,6‑tribromophenol (usually generated with a base such as pyridine or NaOH) attacks dimethyl sulfate in an SN2 process, producing 2,4,6‑tribromoanisole and methyl hydrogen sulfate; conducted under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to room temperature; common solvents include pyridine or DMF; dimethyl sulfate acts as the methylating agent.

Peracid oxidation of a trialkyl phosphite to the corresponding trialkyl phosphate. Peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to tributyl phosphite, producing tributyl phosphate and acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0–25 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, stoichiometric peracid, reaction complete within 1–2 h. No metal catalyst required.

Acylation of sec‑butylamine with acetyl chloride to form N‑sec‑butylacetamide; acid chloride reacts with the amine, displacing chloride as hydrogen chloride; performed in an inert solvent like dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize the evolved HCl.

Coordination complex formation. 2‑(Carboxymethylamino)acetic acid (iminodiacetic acid) reacts with copper(II) chloride in aqueous solution to form copper(II) iminodiacetate, releasing hydrochloric acid. The reaction is performed at ambient temperature or with gentle heating, adjusting pH to favor complexation. Water is the usual solvent; no additional ligands are needed.

Hydride reduction (deoxygenation) of triphenylarsine oxide to triphenylarsine. Sodium borohydride supplies hydride, reducing the As=O bond and generating water and sodium borate as by‑products. Typical conditions: THF/MeOH mixture, 0 °C to rt, 1.5–2 eq NaBH₄, inert atmosphere. Reaction proceeds in 30 min to 1 h.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrodeoxygenation) of 2‑methylhexanol to 2‑methylhexane. Molecular hydrogen adds across the C–O bond in the presence of a metal catalyst, producing water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: Raney Ni or Pd/C (5 wt %), H₂ pressure 30–50 atm, temperature 80–120 °C, solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol. Reaction time 2–6 h.
