Intramolecular Williamson cyclization (base‑promoted epoxide formation); NaOH dehydrohalogenates 1,3‑dichloropropane, displacing one chloride and closing the three‑membered ring to give chlorooxirane (epichloropropane) with NaCl and water as by‑products; the reaction is typically performed in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethanol solution, heated under reflux.

Fluorination of antimony(V) oxide – direct fluorination (oxidation‑reduction) used to prepare antimony pentafluoride, a strong Lewis‑acid fluorinating reagent. The oxygen in Sb2O5 is displaced by fluorine giving SbF5 and O2. Carried out by passing dry F2 gas over solid Sb2O5 at 250–400 °C (sometimes up to 500 °C) in a nickel or Monel reactor under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

N‑methylation of hydrazine (SN2 alkylation); hydrazine attacks methyl iodide, substituting iodide to afford methylhydrazine (CH₃NHNH₂) and HI; the reaction is carried out in anhydrous ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to rt, often with an added base such as Na₂CO₃ or triethylamine to neutralize the generated HI.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination (EAS) of mesitylene; FeBr₃ acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst to generate the bromine electrophile from N‑bromosuccinimide, which substitutes a hydrogen para to a methyl group on 1,3,5‑trimethylbenzene, yielding 2‑bromomesitylene and succinimide as the by‑product; the reaction is typically performed in an inert solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄ at 0 °C to rt with catalytic FeBr₃.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration; converts cyclohexanol to cyclohexene by elimination of water; performed by heating cyclohexanol with concentrated phosphoric acid (≈85 %) at 130–180 °C, often neat or in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene; water is removed to drive the equilibrium.

Type: Double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution. Purpose: Exchange anions to produce thulium(III) chloride and ammonium nitrate. Key transformation: Tm(NO3)3 + 3 NH4Cl ⇌ TmCl3 + 3 NH4NO3. Typical conditions: Dissolve thulium nitrate and ammonium chloride in water, stir at ambient temperature or gently heat (≤80 °C) until complete mixing; the solid TmCl3 may precipitate upon cooling. Common solvent: water. No catalyst required.

Sodium borohydride reduction of chloral hydrate; hydride transfers reduce the gem‑diol (chloral hydrate) to trichloroethanol, producing sodium borate as by‑product; conducted in a protic solvent such as ethanol/water at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere; reaction is quenched with water.

Radical bromination using N‑bromosuccinimide; NBS provides bromine radicals that brominate bromoacetonitrile at the α‑carbon to give dibromoacetonitrile and succinimide; usually run in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂) at room temperature or reflux with light or a peroxide initiator; succinimide precipitates out.

Double‑replacement precipitation; potassium carbonate reacts with barium nitrate in aqueous solution to form insoluble barium carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium nitrate; performed at room temperature with stirring; the BaCO₃ solid is filtered and washed.

Catalytic oxidative conversion of glycerol to sodium pyruvate; glycerol is oxidized in basic medium (NaOH) with copper(II) oxide under an oxygen atmosphere to afford pyruvate anion and water; typically carried out in aqueous NaOH at 120–180 °C under elevated O₂ pressure; copper oxide acts as a heterogeneous catalyst and is recovered by filtration.

Type: diazotization‑hydrolysis (Sandmeyer‑type). Purpose: replace the aromatic amine with a hydroxyl group. Key transformation: 1‑aminoanthraquinone is converted to 1‑hydroxyanthraquinone with loss of N₂; nitrous acid generated from NaNO₂/HCl forms a diazonium intermediate that hydrolyzes to the phenol. Conditions: cold aqueous HCl (0–5 °C), typically 1 M, stirred under ice bath. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Type: acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (protecting carbonyl). Purpose: convert acetaldehyde to its diethyl acetal while generating ethanol as by‑product. Key transformation: acetaldehyde reacts with triethyl orthoformate to give 1,1‑diethoxyethane and ethanol. Conditions: catalytic acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) in anhydrous solvent, reflux with Dean‑Stark to remove ethanol; temperature ≈80–110 °C. Solvent: toluene, benzene, or xylene.

Type: N‑acylation (amide formation) using an acid chloride. Purpose: install a benzoyl group onto phenylurea to afford N‑benzoyl‑3‑phenylurea. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of a urea nitrogen on benzoyl chloride, forming an amide bond; the generated HCl is captured by triethylamine to give triethylammonium chloride. Conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, stoichiometric triethylamine. Solvent: dichloromethane, THF, or chloroform.

Selective oxidation to aldehyde – Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) oxidizes the hydroxymethyl side chain of 5‑hydroxymethylfuran‑2‑carboxylic acid to the corresponding aldehyde, 5‑formylfuran‑2‑carboxylic acid, with water as the only by‑product. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 8‑9) at 0‑25 °C, often in a biphasic system with CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN to improve organic solubility.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl pyrrole‑2‑carboxylate with sodium hydroxide followed by decarboxylation; the ester is hydrolyzed to the carboxylate, which loses CO₂ to afford pyrrole, while ethanol is generated from the ethoxide. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH, heated to 80‑100 °C.

Type: acid‑metal displacement (single‑replacement, redox). Purpose: generate hydrogen gas and form aluminum acetate salt. Key transformation: aluminum metal reduces acetic acid, producing aluminum acetate (Al(OAc)₃) and H₂. Conditions: reflux of aluminum filings or turnings in excess glacial acetic acid, often under nitrogen to avoid oxidation. Solvent: glacial acetic acid (with a small amount of water if needed); no external catalyst.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of an internal alkene. Ozone reacts with the C=C bond of 3‑octene to form a primary ozonide that is reduced (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide) to give the aldehydes propanal and pentanal. Performed in dry dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C under an inert atmosphere; after ozonide formation the reductive work‑up is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature.

Grignard reagent formation (metal insertion); purpose: generate phenylmagnesium bromide for use as a nucleophilic organometallic reagent. Magnesium inserts into the C–Br bond of bromobenzene, yielding Ph‑MgBr. Conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), activation of Mg with a trace of iodine or mercuric chloride, temperature from 0 °C to reflux, moisture‑free environment.

Type: catalytic nitro reduction (NaBH₄/NiCl₂, nickel‑boride system). Purpose: convert a nitroarene to the corresponding aniline. Key transformation: 1‑nitronaphthalene is reduced to 1‑aminonaphthalene; NaBH₄ reduces NiCl₂ to an active nickel‑boride species that transfers hydride to the nitro group. Conditions: NaBH₄ (2–3 eq) and NiCl₂ (10–20 mol %) in ethanol or methanol, 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere. Solvent: ethanol, methanol, or THF.

Type: Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation using an acid anhydride). Purpose: Acylate the secondary amine to give N‑ethyl‑2‑hydroxy‑propionamide while generating propionic acid as by‑product. Key transformation: The lone pair on the ethylamino nitrogen attacks one carbonyl of propionic anhydride, opening the anhydride and forming the amide; the remaining acyl fragment becomes propionic acid. Typical conditions: 1 eq 2‑(ethylamino)ethanol and 1 eq propionic anhydride mixed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine (1–2 eq) at 0 °C → rt for 2–4 h. Common solvents: CH2Cl2, THF, pyridine (acts as both solvent and acid scavenger). No metal catalyst needed.

Metal‑halogen exchange/insertion to form an organolithium reagent; sec‑butyl bromide reacts with elemental lithium to generate sec‑butyl lithium and lithium bromide; carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to –78 °C to avoid side reactions.

Type: heterocycle‑forming cyclocondensation (pyrazole synthesis). Purpose: construction of a 5‑amino‑pyrazole core bearing a nitrile group. Key transformation: nucleophilic addition of the two –NH2 groups of hydrazine to the electrophilic C=C of 2‑amino‑1‑propene‑1,1,3‑tricarbonitrile, followed by intramolecular cyclization and loss of ammonia to give the pyrazole ring. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid or a mild base (NaOAc) to promote cyclization; reaction time 2–6 h. Common solvents/catalysts: ethanol, methanol, acetic acid, sodium acetate.

Acid‑base liberation of hydrogen cyanide; protonation of cyanide ion by hydrochloric acid releases volatile HCN gas while forming potassium chloride. Reaction: KCN + HCl → HCN↑ + KCl. Conducted in dilute aqueous solution, often cooled (0–5 °C) to limit HCN volatilization and in a well‑ventilated fume hood. No catalyst; the gas can be captured in an absorber.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; used to convert soluble mercuric bromide into insoluble mercury(II) sulfide for removal or analysis. Hg^2+ is transferred to thiosulfate which is oxidized to sulfite, while Br⁻ becomes NaBr. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature, often under neutral to slightly acidic conditions; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Type: solid‑state metathesis (high‑temperature inorganic synthesis). Purpose: preparation of the rare‑earth phosphide DyP. Key transformation: exchange of sodium and dysprosium ions between Na₃P and DyBr₃ to form DyP (binary phosphide) and NaBr as by‑product. Typical conditions: intimate mixing of powdered Na₃P and DyBr₃, sealed in an evacuated quartz tube or under argon, heated to 800–1000 °C for several hours (often 12–24 h), then cooled and washed to remove NaBr. Common solvents/catalysts: none; inert atmosphere and high temperature are essential.

Aqueous double‑displacement reaction of silver nitrate with sodium cyanate producing silver cyanate and sodium nitrate; same purpose and key transformation as reaction 2, with sodium as the counter‑ion; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, silver cyanate precipitates, filtered off; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization forming calcium tellurate; purpose is to convert telluric acid (H₆TeO₆) into the calcium salt CaTeO₄ (or Ca₂TeO₅ depending on stoichiometry). Typical conditions: aqueous solution of telluric acid mixed with solid CaO or Ca(OH)₂, the mixture is heated gently (≈80 °C) with stirring; water is produced and the calcium tellurate precipitates, which can be filtered and washed. No special catalyst is needed.

Type: N‑alkylation (SN2 substitution) of an amine. Purpose: introduction of an ethyl group onto the nitrogen of 1,3,4‑thiadiazol‑2‑amine. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the amine nitrogen on ethyl bromide, displacement of bromide ion to give N‑ethyl‑1,3,4‑thiadiazol‑2‑amine and formation of HBr. Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile), presence of a base such as triethylamine, potassium carbonate, or NaH to scavenge HBr, temperature 50–80 °C for 2–12 h. Common solvents/catalysts: DMF, DMSO, K₂CO₃, TEA.

Type: multicomponent Knoevenagel condensation performed in a deep eutectic solvent (DES). Purpose: synthesis of 2‑chloro‑benzylidenemalononitrile via condensation of malononitrile with 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde. Key transformation: activation of malononitrile by the basic DES (choline chloride + urea) leading to deprotonation, nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde, elimination of water to afford the α,β‑unsaturated nitrile. Typical conditions: melt the choline chloride/urea (1:2 molar ratio) at 80–100 °C to form DES, add malononitrile and 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde, stir 1–3 h until completion; water produced remains in the medium. Common solvents/catalysts: the DES itself acts as solvent and catalyst; no additional solvent required.

Type: oxidative conversion of an aldehyde to a carboxylate (bleach oxidation). Purpose: preparation of sodium benzoate from benzaldehyde. Key transformation: oxidation of the aldehydic carbon by hypochlorite to the corresponding carboxylate, with concomitant reduction of OCl⁻ to Cl⁻ and generation of water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOCl solution (≈ 5–10 % active chlorine), pH adjusted to 8–9 with NaHCO₃ or Na₂CO₃, temperature 0–25 °C to minimize side reactions, reaction time 30 min to 2 h. Common solvents/catalysts: water as solvent; often a buffer (bicarbonate) is used to maintain pH.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); dimethylammonium oxalate exchanges cations with calcium chloride, forming insoluble calcium oxalate precipitate and soluble dimethylammonium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

General type: acylation of an amine using an anhydride. Purpose: selective mono‑acetylation of m‑phenylenediamine to give 3‑aminoacetanilide. Key transformation: one –NH2 reacts with acetic anhydride, forming an acetamide and producing one equivalent of acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: excess acetic anhydride, heated reflux or 80–100 °C, often in pyridine, DMF or neat; the reaction may be carried out under nitrogen; the resulting acetic acid is removed on work‑up.

Type: hydrolysis of a sulfonyl fluoride. Purpose: conversion of p‑aminobenzenesulfonyl fluoride to sulfanilic acid (p‑aminobenzenesulfonic acid). Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the sulfur atom, cleavage of the S–F bond, release of HF and formation of the sulfonic acid group. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature or gently heated (40–60 °C), sometimes with a weak base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) to neutralize HF and drive the reaction to completion; reaction time 1–4 h. Common solvents/catalysts: water, optional mild base; no special catalyst required.

Reaction type: alkaline digestion / dissolution. Purpose: break down aluminum borate to soluble aluminate and borate species for further processing or analysis. Key transformation: Al₂O₃·B₂O₃ (simplified formula for aluminum borate) + 2 NaOH → 2 NaAlO₂ + Na₂B₄O₇ + H₂O (balanced stoichiometry varies with exact borate). Typical conditions: solid aluminum borate mixed with concentrated NaOH solution (5–10 M) and heated to 80–120 °C under stirring for 1–3 h. Solvent: aqueous NaOH; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 4‑fluoro‑1‑nitrobenzene by piperazine; the basic potassium carbonate deprotonates the piperazine nitrogen which attacks the electron‑deficient aromatic carbon bearing fluorine, displacing fluoride to give 1‑(4‑nitrophenyl)piperazine. Typically performed under microwave heating (≈120–150 °C) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO; no metal catalyst is required. Purpose: synthesis of aryl‑piperazine intermediates for pharmaceuticals.

Halogen exchange / radical halogenation of carbon tetraiodide with chlorine. Chlorine abstracts an iodine atom from CI₄, generating iodine monochloride (ICl) and the mixed halomethane chlorotriiodomethane (CClI₃). Usually carried out under UV irradiation or thermal conditions in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) to promote radical formation. Purpose: preparation of mixed‑halogen reagents.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol (2‑hexanol) to the corresponding ketone (2‑hexanone). Common oxidants include pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) on silica, Dess–Martin periodinane, or catalytic aerobic oxidation over copper or TEMPO‑Cu complexes in dichloromethane or acetonitrile. Conditions are mild (0 °C to rt) and the reaction proceeds with retention of the carbon skeleton. Purpose: functional‑group interconversion.

Hydrolysis (amide cleavage); conversion of N‑phenylprop‑2‑enamide back to aniline and acrylic acid; cleavage of the amide bond by water under acidic (e.g., 6 M HCl, reflux) or basic (e.g., 2 M NaOH, reflux) conditions; usually performed in aqueous ethanol or water/THF mixture; temperature 80–120 °C; acid or base serves as catalyst.

Type: acid leaching / metathesis of a silicate mineral. Purpose: dissolve zirconium silicate to recover zirconium as its soluble chloride and generate soluble silicic acid. Key transformation: protons from HCl attack the Si–O and Zr–O bonds, forming H4SiO4 (silicic acid) and ZrCl4 in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (4 M or concentrated) heated to reflux≈80–100 °C) for several hours; excess acid ensures complete conversion. Solvent is water; no additional catalyst required.

Alkoxide exchange (proton transfer) between isobutanol and sodium ethoxide in anhydrous ethanol. Sodium ethoxide abstracts a proton from isobutanol, generating ethanol and sodium isobutoxide. The reaction is driven to completion by using excess sodium ethoxide and refluxing the mixture under dry, inert atmosphere. Purpose: preparation of a specific alkoxide for subsequent synthetic steps.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between aqueous barium chloride and thallium(I) selenate. The insoluble barium selenate precipitates, while thallium(I) chloride remains in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the solid barium selenate is filtered off and washed. Purpose: selective precipitation to separate barium from thallium salts.

Halide‑acetate metathesis (transmetalation); purpose is to exchange the chloride ligand on triphenyl‑tin for acetate, yielding a more reactive or less corrosive organotin reagent. Key transformation: Sn‑Cl bond is replaced by Sn‑OAc, Ag⁺ precipitates as AgCl. Typical conditions: ambient to mild heating, inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF), stoichiometric amounts, filtration to remove AgCl.

Acyl‑chloride esterification; formation of diphenyl oxalate from phenol and oxalyl chloride in the presence of a base. Key transformation: oxalyl chloride reacts with phenolic OH to give phenyl oxalate ester, while triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl as triethylammonium chloride. Conditions: low temperature (0 °C → rt), anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Gas‑phase chlorination (oxidative halogenation) of gallium arsenide; purpose is to convert the solid semiconductor into volatile gallium trichloride and arsenic trichloride for purification or analytical distillation. Key transformation: GaAs + 3 Cl₂ → GaCl₃ + AsCl₃. Conditions: high temperature (≈500–800 °C) in a quartz tube under a flow of dry Cl₂ gas; no solvent, reaction occurs in the gas phase.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; purpose is to saturate the C=C bond of 2,4‑dimethylpent‑2‑ene to give the corresponding alkane. Key transformation: addition of H₂ across the double bond to form 2,4‑dimethylpentane. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % w/w) as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–80 °C, stirring under inert atmosphere.

Thioether hydrogenolysis; cleavage of the C–S bond in methyl cyclohexyl sulfide to give cyclohexane and methanethiol. Usually carried out under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with Raney‑Ni or Pd/C catalyst in an alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 50–100 °C.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a carboxylate salt; purpose is to convert 2,6‑dihydroxybenzoic acid into its water‑soluble sodium salt. Key transformation: deprotonation of the carboxylic acid by NaOH, yielding water and sodium 2,6‑dihydroxybenzoate. Conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, typically stoichiometric NaOH, stirring until dissolution; no catalyst required.

Redox displacement / halide exchange between iodide and gold(III) chloride; purpose is to reduce Au(III) to Au(I) as gold(I) iodide while oxidizing iodide to elemental iodine. Key transformation: 3 KI + AuCl₃ → AuI + I₂ + 3 KCl. Conditions: aqueous medium (often mildly acidic), ambient temperature, stoichiometric reagents; reaction proceeds spontaneously without added catalyst.

Oxidation of a benzylic methyl group on 2‑methylnaphthalene to a carboxylic acid using acidic dichromate; a strong oxidizing (Jones‑type) reaction performed in concentrated H₂SO₄ (often reflux) with Na₂Cr₂O₇ as oxidant; converts –CH₃ to –CO₂H, yielding 2‑naphthoic acid; typical solvent is the acid medium itself, no additional catalyst.

Combustion (complete oxidation) of 1,1,1‑trifluoroethane with O₂; high‑temperature flame or heated reactor in excess oxygen; produces CO₂, H₂O and HF as the only gaseous products; no catalyst required, reaction proceeds spontaneously under ignition conditions.

Oxidative cyclodehydrogenation (Scholl reaction) of 1,1′‑binaphthyl to perylene using FeCl₃ as the oxidant; FeCl₃ abstracts electrons and HCl, being reduced to FeCl₂; typically carried out in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or nitromethane at room temperature to reflux; purpose is to form a fused polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon.

N‑acylation of benzylamine with acetyl chloride to give N‑acetylbenzylamine; nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) producing HCl as by‑product; usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or THF at 0 °C to rt, with a tertiary amine base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl.

Hydrolysis/quench of lithium diisopropylamide (LDA·THF) with water; acid‑base neutralization where LDA abstracts a proton from water yielding lithium hydroxide and regenerating diisopropylamine; carried out in THF at 0 °C to rt; water is added dropwise to a solution of LDA.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 O‑alkylation) of 2‑methoxyphenol. NaOH deprotonates the phenol to the phenoxide, which attacks methyl iodide to afford 1,2‑dimethoxybenzene (veratrole) with NaI as by‑product. Usually performed in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone at 0 °C to rt.

Acid‑base metathesis between hydrofluoric acid and lithium oxalate; HF protonates the oxalate anion to give oxalic acid and lithium fluoride; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with gentle heating to ensure complete reaction; LiF may precipitate.

Double‑displacement precipitation with acid‑base decomposition; aqueous silver nitrate reacts with sodium bicarbonate to precipitate silver carbonate, while sodium nitrate remains in solution; carbon dioxide gas and water are released as the bicarbonate decomposes; carried out at room temperature in water, no catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (halide to cyanide). Purpose: install a benzylic nitrile functionality. Key transformation: bromide is displaced by cyanide ion, giving 4‑(cyanomethyl)phenol and NaBr. Typical conditions: NaCN (1–1.5 equiv) in dry DMF or DMSO, heated 50–80 °C, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst.

Double displacement (acid‑base metathesis); HF protonates the sulfate and exchanges halide to give palladium(II) fluoride and sulfuric acid; usually carried out in concentrated aqueous HF at room temperature; no additional catalyst, solvent is the HF solution itself.

Nucleophilic addition of an organolithium to an aldehyde (Grignard‑type addition); phenyl lithium adds to the carbonyl of benzaldehyde forming a benzylic alkoxide that upon aqueous work‑up yields diphenylmethanol; performed under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, typically at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by quench with dilute acid or NH₄Cl.

Wolff‑Kishner reduction of a ketone; hydrazine reacts with the naphthyl ethanone in basic medium to give a hydrazone which, upon heating, decomposes to nitrogen, water and the corresponding alkane (1‑ethylnaphthalene); carried out with excess KOH in high‑boiling polar solvents such as ethylene glycol or diethylene glycol, refluxing (≈180–200 °C).

Selenium dioxide oxidation (Riley oxidation) of benzylic methyl groups to aldehydes; SeO₂ oxidizes the two methyl groups of 1,3‑dimethylbenzene to give isophthalaldehyde while being reduced to selenous acid; typically performed by refluxing the aromatic substrate with SeO₂ in water or a water‑compatible solvent (e.g., dioxane/water), often with a catalytic amount of a co‑oxidant; reaction temperature 80–120 °C.

Type: Esterification of a sulfonic acid (Fischer‑type sulfonate formation). Purpose: Prepare the butyl methanesulfonate (mesylate) as a good leaving group. Key transformation: condensation of methanesulfonic acid with n‑butanol, eliminating water to give the sulfonate ester. Typical conditions: reflux of methanesulfonic acid and butanol (1:1 mol) in toluene or benzene with Dean–Stark apparatus to remove water; alternatively, azeotropic removal of water under reduced pressure. No external catalyst required beyond the acid itself.

Electrophilic O‑methylation (alkylation) of phenol with methyl triflate – phenoxide attacks the methyl group of MeOTf, forming anisole and generating triflic acid. Reaction is fast, performed at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane or acetonitrile, often in the presence of a non‑nucleophilic base (pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize the acid.

Acid‑base double displacement; nitric acid protonates the tellurate anion to produce telluric acid while Ba²⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to form soluble barium nitrate. Conducted in aqueous solution with stirring and gentle heating; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Mercury(II) acetate‑mediated dehydrohalogenation of 2,3‑dibromobicyclo[2.2.1]heptane to give bicyclo[2.2.1]hept‑2‑ene; the reaction proceeds via formation of an organomercury intermediate and elimination of two bromide ions, generating HgBr₂ and acetic acid as by‑products; generally carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature with stoichiometric Hg(OAc)₂.

Electrophilic aromatic formylation (Gattermann–Koch/Duff type) using hexamethylenetetramine and trifluoroacetic acid; the combination generates a formyl cation equivalent that installs a CHO group at the 9‑position of anthracene to give 9‑anthracenecarboxaldehyde; conducted by heating anthracene with HMTA in excess TFA (often neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent) at 60–80 °C; no external metal catalyst required.

Boron tribromide mediated cleavage of aryl methyl ethers (demethylation); BBr₃ attacks the methoxy group of 2,4‑dibromoanisole, forming a phenolic bromide and releasing methyl bromide; typically performed in dry dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen, then warmed to room temperature; reagents are used in stoichiometric excess, and the reaction is quenched with aqueous work‑up.

Chloromethane + water -> methanol + hydrogen chloride: hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution, SN2) of a primary alkyl halide; purpose is conversion of CH3Cl to methanol; key transformation is attack of water oxygen on the methyl carbon displacing Cl‑; generally slow at ambient temperature, accelerated by heating (reflux) and often acid or base catalysis; performed in aqueous media, sometimes under steam or in sealed vessels.

Type: Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction. Purpose: Oxidize bromic acid (HBrO3) to perbromic acid (HBrO4) while reducing hydrogen peroxide to water. Key transformation: H2O2 + HBrO3 → H2O + HBrO4 (overall transfer of two electrons from peroxide to bromine). Typical conditions: Conduct in dilute acidic aqueous solution (pH ≈ 1–2) at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control the highly oxidative environment; reaction proceeds rapidly, often in the presence of excess HCl to stabilize perbromic acid. Solvent: water. No additional catalyst is generally employed.

1. Metathesis/precipitation (double displacement) in aqueous solution; ammonium hydroxide reacts with chromium(III) bromide to give insoluble chromium(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium bromide; performed by mixing aqueous NH4OH and CrBr3 at room temperature; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

2. Hydrolysis of a sulfonyl chloride; water attacks 2,4,6‑trimethylbenzenesulfonyl chloride forming the corresponding sulfonic acid and releasing hydrogen chloride; typically carried out in water or aqueous organic solvent at 0‑25 °C, sometimes acid‑catalyzed; solvent is water; no special catalyst needed.

3. Transesterification; dimethyl decanedioate reacts with ethanol to exchange the methyl ester groups for ethyl groups, producing diethyl decanedioate and methanol; catalyzed by acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOMe), refluxed in excess ethanol which also serves as solvent; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium forward.

4. Metallothermic reduction (metal displacement) of scandium(III) chloride by calcium; solid‑state high‑temperature reaction in an inert atmosphere (often >800 °C) that yields scandium metal and calcium chloride; performed in a sealed tube or furnace with no solvent; calcium acts as the reducing agent, no catalyst required.

Oxidative dimerization; used to synthesize the indigo dye from indoxyl. Two indoxyl molecules are oxidized by hydrogen peroxide and couple to form indigo, with water as the only by‑product. Typically performed in aqueous or ethanol/water solution at ambient temperature, pH kept mildly acidic (often with a carbonate buffer); hydrogen peroxide is the oxidant, no additional catalyst required.
Dehalogenation (elimination of dibromide); forms alkene via zinc-mediated reductive elimination; zinc dust in ethanol acts as reducing agent; eliminates 1,2-dibromide to form double bond.

Catalytic hydrogenation reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an amine; converts 4‑nitro‑N,N‑dimethylaniline to 4‑amino‑N,N‑dimethylaniline. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure of 1–5 atm, 5 % Pd/C (or PtO₂, Raney Ni) as catalyst, ethanol or methanol as solvent, temperature 25‑50 °C. Reaction proceeds via nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates to give the aniline.

Single‑replacement / acid‑metal redox reaction. Chromium metal is oxidized from 0 to +3 while dilute sulfuric acid is reduced, releasing H₂ gas. Used to generate chromium(III) sulfate and liberate hydrogen. Typically performed with aqueous H₂SO₄ (≈1 M) at 50–80 °C; vigorous stirring helps. No special catalyst required.

5. Photochemical radical chlorination using N‑chlorosuccinimide; light activates NCS to generate chlorine radicals that chlorinate the methyl group of 5‑methylfurfural, giving 5‑chloromethylfurfural and succinimide as byproduct; carried out in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane under UV/visible illumination at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization); used to convert a lithium arsenate salt into arsenic acid; chloride ions exchange with arsenate and protons protonate the AsO4³⁻ to give H3AsO4 while Li⁺ forms LiCl; performed in aqueous solution with dilute HCl at ambient temperature; water serves as solvent.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of a metal acetate; employed to obtain terbium(III) oxide from its acetate precursor; the acetate ligands break down, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and leaving Tb₂O₃ as the solid residue; carried out by heating the solid to 400–800 °C in air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an internal alkyne; purpose is full saturation of the C≡C bond to give an alkane; two equivalents of H₂ add across the triple bond converting 2‑pentyne to pentane; typical conditions use H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni in a solvent like ethanol or THF at 25–80 °C.

Acyl exchange (transacylation) between a carboxylic acid and an acid anhydride; used to generate benzoyl acetate while converting benzoic anhydride to benzoic acid; one acetyl group is transferred from acetic acid to the benzoic anhydride carbonyl; usually performed by refluxing the mixture in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, often with catalytic DMAP or a trace acid to accelerate the process.

Type: Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation). Purpose: preparation of methyl 2‑ethylhexanoate. Key transformation: protonated 2‑ethylhexanoic acid reacts with methanol; water is eliminated to give the methyl ester. Typical conditions: excess methanol as solvent, catalytic amount of strong acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH), reflux 3‑6 h; removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic distillation) drives equilibrium.
Acid‑base neutralization; hydrogen bromide reacts with potassium hydroxide in water to produce potassium bromide and water; carried out at room temperature in aqueous medium, no catalyst required.

Methanolysis (transesterification) of a phenyl N‑phenylcarbamate; purpose is to cleave the phenoxy fragment to afford phenol and a methyl phenylcarbamate; methanol attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing phenoxide; reaction is typically run under reflux in methanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOMe) to promote the nucleophilic substitution.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; converts 1H‑pyrazol‑3‑ylmethanol to pyrazole‑3‑carboxylic acid; the –CH₂OH group is oxidized through aldehyde and acid intermediates to the –COOH function; performed in aqueous alkaline medium (NaOH or KOH) with KMnO₄ at reflux, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the product.

Acid‑chloride hydrolysis; 4‑methylbenzoyl chloride reacts with water to give 4‑methylbenzoic acid and HCl. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in aqueous medium; the HCl formed is often neutralized with NaOH or Na2CO3. Solvent can be a mixture of water and an organic solvent such as ether.

LiAlH₄ reduction of a carboxylic acid; reduces 3‑bromopropanoic acid to the primary alcohol 3‑bromo‑1‑propanol while preserving the bromide. Key transformation: conversion of –CO₂H to –CH₂OH. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to rt, addition of LiAlH₄ under inert atmosphere, followed by careful aqueous work‑up (e.g., dilute HCl) to quench excess hydride and generate Al(OH)₃ precipitate.

Acid‑base exchange/neutralization; ammonium perrhenate reacts with potassium hydroxide, the NH₄⁺ is deprotonated to release NH₃ gas, water forms, and the perrhenate anion pairs with K⁺ to give potassium perrhenate. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off NH₃; no catalyst required.

Ammonolysis (nitride synthesis); formation of dysprosium nitride. Dy2O3 is placed in a tubular furnace and heated to 800‑1200 °C while flowing NH3 (often with a small H2 stream to aid water removal). The oxide reacts with ammonia, releasing H2O and generating DyN solid. No liquid solvent; gas‑solid reaction.

Mannich-type condensation; purpose is to install a 3‑pyrrolyl side chain on ethylenediamine. Formaldehyde reacts with ethylenediamine to form an iminium intermediate, which is attacked by pyrrole at its C‑3 position, giving 2‑(1H‑pyrrol‑3‑yl)ethan‑1‑amine and water. Typically performed in a polar protic solvent (e.g., methanol or ethanol) at ambient temperature or gentle reflux; acid catalysis (e.g., acetic acid) may be used to promote iminium formation.

Direct chlorination of chromium(VI) oxide with concentrated HCl to give chromyl chloride and water; this is an anhydride formation reaction used to prepare CrO2Cl2; key step is replacement of oxygen by chloride to form the mixed oxide chloride; carried out with excess conc. HCl, mild heating, typically neat or in a non‑reactive glass vessel.

General type: Precipitation (double displacement). Purpose: Synthesis of silver azide (AgN3). Key transformation: Sodium azide reacts with silver nitrate to form insoluble AgN3. Conditions: Aqueous solution, room temperature. Solvent: Water. Catalyst: None.

Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2); purpose is to convert an alkyl bromide to the corresponding alkyl iodide. Sodium iodide nucleophilically displaces bromide from ethyl bromoacetate, yielding ethyl iodoacetate and precipitating sodium bromide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone (or DMF) where NaBr is insoluble; reaction proceeds at reflux or room temperature until complete precipitation of NaBr.

Type: Appel‑type halogenation (alcohol to bromide). Purpose: replace the hydroxyl group of diphenhydramine (or the benzylic ether carbon bearing a hydroxyl in derivatives) with bromine to give bromodiphenhydramine. Key transformation: thionyl bromide activates the C–OH bond, forming an alkyl bromide while releasing HBr and SO2 gases. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane as solvent, 0 °C to room temperature, catalytic pyridine or triamine to capture HBr; reagents added dropwise under inert atmosphere. By‑products (HBr, SO2) are vented or trapped.

Oxidative sulfoxidation; purpose is to oxidize the thioether of fenbendazole to the sulfoxide (oxfendazole). Sodium periodate serves as a stoichiometric oxidant, converting the sulfide to a sulfoxide while itself being reduced from periodate (IO₄⁻) to iodate (IO₃⁻). The reaction is usually performed in a mixed aqueous/acetone medium at 0–25 °C, often with a catalytic amount of a phase‑transfer agent to improve contact between phases.

Metathesis (double displacement) of carbonate and acetate salts; purpose is to generate insoluble silver carbonate while exchanging the cation to sodium. Sodium carbonate reacts with silver acetate in aqueous solution, precipitating silver carbonate and forming soluble sodium acetate. The reaction is carried out in water at ambient temperature; the solid silver carbonate is isolated by filtration and washing.

Gas‑solid acid–base/precipitation synthesis of a metal selenide; purpose is to prepare cobalt(II) selenide from cobalt(II) carbonate and hydrogen selenide. H₂Se gas protonates the carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O, while the selenide anion combines with cobalt(II) to precipitate CoSe (cobalt selenide). Conducted in a sealed tube or flow reactor under an inert atmosphere, typically at elevated temperature (100–200 °C) to drive off CO₂ and promote formation of the black CoSe solid.

Reduction of cadmium oxide by hydrogen telluride (H₂Te) to form cadmium telluride and water; gas‑solid reaction performed at 300–600 °C in an inert flow of H₂Te (often generated in situ) to avoid oxidation; no additional catalyst.

Radical oxidation: an acetyl radical reacts with hydrogen peroxide, producing acetic acid and a hydroxyl radical. Occurs in the gas phase or solution under radical‑generating conditions (e.g., UV irradiation, high temperature); no specific solvent or catalyst is required, and the process is relevant to atmospheric or combustion chemistry.

Peracid epoxidation; converts cyclopentene to 1,2‑epoxycyclopentane using peracetic acid. Key transformation is insertion of an oxygen across the C=C bond (alkene to epoxide) with acetic acid generated as by‑product. Typically performed in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic amination (SN2) of an α‑chloro ketone; dry ammonium carbonate furnishes ammonia that displaces chloride on α‑chloroacetophenone, yielding phenacylamine. The carbonate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O, which are also formed. Usually carried out in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, water/ethanol mixture) with gentle heating (reflux) to drive off CO₂.

Transesterification (alcoholysis); purpose is to replace the octan‑2‑yl group of the acetate with an ethyl group, producing ethyl acetate and 2‑octanol. Transformation: R'OCOCH3 + EtOH → EtOCOCH3 + R'OH. Usually catalyzed by acid (H2SO4, p‑TsOH) or base (NaOEt) under reflux with excess ethanol; removal of ethyl acetate (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) drives the reaction. Solvent can be ethanol itself or anhydrous toluene.

Oxidative combustion of trimethylindium, where oxygen oxidizes the methyl groups to carbon dioxide and water while forming indium oxide; usually carried out by heating the compound in air or flowing O₂ at 300–500 °C, without solvent.

Alkylation of a selenide (SN2); sodium hydroselenide (SeH⁻) attacks methyl iodide to give methylselenol (CH₃SeH) with NaI as by‑product. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0–25 °C to minimize side reactions; often performed under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of the selenol.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis; aqueous H₂SO₄ protonates the aminoacetaldehyde dimethyl acetal, promoting cleavage to the free aldehyde (aminoacetaldehyde) and two equivalents of methanol. Reaction is run in dilute sulfuric acid aqueous solution, typically at reflux temperature (≈80 °C) until completion; work‑up involves neutralization and extraction.

Acid–base reaction; HF reacts with iron(II) oxide to give iron(II) fluoride (FeF₂) and water; key transformation is conversion of Fe‑O to Fe‑F; usually carried out in aqueous HF at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Redox oxidation of Fe(II) by permanganate in acid; potassium permanganate oxidizes ferrous acetate (Fe²⁺) to ferric acetate (Fe³⁺) while being reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn(II) sulfate. Sulfuric acid provides the acidic medium and supplies the sulfate counter‑ions. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating; stoichiometry is adjusted to consume KMnO₄ completely, yielding water as the only neutral by‑product.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; sodium methoxide in methanol catalyzes exchange of the ethoxy group of ethyl cyclopentanecarboxylate for a methoxy group, affording methyl cyclopentanecarboxylate and ethanol; conducted at reflux in methanol solvent, using catalytic amounts of NaOMe, no further catalyst required.

Reductive amination of cyclopropanone; ammonia adds to the carbonyl of cyclopropanone forming an imine intermediate, which is then reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to give cyclopropylamine. The reaction proceeds in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol, buffered to mildly acidic pH (≈4–6) to facilitate imine formation, usually at 0–25 °C. Water is generated as the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an organic azide to a primary amine; purpose is to replace the –N₃ group with –NH₂ while releasing N₂ gas. Key transformation: reduction of the azide nitrogen to amine; nitrogen gas eliminated. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate) at room temperature to moderate heating.

Metathesis/ion‑exchange (double displacement) to form a calcium salt. Purpose: exchange Na⁺ for Ca²⁺, isolating calcium 2‑hydroxypropanoate. Key transformation: sodium 2‑hydroxypropanoate reacts with Ca(OH)₂ to give calcium 2‑hydroxypropanoate and NaOH. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric mixing of the two salts at ambient temperature; the calcium salt often precipitates and is filtered.

Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction; manganese dioxide oxidizes iodide to iodine while being reduced to manganese(II) iodide; MnO2 + 4 HI → MnI2 + 2 I2 + 2 H2O; performed by heating solid MnO2 in aqueous HI (often under reflux); water solvent, no catalyst; commonly used for laboratory iodine preparation.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of calcium titanate (CaTiO₃); a ceramic perovskite preparation. Key transformation: solid‑state combination of CaO and TiO₂ to form the mixed oxide lattice, releasing no volatile by‑products. Typical conditions: intimate mixing of dry powders followed by heating at 1000–1300 °C in a furnace for several hours under air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of ethyl 2‑methoxybenzoate to 2‑methoxybenzoic acid; purpose is to convert the ethyl ester into the free acid while generating ethanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon, displacement of ethanol. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl (concentrated or 1 M) for 2–6 h, often in a mixture with a water‑miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF or dioxane) to improve solubility; product isolated by extraction and acidification.

Salt metathesis (ion exchange) to generate tetrabutylammonium fluoride from the chloride salt using sodium fluoride. Performed in a polar solvent such as acetonitrile or water; NaCl precipitates and is removed, leaving soluble TBAF for subsequent use.

TEMPO‑mediated oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using sodium hypochlorite; purpose is selective conversion of 2‑hexanol to 2‑hexanone under mild conditions. Key transformation: catalytic oxidation of the –CH(OH)– group to a carbonyl, with NaOCl as terminal oxidant and TEMPO as redox carrier. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 8–9, NaHCO₃), NaOCl (bleach, 5–10 % w/v), catalytic TEMPO (≈ 5 mol %), sometimes NaBr as co‑catalyst, at 0 °C to room temperature; solvent may be a biphasic mixture of CH₂Cl₂/water or MeCN/water.

Hydrolysis of methyl (9Z,12Z)-octadeca-9,12-dienoate (methyl linoleate) to the corresponding free fatty acid (linoleic acid); purpose is to obtain the acid from its methyl ester. Key transformation: cleavage of the methyl ester bond by water, producing methanol and the diene‑containing carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: either base‑catalyzed saponification (NaOH or KOH, aqueous ethanol, reflux 2–4 h) followed by acidification with dilute HCl, or acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (conc. H₂SO₄, reflux) in water or water‑alcohol mixture; product isolated by extraction and acid work‑up.

Reaction of elemental beryllium with concentrated sulfuric acid; a redox acid‑metal reaction that generates hydrogen gas and beryllium sulfate. Key transformation: oxidation of Be⁰ to Be²⁺ and reduction of H⁺ to H₂. Typical conditions: addition of Be metal to hot (≈ 80–100 °C) concentrated H₂SO₄ under a fume hood; hydrogen gas evolves, and the aqueous solution contains BeSO₄; no additional solvent or catalyst required.

Reduction of an organic hydroperoxide to the corresponding alcohol using sodium sulfite as a stoichiometric reducing agent. Sodium sulfite donates electrons, converting the O‑O bond of ethylbenzene hydroperoxide into a hydroxyl group, forming 1‑phenylethanol while being oxidized to sodium sulfate. Typically carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (azidation); purpose is to install an azide handle for further click chemistry; iodide is displaced by azide ion from sodium azide, giving 1‑azidopentane and sodium iodide; reaction is usually run in DMF, DMSO, or acetone at 40–80 °C; azide provides a versatile functional group for later cycloaddition.

Phosgene (diphosgene) mediated synthesis of phenyl isocyanate from aniline. The amine attacks the carbonyl carbon of diphosgene, releasing two equivalents of HCl and giving phenyl isocyanate. Performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0–5 °C under inert atmosphere, often with a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge HCl.

Acid‑base metathesis of aluminium selenide with hydrobromic acid to generate hydrogen selenide gas and aluminium bromide. HBr protonates the selenide anion, liberating H₂Se, while Al³⁺ forms AlBr₃. Conducted in aqueous HBr solution, typically at reflux; the reaction is carried out in a sealed system to capture the toxic H₂Se gas.

Acid–base neutralization and salt formation; tungstic acid is neutralized by ammonium hydroxide to generate water and the ammonium tungstate salt (NH4)2WO4; typically performed in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient to mildly elevated temperature; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

TEMPO‑catalyzed oxidation of ethyl lactate to ethyl pyruvate using sodium hypochlorite as the terminal oxidant. TEMPO (a nitroxyl radical) abstracts the α‑hydrogen of the secondary alcohol, and NaOCl re‑oxidizes TEMPO, delivering the ketone product. Typical conditions: biphasic mixture of water and an organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN), pH 8–9 buffered with sodium bicarbonate, ambient temperature, catalytic amount of TEMPO.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction used to prepare ammonium dichromate; sodium dichromate reacts with ammonium chloride in aqueous solution, exchanging cations to give ammonium dichromate and sodium chloride; typically performed at room temperature with stirring, no catalyst required, water as solvent.

DCC‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification) to synthesize meclofenoxate; p‑chlorophenoxyacetic acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide, then reacts with dimethylaminoethanol to form the ester (meclofenoxate) while generating dicyclohexylurea as by‑product; carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is mandatory, though a catalytic amount of DMAP can accelerate the reaction.

Catalytic hydrogenation of (3Z)-hexa‑1,3,5‑triene to hexane; hydrogen gas is applied in the presence of palladium on carbon (Pd/C) to reduce all three C=C bonds, yielding the fully saturated alkane; typical conditions are 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate or THF, ambient to 50 °C; reaction is heterogeneous and does not require added reagents.

Metathesis (acid‑base) reaction in aqueous medium; ammonium hydroxide replaces sodium in tetrasodium pyrophosphate producing soluble ammonium pyrophosphate and NaOH; done at room temperature in water; no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide ring‑opening (hydrolysis) to give a vicinal diol; protonation of the epoxide oxygen followed by nucleophilic attack of water yields 1,2‑butanediol; generally carried out in dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) in water or a water‑mixed organic solvent at 0–50 °C; acid acts as catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose: form the sodium salt of 2‑methylpropanoic acid; key transformation: CH3CH2C(O)OH + NaOH → CH3CH2C(O)ONa + H2O; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed epoxide ring opening of glycidyl acetate; hydroxide ion attacks the less‑substituted carbon of the epoxide, opening the ring to give 2,3‑dihydroxypropyl acetate. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH (often 1 M) at 0 °C to rt, sometimes with co‑solvent (MeOH, ethanol) to aid solubilization; product isolated after acidification and extraction.

Acid–base neutralization / salt formation converting ammonium chloride and perrhenic acid into ammonium perrhenate and releasing hydrochloric acid; performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off HCl gas; no catalyst needed; the resulting ammonium perrhenate can be isolated by evaporation or crystallisation.

Acidic ether cleavage (hydrohalogenation) of a primary alkyl methyl ether; HBr protonates the ether oxygen, then bromide attacks the primary carbon displacing methanol and forming 1‑bromobutane. Conditions: excess HBr, reflux in a polar protic solvent (e.g., glacial acetic acid or aqueous HBr); temperature 60–80 °C.

Nucleophilic substitution of benzylic bromide with aqueous ammonia to form a primary amine; the bromide is displaced by NH₃, yielding 2‑phenyl‑1‑propanamine and ammonium bromide; performed in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia solution, often at reflux or room temperature, sometimes with ethanol as co‑solvent.

Electrophilic addition/oxidation of trimethylphosphine by bromine forming trimethylphosphonium bromide; carried out in a non‑protic solvent (CH2Cl2, CS2) at 0 °C to rt, with stoichiometric Br2; no catalyst needed

Oxidative conversion of cyclopropylmethyl bromide to cyclopropanecarboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; KMnO₄ in aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or KOH) oxidises the primary bromide to the carboxylic acid while being reduced to insoluble MnO₂, with KBr formed as a by‑product; reaction is typically run under reflux for several hours, followed by filtration to remove MnO₂ and acidification to isolate the acid.

Halide exchange (metathesis) converting benzyltrimethylammonium chloride to the iodide salt; aqueous hydroiodic acid swaps the chloride for iodide, producing benzyltrimethylammonium iodide and liberating HCl; usually carried out at room temperature or mild heating, aqueous medium, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (methylation) where dimethyl sulfate transfers a methyl group to selenide ion, forming dimethyl selenide and potassium sulfate. Typically carried out in aprotic polar solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 50‑100 °C; no catalyst required though careful exclusion of moisture is essential.

Thermal decomposition/disproportionation of mercuric iodide upon strong heating, yielding metallic mercury and iodine vapor. Carried out by heating HgI₂ above its melting point (~259 °C) in a sealed tube or under inert gas.

Halogenolysis of silicon dioxide with concentrated hydroiodic acid, cleaving Si‑O bonds to give silicon tetraiodide and water. Usually performed by refluxing SiO₂ in 57 % HI (often with excess HI) at 150‑200 °C under inert atmosphere; the HI acts as both reagent and solvent.

Acid–base deprotonation of ammonium bromide by potassium hydride, producing ammonia, hydrogen gas and potassium bromide. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., THF) under inert atmosphere at room temperature; KH serves as the strong base, no additional catalyst needed.

Silyl‑ester formation (esterification) where the acidic proton of acetic acid reacts with triethylchlorosilane, yielding triethylsilyl acetate and HCl. Performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; used to convert a soluble acetate salt into an insoluble sulfate and regenerate acetic acid; the acetate anion exchanges with the sulfate anion forming solid SrSO4 and free CH3COOH; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Metathesis/complexation in aqueous solution where ferric sulfate reacts with citric acid to form ferric citrate complex and liberate sulfuric acid. Typically done by mixing aqueous solutions of the reagents at ambient temperature or mild heating; no catalyst required.

Oxidative cyclization (disulfide formation) – iodine oxidizes the two thiol groups of 1,4‑butanedithiol, generating a six‑membered cyclic sulfide (1,4‑dithiane) while being reduced to 2 HI. Used to protect di‑thiols as dithiane groups. Typical conditions: reflux in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, often with a base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize the generated HI.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation – fuming (concentrated) sulfuric acid acts as electrophile, inserting a sulfonic acid group para to the bromine on bromobenzene, affording 4‑bromobenzenesulfonic acid and water. Standard conditions: excess conc. H₂SO₄, heating to 80–150 °C; the reaction is performed neat (acid serves as solvent).

Carbothermic reduction of a metal oxide – solid zinc oxide is reduced by carbon at high temperature, producing metallic zinc and carbon monoxide. Typical industrial conditions: temperatures of 900–1100 °C in a furnace under an inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent, solid‑state reaction.

Type: direct fluorination (halogenation oxidation). Purpose: synthesis of TiF4 by direct fluorine attack; useful in small‑scale or specialized processes. Key transformation: TiO2 is fluorinated to TiF4 with concurrent release of O2. Conditions: flow of F2 gas over solid TiO2 at 300–500 °C in a fluorine‑compatible reactor (e.g., nickel, Monel). No solvent; no catalyst.

Redox reaction: sodium dithionite acts as a reducing agent while hydrogen peroxide is reduced to water; the dithionite is oxidized to sulfate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often under neutral to slightly acidic conditions; no special catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed dimerization (formaldehyde self‑condensation) – two molecules of formaldehyde undergo an aldol‑type condensation to give glycolaldehyde (HOCH₂‑CHO). Performed in aqueous basic medium (e.g., Ca(OH)₂ or NaOH) at modest temperature (0–50 °C). The reaction is the initial step of the formose pathway.

Type: Swern oxidation (DMSO‑mediated oxidation of an alcohol to a carbonyl). Purpose: to oxidize 3‑hydroxypropionic acid to the corresponding keto‑acid (3‑oxopropanoic acid) under mild, low‑temperature conditions. Key transformation: dimethyl sulfoxide is activated by oxalyl chloride to form the chlorodimethyl‑sulfonium intermediate, which reacts with the hydroxyacid; subsequent addition of triethylamine abstracts the proton, yielding dimethyl sulfide, carbon dioxide, triethylammonium chloride, and the oxidized product. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane as solvent, temperature maintained at –78 °C to 0 °C during oxalyl chloride addition, followed by gradual warming after substrate addition; stoichiometric amounts of DMSO, oxalyl chloride, and triethylamine are used, and the reaction is performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere.

Type: nucleophilic hydride reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Purpose: convert 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde into the corresponding benzyl alcohol for further functionalization. Key transformation: delivery of a hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming a C‑H bond and generating the alcohol; sodium borohydride is oxidized to sodium borate. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in a polar protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or isopropanol; reaction is usually performed under inert atmosphere but not essential. No additional catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis) redox reaction; elemental holmium metal reacts with chlorine gas to form holmium(III) chloride; metal is oxidized and chlorine reduced; performed at elevated temperature (300‑500 °C) under dry chlorine flow in an inert or vacuum‑tight vessel; no solvent or catalyst.

Condensation (hydrazone formation); hydrazine adds to the carbonyl and eliminates water to give acetone hydrazone; usually carried out in ethanol or methanol at room temperature or under reflux; a catalytic amount of acetic acid speeds the reaction; product is isolated by cooling and filtration.

Type: selective partial reduction of a nitro group to a hydroxylamine. Purpose: obtain phenylhydroxylamine, an intermediate for azo coupling or heterocycle synthesis. Key transformation: two‑electron reduction of the nitro group (–NO2) to the N‑hydroxyamine (–NHOH) while sodium dithionite is oxidized to sulfite. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, pH adjusted to neutral or slightly basic, temperature 0–25 °C; excess sodium dithionite is used. No external catalyst; the dithionite itself acts as the reducing agent.

Type: Friedel‑Crafts acylation of an electron‑rich heteroaromatic ring. Purpose: install an acetyl carbonyl at the 2‑position of thiophene to give 2‑acetylthiophene, a building block for further functionalization. Key transformation: electrophilic attack of the acylium ion (generated from acetyl chloride) on thiophene, followed by deprotonation; BF₃·OEt₂ serves as Lewis‑acid catalyst and HCl is released as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane (or chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; stoichiometric BF₃·OEt₂ (1–1.2 equiv) and acetyl chloride (1.1 equiv) are used.

Hofmann β‑elimination of benzyltrimethylammonium hydroxide yielding trimethylamine, styrene (the alkene), and water. The quaternary ammonium hydroxide undergoes thermal decomposition, typically heated to 100‑150 °C under reflux in water or a high‑boiling solvent.

Type: base‑mediated liberation of a free amine from its hydrochloride salt with concurrent carbonate decomposition. Purpose: generate ethanolamine free base and evolve CO₂ for subsequent use. Key transformation: sodium carbonate neutralizes the hydrochloride, forming sodium chloride and water; the carbonate ion decomposes to CO₂ and OH⁻, which assists in deprotonating the amine. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension at ambient temperature or gentle heating (≤50 °C); stoichiometric amounts (1 equiv Na₂CO₃ per 2 equiv ethanolamine·HCl) are mixed, and the evolution of CO₂ is observed. No special catalyst required.

Type: N‑alkylation of an indole nitrogen via SN2 displacement. Purpose: introduce an ethyl substituent on the indole nitrogen of 5‑methoxytryptamine to afford the N‑ethyl derivative, useful in medicinal chemistry. Key transformation: deprotonation of the indole NH by sodium hydride generates a nucleophilic nitrogen anion, which attacks ethyl iodide, displacing iodide and forming the N‑ethyl bond; NaI and H₂ gas are formed as by‑products. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; NaH is added in slight excess, followed by ethyl iodide (1.1–1.5 equiv). No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol-to-alkyl chloride) using thionyl chloride; purpose is to convert the primary hydroxymethyl group of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural into a chloromethyl group. Key transformation: R‑CH₂OH → R‑CH₂Cl with loss of HCl and SO₂ gases. Typical conditions: anhydrous solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; pyridine often serves as both solvent and HCl scavenger.

Type: direct halogenation/oxidative addition (solid‑state synthesis of metal halide); purpose: form iridium(III) iodide; key transformation: Ir(s) + 3 I2 → IrI3(s); typical conditions: heating iridium metal in excess iodine, sealed tube or inert atmosphere at 200–300 °C; usually conducted without solvent or in molten iodine.

Reductive dehalogenation using zinc (metal‑mediated elimination); purpose is to remove two bromine atoms from 2,3‑dibromo‑2‑methylpropanoic acid and generate the α‑β unsaturated acid (methacrylic acid); key transformation is zinc insertion and elimination of ZnBr2 to form a C=C double bond; typical conditions are reflux of the substrate with Zn dust in ethanol or THF under nitrogen; product ZnBr2 stays in solution or precipitates.

Solid‑state metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction; yttrium chloride reacts with sodium phosphide (Na₃P) to exchange anions and produce yttrium phosphide and sodium chloride. The mixture of dry YCl₃ and Na₃P powders is heated in a sealed, evacuated ampoule or under flowing argon. Typical temperature range is 600‑900 °C for 4‑12 h, allowing NaCl to melt/evaporate and drive the equilibrium toward YP formation. No solvent; the reaction may be assisted by a brief grinding of the reagents to increase contact.

Thermal decomposition of a metal dithiocarbamate; purpose is to generate carbon disulfide and free amine while forming insoluble metal sulfide. Key transformation: Ag(SC(S)NEt₂) → CS₂ + HNEt₂ + Ag₂S (often written as AgS). Typical conditions: heating to 150–200 °C in a sealed tube or under nitrogen; no additional solvent required, although a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., refluxing dioxane) can be employed to aid heat transfer.

Oxidation. Converts a hydrazo (-N-N-) bond to an azo (-N=N-) bond. Purpose: Synthesis of azobenzene from hydrazobenzene. Key transformation: Oxidative dehydrogenation of the azane-azene system. Reaction conditions: Copper(II) chloride (CuCl2) as a catalyst and oxidizing agent under mild heating. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is formed as a byproduct. Synthesis typically occurs in aqueous or aqueous-ethanolic solvents at moderately acidic pH.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acyl chloride with an alcohol; purpose is to form an ester (ethyl heptanoate). Key transformation: Heptanoyl chloride + EtOH → EtO‑C(O)‑(CH₂)₅‑CH₃ + HCl. Typical conditions: dry organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, with a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or 2,6‑lutidine) to capture the generated HCl.

Acid–base neutralization/precipitation reaction; purpose is to convert a basic carbonate into the corresponding metal sulfate while evolving CO₂. Key transformation: Nd₂(CO₃)₃ + 3 H₂SO₄ → Nd₂(SO₄)₃ + 3 CO₂↑ + 3 H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, gentle heating to promote CO₂ release, stoichiometric addition of sulfuric acid under stirring.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange anions and cations, forming copper(II) fluoride and potassium sulfate. Key transformation: CuSO₄ + 2 KF → CuF₂ (precipitate) + K₂SO₄ (soluble). Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; optional mild heating to improve crystallization of CuF₂.

Free‑radical chlorination (substitution). Chlorine gas abstracts a hydrogen atom from the primary carbon of 2,2,4‑trimethylpentane, forming 1‑chloro‑2,2,4‑trimethylpentane and HCl. Reaction proceeds via a radical chain mechanism, initiated by heat or UV light. Typical set‑up: Cl₂ (excess), CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂ as solvent, 60–120 °C, inert atmosphere.

A redox reaction where dihydroxyacetone phosphate is reduced to L-alpha-glycerophosphate using ubiquinol as the electron donor, which is oxidized to ubiquinone. This enzymatic process occurs in biological systems, facilitated by enzymes like glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase in aqueous environments. Purpose: part of the glycerophosphate shuttle for energy metabolism.

Precipitation/metathesis reaction forming an insoluble metal silicate; purpose is to isolate zirconium silicate and regenerate nitric acid. Key transformation: H₄SiO₄ + Zr(NO₃)₄ → ZrSiO₄ (solid) + 4 HNO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH adjustment (often slight acidity), heating to ~80 °C with continuous stirring to promote nucleation of ZrSiO₄; the product is filtered and washed.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of laurolactam to 12‑aminododecanoic acid; water attacks the carbonyl of the lactam, opening the ring to give the corresponding ω‑amino acid; usually carried out in aqueous HCl or NaOH at reflux (80‑120 °C), sometimes with a co‑solvent (e.g., ethanol); purpose is to obtain the linear amino acid from the cyclic lactam.

Reductive dehalogenation of a tertiary alkyl iodide using zinc dust; purpose is to replace the C–I bond with a C–H bond to afford the saturated alkane; key transformation involves single‑electron transfer from Zn to generate an alkyl radical that captures a hydrogen atom, with ZnI2 formed as the inorganic by‑product; reaction is usually performed by stirring zinc dust in refluxing ethanol or aqueous ethanol, sometimes under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to replace the ethoxy group of the ester, producing ethyl acetate and 2‑fluoroethanol; ethanol attacks the protonated carbonyl of 2‑fluoroethyl acetate, yielding ethyl acetate and the fluorinated alcohol; typical conditions: reflux in excess ethanol with 5–10 % strong acid (H₂SO₄, HCl) for 1–4 h; solvent is the ethanol reactant.

Electrophilic halogenation of a nucleoside; purpose is to prepare the antiviral analogue idoxuridine. Iodine replaces the C‑5 hydrogen of the uracil ring in 2′‑deoxyuridine, giving 5‑iodo‑2′‑deoxyuridine and generating HI. Usually carried out in methanol or aqueous methanol under reflux, often with a weak base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to facilitate formation of the electrophilic I⁺ species.

Metathesis/precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction; purpose is to exchange chloride for fluoride to isolate low‑solubility SmF3; key transformation: SmCl3(aq) + 3 NH4F(aq) → SmF3(s) + 3 NH4Cl(aq); typical conditions: aqueous solutions mixed at ambient temperature, often followed by gentle heating (30–50 °C) to improve precipitation; water solvent, no catalyst; ethanol or acetone may be added to aid solid recovery.

SN2 O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of cyclohexanol with methyl triflate; used to install a methyl ether protecting group. The hydroxyl oxygen attacks MeOTf, displacing triflate and forming cyclohexyl methyl ether while producing triflic acid. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; a mild base such as pyridine or triethylamine is often added to scavenge the generated HOTf.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of normorphine with allyl iodide to give nalorphine, an opioid antagonist; HI is released as by‑product. The secondary amine nitrogen of normorphine attacks the allyl carbon, displacing I⁻. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or acetone) with a base (e.g., K₂CO₃ or NaH) at 0–25 °C to suppress side reactions and capture the generated HI.

Acid–base protonation of sodium selenide; purpose is to generate the hydrogen selenide anion (NaHSe) from Na₂Se. One equivalent of HCl protonates Se²⁻ to give NaHSe and NaCl. Performed in aqueous solution at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control the release of H₂Se gas; no catalyst required.

Grignard carboxylation; phenylmagnesium bromide adds to carbon dioxide to give the magnesium benzoate intermediate, which after protonationor directly in the presence of NaOH) affords sodium benzoate. Key transformation is formation of a new carbon‑carbon bond between the aryl nucleophile and CO2. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) under anhydrous conditions, followed by aqueous work‑up with NaOH to isolate the sodium salt.

Multicomponent reductive amination (Mannich‑type) of ammonia with three equivalents of 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde, followed by NaBH₄ reduction; provides tris(2‑pyridylmethyl)amine, a tetradentate N‑donor ligand. Each aldehyde forms an imine with ammonia, which is subsequently reduced by NaBH₄ to the secondary amine. Conducted in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to rt, using stoichiometric NaBH₄; no additional catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement metathesis/precipitation in aqueous solution. Magnesium bromide solution is mixed with aqueous ammonium carbonate; insoluble MgCO₃ precipitates while ammonium bromide remains in solution (MgBr₂ + (NH₄)₂CO₃ → MgCO₃↓ + 2 NH₄Br). Reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring; the solid carbonate is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine using palladium on carbon (Pd/C); similar purpose as above. The nitrile is treated with H2 (1–3 atm) in the presence of Pd/C (5–10 wt %) in ethanol or methanol at room temperature to 60 °C, yielding 4‑methoxybenzylamine after work‑up. Reaction proceeds via imine/intermediate amide and is complete within several hours.

Redox (acidic oxidation‑reduction) reaction; classical preparation of chlorine gas. MnO₂ is reduced by concentrated HCl, generating Mn²⁺ (as MnCl₂), water, and Cl₂. Typically performed by heating MnO₂ with excess conc. HCl in a dry glass apparatus; the chlorine gas is distilled off. No solvent; reaction carried out under reflux or in a distillation setup.

Radical benzylic bromination of 1‑methyl‑2‑nitrobenzene using N‑bromosuccinimide; type: free‑radical halogenation. Purpose: convert the methyl group to a bromomethyl substituent. Key transformation: homolytic cleavage of NBS to generate Br·, which abstracts a benzylic hydrogen; the resulting benzylic radical recombines with Br· to give 1‑(bromomethyl)-2‑nitrobenzene. Typical conditions: reflux in carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often under UV light or with a radical initiator such as AIBN; reaction time 1–4 h. Common solvents/catalysts: CCl₄ or CHCl₃ as solvent, AIBN or benzoyl peroxide as initiator, and a small amount of light.

Nickel‑catalyzed reductive homocoupling (Ullmann‑type) of 2‑bromopyrimidine to give 2,2‑bipyrimidine Zn dust reduces Ni(II)Cl₂ in the presence of the diphosphine ligand dppe to a Ni(0) species, which mediates C–C bond formation between two aryl bromides; ZnBr₂ is formed as a by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (DMF or THF) under nitrogen, reflux temperature (80‑110 °C), with Zn dust added in excess.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) between 2-chloropyridine and sodium cyanide. Purpose: replaces chlorine with a cyanide group. Key transformation: chloro-to-cyano substitution via an anionic intermediate. Conditions: polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF), elevated temperature, often under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (aminolysis of a thioester). Aniline attacks the carbonyl of S‑ethyl propanethioate, displacing ethanethiol and forming N‑phenylpropanamide. Usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at room temperature; a mild base (e.g., triethylamine) may be added to scavenge the released HCl, but the reaction proceeds without external heating.

Aqueous precipitation followed by calcination to afford a rare‑earth oxide. GdCl₃ reacts with excess NaOH to precipitate Gd(OH)₃, which upon heating dehydrates to Gd₂O₃, releasing water and forming NaCl. Performed in water with vigorous stirring at 0‑5 °C to control precipitation, then the solid is filtered, washed, dried, and calcined at 800‑1000 °C in air to obtain the oxide.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction forming a less‑soluble calcium salt. Calcium chloride in aqueous solution reacts with two equivalents of potassium sorbate; KCl remains soluble while calcium sorbate precipitates. The mixture is stirred at ambient temperature, the precipitate filtered, and washed. No special catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction of yttrium sulfate with sodium hydroxide forming yttrium hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst.

Esterification of an acyl chloride with an alcohol (nucleophilic acyl substitution); methanol attacks dichloroacetyl chloride to form methyl dichloroacetate and HCl. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, often with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to trap the generated HCl.

2-chloroheptane undergoes a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction with sodium iodide. The purpose is to replace the chloride with iodide via the Finkelstein reaction. Key transformation includes halogen exchange. Reaction conditions are typically in acetone, where sodium chloride precipitates out.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrite (ester of nitrous acid); water cleaves the O–N bond of isopropyl nitrite, yielding isopropanol and nitrous acid. Usually carried out at ambient temperature in aqueous media; acid or base catalysis can accelerate the reaction but is not required for simple hydrolysis.

Halogen exchange (halogen‑atom transfer) between potassium iodide and N‑bromosuccinimide, producing N‑iodosuccinimide and potassium bromide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile at room temperature under stirring; the reaction proceeds readily without additional catalysts.

Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2) reaction. Sodium iodide in acetone replaces bromide on 1‑bromohexane to give 1‑iodohexane, with NaBr precipitating out of solution. Reaction is performed under reflux in dry acetone; the insoluble NaBr removal shifts the equilibrium toward product formation. No additional catalyst is required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 substitution); methanol is deprotonated (e.g., with NaH or K2CO3) to form methoxide, which attacks 2‑chloropropane to give isopropyl methyl ether, with chloride abstracted as HCl (or captured by the base). Reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at reflux or elevated temperature, under anhydrous conditions to avoid competing protonation of the alkoxide.

Redox oxidation of the tellurite ion by hydrogen peroxide forming potassium tellurate and water; carried out in aqueous solution under mildly acidic conditions to stabilize H₂O₂, at ambient to moderate temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Radical peroxide formation (peroxyester synthesis); tert‑butyl hydroperoxide oxidatively esterifies benzoic acid to produce tert‑butyl peroxybenzoate, releasing water. The key transformation is the generation of the O–O peroxide linkage attached to the benzoate. Often catalyzed by a metal ion (e.g., Fe(II) or Cu(I)) or a Lewis acid, carried out in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen to prevent unwanted side reactions.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to convert 4‑methoxybenzo acid into its methyl ester. Key transformation: acid‑catalyzed condensation of a carboxylic acid with methanol, releasing water. Typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol with catalytic conc. H₂SO₄, removal of water to drive equilibrium. Common solvent: methanol itself; catalyst: sulfuric acid.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (halogenation); purpose is to introduce a third chlorine onto the benzene ring. Key transformation: substitution of a hydrogen on 1,2‑dichlorobenzene by chlorine via an electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism. Typical conditions: Cl₂ gas in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃, at ambient or mildly elevated temperature. Common solvent: carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichloromethane.

Oxidative metal oxidation; purpose is to oxidize elemental aluminum to its oxide while reducing ozone. Key transformation: ozone (O₃) acts as a strong oxidant, converting Al metal to Al₂O₃ and liberating O₂ gas. Typical conditions: dry ozone gas passed over heated aluminum (often 200–400 °C) in a flow reactor; no solvent. Catalyst: none required; reaction is driven by the high oxidizing potential of ozone.

Carbodiimide‑mediated peptide coupling; purpose is to form an amide bond between vanillic acid and glycine. Key transformation: activation of the carboxyl group of vanillic acid by DCC to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, followed by nucleophilic attack by the amino group of glycine, yielding N‑(4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzoyl)glycine and dicyclohexylurea by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in an aprotic polar solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or DMF) with a base such as triethylamine; catalytic DMAP often added to accelerate acyl transfer.

Perborate formation (addition of peroxide). Boric acid reacts with hydrogen peroxide to yield perboric acid and water. Used to produce bleaching/peroxide‑releasing agents. The transformation links a peroxy O‑O bond to boron, producing H2BO4·H2O. Carried out at 0–25 °C in aqueous solution, slowly adding H2O2 to a solution of H3BO3; no catalyst, water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (acetalization). Butanal reacts with excess methanol under catalytic acid (e.g., p‑TsOH or HCl) to give 1,1‑dimethoxybutane. Typical conditions: dry methanol, catalytic acid, reflux or Dean‑Stark removal of water, inert atmosphere; methanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Phenolic O‑methylation (alkylation) using dimethyl sulfate; purpose is to methylate the 3‑hydroxyl of 17α‑ethynyl estradiol, producing mestranol. Key transformation: SN2 attack of the phenoxide anion on the methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, generating a methyl ether and methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. Typical conditions: dissolved in acetone or DMF, base (e.g., K₂CO₃ or NaH) at 0 °C to rt; reaction protected from moisture. Common solvent: acetone; catalyst: none beyond the base.

Peracid oxidation of pyridine nitrogen; purpose is to obtain the N‑oxide of 2‑ethylpyridine. Key transformation: transfer of an oxygen atom from peracetic acid to the lone pair on the pyridine nitrogen, forming the N‑oxide and acetic acid. Typical conditions: stoichiometric peracetic acid in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or acetonitrile) at 0 °C to rt, often under inert atmosphere. Common solvent: dichloromethane; catalyst: none required.

Nucleophilic addition of an organolithium reagent to a ketone; the phenyl lithium attacks the carbonyl of benzophenone to give a tertiary alkoxide which upon aqueous work‑up furnishes triphenylmethanol.
