Key transformation: P₂O₅ abstracts water from hexanamide, forming hexanenitrile and generating one equivalent of water. Typical conditions: excess dry phosphorus pentoxide (1.5–2 equiv) under anhydrous conditions, heating to 120–150 °C in a dry, inert atmosphere. Solvent: often performed solvent‑free or in a high‑boiling, aprotic solvent like toluene or xylene; no catalyst needed.

Chemical reduction of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone to an allylic alcohol using sodium borohydride; selective carbonyl reduction while leaving the conjugated double bond intact; typically performed in methanol, ethanol or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH₄ is added portionwise and the reaction is quenched with water; yields 4‑hydroxy‑2‑nonenal after work‑up.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; elemental yttrium is oxidized by chlorine gas to give yttrium(III) chloride (YCl₃). Conducted by passing dry Cl₂ over heated Y metal (≈300‑500 °C) in a quartz or stainless‑steel under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Carbothermic reduction; purpose: synthesis of zirconium carbide from oxide; key transformation: O atoms are removed from ZrO2 and replaced by C, forming ZrC and CO gas; typical conditions: high temperature (1500–2000 °C) in a closed furnace under inert atmosphere; no solvent, solid‑state reaction.

Palladium‑catalyzed C–N cross‑coupling (azidation of an aryl halide); iodobenzene reacts with sodium azide in the presence of Pd(OAc)₂ and triphenylphosphine to afford phenyl azide, with NaI as by‑product. Typical conditions: DMF or dioxane as solvent, 80‑120 °C, inert atmosphere, 1–5 mol % Pd catalyst, excess NaN₃ (2‑3 equiv). No additional base is required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (elimination) of 2‑hydroxyethanesulfonic acid to give vinylsulfonic acid and water. Performed by heating the sulfonic acid neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., chlorobenzene) with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ (≈10 equiv) at 150‑200 °C; the water formed is removed by distillation. No metal catalyst is involved.

Metal‑mediated reduction of a nitro aromatic compound (Zn/NH₄Cl reduction). Zinc in the presence of ammonium chloride reduces nitrobenzene toiline, generating hydrogen gas and converting Zn to ZnCl₂; ammonia is liberated from NH₄Cl. Typically carried out in refluxing ethanol (or ethanol/water) under an inert atmosphere, at 70–80 °C, with Zn as the reducing agent NH₄Cl providing protons.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation): Scandium oxide reacts with excess acetic acid to give scandium acetate and water. Typically performed by stirring Sc2O3 in glacial acetic acid and heating under reflux to drive off water; no catalyst required. Purpose is to prepare a soluble Sc(III) acetate for further synthesis.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of an acid chloride: Ammonia attacks the carbonyl of heptanoyl chloride, displacing chloride to form heptanamide while HCl is generated. Usually carried out at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: Aqueous silver nitrate exchanges anions with palladium bromide, precipitating insoluble AgBr and leaving palladium nitrate in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; the reaction is driven to completion by the low solubility of AgBr. No catalyst needed.

Alcoholysis of tributyltin chloride with methanol to afford tributyltin methoxide and hydrogen chloride; conducted by refluxing the tin chloride in excess methanol, sometimes with a base (e.g., pyridine) to capture HCl.

Acid‑base neutralization; produces cadmium acetate, a soluble salt useful in further syntheses. Cd(OH)₂ reacts with acetic acid, exchanging OH⁻ for CH₃COO⁻ to yield Cd(CH₃COO)₂ and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle reflux to ensure complete dissolution; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Acidbase metathesis (salt exchange): Hydrochloric acid protonates the tellurate anion, converting potassium tellurate to telluric acid while forming soluble potassium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution, often at room temperature; no special reagents or catalysts are required.

Phosphorylation via POCl3 (condensation): 4‑Nitrophenol is reacted with phosphorus oxychloride in the presence of triethylamine, which scavenges the generated HCl, yielding 4‑nitrophenyl phosphate as its triethylammonium chloride salt. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, dropwise addition of POCl3; no additional catalyst. Purpose is preparation of an activated phosphate ester.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination (halogenation): Tribromoisocyanuric acid serves as a source of Br⁺ to brominate phenol preferentially at the para position, producing 4‑bromophenol and isocyanuric acid as by‑product. Reactions are usually run in acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C; the process is catalyst‑free and may include a mild base to neutralize any HBr formed. Goal is selective para‑bromination of phenol.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; used toesize nickel selenide (NiSe). Hydrogen selenide gas is bubbled through an aqueous solution of nickel nitrate, causing the formation of insoluble NiSe solid and release of nitric acid into the solution. Typically performed under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to prevent oxidation of H2Se; water is the solvent.

Thermal decomposition; solid beryllium hydride decomposes on heating to metallic beryllium and hydrogen gas. Usually performed under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at temperatures above ~600 °C; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Redox halogen exchange (displacement): Chlorine gas oxidizes bromide ions from lithium bromide to elemental bromine while being reduced to chloride, giving bromine and lithium chloride. Conducted by bubbling Cl₂ through an aqueous LiBr solution at 0–25 °C; no catalyst is needed. The reaction provides an in‑situ source of Br₂.

Acid–base reaction; thorium carbonate is converted to its nitrate salt by reaction with nitric acid. Aqueous HNO₃ (moderate concentration, 1–6 M) is added to a suspension of ThCO₃, often with mild heating to accelerate dissolution. The products are thorium nitrate in solution, carbon dioxide gas, and water. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of the nitroxyl radical TEMPO to the corresponding amine; hydrogen gas reduces the N‑O bond yielding 2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine and water; usually performed under H₂ (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C or Raney Ni in a polar solvent (ethanol, THF).

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using sodium cyanoborohydride; mild hydride transfer that converts cyclohexylcarbaldehyde into cyclohexylmethanol; usually performed in methanol or aqueous methanol at pH 7‑8, often at room temperature to gentle heating; no additional catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed amination (Buchwald‑Hartwig coupling) of an aryl bromide with ammonia, forming the C–N bond to give 2‑methoxy‑5‑methylaniline; typical conditions employ Pd(OAc)₂ or Pd₂(dba)₃ with a phosphine ligand, a strong base such as NaOtBu, solvent like toluene or dioxane, and heating to 80‑120 °C.

SN2 substitution of a primary bromide by acetate ion to produce an alkyl acetate ester; commonly carried out with potassium acetate in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often under reflux; the acetate anion serves as nucleophile, and the reaction proceeds without added catalyst; purpose is synthesis of an ester from an alkyl halide.

Thermal decomposition of trichloroacetic acid to generate chloroform and carbon dioxide; a decarboxylation/haloform‑type reaction; carried out by heating the acid (≈150‑200 °C) neat or in a high‑boiling solvent; no catalyst needed.

Redox reduction of tellurium dioxide by carbon monoxide, producing elemental tellurium and carbon dioxide; a gas‑solid oxidation‑reduction reaction performed at elevated temperature (≈400‑500 °C) under a flow of CO; no solvent or additional catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑replacement (metathesis) between sodium oxalate and magnesium chloride, yielding magnesium oxalate precipitate and sodium chloride; conducted by mixing aqueous solutions of Na₂C₂O₄ and MgCl₂ at ambient temperature; water serves as the solvent.

Hydrolysis of benzyl isothiocyanate with water; neutral hydrolysis that converts the –N=C=S group into benzyl amine while releasing carbonyl sulfide (OCS) gas; typically carried out by stirring the substrate in water or a water‑compatible organic solvent (e.g., MeOH/H₂O) at reflux; no catalyst is required, although a small amount of acid or base can accelerate the reaction.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification of ethyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑phenylacetate with methanol, exchanging the ethoxy group for a methoxy group to afford methyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑phenylacetate and ethanol; typically refluxed in excess methanol with catalytic H₂SO₄ or NaOCH₃; methanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Direct fluorination (oxidation‑reduction) of lanthanum sesquioxide; fluorine gas attacks the oxide lattice, producing lanthanum fluoride (LaF₃) and liberating O₂; conducted at elevated temperature (400–800 °C) in an inert reactor, often under controlled F₂ flow; no solvent or catalyst.

Volatilization/decomposition; ammonium hydroxide in solution releases ammonia gas and water, especially upon heating or reducing pressure; essentially the reverse of reaction 3; performed by gentle heating (≈60‑80 °C) or by sparging; no catalyst.

Redox reaction; chromyl chloride reacts with hydrogen peroxide, oxidizing chloride to chlorine gas while converting chromyl chloride to chromium(VI) oxide (CrO₃). Typically performed in dilute aqueous solution at 0–25 °C; excess H₂O₂ added slowly with stirring; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of HCl to an alkene; Markovnikov addition installs a chloride at the more substituted carbon. The reaction proceeds by protonation of the double bond to form a carbocation followed by capture of Cl⁻. It is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; no catalyst is required.

Carbothermic reduction (metal‑oxide reduction by carbon). Chromium(III) oxide is reduced to metallic chromium while carbon is oxidized to CO. Employed in high‑temperature metallurgy to produce chromium metal from its ore. Conducted in a furnace at 1700–1900 °C under inert or reducing atmosphere, using solid carbon or coke as the reductant. No solvent; reaction occurs in the solid state.

Carbonate neutralization (acid–base reaction); converts the hydrochloride salt of 1,4,7‑triazacyclononane to the free base while evolving CO₂. Potassium carbonate is used in water or aqueous‑acetone mixture, typically at room temperature; the reaction releases potassium chloride, carbon dioxide gas, and water.

Acid‑base and redox reaction; metabisulfite reacts with nitric acid, the sulfite portion is oxidized to sulfur dioxide and the acid is neutralized to give sodium nitrate and water; usually performed in dilute aqueous nitric acid at 0–25 °C to control SO₂ evolution; water is the reaction medium, no additional catalyst.

Reduction of an acid chloride to a primary alcohol; trichloroacetyl chloride is reduced by sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)aluminium hydride (Red‑Al) to give trichloroethanol. Conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in anhydrous THF at –78 °C to 0 °C, then allowed to warm to room temperature the reaction is quenched with aqueous NH₄Cl before work‑up.

Salt formation (acid‑base reaction); the diamine N‑(1‑naphthyl)ethylenediamine is protonated by two equivalents hydrochloric acid to afford its dihydrochloride salt. Usually carried out in aqueous HCl at ambient temperature; the product precipitates upon evaporation or addition of a non‑solvent such as acetone.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl phosphate ester; water cleaves the ethoxy group of ethyl dimethyl phosphate to afford dimethyl phosphate and ethanol; generally performed in aqueous acidic or basic medium at moderate temperature (often reflux); solvent is water or an aqueous buffer.

Hydrogenation (reduction) of a high‑oxidation‑state metal oxide; rhenium(VI) oxide (e.g., ReO₃) is reduced by H₂ gas to rhenium(IV) oxide (ReO₂) with formation of water. Performed in a tubular furnace or flow reactor at 300–500 °C under a flow of H₂ (1–5 atm); solid oxide is supported on inert carrier, no solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone; p‑hydroxybenzalacetone undergoes selective reduction of the C=C double bond to afford 4‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)‑2‑butanone. Typical conditions: H₂ (1–3 atm), 10 % Pd/C or PtO₂ as catalyst, ethanol or methanol as solvent, 25–50 °C; reaction monitored until disappearance of the olefinic proton signal.

Reductive carbonylation to form a metal carbonyl; iron(II) chloride reacts with sodium metal under a CO atmosphere to generate iron pentacarbonyl and Na. Conducted in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether under CO pressure (5–10 atm) at 0–25 °C; sodium is added as a dispersion, and the volatile Fe(CO)₅ is removed by low‑temperature distillation, leaving NaCl as solid by‑product.

Metal reduction (single‑electron transfer) where sodium reduces uranium(III) to metallic uranium, forming sodium iodide; usually carried out in a dry, oxygen‑free environment at 150‑250 °C, often in a sealed tube or molten salt medium or dry ether/THF under inert gas; no solvent in solid‑state; purpose is preparation of uranium metal and NaI.

Redox reduction of a mixed metal oxide; hydrogen gas reduces lead tetroxide (Pb3O4) to lead(II) oxide (PbO) while being oxidized to water. Typically carried out at high temperature (400–600 °C) in a flow of H₂ gas, no solvent needed, often under inert atmosphere.

Type: hydrolysis of an acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: convert the reactive 3‑methylthiophene‑2‑carbonyl chloride to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing chloride as HCl and forming 3‑methylthiophene‑2‑carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: addition of the acid chloride to ice‑cold water or dilute aq. NaHCO₃ under stirring, maintaining temperature ≤5 °C, then warming to rt. Common solvents/catalysts: aqueous medium, sometimes pyridine or a non‑nucleophilic base (triethylamine) is used to neutralize HCl generated.

Hydride reduction (dehalogenation) of a primary alkyl chloride; lithium aluminium hydride (LAH) delivers hydride to replace the chloride of 3‑chlorohexane, yielding hexane. Conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, quenched with water; no additional catalyst required.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2); purpose is preparation of benzylamine; key transformation is amide ion displacement of chloride in benzyl chloride to afford benzylamine and KCl; usually run in dry THF or DMF, cooled to 0 °C then allowed to warm to ambient, under inert atmosphere.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; ammonium phosphate reacts with magnesium nitrate in water to form soluble ammonium nitrate and insoluble magnesium phosphate, which precipitates. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; cadmium sulfide reacts with silver nitrate to give soluble cadmium nitrate and insoluble silver sulfide (Ag₂S) precipitate. Conducted in water at room temperature, no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of vinyl acetate; water (often as aqueous NaOH/KOH) cleaves the acetate ester to produce acetic acid (after acid work‑up) and acetaldehyde (from the transient vinyl alcohol). Typical conditions: aqueous base, 50–80 °C, followed by acidification; solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Alcohol mesylation (formation of a sulfonate ester); octanol reacts with methanesulfonyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine, which scavenges the generated HCl, yielding octyl methanesulfonate and triethylammonium chloride. Performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic chlorination (halogenation) of Salinosporamide B using N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) to install a chlorine atom and form (-)-Salinosporamide A. The reaction proceeds via transfer of Cl⁺ from NCS to the allylic/activated carbon of precursor. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or methanol, at 0 °C to room temperature, often buffered (pH ≈ 7–8) to control acidity; NCS serves as both chlorinating reagent and oxidant.

Oxidation‑redox reaction; converts Cu(I) to Cu(II) for preparation of copper(II) chloride. Key transformation: 2 CuCl + Cl₂ → 2 CuCl₂. Typically performed in aqueous chloride solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no required.
Acid–base dissolution; dysprosium(III) oxide reacts with hydrobromic acid to form dysprosium(III) bromide hydrate and water; performed in aqueous HBr, often refluxed to ensure complete conversion.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (alkaline saponification) of an alkyl nitrate. Benzyl nitrate is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide; hydroxide attacks the nitrate ester, yielding benzyl alcohol, sodium nitrate, and water. Reaction is performed at moderate heat (50–80 °C) in aqueous NaOH solution, often in methanol or ethanol as co‑solvent to aid dissolution. Provides a clean method for nitrate removal under basic conditions.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) forming a thioether (Williamson‑type thiolation). Methyl iodide reacts with the thiolate anion from sodium methyl mercaptan to give dimethyl sulfide and NaI. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, usually at 0–25 °C; no additional catalyst needed.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) to produce isopropyl methyl ether. Sodium isopropoxideplaces iodide from methyl iodide, yielding the ether and NaI. Performed in dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO) under inert atmosphere, mild temperatures (0–50 °C); no catalyst required.

Peroxide condensation (acetal formation) yielding triacetone triperoxide (TATP), a primary explosive. Three acetone molecules condense with three H₂O₂ molecules, releasing three water molecules. Carried out in acetone (as solvent and reactant) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) at 0–5 °C to control exotherm; reaction is highly sensitive and must be conducted with extreme safety precautions.

Ozonolysis of allyl alcohol with dimethyl sulfide as reductive work‑up. Ozone adds across the C=C bond of allyl alcohol; subsequent reduction by DMS cleaves the ozonide to give formaldehyde and glycolaldehyde. Typical conditions: O₃ bubbled through a solution of allyl alcohol in CH₂Cl₂ at –78 °C, followed by addition of excess DMS at the same temperature; no metal catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation; iron(III) chloride reacts with ammonium arsenate to give insoluble iron(III) arsenate and soluble ammonium chloride; aqueous solution, stirring, often at room temperature; no catalyst.

acid-base reaction, purpose proton transfer forming amine salt, transformation triethylamine protonated to ammonium ion with tetrafluoroborate counterion. conditions typically in diethyl ether as solvent.
Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl 3‑aminopropanoate to β‑alanine and methanol; carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) under reflux; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne amide; pent‑4‑ynamide is exposed to H2 gas (1–5 atm) over Pd/C in a protic solvent such as EtOH or MeOH at room temperature or slight heating, saturating the C≡C bond to give pentanamide.

Swern oxidation; purpose is to convert tribromoethanol to tribromoacetaldehyde. Key transformation is oxidation of a primary brominated alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde via activation of DMSO with oxalyl chloride to form a chlorosulfonium intermediate, which reacts with the alcohol and is deprotonated by triethylamine. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane, temperature –78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). Reagents are used in stoichiometric amounts; no catalyst beyond the reagents themselves.

Acid‑catalyzed formation of a sulfonate ester (mesylation); purpose is to prepare isopropyl methanesulfonate as a good leaving group. Key transformation is substitution of the hydroxyl hydrogen of isopropanol by the methanesulfonyl group, generating water as a by‑product. Typical conditions: neat or solvent‑free methanesulfonic acid, heating to 60–80 °C for 1–2 h, often under reflux; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to exchange ions and isolate insoluble barium chromate. Key transformation is formation of solid BaCrO₄ and soluble CsCl from BaCl₂ and Cs₂CrO₄. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) of cadmium sulfide; purpose is to synthesize CdS solid. Key transformation is exchange of Cd²⁺ and S²⁻ ions to precipitate CdS while forming soluble KNO₃. Conducted in water at room temperature with vigorous stirring; no catalyst needed.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of thiophene; purpose is to introduce an acetyl carbonyl at the 2‑position of the heteroaromatic ring. Acetyl chloride reacts with AlCl3 to generate the acylium ion (CH3CO⁺) which electrophilically attacks thiophene, producing 2‑acetylthiophene and HCl. Usually performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon disulfide at 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; AlCl3 is used in stoichiometric excess.

Limited‑carbonate acid‑base reaction and metathesis leading to bismuth subnitrate; purpose is to convert bismuth nitrate to insoluble bismuth subnitrate while generating potassium nitrate. Key transformations: carbonate reacts with nitric acid generated in situ, releasing CO₂ and H₂O; Bi³⁺ precipitates as basic nitrate (Bi₅O(OH)₉·nH₂O), and K⁺ combines with NO₃⁻ to give KNO₃. Performed in aqueous solution, mild heating (≈50 °C) improves precipitation; no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis (halide exchange) used to replace the PF6 counter‑anion of Cu(I) with chloride and liberate coordinated acetonitrile. Key transformation: [Cu(CH3CN)4]PF6 + NaCl → CuCl (precipitate) + NaPF6 + 4 CH3CN. Typically performed in dry acetonitrile at room temperature under inert atmosphere; the insoluble CuCl precipitates and is filtered off. No catalyst required.

Magnesiothermic reduction of zirconium difluoride; magnesium reduces ZrF2 to zirconium metal, producing magnesium fluoride as the by‑product. The mixture is heated under inert atmosphere (argon) to 800–1100 °C, typically in a sealed tube or furnace to prevent oxidation. No catalyst or solvent is used; the process relies on the high thermodynamic driving force of Mg→MgF2 formation.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of 1‑chloro‑2‑iodoethane with water; the chloride is displaced by OH⁻ to give 2‑iodoethanol and HCl. Typically carried out in dilute aqueous medium at ambient to mild heating; no catalyst required, HCl can be neutralized with base if needed.

Acid‑catalyzed tert‑butyl ester deprotection (acidolysis). Trifluoroacetic acid protonates the carbonyl of tert‑butyl 2‑hydroxybenzoate, generating a tert‑butyl cation that eliminates isobutylene, yielding salicylic acid. Common conditions: excess TFA (often 1–3 equiv) in dichloromethane or neat, 0 °C to 60 °C, reaction time 1–4 h. No metal catalyst; the acid itself drives the transformation.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling (condensation). Purpose: form N‑ethylbenzamide from benzoic acid and ethylamine. Key transformation: activation of the carboxyl group by DCC to a O‑acylurea intermediate, nucleophilic attack by ethylamine gives the amide and dicyclohexylurea precipitates. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane (or DMF) at 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, optional catalytic DMAP. Byproduct dicyclohexylurea is filtered off.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of barium aluminide. Molecular oxygen oxidizes BaAl intermetallic to the corresponding binary oxides, BaO and Al2O3. Typical conditions: heating the solid BaAl in flowing O2 or air at 800–1000 °C for several hours until complete conversion. No solvent; the reaction is heterogeneous and exothermic.

N‑alkylation of 4‑piperidone via SN2 substitution. Benzyl chloride acts as electrophile; the nitrogen of 4‑piperidone attacks, displacing chloride to give N‑benzyl‑4‑piperidone. Usually carried out with a base (e.g., NaH, K2CO3) in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, at reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours under nitrogen. No transition‑metal catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Buchwald‑Hartwig amination of an aryl bromide with ammonia to form 2‑methoxy‑5‑methylaniline. Pd(OAc)2 combined with tri‑tert‑butylphosphine (Ligand) and a strong base (e.g., NaOtBu) mediates C–N bond formation. Typical conditions: ammonia (gas or aqueous solution, 1–3 equiv), Pd(OAc)2 (1–5 mol %), t‑Bu3P (2–10 mol %), toluene or dioxane as solvent, 80–120 °C for 12–24 h under inert atmosphere. The reaction yields the aniline product after aqueous work‑up.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Deprotonation of catechol by two equivalents of NaOH generates the sodium catecholate dianion and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with stirring until dissolution is complete. No catalyst required.

Acid chloride activation / Vilsmeier reagent formation. The reaction converts N,N‑dimethylformamide (DMF) into the chloro‑N,N‑dimethylformiminium chloride (Vilsmeier reagent) by treatment with thionyl chloride. Purpose: generate a powerful electrophilic iminium species used for formylation of activated aromatic rings and heterocycles. Key transformation: DMF oxygen is replaced by chlorine, forming an iminium cation and releasing HCl and SO₂ gases. Typical conditions: anhydrous, inert atmosphere, often performed neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature; gases evolve and are vented. No catalyst required.

Acyl chloride aminolysis (amide formation). Oleoyl chloride reacts with ammonia to give oleamide and hydrogen chloride. Purpose: synthesis of long‑chain fatty amides used in surfactants, cosmetics, or pharmaceuticals. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of ammonia on the carbonyl carbon of the acid chloride, displacement of chloride, followed by proton transfer to release HCl. Typical conditions: gaseous or aqueous NH₃ at 0 °C to 25 °C, often in anhydrous solvent such as THF or ether; excess ammonia or a base (e.g., pyridine) may be employed to trap HCl. No catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of bromide by cyanide on bromodifluoromethane to give 2,2‑difluoroacetonitrile and NaBr; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often at mild heating (40–80 °C), using NaCN as the nucleophile.

Acid–base halogenation of a metal oxide. Yttrium oxide is reduced by hydrogen iodide to give yttrium iodide, water, and hydrogen iodide is consumed. Purpose: preparation of anhydrous yttrium iodide for use as a precursor in materials synthesis. Key transformation: protonation of the oxide oxygen to form water while iodide anion coordinates yttrium, producing YI₃. Typical conditions: excess HI (often 57 % aqueous) heated under reflux in a sealed tube or round‑bottom flask; removal of water by azeotropic distillation may be employed. No catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a vicinal dihalide. Sodium phenoxide attacks 1,2‑dibromoethane, displacing bromide to form phenoxyethyl bromide (2‑bromoethyl phenyl ether) and sodium bromide. Purpose: synthesis of aryl alkyl ethers. Key transformation: phenoxide oxygen performs backside attack on a primary carbon bearing bromide, forming a C‑O bond while retaining the second bromide. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, ambient or gently heated temperature (20‑50 °C), stoichiometric amounts of Na phenoxide; inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation. No additional catalyst.

Metal‑amido base generation (metalation). Potassium metal deprotonates hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) to produce potassium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (KHMDS) and hydrogen gas. Purpose: preparation of a strong, non‑nucleophilic base used for deprotonation and metallation reactions. Key transformation: single‑electron transfer from K to HMDS, followed by proton abstraction, yielding H₂ and the potassium amide. Typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free environment; THF or diethyl ether as solvent; low to moderate temperature (0 °C to reflux) to control H₂ evolution. No catalyst.

Salt formation (acid–base neutralization). Dothiepin reacts with hydrochloric acid to give dothiepin hydrochloride, the pharmaceutically used salt form. Purpose: improve solubility, stability, and handling of the active pharmaceutical ingredient. Key transformation: protonation of the tertiary amine nitrogen of dothiepin by HCl, forming the corresponding ammonium chloride salt. Typical conditions: dissolve dothiepin in ethanol, methanol, or isopropanol; add aqueous HCl or gaseous HCl at 0 °C to room temperature; stir until precipitation occurs; isolate the solid by filtration and drying. No catalyst needed.

Acid‑base deprotonation (salt formation). A strong alkoxide base (sodium methoxide) abstracts the N‑H proton of imidazole, generating the sodium imidazolate anion and methanol. Typically performed at ambient temperature in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or in methanol itself; no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic nitrosation of urea. Nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO2/HCl) nitrosates the urea nitrogen to give N‑nitrourea and water as by‑product. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium, usually 0–5 °C to limit decomposition; water is the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Oxidative condensation to form 1,5‑diphenylcarbazone. Phenylhydrazine reacts with benzaldehyde to give a phenylhydrazone, which in the presence of molecular oxygen and catalytic Cu(II) chloride undergoes oxidative coupling to the diphenylcarbazone. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or acetic acid, atmospheric O₂, catalytic CuCl₂ (≈5 mol %); reaction time 2–6 h.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of tert‑butyl formate. Hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl of the formate ester, cleaving the C–O bond to afford tert‑butyl alcohol and sodium formate. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at reflux (≈80 °C); water/ethanol mixture is common solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Reduction of a selenocyanate to a selenol; sodium borohydride reduces methyl selenocyanate to methyl selenol, generating sodium cyanoborohydride as by‑product; carried out in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is typically performed under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; calcium chloride exchanges ions with ammonium valerate, giving calcium valerate (often less soluble) and ammonium chloride; allows isolation of calcium valerate by filtration; performed in aqueous solution with stirring, sometimes warmed slightly to improve dissolution; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using dimethyl sulfoxide activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (offatt oxidation). The DMSO serves as the oxygen source, the primary alcohol is converted to the corresponding aldehyde, dimethyl sulfide is released as a volatile by‑product, and dicyclohexylurea forms from the coupling agent. Typically carried out at 0 – 25 °C under inert atmosphere in aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF. No additional metal catalysts are required.

Base‑induced dehydrofluorination (elimination). Strong base (KOH) abstracts a proton and a fluoride from 1,1,1,2,3,3,3‑heptafluoropropane, generating the fluoroalkene hexafluoropropene, water from the hydroxide, and potassium fluoride. Typically performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO or DMF at elevated temperature (100‑150 °C).

Base‑mediated SN2 alkylation (esterification). Jasmonic acid is deprotonated by NaOH to form the carboxylate, which then attacks methyl iodide to give the methyl ester (‑‑‑methyl jasmonate) and sodium iodide. Conducted in a biphasic water/organic system or aqueous methanol, often at 0‑25 °C, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the ester.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt formation) with liberation of a volatile acid. Dilute sulfuric acid protonates the azide anion of silver azide, displacing silver to precipitate silver sulfate and releasing hydrazoic acid (HN₃) into the solution. Reaction is carried out in cold aqueous medium (0‑5 °C) under strict safety controls because HN₃ is highly toxic and explosive.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (Fischer ether synthesis). A mixture of 1‑butanol and 1‑propanol is heated with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., conc. H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH). The acids protonate the hydroxyl groups, facilitating loss of water and forming the mixed ether 1‑propoxybutane. Typical conditions: excess alcohol, 140‑180 °C, removal of water to drive equilibrium.

Acid‑catalyzed redox generation of chlorine dioxide from sodium chlorite; purpose is in‑situ ClO2 production for bleaching, disinfection or oxidation; chlorite ion is oxidized to ClO2 while sulfate forms; carried out in aqueous solution with dilute H2SO4, low temperature (0‑5 °C) and slow addition of acid; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Isotopic exchange between D₂O and H₂; hydrogen gas reduces deuterium oxide to produce D₂ gas and H₂O. Conducted at elevated temperatures (200‑500 °C) in the gas phase over a metal catalyst such as Pt, Pd or Ni and Ni.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). In aqueous solution, oxalic acid exchanges its protons with cadmium acetate: cadmium oxalate precipitates as an insoluble solid, while acetic acid remains in solution. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid is filtered and washed to isolate cadmium oxalate.

Nucleophilic addition of an organolithium reagent to an aldehyde; butyl lithium adds to the carbonyl of benzaldehyde to form a benzylic alkoxide which on aqueous work‑up (water) is protonated, giving 1‑phenyl‑1‑butanol and lithium hydroxide as the by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF or diethyl ether, −78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen or argon, followed by quench with dilute acid or water.

N‑alkylation (SN2 substitution) of 5,5‑diethylbarbituric acid using methyl p‑toluenesulfonate as the alkylating agent; pyridine acts as a base to deprotonate the barbituric nitrogen and as the counter‑ion, forming pyridinium p‑toluenesulfonate. Usually carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetone, DMF or acetonitrile at reflux or 50‑80 °C under inert atmosphere.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation) of iodine trichloride; upon heating ICl₃ breaks down to molecular chlorine gas and iodine monochloride (ICl). The reaction proceeds in the gas phase or in a dry, inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) at elevated temperature (typically > 50 °C).

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; used to convert benzoic acid into its tert‑butyl ester for protecting group or fragrance synthesis; key transformation is condensation of the carboxylic acid carbonyl with tert‑butanol forming tert‑butyl benzoate and water; typical conditions are reflux in a non‑polar solvent (toluene or benzene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, often employing a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water and drive the equilibrium to completion.

Friedel‑Crafts methylation: naphthalene reacts with dimethyl sulfate in the presence of AlCl₃ (anhydrous, inert atmosphere, typically in CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂, 0 °C → rt) to give 1‑methylnaphthalene as the major product, with methyl hydrogen sulfate formed as the acid by‑product.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; Fe₂(SO₄)₃ reacts with CaCl₂ to exchange anions, forming soluble FeCl₃ and insoluble CaSO₄ which precipitates. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid calcium sulfate is removed by filtration.

Acid‑base gas absorption; CO₂ reacts with aqueous KOH to give potassium bicarbonate (KHCO₃). Performed water or dilute KOH solution at room temperature, often under atmospheric pressure; excess base can be used to drive the reaction to completion.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of 4‑mercaptobenzoic acid with ethanol to afford ethyl 4‑mercaptobenzoate; converts the carboxylic acid to an ethyl ester, water is formed; carried out by refluxing ethanol in the presence of a catalytic acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or TsOH); ethanol serves as solvent.

Neutralization of selenous acid with potassium hydroxide; the acid–base reaction yields water and dipotassium selenite (K₂SeO₃). Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric amounts of KOH are added to a cooled solution of H₂SeO₃, then the mixture is allowed to warm and the product is isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Acid hydrolysis of a metal nitride; produces a metal chloride and ammonium chloride. ZrN reacts with aqueous HCl, where the nitride is protonated to release NH₄⁺ (forming NH₄Cl) and Zr⁴⁺ is chlorinated to give ZrCl₄ (or ZrCl₂ depending on stoichiometry). Reaction conducted at room temperature to 80 °C in concentrated HCl solution, often under reflux to drive completion. No catalyst; aqueous HCl serves as both reagent and solvent.

Thermal aqueous decomposition of a β‑ureido acid; β‑ureidoisobutyric acid hydrolyzes and decarboxylates to β‑aminoisobutyric acid while evolving CO₂ and NH₃; the reaction proceeds by cleavage of the ureido C‑N bond and loss of carbon dioxide; generally achieved by heating an aqueous solution (reflux, 80–100 °C) without added reagents.

Oxidation of hydroquinone to 1,4‑benzoquinone; hydrogen peroxide serves as the oxidant, converting the two phenolic OH groups to carbonyls; generally carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., water/acetone) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, sometimes with a catalytic base.

Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidation of (4‑iodophenyl)methanol to 4‑iodobenzaldehyde; the primary alcohol is selectively oxidized to the aldehyde while the periodinane by‑product generates acetic acid; reactions are run in an anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Direct fluorination of hydrazine with elemental fluorine; fluorine gas attacks the N‑H bonds, producing hydrogen fluoride and dinitrogen tetrafluoride (N₂F₄) as the major nitrogen‑fluorine product; performed in the gas phase at low temperature with strict safety controls, no solvent.

Base‑catalyzed trans‑esterification of octyl acetate with sodium methoxide; the methoxide attacks the carbonyl, exchanging the octyl alkoxy group for a methyl group and forming methyl acetate while the octylate anion pairs with sodium; commonly conducted in methanol or THF at reflux under anhydrous conditions.

Oxidative cleavage of 7‑methyl‑1‑octene using ozone followed by hydrogen peroxide work‑up; ozone adds across the terminal double bond to give a ozonide which is reduced by H₂O₂ to afford formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and 6‑methylheptanal from the internal fragment; usually performed in an inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by aqueous H₂O₂ quench.

Solid‑state high‑temperature synthesis (oxide fusion); combines SiO₂ and Na₂O to form the alkaline silicate Na₂SiO₃ (sodium metasilicate). Purpose is to generate a water‑soluble silicate used in detergents, cements, and glass frits. Key is the formation of Si–O–Na bridges through condensation of oxide ions. Typical conditions: mix stoichiometric powders, heat to 900–1100 °C in a furnace under air or inert gas; no solvent, the melt acts as medium.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Magnesium sulfate reacts with sodium tungstate to exchange cations, yielding Na₂SO₄ and sparingly soluble magnesium tungstate (MgWO₄) which precipitates. Purpose is preparation of MgWO₄ for pigments or catalytic supports. Usually performed in water at ambient or mildly elevated temperature with stirring; the solid product is filtered and washed. No special catalyst required.

Chlorination of an ester using phosphorus pentachloride; transforms ethyl 2‑butoxyacetate into 2‑butoxyacetyl chloride while cleaving the ethoxy group to give ethyl chloride and phosphorus oxychloride as by‑products. Performed anhydrously in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or CS₂ at 0 °C → rt under inert atmosphere; excess PCl₅ is removed during work‑up.

Hydrolysis (protonolysis) of tributyltin methoxide; purpose is to replace the methoxy ligand with hydroxide, producing methanol; key transformation is cleavage of the Sn–OCH₃ bond to form Sn–OH and release CH₃OH; typical conditions involve an aqueous workup at ambient temperature, often in a biphasic system with an organic solvent such as THF or toluene; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a diamine; 2‑aminoacetonitrile is hydrogenated over Raney nickel under H₂ pressure (≈50 atm) in ethanol or methanol at 50‑80 °C, reducing the –CN group to a primary amine and producing ethylenediamine; Raney Ni catalyst, protic solvent.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of 4‑nitrophenyl acetate. Water (often as NaOH solution) attacks the carbonyl carbon, cleaving the ester to give acetic acid and 4‑nitrophenol. Purpose is deprotection of the nitrophenyl group or generation of the chromogenic phenol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH at 25–80 °C, followed by acidification to liberate the phenol; solvent can be mixed water‑acetone. No metal catalyst needed.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann ether synthesis (C–O bond formation). Sodium isopropoxide acts as the nucleophile, displacing bromide from 2‑bromopropane under CuI catalysis to give di‑isopropyl ether and NaBr. Purpose is construction of symmetrical ethers. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, refluxed under nitrogen; CuI (5–10 mol %) may be assisted by a bidentate ligand (e.g., 1,10‑phenanthroline). No additional base beyond the alkoxide is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a ketone to a secondary alcohol. 1‑Phenylbutan‑1‑one is reduced by H₂ in the presence of Pd/C to give 1‑phenylbutan‑1‑ol. Purpose is selective carbonyl reduction. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, solvent (EtOH, MeOH, or EtOAc), room temperature to 50 °C, Pd/C (5 wt %). Reaction proceeds via surface adsorption of H₂ and the ketone, delivering hydride to the carbonyl carbon.

Synthesis of bis(2‑chloroethyl)sulfide (mustard gas) from sulfur monochloride and ethylene; a chlorosulfonium‑mediated addition/substitution reaction. Ethylene adds across the S–Cl bonds, forming the dichloroethyl sulfide and precipitating elemental sulfur. Reaction carried out in an inert organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) under reflux with a Lewis‑acid catalyst such as FeCl3 or AlCl3; temperature around 50–80 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of a tertiary alkene; adds water across the double bond to form a tertiary alcohol. Sulfuric acid protonates the double bond, generating a carbocation that is captured by water, giving 2,3‑dimethylbutan‑2‑ol after deprotonation. Conducted with dilute H₂SO₄ (10–20 % v/v) at 0 °C to reflux in an aqueous‑organic mixture (e.g., H₂O/CH₂Cl₂) or neat acid; the reaction is exothermic and often run under cooling initially.

Electrophilic sulfonation (sulfation) of indoxyl using fuming (oleum) sulfuric acid. The strong SO₃/H₂SO₄ mixture transfers a sulfate group to the phenolic oxygen of indoxyl, forming indoxyl sulfate and water. Purpose is preparation of the biologically relevant indoxyl sulfate metabolite. Conducted by adding indoxyl to cooled fuming H₂SO₄ (0–5 °C), then stirring at 0–25 °C; the reaction mixture itself is the solvent, and no added catalyst is required.

Double displacement/acid‑base reaction; purpose is to exchange ions and precipitate insoluble silver bromide; HBr protonates acetate to give acetic acid while Ag⁺ combines with Br⁻ to form AgBr solid; typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; ammonium carbonate reacts with beryllium chloride to form insoluble beryllium carbonate and soluble ammonium chloride; carried out in water, typically at room temperature; the beryllium carbonate precipitate is collected by filtration; no catalyst needed.

Salt metathesis (anion exchange) between pyridinium PF6⁻ and LiCl. Purpose: replace PF6⁻ with Cl⁻ on the pyridinium cation. Key transformation: [C5H5NH]PF6 + LiCl → [C5H5NH]Cl + LiPF6. Typical conditions: ambient temperature, polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, stirring to equilibrium; both salts remain soluble, so reaction proceeds by equilibrium shift; isolation achieved by solvent removal or precipitation of one salt if a suitable anti‑solvent is added.

Halogenation of an organolithium; n‑butyllithium reacts with chlorine to produce n‑butyl chloride and lithium chloride. Carried out at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in dry ether or THF with inert gas protection; Cl₂ introduced dropwise to avoid uncontrolled radical chlorination. Purpose: synthesis of the corresponding alkyl chloride from the organolithium reagent.

Acid‑base deprotonation (salt formation); purpose is to generate the sodium salt of phenytoin for increased solubility or subsequent reactions; sodium amide abstracts the acidic N‑H proton of phenytoin, releasing NH₃ and forming Phenytoin‑Na; performed in an aprotic, moisture‑free solvent such as THF or liquid NH₃ at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C); no added catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) under acidic or basic conditions; purpose is to cleave the phenyl ester to afford phenol and the free furan‑2‑carboxylic acid; water adds across the carbonyl, breaking the C–O(Ph) bond and protonating the leaving phenoxide, which becomes phenol; usually heated in aqueous acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (NaOH) at reflux; water is the reaction medium; acid or base serves as catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; palladium(II) chloride reacts with sodium hydroxide to exchange chloride for hydroxide, yielding insoluble palladium(II) hydroxide and soluble sodium chloride. Performed in water at ambient temperature with an aqueous NaOH solution; the product precipitates and is filtered.

Lithium‑halogen exchange; purpose is to generate a vinyl organolithium reagent (vinyllithium) while transferring the iodine to the sec‑butyl group; sec‑BuLi attacks the C–I bond of iodoethene, delivering Li⁺ to the vinyl carbon and forming 2‑iodobutane as the by‑product; carried out at low temperature (–78 °C to –20 °C) in dry inert atmosphere; no external catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state combination (synthesis of an iron(II) silicate); purpose is to form the mixed oxide FeSiO₃ from its binary oxides; SiO₂ and FeO react and rearrange to give iron(II) silicate lattice; performed by grinding the powders together and heating in a furnace at 900–1200 °C in air or inert gas; no solvent; catalyst not required.

Base‑mediated decomposition of trichloroisocyanuric acid; purpose is to generate hypochlorite (bleach) and cyanuric acid while consuming the chlorinated reagent; NaOH hydrolyzes the N‑Cl bonds, producing NaCl, NaClO (hypochlorite) and cyanuric acid as the residual ring; typically conducted in aqueous solution at ambient or modestly elevated temperature (0–30 °C); water is the solvent; the hydroxide ion acts as the catalyst/base.

Double displacement/metathesis precipitation: aqueous ammonium hydroxide reacts with yttrium iodide, exchanging ions to give soluble ammonium iodide and insoluble yttrium hydroxide precipitate. Performed in water at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid dissolution/redox of sodium bismuthate: concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with sodium bismuthate, reducing Bi(V) to Bi(III) and forming bismuth(III) sulfate and sodium sulfate while generating water. Typically carried out in aqueous medium with heating; no external catalyst.
Acid‑base neutralization of an acid salt: aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes sodium bisulfate, producing water and sodium sulfate. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst.

Enzyme‑catalyzed analogous reaction of O‑acetyl‑L‑serine with hydrogen selenide to afford L‑selenocysteine; selenocysteine synthase (a PLP enzyme) transfers Se⁻ to the substrate, displacing acetate; performed in aqueous buffer, pH 7–8, under anaerobic conditions to avoid oxidation of H2Se.

Acyl chloride synthesis: 1‑adamantanecarboxylic acid is treated with oxalyl chloride, converting the carboxylic acid to the corresponding acid chloride (1‑adamantanecarbonyl chloride) and liberating carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen chloride gases. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMF.

Salt‑base conversion to free base: disopyramide phosphate is treated with calcium hydroxide, which neutralizes the phosphate anion, precipitating calcium phosphate and releasing free‑base disopyramide into solution. Performed in water with gentle heating; filtration isolates the product; no catalyst.

Peroxidase‑catalyzed oxidative hydroxylation of resorcinol with hydrogen peroxide. Purpose: introduce a third hydroxyl group to give 1,2,4‑benzenetriol. Key transformation: C₆H₄(OH)₂ + H₂O₂ → C₆H₃(OH)₃ + H₂O (catalyzed by peroxidase). Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 7), ambient temperature, low H₂O₂ concentration (≤ 10 mM) to avoid over‑oxidation. Enzyme: horseradish peroxidase or similar; no organic solvent required.

N‑Acetylation of serotonin using acetyl chloride and triethylamine. Purpose: protect the primary amine or modify serotonin pharmacologically. Key transformation: 5‑HT (NH₂) + CH₃COCl → 5‑HT‑NHCOCH₃ + Et₃N·HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric triethylamine as HCl scavenger, reaction time 1–3 h. No additional catalyst; inert atmosphere often employed.

Acid-base neutralization (salt formation); acetic acid protonates mercury(II) hydroxide to give mercury(II) acetate and water; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Selective reduction of aldehydes to primary alcohols; NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the two aldehyde groups of pyrrole‑2,5‑dicarbaldehyde to afford 2,5‑bis(hydroxymethyl)pyrrole; performed in methanol, ethanol or isopropanol at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction quenched with water; inert atmosphere optional.

Multicomponent Debus‑Radziszewski condensation; aldehydes (acetaldehyde, glyoxal) and ammonium acetate combine to form a substituted imidazole (2‑ethyl‑1H‑imidazole) with acetic acid and water as by‑products; usually carried out in ethanol or water under reflux for several hours, no external catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of diisopropyl fluorophosphate; the P–F bond is replaced by a P–OH bond, producing diisopropyl phosphate and hydrogen fluoride. Usually carried out in aqueous buffer or dilute NaOH at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and the base scavenges the liberated HF.

Acid‑base (double displacement) reaction of lead(II) sulfide with aqueous sulfuric acid yielding lead(II) sulfate precipitate and hydrogen sulfide gas; carried out at ambient to mildly heated conditions with dilute H₂SO₄; aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Base‑promoted tautomerization/hydration of a cyclic ketone; aqueous NaOH adds to tropone and induces rearrangement to the hydroxy‑ketone tropolone; performed in aqueous alkaline medium at moderate temperature, often with stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type) nucleophilic substitution; fluoride ion from cesium fluoride displaces iodide on methyl iodide to give methyl fluoride insoluble cesium iodide; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, typically at reflux; cesium fluoride acts asophile, no metal catalyst.

Hydrolysis/decomposition; aqueous dissociation of sodium hydrogen selenide to generate sodium hydroxide and hydrogen selenide gas; occurs spontaneously in water, often at room temperature; no catalyst; gas is collected or trapped.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage (hydrolysis). Water in the presence of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, HCl) at reflux protonates the ether oxygen, enabling nucleophilic attack by water on the ethyl groups. Both ethyl fragments are converted to ethanol; the reaction is used to degrade diethyl ether to its corresponding alcohols. Typical solvent is excess aqueous acid; temperature 80‑100 °C.

Copper‑catalyzed N‑alkylation (Ullmann‑type coupling tryptamine nitrogen reacts with benzyl bromide in the presence of CuI and a diamine ligand (N,N‑dimethylethylenediamine) to give N‑benzyltryptamine and HBr; typically run in DMF or DMSO at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere; CuI serves as catalyst, the diamine as ligand.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); purpose: removal of aryl bromide to afford acetophenone; key transformation: C‑Br bond reduced, forming H‑Br as by‑product; typical conditions: H2 (1–3 atm) over Pd/C (10 % loading) in ethanol or methanol at room temperature to reflux; solvent: ethanol, methanol; catalyst: palladium on carbon.

Reaction type: Hydride reduction; Purpose: Converts aldehydes to primary alcohols; Key transformation: Sodium borohydride reduces aldehyde carbonyl; Reaction conditions: Mild (room temperature), no strong base required; Solvents/catalysts: Ethanol/water mixture; NaBH4.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of 4‑bromophenol; the activated phenolic ring undergoes ortho/para bromination yielding 2,4,6‑tribromophenol and HBr. Usually carried out with Br2 (1.5 equiv) at 0 °C in acetic acid or water; no external catalyst is required.

Halide exchange (fluorination) with hydrofluoric acid; converts titanium(III) chloride to titanium(III) fluoride and releases hydrogen chloride; TiCl3 + 3 HF → TiF3 + 3 HCl; performed in aqueous HF solution, typically 0–100 °C, often with excess HF to drive the reaction; no external catalyst, HF serves both solvent and fluorinating agent.

Deamination of adenine by nitrous acid. NaNO₂/HCl generates nitrous acid, which diazotizes the exocyclic amine of adenine. Subsequent hydrolysis replaces the –NH₂ group with a carbonyl, yielding hypoxanthine (6‑hydroxypurine). Reaction is performed at 0‑5 °C to control nitrosation, then warmed gently; aqueous acidic medium is required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; lead(II) acetate reacts with oxalic acid to produce insoluble lead(II) oxalate as a white precipitate while acetic acid is liberated. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst.

Mild hydride reduction of a nitrile using sodium borohydride and cobalt(II) chloride as a catalyst. NaBH4 in the presence of CoCl2 generates a cobalt–hydride species that reduces the –C≡N to –CH2NH2, affording cyclobutylamine. Typical conditions: methanol or ethanol as solvent, CoCl2 (10–20 mol %), NaBH4 (2–3 equiv), temperature 0 °C to room temperature, reaction 1–3 h. No additional acid or base needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a benzylic chloride with piperidine. Piperidine attacks the carbon bearing the chlorine in 2‑chloro‑1‑phenoxyethane, displacing chloride as HCl and forming piperoxan (phenoxyethyl‑piperidine). The reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or ethanol, often with an added base (e.g., triethylamine or Na₂CO₃) to scavenge HCl; temperatures range from room temperature to reflux.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of benzyl chloride (SN2). Aqueous NaOH attacks the benzylic carbon of 3‑nitrobenzyl chloride, substituting chloride with a hydroxyl group to give 3‑nitrobenzyl alcohol, while NaCl precipitates. The reaction is typically performed in aqueous solution at reflux (≈80 °C) or under mild heating; no special catalyst is required.

Acid‑carbonate reaction with gas evolution; nickel(II) carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid to give nickel(II) chloride, carbon dioxide gas, and water; performed in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating to release CO₂; water serves as the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Amidoxime formation from nitrile and hydroxylamine. Hydroxylamine adds to the electrophilic carbon of benzonitrile, followed by proton transfers to give N′‑hydroxy‑benzenecarboximidamide (benzamidoxime). The reaction proceeds in ethanol or methanol/water mixtures at 50‑100 °C, often under neutral or mildly basic conditions; no metal catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose to saturate the C=C bond of phenyl vinyl ketone producing phenylacetone; key transformation is reduction of the alkene while leaving the carbonyl unchanged; typical conditions use H₂ gas (1‑5 atm) over 5‑10 % Pd/C at room temperature to reflux in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate.

Reaction type: hydride reduction of a metal halide. Purpose: synthesize stannane (SnH4). Key transformation: LiAlH4 transfers hydride to SnI4, converting Sn–I bonds to Sn–H and generating AlH3 and LiI as by‑products Typical conditions: dry ether (THF or diethyl ether), inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), 0 °C to reflux, stoichiometric LiAlH4 (4 equiv). No catalyst required.

Trans‑nitrosation (nitrosothiol exchange). S‑Nitroso‑L‑cysteine transfers its nitroso group to reduced glutathione (GSH), yielding L‑cysteine and S‑nitrosoglutathione (GS‑NO). The reaction proceeds in physiological buffer (pH 7–7.4) at 37 °C, typically under anaerobic conditions to prevent NO oxidation. No external catalyst is required; the reaction is driven by the nucleophilicity of GSH thiolate.

Sandmeyer‑type diazotization‑substitution; purpose to replace the para‑amino group of 4‑aminophenylacetic acid with a thiol group; key transformation involves formation of the diazonium salt (HCl/NaNO₂, 0‑5 °C) followed by nucleophilic attack by sulfide (KSH) to give 4‑mercaptophenylacetic acid with evolution of N₂ and H₂O; carried out in aqueous HCl at 0‑5 °C for diazotization, then addition of KSH solution (often with catalytic Cu(I) such as CuCl) at 0‑25 °C; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of nitro groups; purpose to reduce 2,4‑dinitrotoluene to 2,4‑diaminotoluene; key transformation is conversion of both nitro groups to primary amines; typical conditions employ H₂ pressure (1‑5 atm) with Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni catalyst in ethanol or methanol at 25‑80 °C.

Thermal disproportionation (decomposition); purpose to separate lead tetroxide into its distinct oxidation‑state oxides; key transformation is Pb₃O₄ → PbO₂ (lead(IV) oxide) + 2 PbO (lead(II) oxide); carried out by heating solid Pb₃O₄ to 400‑500 °C in air, no solvent required.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a vicinal dibromide to a diol. Purpose: Replace bromine atoms with hydroxyl groups to give cyclopentane‑1,2‑diol. Key transformation: Two SN2 attacks by OH⁻ on the carbon atoms bearing bromine, forming C‑OH bonds and releasing Br⁻ as NaBr. Typical conditions: Aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux for 1–3 h. Common solvents/catalysts: Water or aqueous ethanol; no additional catalyst needed.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; purpose to introduce a methyl substituent at the 7‑position of benz[a]anthracene; key transformation is electrophilic aromatic substitution using a methyl electrophile generated from dimethyl sulfate and AlCl₃, yielding 7‑methylbenz[a]anthracene; conditions include anhydrous AlCl₃ (1‑2 equiv) in a dry non‑protic solvent such as carbon disulfide, dichloromethane or nitrobenzene, temperature ranging from 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere.

Photochemical halogen exchange (radical substitution); UV light cleaves Br2 to Br· radicals which replace chlorine atoms in dichlorodifluoromethane, yielding dibromodifluoromethane and chlorine gas. Typically performed in the gas phase or in an inert solvent under UV irradiation, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed decomposition of sodium formaldehyde sulfoxylate (rongalite); HCl protonates the sulfoxylate, leading to release of formaldehyde, sulfur dioxide, and water while forming NaCl. Conducted in aqueous HCl at 0–25 °C; water is the solvent, no external catalyst needed.

Reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an amine using tin(II) chloride in hydrochloric acid (SnCl2/HCl reduction). The nitro‑biphenyl is reduced to 4‑aminobiphenyl with concomitant oxidation of SnCl2 to SnCl4 and generation of water. Reaction is carried out in aqueous HCl, typically reflux; water is the solvent and SnCl2 serves as the reducing agent.

Oxidative coupling of ethyl xanthate anions with bromine to form diethyl dixanthogen (a disulfide) and sodium bromide. Br2 acts as the oxidant, linking two xanthate radicals. Usually performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of allyl alcohol to acrolein with concomitant release of hydrogen gas. Conducted over metal oxide or supported metal catalysts (e.g., Cu, Ag, Pd) at 250–350 °C in the gas phase or sealed reactor; often under inert atmosphere. No solvent; heat provides the driving force.

Hydrolysis of triethyl borate (ester cleavage) to give boric acid and ethanol. Reaction proceeds in water, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C); can be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed but also occurs readily under neutral conditions. No special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed isomerization of an allylic alcohol; cis‑3,7‑dimethyl‑2,6‑octadien‑1‑ol treated with dilute H₂SO₄ rearranges to the more stable trans‑isomer via carbocation intermediate; performed at 0–25 °C in aqueous sulfuric acid or a dilute acid solution, no organic solvent required.

Acid‑base reaction (proton transfer). Purpose: generate hydrogen gas and a stable fluoride salt. Key transformation: HF donates a proton to LiH, producing H2 gas and LiF solid. Typical conditions: anhydrous HF mixed with LiH at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; often performed in an inert‐dry solvent such as THF or in liquid HF under a nitrogen atmosphere. No additional catalyst required.

Strong reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride – complete reduction of both the acyl carbonyl and the ester alkoxy fragment. LiAlH4 converts 2-(dimethylamino)ethyl benzoate into the corresponding primary alcohols: benzyl alcohol from the benzoate carbonyl and 2-(dimethylamino)ethanol from the original alkoxy side chain. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere.

Direct combination / synthesis (fluorination) reaction. Purpose: preparation of cerium(III) fluoride, a lanthanide halide used in optics and ceramics. Key transformation: elemental cerium is oxidized by elemental fluorine to CeF3, with a net oxidation state change from 0 to +3. Typical conditions: fluorine gas passed over powdered Ce at 300–500 °C in a nickel or steel reactor; excess2 ensures complete conversion. No solvent; reaction is gas‑solid.

Oxidative decomposition (solid‑state oxidation). Purpose: convert cadmium telluride into its constituent oxides, often for waste processing or material recycling. Key transformation: O2 oxidizes CdTe, breaking the Cd–Te bond to give CdO and TeO2. Typical conditions: heating of CdTe powder in a flowing air or O2 stream at 500–800 °C; usually performed in a ceramic crucible. No solvent; reaction is gas‑solid.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration (electrophilic addition) of an alkene. Purpose: synthesize dodecan‑2‑ol from dodec‑1‑ene. Key transformation: protonation of the double bond forms a secondary carbocation (Markovnikov orientation), which is captured by water to give the secondary alcohol after deprotonation. Typical conditions: dilute sulfuric acid (≈5–10 % H2SO4) with excess water, temperature 0–50 °C, often in a biphasic system (aqueous acid and organic alkene). No additional catalyst beyond H2SO4.

Metathesis (acid‑base double displacement) reaction. Purpose: exchange of cations to produce soluble oxalic acid and potassium perrhenate salt. Key transformation: potassium oxalate reacts with perrhenic acid (HReO4); K⁺ pairs with ReO₄⁻ to form KReO₄, while H⁺ pairs with C₂O₄²⁻ to give H₂C₂O₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature to reflux (≈80 °C) to ensure complete ion exchange; pH neutral to slightly acidic. Water is the solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid digestion / fluorination of a silicate. Purpose: convert magnesium orthosilicate into soluble magnesium fluoride and volatile silicon tetrafluoride, useful in fluoride production or silica removal. Key transformation: HF protonates and fluoridates the silicate framework, releasing SiF₄ gas and forming MgF₂ solid. Typical conditions: concentrated HF (≈48 % aqueous) heated gently (50–100 °C) in a PTFE or glass reactor resistant to HF; SiF₄ evolves and is vented through a scrubber. No catalyst; reaction relies on the strong acidity and fluorinating power of HF.

Type: Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification of phenoxide). Purpose: formation of phenyl acetate ester. Key transformation: phenoxide O‑ attacks acetyl chloride, releasing Cl⁻ which combines with Li⁺ to give LiCl; acetate ester produced. Typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C) in anhydrous pyridine or dichloromethane, pyridine acts as solvent and HCl scavenger; inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; base‑exchange of the acidic manganese formate salt with sodium hydroxide; precipitates insoluble manganese hydroxide while forming soluble sodium formate; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

O‑Methylation (alkylation of phenol); the phenolic hydroxyl of 3‑hydroxybenzaldehyde is methylated with methyl iodide in the presence of potassium carbonate as a base, affording 3‑methoxybenzaldehyde. The reaction is run in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at reflux; after cooling the mixture is filtered to remove inorganic salts and the product is extracted.

Catalytic dehydrogenative cracking of isopentane to give 2‑methyl‑1‑butene and hydrogen; a high‑temperature (400–600 °C) gas‑phase reaction over metal oxides (e.g., Cr₂O₃) or supported Pt catalysts; no solvent required.

Oxidation–reduction (oxidative dehydrogenation) of phenol to para‑benzoquinone using cerium(IV) sulfate as the oxidant; Ce(IV) is reduced to Ce(III) while phenol loses two hydrog to become quinone; performed in dilute aqueous acidic medium (often sulfuric acid) at room temperature to 40 °C; water is the only by‑product; no additional catalyst needed.

Nitration (formation of a nitrate ester) of tert‑butanol with cold concentrated nitric acid in the presence of sulfuric acid as a dehydrating catalyst; yields tert‑butyl nitrate and water; reaction is conducted at 0 °C to 5 °C to suppress oxidation of the alcohol; mixture of HNO₃/H₂SO₄ serves both as nitrating and acid medium; no organic solvent is required.

Macrocyclic condensation (SN2 polyalkylation) forming a 2,2,2‑cryptand from tris(2‑aminoethyl)amine and 2,2‑bis(bromomethyl)1,3‑propanediol in basic medium; NaOH deprotonates the amine groups, promoting nucleophilic attack on the bromomethyl electrophiles; water is released and NaBr formed; typically run in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution at reflux (50–80 °C) under inert atmosphere; no external catalyst.

Acid dissolution of holmium oxide; solid Ho₂O₃ is added to aqueous nitric acid (usually 1–6 M) and heated under reflux. The oxide is converted to soluble holmium(III) nitrate, Ho(NO₃)₃, with formation of water. No catalyst; water serves as solvent.

Acid‑base salt metathesis with gas evolution; converts copper(I) cyanide to copper(I) chloride and releases hydrogen cyanide. CuCN is treated with dilute HCl, forming CuCl precipitate and HCN gas. Performed at 0–25 °C in aqueous HCl, under a fume hood; no catalyst needed.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) reaction; replaces fluorine atoms of thiothionyl fluoride with chlorine from hydrogen chloride, yielding disulfur dichloride and hydrogen fluoride. Typically performed in the gas phase or in an inert non‑polar solvent at elevated temperature (150‑250 °C); no catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization; thiocyanic acid (HSCN) reacts with aqueous potassium hydroxide to form potassium thiocyanate (KSCN) and water. Conducted at room temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (chlorination) of 3‑ethylphenol; chlorine gas attacks the activated aromatic ring ortho to the hydroxyl group, producing 2‑chloro‑3‑ethylphenol and hydrogen chloride. Conducted in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often at 0 °C to 25 °C; a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl₃) may be used to increase the rate.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) between potassium hydroxide and ammonium lactate; the strong base deprotonates the ammonium ion, liberating ammonia gas and forming potassium lactate. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst needed.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose: preparation of 3‑nitropropanoyl chloride; key transformation: SOCl₂ reacts with 3‑nitropropionic acid, forming the acyl chloride while releasing SO₂ and HCl gases; typical conditions: reflux or gentle heating in anhydrous solvent (dry dichloromethane, chloroform, or toluene), often with a catalytic amount of DMF to activate SOCl₂; solvent/catalyst: dry CH₂Cl₂ (or toluene) and catalytic DMF; gases evolve and are removed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) via Williamson ether synthesis. Purpose: Ethers formation through coupling of alkoxide and alkyl halide. Transformation: Sodium ethoxide displaces iodide from methyl iodide. Conditions: Heated if necessary; solvent: ethanol or polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF).

Strong‑base induced elimination (E2 dehydrohalogenation); potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 6‑bromo‑1‑hexene, eliminating HBr to give 1,5‑hexadiene and potassium bromide. Reaction is performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMSO, typically at 0 °C to reflux, with no additional catalyst.

Acid‑salt metathesis/precipitation: barium fluoride is treated with concentrated sulfuric acid, yielding insoluble barium sulfate as a precipitate and liberating hydrofluoric acid gas; performed by mixing solid BaF2 with hot H2SO4, usually under reflux or with gentle heating, no solvent or catalyst besides the acid.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium phosphate tribasic; upon heating the solid salt breaks down to release ammonia gas and phosphoric acid. Conducted by direct heating of the solid (generally >200 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (metal acetate formation) between thulium hydroxide and acetic acid; the hydroxide is neutralized to water while thulium is converted to thulium acetate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating or reflux to drive off water; no catalyst is necessary.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; exchanges the cations between ammonium perchlorate and potassium hexafluorophosphate to give potassium perchlorate and ammonium hexafluorophosphate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the salts may precipitate depending on solubility. No catalyst required; water is the common solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); the sulfonamide NH group of sulfacetamide is deprotonated by sodium hydroxide, producing the sodium salt of sulfacetamide and water. Performed in water or dilute aqueous base at room temperature; stirring ensures complete conversion. No special catalyst.

Acidic cleavage of a methyl ether with hydroiodic acid; purpose is conversion of propargyl methyl ether to propargyl alcohol while forming methyl iodide. Key transformation: protonation of the ether oxygen followed by SN2 attack of iodide on the methyl group, displacing the alcohol. Typical conditions: excess HI, reflux in aqueous or alcoholic medium, often 80–100 °C for several hours.

Reaction type: hydrolysis of iodine azide. Purpose: generate hydrazoic acid (HN3) and hydrogen iodide. Key transformation: water attacks IN3, cleaving the I–N bond to give HN3 and HI. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at 0–25 °C to control exotherm; reaction performed in dilute solution, no catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (carbonation) reaction; aqueous cesium hydroxide reacts readily with carbon dioxide gas at room temperature, forming soluble cesium carbonate and water; typically performed in water or aqueous ethanol; no additional catalyst.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; sodium sulfide and calcium nitrate exchange anions to form soluble sodium nitrate and insoluble calcium sulfide, which precipitates. Conducted in aqueous solution with stirring at room temperature or slight heating to improve solubility. No catalyst required.

Thermal decarboxylation (pyrolysis) of cyanoacetic acid to yield acetonitrile and carbon dioxide. Heat the neat acid to 200–250 °C under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); no solvent or catalyst is required.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkyne to a 1,2‑diketone; cold, dilute KMnO4 oxidizes cyclooctyne to cyclooctane‑1,2‑dione. The alkyne is treated with an aqueous solution of KMnO4 at 0 °C (often in a mixture of water/acetone). Under these mild conditions the alkyne is converted directly to the vicinal diketone without over‑oxidation; the reaction is typically quenched with a dilute acid and the product isolated by extraction.

Metal‑alcohol acid‑base reaction producing an alkoxide; sodium metal transfers a proton to methanol, generating sodium methoxide and hydrogen gas; carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF under nitrogen or argon, with finely divided Na added to excess dry methanol; exothermic; used to prepare sodium methoxide as a strong base.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange; sodium tungstate reacts with ammonium chloride in water, exchanging cations to afford ammonium tungstate ((NH4)2WO4) and sodium chloride. Reaction is carried out at room temperature with stirring; aqueous medium, no catalyst required.

Oxidative digestion of nickel arsenide with concentrated nitric acid; the strong oxidizing HNO₃ converts arsenide to arsenic acid, oxidizes nickel to nickel(II) nitrate, and reduces nitrate to nitrogen dioxide gas while generating water. Reaction is performed under reflux with concentrated (≈  %) HNO₃, typically in a glass flask equipped with a gas‑scrubbing outlet for NO₂. No additional catalyst; heat and excess acid drive the process.

Diazo methylation (esterification) of a carboxlic acid; diazomethane reacts with isovaleric acid to give methyl isovalerate and nitrogen gas. Performed at 0 °C to −10 °C in an inert, aprotic solvent such as di ether or THF, under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). The reaction proceeds without catalyst; the evolution of N₂ drives it to completion.

Ozonolysis of a Z‑alkene; oxidative cleavage of the carbon–carbon double bond to afford carbonyl fragments. Typically performed by bubbling O₃ through a solution of the alkene in dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide) to give the aldehyde (acetaldehyde) and ketone (2‑pentanone). No catalyst required; solvent is an aprotic halogenated hydrocarbon.

Wöhler rearrangement; thermal isomerization of ammonium cyanate to urea. Heating solid ammonium cyanate causes intramolecular rearrangement of the cyanate group to the carbonyl of urea. No solvent or catalyst required; typically heated to 150‑200 °C.

Alcoholysis/transesterification of a trimethylsilyl ester with methanol; methanol attacks the Si‑O bond, yielding methyl benzoate and trimethylsilanol. Typically refluxing in excess methanol, optionally acid‑ or base‑catalyzed (e.g., a catalytic amount of HCl or NaOMe) to accelerate the process.

Williamson ether synthesis; nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of phenoxide on methyl iodide to form methyl phenyl ether (anisole). Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as dry acetone or DMF, often at reflux. Sodium phenolate is generated in situ from phenol and NaOH, and NaI precipitates out, driving the reaction forward.

Reaction type: ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: cleave 2‑hydroxypropyl octadecanoate into octadecanoic (stearic) acid and 1,2‑propanediol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water (or OH⁻) on the ester carbonyl, breaking the C–O bond. Typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H2SO4) or base (NaOH) under reflux; solvent is water or water‑organic mixture; acidic work‑up yields free acid.

Condensation formaldehyde with methylamine to give 1,3,5‑trimethyl‑1,3,5‑triazacyclohexane (a hexahydro‑1,3,5‑triazine) with of water. The reaction proceeds via successive imine formation and cyclization (Mannich‑type condensation). Usually carried out in ethanol or methanol at room temperature to 60 °C, with removal of water (e.g., by azeotropic distillation or molecular sieves) to drive the equilibrium toward the cyclic product.

Acylation (acetylation) of the amino group of glycine with acetic anhydride, producing N‑acetylglycine and one equivalent of acetic acid. Reaction is performed neat or in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated acid and catalyze the process.

Halide exchange (metathesis) between hydrogen bromide and titanium tetrachloride, yielding titanium tetrabromide and hydrogen chloride gas. Conducted in anhydrous, non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dry benzene) at low to moderate temperature under an inert atmosphere; the reaction proceeds without a catalyst, the gaseous HCl is removed to shift equilibrium toward TiBr₄ formation.

Acid‑base (salt metathesis) reaction; aqueous HCl protonates aluminium molybdate, displacing molybdate to form molybdic acid (H2MoO4) and generating aluminium chloride. Typically carried out in water with excess HCl, heated gently to promote dissolution; common solvent is water, no additional catalyst required.

Metal carbonyl synthesis via high‑pressure CO reduction; solid chromium(III) bromide is reduced by sodium metal in a carbon monoxide atmosphere to give chromium hexacarbonyl Cr(CO)6 and sodium bromide. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, CO pressure (≈30–50 atm), inert atmosphere (argon), temperature around 150–200 °C; solvents are rarely used, reaction performed in sealed steel autoclave.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of urea; water attacks urea yielding ammonia and carbamic acid (NH2COOH), which can further decompose to a second molecule of ammonia and carbon dioxide. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; no catalyst needed, reaction proceeds spontaneously; often observed in biological or industrial urea hydrolysis.
