Purpose: conversion of soluble AgF to insoluble AgCl, allowing removal of silver as a precipitate and formation of sodium fluoride in solution. Key transformation: AgF + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaF. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature; reaction proceeds spontaneously. Common solvents/catalysts: water; no catalyst required.

Reductive de‑oxygenation of a metal oxide. Thallium(I) oxide is reduced by hydrogen gas to metallic thallium with water as the by‑product. Conducted at high temperature (≈400‑600 °C) in a flow of hydrogen; typically a tubular furnace, no solvent needed.

Formation of a sulfonate ester (mesylation) of an alcohol; 1‑propanol reacts with methanesulfonyl chloride, pyridine scavenges the generated HCl to give propyl methanesulfonate and pyridinium chloride; performed at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine as solvent.

Oxidation of uranium nitride with oxygen to afford uranium dioxide and nitrogen gas; used to convert UN to the more stable UO2 oxide; O2 attacks the UN lattice, breaking U‑N bonds and forming U‑O bonds while N is released as N2; typically performed at 500–700 °C in flowing O2 or air; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification with ethanol; converts tert‑butyl methacrylate into ethyl methacrylate and tert‑butanol. Conditions similar to the methyl case: excess ethanol, catalytic p‑TsOH or H₂SO₄, reflux 3–6 h. Ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent; removal of tert‑butanol shifts the reaction forward.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkyne to a 1,2‑diketone; osmium tetroxide adds across the triple bond of 2‑butyne forming a cyclic osmate intermediate that hydrolyzes to give 2,3‑butanedione while OsO₄ is reduced to osmium dioxide. Typically catalytic OsO₄ (1–5 mol %) with a co‑oxidant such as N‑methylmorpholine N‑oxide or H₂O₂ in a mixed tert‑butanol/water solvent, carried out at 0 °C to room temperature.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an ester; purpose is to convert the ester into the corresponding primary alcohols. LiAlH₄ reduces the carbonyl of 3‑methylbutyl benzoate to give benzyl alcohol while the original alkoxy fragment is released as 3‑methylbutanol. Reaction carried out in anhydrous THF (or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful aqueous work‑up.

Metathesis (halide exchange) precipitation; silver acetate exchanges its acetate anion with the chloride of phenylmercuric chloride, producing insoluble silver chloride which precipitates and soluble phenylmercuric acetate. Usually performed in water or an alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at ambient temperature; stirring until complete precipitation. No catalyst needed.

Alkylation of acetate with tertiary halide 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane proceeds mainly via an SN1/ion‑pair pathway to give tert‑butyl acetate and cesium bromide; requires a highly polar solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or acetone) and often heating; cesium acetate supplies acetate, sometimes a silver salt is added to facilitate halide removal; reaction is slower due to carbocation formation.

N‑alkylation via SN2 nucleophilic substitution; pyrrolidine attacks one carbon of 1,2‑dichloroethane, displacing chloride and forming 1‑(2‑chloroethyl)pyrrolidine while releasing HCl. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or DMF, often refluxed; a base (e.g., triethylamine) may be added to scavenge the liberated HCl, but the stoichiometric equation shows HCl as product.

Acid‑base reaction; ammonia reacts with carbonic acid (H₂CO₃, generated from CO₂ and water) to give ammonium carbonate ((NH₄)₂CO₃). Performed by bubbling CO₂ through aqueous ammonia at room temperature; no catalyst.

Aerobic oxidation (redox); molecular oxygen oxidizes 2,6‑dimethoxyhydroquinone to the corresponding 2,6‑dimethoxy‑1,4‑benzoquinone. Reaction commonly uses a metal catalyst (e.g., CuCl₂, Fe‑porphyrin, or cobalt salen) or a quinone‑mediated system, in solvents like methanol, acetonitrile, or dichloromethane, under an O₂ atmosphere at room temperature to 60 °C. No additional oxidants required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; converts the C=C bond of dimethyl maleate to the saturated dimethyl succinate. Hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) is introduced over a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni. The reaction is usually carried out in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) or ethyl acetate at 20–50 °C. The purpose is to reduce the unsaturated ester to a saturated di‑ester.

General type: diazomethyl esterification (methylation of carboxylic acids). Purpose: preparation of methyl picolinate under mild conditions. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the carboxylate on diazomethane, forming the methyl ester and liberating nitrogen gas. Typical conditions: addition of freshly prepared diazomethane solution (in ether or CH₂Cl₂) to a solution of picolinic acid at 0–5 °C under inert atmosphere, stirring until gas evolution ceases. Solvent/catalyst: anhydrous diethyl ether or dichloromethane; no external catalyst required.

Metathesis (anion exchange) double displacement; sodium acetate swaps its acetate ion with the nitrate of phenylmercuric nitrate, yielding soluble sodium nitrate and phenylmercuric acetate. Performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic media (e.g., water/ethanol) at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Precipitation/ionic exchange; ammonium oxalate reacts with manganese(II) chloride in water to form insoluble manganese(II) oxalate precipitate and soluble ammonium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution, usually at 0–25 °C to maximize precipitation; the solid MnC₂O₄ is filtered off. No catalyst needed.

Electrophilic halogenation of furan using N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS). This is an electrophilic aromatic substitution that installs a chlorine atom at the 2‑position of the heteroaromatic ring. Typically performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, protected from light. No additional catalyst is required; succinimide is formed as a by‑product.

Metathesis/precipitation synthesis of cobalt(II) selenide (CoSe) from cobalt(II) chloride and sodium selenide. In aqueous solution the sodium ions exchange with cobalt, yielding insoluble cobalt selenide as a solid precipitate and sodium chloride remaining in solution. The reaction is usually carried out at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; water or dilute ethanol can be used as solvent. No external catalyst is needed.

Thermal decomposition (thermolysis) of iron pentacarbonyl; purpose is to regenerate metallic iron and release CO gas. Fe(CO)5 is heated to 180–200 °C under an inert gas flow (N₂ or Ar). The reaction is carried out without solvent, often in a tube furnace; the iron precipitates as a fine powder while CO evolves.

Oxidation of tungsten(IV) chloride (WCl4) to tungsten(VI) chloride (WCl6) by chlorine gas. Chlorine acts as an oxidizing agent, raising the oxidation state of tungsten from +4 to +6. The reaction is conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in a dry non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, and may require gentle heating and a flow of Cl2. No catalyst is employed.

Redox (disproportionation) reaction between chloric acid (HClO3) and sodium thiosulfate (Na2S2O3). Chloric acid is reduced to chloride while thiosulfate is oxidized to sulfate, liberating elemental sulfur. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution, typically at low temperature (0–5 °C) with continuous stirring to control gas evolution. No catalyst is required; the acidic medium provides the necessary proton source.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 2,3‑dimethylbutane‑2,3‑diol to give 2,3‑dimethyl‑2‑butene. The vicinal diol loses a molecule of water via an E1/E2 elimination mechanism, commonly using concentrated sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid as the catalyst. The reaction is performed neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene under reflux. No additional catalyst beyond the strong acid is needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of carbonyl dichloride (phosgene, COCl2) with two equivalents of aniline to afford N,N‑diphenylurea and hydrogen chloride. The reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent like dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) added to scavenge the generated HCl. No metal catalyst is required.

Halogenation / acyl chloride formation; PCl5 converts an ester into an acyl chloride (propionyl chloride) while the alkoxy group is displaced as an alkyl chloride (ethyl chloride). Typically performed under anhydrous conditions, refluxing in a non‑polar solvent such as CH2Cl2 or CCl4, often with pyridine to scavenge HCl.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation); CrO3/H2SO4 in acetone oxidizes the primary alcohol 4‑phenyl‑1‑butanol to the corresponding carboxylic acid (4‑phenylbutyric acid). Reaction is run at 0 °C to rt, aqueous acetone as solvent, and excess Jones reagent is added dropwise.

Aqueous double‑replacement precipitation; mercurous nitrate reacts with potassium iodide to form insoluble mercurous iodide (Hg2I2) precipitate and soluble potassium nitrate (KNO3); performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; calcium bromide reacts with ammonium sulfate in aqueous solution to give insoluble calcium sulfate precipitate and soluble ammonium bromide. Conducted at ambient temperature with water as solvent; product CaSO4 is filtered off.

Acid‑base displacement; sulfuric acid protonates magnesium tungstate, forming tungstic acid (H2WO4) which precipitates, while magnesium sulfate remains in solution. Usually carried out in water with gentle heating to aid dissolution and precipitation of H2WO4.

Fluorination of magnesium silicide with elemental fluorine; an aggressive fluorination that forms magnesium fluoride solid and silicon tetrafluoride gas; carried out in a fluorine‑compatible vessel at 200–400 °C, often with a carrier gas such as nitrogen or argon; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; potassium carbonate reacts with lead(II) hydroxide in aqueous medium to produce lead(II) carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium hydroxide. Performed at room temperature or with mild heating; water is the solvent.

Synthesis (direct combination) of a metal halide; elemental protactinium metal reacts vigorously with chlorine gas to afford protactinium(V) chloride (PaCl5). Requires dry, inert atmosphere, elevated temperature (often 300–400 °C) and a flow of Cl2 gas; no solvent is used.

Alcohol‑to‑chloride substitution; conversion of triphenylmethanol to triphenylmethyl chloride using phosphorus pentachloride. PCl5 reacts with the hydroxyl group, generating HCl and POCl3. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in a dry non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, starting at 0  and then warming to reflux, under an inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst is required.

Redox (halogen oxidation) reaction; chlorine oxidizes zinc sulfide to elemental sulfur while being reduced to zinc chloride. Usually carried out by bubbling Cl₂ gas through a suspension of ZnS in water or dilute acid and heating gently. Reaction proceeds without a catalyst; stoichiometric Cl₂ is consumed.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; cobalt(II) sulfate reacts with potassium phosphate in aqueous solution to give insoluble cobalt(II) phosphate precipitate and soluble potassium sulfate. Conducted at room temperature in water with stirring the cobalt phosphate solid is filtered and washed. No special catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis; aqueous sodium hydroxide displaces the iodide of 2,2‑dimethyl‑1‑iodopropane to afford 2,2‑dimethyl‑1‑prool and sodium iodide. Performed in warm aqueous NaOH (≈50–80 °C) or a water/ethanol mixture to improve solubility. Excess NaOH drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst required.

Dehydrization (anhydride formation); itaconic acid reacts with acetic anhydride, which acts as a dehydrating agent, to produce itaconic anhydride and two equivalents of acetic acid. The reaction is carried out under reflux in a dry non‑protic solvent such as toluene or benzene, often with a catalytic amount of pyridine to scavenge the generated acid. Temperature 80–120 °C; inert atmosphere recommended.

Hydrolysis reaction; gallium(III) iodide reacts with water to form insoluble gallium hydroxide precipitate and hydroiodic acid; essentially an acid‑base hydrolysis of a metal halide. Typically carried out by adding solid GaI3 to aqueous water, often with gentle heating and stirring; no special solvent needed, reaction proceeds in water.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis. Purpose: regenerate formaldehyde and ethylene glycol from the cyclic acetal 1,3-dioxolane. Key transformation: protonation of acetal oxygen followed by water attack cleaves the ring, yielding formaldehyde and ethylene glycol. Typical conditions: dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) in water, ambient to reflux temperature. Solvent: aqueous acid. Catalyst: acid.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation); 3‑Cyclopenten‑1‑ol is oxidized by chromic acid (generated from chromium(VI) oxide in sulfuric acid) to 3‑cyclopenten‑1‑one, with water as by‑product. Conducted in an acetone‑water mixture at 0–25 °C under acidic conditions; stoichiometric Cr(VI) reagent is used. No additional catalyst is needed.

Neutral hydrolysis of glycol monobutyl ether acetate to glycol monobutyl ether and acetic acid. This is an ester hydrolysis (acetate cleavage) without added acid or base, driven by water at elevated temperature. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, temperature 90–120 °C, reaction time 1–3 h. No catalyst is required, although a small amount of acid can accelerate the process. The reaction is often performed in water or a water‑ethanol mixture.

Free radical halogenation (monochlorination) of cyclohexane. UV light or heat initiates homolysis of Cl₂, generating chlorine radicals that abstract a hydrogen atom from cyclohexane to form cyclohexyl radical, which then recombines with Cl· to give chlorocyclohexane; HCl is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: dilute Cl₂ (1 equiv) in inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, irradiated with UV or heated to 50–80 °C. Purpose: synthesis of a mono‑chlorinated cyclohexane for further functionalization.

Acid‑catalyzed Pictet–Spengler condensation between dopamine (as the amine component) and 4‑hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde to afford the tetrahydroisoquinoline alkaloid higenamine. Trifluoroacetic acid protonates the aldehyde, facilitating imine formation, followed by intramolecular cyclization onto the phenolic ring and subsequent deprotonation. Typical conditions: 1–2 equiv TFA in dichloromethane or acetonitrile, reaction at 0 °C to room temperature for 1–4 h, often with removal of water (e.g., molecular sieves) to drive equilibrium. Purpose: construction of the benzo‑tetrahydroisoquinoline core of higenamine.

Base‑promoted cleavage of a symmetrical ether (alkyl‑alkyl ether cleavage). Heated sodium hydroxide (often 2–3 equiv) attacks the less hindered carbon of di‑n‑butyl ether via SN2, giving n‑butanol and sodium n‑butoxide. Conditions: reflux in aqueous ethanol or water, temperature 80–100 °C. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic substitution and is sometimes called alkaline hydrolysis of ethers. Purpose: generation of a primary alcohol and its alkoxide for subsequent alkylation or other transformations.

Oxidation of a thiol to a disulfide using manganese(IV) dioxide. Two molecules of ethyl mercaptan are oxidized; MnO₂ abstracts hydrogen atoms, forming ethyl disulfide and reducing Mn(IV) to Mn(II) oxide (often reported as MnO). Typical conditions: ambient temperature or gentle heating, solvent such as dichloromethane, acetonitrile, or a mixture with water; stoichiometric amount of MnO₂ (≈1 equiv per thiol). Purpose: preparation of symmetrical disulfides as protecting groups or intermediates.

Oxygen‑transfer oxidation of trimethylsulfonium iodide to the corresponding sulfoxonium salt (trimethylsulfoxonium iodide) using peracetic acid. The peracid delivers an oxygen atom to the sulfonium center, generating the sulfoxonium ylide precursor and producing acetic acid as the only by‑product. Conditions: low temperature (0–5 °C) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, slow addition of peracetic acid (1 equiv) to a solution of the sulfonium salt, then stirring at room temperature for 30 min to 1 h. Purpose: preparation of a stable sulfoxonium salt for use in cyclopropanation or epoxidation reactions (Corey–Chaykovsky reagents).

Acid–base reaction of samarium oxide with sulfuric acid; forms samarium(III) sulfate. Purpose: generation of sulfate salt for precipitation or analytical work. Key transformation: Sm2O3 + 3 H2SO4 → Sm2(SO4)3 + 3 H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous sulfuric acid (dilute to moderate concentration), heating (70–100 °C) to ensure complete reaction. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Selenium dioxide oxidation of the benzylic (allylic) methyl group of 2‑methylthiophene to the corresponding aldehyde, thiophene‑2‑carboxaldehyde. SeO₂ acts as an oxidant, converting the methyl substituent via a “ene”‑type mechanism to an aldehyde while elemental selenium precipitates. Typical conditions: reflux in 1,4‑dioxane, pyridine, or tert‑butanol as solvent; catalytic or stoichiometric SeO₂ (0.5–1 equiv), reaction time 2–6 h; often a small amount of water is present to facilitate the oxidation. Purpose: functionalization of heteroaryl methyl groups to aldehydes for further cross‑coupling or condensation chemistry.

Direct chlorination of elemental sulfur; synthesis (halogenation) reaction to prepare sulfur dichloride (SCl2) as a chlorinating reagent; elemental sulfur (S8) is exposed to excess chlorine gas at elevated temperature (≈200‑250 °C) under anhydrous, inert conditions, often in the gas phase without solvent; the reaction proceeds via oxidative addition of Cl2 to S–S bonds forming SCl2.

Technetium dioxide (TcO2) + hydrogen peroxide + nitric acid → pertechnic acid (HTcO4) + water (H2O). Oxidative dissolution (redox) of Tc(IV) to Tc(VII) using H2O2 and HNO3 as oxidants. Employed to regenerate pertechnetate from TcO2. Conducted in aqueous solution with concentrated HNO3 and excess H2O2, temperature 0–60 °C; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: dehydrative cyclodehydration (intramolecular cyclization) to form a benzoxazolinone. Purpose: construction of a heterocyclic lactam (benzoxazolin‑2‑one) from an N‑hydroxyamide. Key transformation: N‑hydroxybenzamide + POCl3 → benzoxazolin‑2‑one + HCl (g). Typical conditions: POCl3 added dropwise to a solution of N‑hydroxybenzamide in anhydrous pyridine or CH2Cl2 at 0 °C, then warmed to rt or gentle reflux for 1–3 h. HCl generated is neutralized by the pyridine base. No metal catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation; introduces a chlorine atom onto the 2‑position of the selenophene ring. Typically performed with Cl2 (1–2 equiv) in an anhydrous non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or CH2Cl2 at 0 °C to room temperature, using a Lewis‑acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl3, AlCl3) to activate Cl2; the reaction yields 2‑chloroselenophene as the major product.

Metal‑acid redox/displacement; solid magnesium reacts with ammonium bromide upon heating (typically 200‑300 °C) in the absence of solvent, generating magnesium bromide, ammonia gas, and hydrogen gas; employed to produce MgBr₂ and evolve gases.

Acid–base exchange (protonation of an anion); nitric acid protonates the arsenate ion of potassium arsenate, yielding arsenic acid and potassium nitrate; carried out by dissolving K₃AsO₄ in aqueous HNO₃ at ambient temperature, producing soluble H₃AsO₄ and KNO₃ in the same solution.

Dehydrative conversion of a fluorinated amide to the corresponding nitrile; phosphorus pentoxide acts as a strong dehydrating agent to remove water from 2,2‑difluoroacetamide, yielding 2,2‑difluoroacetonitrile; typically performed by heating the amide with P2O5 (often under reflux) in a dry, inert environment; no solvent or catalyst is essential, though a high‑boiling aprotic solvent such as toluene may be used to improve mixing.

Dissolution of tribasic ammonium phosphate in water to give an aqueous ammonium phosphate solution; purpose is preparation of buffer, fertilizer or reagent solution; solid (NH4)3PO4 dissolves, furnishing NH4⁺ and PO4³⁻ ions; performed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is involved.

Thermal decomposition of sodium germanate; heating solid Na2GeO3 at elevated temperatures (typically >600 °C) in the presence of air or inert gas leads to breakdown into sodium oxide (Na2O) and germanium dioxide (GeO2); solid‑state reaction without solvent or catalyst.

Type: electrophilic addition (nitroso‑chlorination) to an alkene. Purpose: synthesize β‑chloro‑nitroso substituted ethane. Key transformation: the π‑bond of ethylene attacks the electrophilic NO⁺/Cl⁻ pair of NOCl, forming a three‑center intermediate that collapses to 1‑chloro‑2‑nitrosoethane. Conditions: inert, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, temperature around 0‑25 °C to suppress side reactions; generally no additional catalyst is needed.

Aerobic oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; isobutyl alcohol is oxidized by molecular oxygen to isobutyric acid with water as the by‑product; the reaction generally requires a homogeneous or heterogeneous metal catalyst (e.g., TEMPO/NaClO, Au, Pt, Pd on carbon) and is carried out in polar aprotic solvents (acetonitrile, methanol) under O₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 60‑100 °C; the purpose is to obtain the corresponding acid from the alcohol.
Acid‑base neutralization; NaOH reacts with formic acid to afford water and sodium formate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; simple stirring is sufficient.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of chlorine atoms on a purine ring by ammonia; aqueous ammonia replaces the two chlorine substituents of 2,6‑dichloropurine to give 2,6‑diaminopurine; the reaction is conducted by heating the substrate with excess NH₃(aq) (typically 80‑100 °C) under reflux; water serves as both solvent and nucleophile; no additional catalyst is required.

Hydride reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; benzaldehyde is reduced by sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)aluminum hydride (a “Red‑Al” type reagent) to give benzyl alcohol; the reaction is performed in anhydrous THF or toluene at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; the purpose is selective conversion of the carbonyl group to an alcohol without over‑reduction; the aluminum hydride acts as the reducing agent, no external catalyst is needed.

This is a hydrolysis reaction. The purpose is to convert 4-nitrobenzenesulfonyl chloride into 4-nitrobenzenesulfonic acid. The key transformation involves nucleophilic attack by water on the sulfonyl chloride group, releasing hydrogen chloride as a byproduct. Reaction conditions typically include aqueous media, often under mild heating or ambient temperature, with no specific catalyst required. Common solvents may include water or mixtures with organic solvents like THF.

This is an ester hydrolysis reaction. The purpose is to cleave prop-2-ynyl 2,2-dimethylpropanoate into its corresponding carboxylic acid and alcohol. The key transformation involves water breaking the ester bond, yielding 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid and prop-2-yn-1-ol. The reaction typically occurs under acidic or basic aqueous conditions; if acidic, dilute HCl or H2SO4 may be used. Common solvents include water, ethanol, or mixtures.

Acid‑base reaction of a carbonate with sulfuric acid; yields beryllium sulfate. Key transformation: BeCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → BeSO₄ + CO₂↑ + H₂O. Reaction is performed by stirring BeCO₃ into dilute aqueous H₂SO₄ (0.5–2 M) at ambient temperature or with mild heating (≤50 °C) until CO₂ evolution stops. No catalyst needed; the resulting BeSO₄ remains in solution.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to prepare rubidium hydroxide by exchanging cations; Na⁺ swaps with Rb⁺ while OH⁻ and Br⁻ remain paired; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and the products remain dissolved, after which RbOH can be isolated by evaporation.

This is an electrophilic aromatic substitution. The purpose is to iodinate phenol at the ortho position to form 2-iodophenol. Hydrogen peroxide acts as an oxidizing agent, converting iodine to a reactive electrophilic iodinating species (hypervalent iodine species or HOI). The reaction likely proceeds in acidic conditions (e.g., H2SO4) to facilitate electrophilic iodine generation. Common solvents may include aqueous mixtures or acetic acid.

This is a precipitation/double displacement reaction. The purpose is to synthesize cerous oxalate from cerium(III) chloride and ammonium oxalate. The key transformation involves Ce³+ and oxalate ions forming an insoluble complex (cerous oxalate). The reaction typically occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperatures. No catalyst is required, and water is the common solvent.

Nucleophilic O‑methylation (SN2) of 3‑methoxyphenol with methyl iodide; purpose is to install a second methoxy group to give 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene. The phenolic OH is deprotonated with a base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaH) and then reacts with MeI in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone at reflux. By‑product is hydrogen iodide, which is neutralized by the base.

This is an acid-base (gas evolution) reaction. The purpose is to produce hydrogen selenide gas by protonating magnesium selenide with a strong acid. Perchloric acid donates protons to selenide, forming H2Se gas and magnesium perchlorate. The reaction occurs under acidic aqueous conditions, often with cold dilute perchloric acid to control gas release. Water is the primary solvent.

Reaction type: Lewis‑acid mediated ether cleavage (aryl‑alkyl ether deprotection). Purpose: Convert an allyl phenyl ether into the free phenol while generating allyl bromide as the side‑product. Key transformation: BBr₃ attacks the oxygen, cleaving the Ar‑O‑CH₂CH=CH₂ bond to give phenol (Ar‑OH) and allyl bromide (CH₂=CH‑CH₂Br). Typical conditions: Anhydrous environment, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, dissolved in a non‑protic such as dichloromethane or chloroform; reaction is quenched with methanol or water after completion.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to convert soluble Yb(III) nitrate into insoluble YbF3 for isolation; Yb^3+ exchanges nitrate for fluoride producing YbF3 solid and NH4NO3 in solution; typically performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; water is the usual solvent, no catalyst required.

Double displacement (hydrolysis) precipitation; addition of aqueous ammonium hydroxide to a cadmium iodide solution precipitates cadmium hydroxide, while ammonium iodide stays in solution. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst is needed. It is often used to separate cadmium as a hydroxide precipitate.

Reaction type: Oxidative dissolution (acid digestion) of a metal in aqua regia. Purpose: Solubilize copper as Cu²⁺ for analysis, refining, or further chemistry. Key transformation: Copper metal is oxidized by the mixture of concentrated HCl and HNO₃; chloride complexes Cu²⁺ as CuCl₂, while chlorine gas and nitrogen dioxide are liberated. Typical conditions: Freshly prepared aqua regia (3 parts HCl : 1 part HNO) at ambient temperature or with gentle reflux; performed in a glass vessel with venting, no special solvent needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement reaction; sulfurous acid (H2SO3) reacts with silver oxalate (Ag2C2O4) in water, forming silver sulfite (Ag2SO3) precipitate and oxalic acid (H2C2O4) in solution; performed at room temperature in water; the oxalic acid may further decompose if heated.

Reaction type: Nucleophilic substitution of a chlorosilane by a Grignard reagent (organometallic Si‑C bond formation). Purpose: Synthesize tetramethylsilane (Me₄), a volatile silicon standard. Key transformation: Two equivalents of MeMgBr attack the Si center of Cl₂SiMe₂, displacing chloride as MgBrCl and installing two additional methyl groups, ultimately yielding SiMe₄ after work. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ethereal solvent (diethyl ether or THF), 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; the reaction mixture is quenched with aqueous ammonium chloride or dilute acid to remove magnesium salts.

Reaction type: Aerobic microbial oxidation of a straight‑chain alkane to the corresponding terminal fatty acid. Purpose: Bioconversion of nonane to the valuable monocarboxylic acid nonanoic acid. Key transformation: Three molecules of O₂ are reduced, inserting an oxygen atom at the terminal carbon of nonane, forming nonanoic acid and water; the overall stoichiometry yields two equivalents of nonanoic acid and two equivalents of water from two nonane molecules. Typical conditions: Cultures of alkane‑degrading bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas spp.) in aqueous mineral medium, aerobic shaking incubator, temperature 20–30 °C, pH neutral; oxygen supplied by sparging or agitation.

Reaction type: Base‑promoted hydrolysis of an anhydride followed neutralization (acid‑base reaction). Purpose: Prepare potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP), a primary standard for acid‑base titrations, while generating potassium bicarbonate as a by‑product. Key transformation: Water opens the phthalic anhydride ring to give phthalic acid; the carbonate from K₂CO₃ reacts with the acid to form KHC₈H₄O₄ (monobasic potassium phthalate) and KHCO₃. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution, mild heating (30–60 °C) and stirring until dissolution; no additional solvent needed beyond water.

Reaction type: Acid-carbonate. Purpose: Dissolution of bismuth carbonate with nitric acid. Key transformations: Nitric acid protonates carbonate, releasing CO2 gas, while forming water and soluble bismuth nitrate. Conditions: Cold aqueous solution. Solvents: Water. No catalyst required.

Reaction type: Hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid (acidic or basic conditions). Purpose: Convert 3‑(methylamino)propionitrile into the corresponding carboxylic acid, 3‑(methylamino)propanoic acid, releasing ammonia. Key transformation: Two water molecules add across the C≡N triple bond, first forming an amide intermediate then ay; the nitrile nitrogen leaves as NH₃. Typical conditions: Aqueous acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) or base (NaOH) heated to reflux (100 °C) for several hours; after completion, the reaction mixture is neutralized and the product isolated by acidification or extraction.

Strong‑base induced dehydrohalogenation (E2) of 1,2‑dibromo‑1‑methylcyclopentane with potassium tert‑butoxide; purpose is to eliminate HBr and form a mono‑alkene; key transformation is removal of a bromine atom and a vicinal hydrogen to give 1‑methylcyclopentene, with KBr and tert‑butanol as by‑products; typically run in anhydrous THF or DMSO under nitrogen at 0 °C to room temperature using stoichiometric KOtBu.

Acid‑base neutralisation; LDA is protonated by water to give the conjugate acid diisopropylamine and lithium hydroxide. Typically performed as a quench of a LDA solution in an aprotic solvent such as THF, with addition of dilute water at 0 °C to rt. No catalyst required; the reaction is rapid and exothermic.

Nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether synthesis); methanol is deprotonated (often with NaH, K2CO3 or pyridine) to generate methoxide which attacks propargyl bromide displacing bromide to form propargyl methyl ether. Commonly carried out in refluxing methanol or in anhydrous DMF/acetone with a mild base; the by‑product is HBr (often scavenged by the base).

Acyl‑substitution (esterification with an acid chloride); the two primary hydroxyl groups of triethylene glycol react with acetyl chloride to give the diacetate and two equivalents of HCl. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, using a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to capture the liberated HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

SN2 alkylation with acetate (Williamson‑type ester formation); purpose: synthesize octyl acetate from 1‑chlorooctane. Sodium acetate acts as nucleophile, substituting Cl⁻ to give the ester. Typical conditions: NaOAc (2 equiv) in polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or DMSO, reflux (≈80–120 °C) for several hours; NaCl precipitates and is filtered off. No catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; potassium acetate supplies acetate anion which attacks isopropyl bromide, displacing bromide to afford isopropyl acetate and KBr. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF under reflux; excess acetate and removal of KBr (by filtration) improve yield. No additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement/precipitation (metathesis) reaction; aqueous hydrobromic acid reacts with lead(II) acetate, exchanging anions to produce insoluble lead(II) bromide precipitate and acetic acid in solution. Carried out at room temperature in water; the solid PbBr₂ is filtered off and the filtrate contains the liberated acetic acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction); molecular hydrogen adds across the unsaturated bond(s) of anabaseine in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni, converting it to the saturated alkaloid anabasine. Typical conditions are H₂ at 1–5 atm, catalyst loading 5–10 wt % in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or methanol) at reflux or 50–80 °C. The reaction is selective for reduction of the C=C or C≡C functionality while leaving the heterocyclic nitrogen atoms untouched.

Ester hydrolysis (acidic or basic); the acetate protecting group on 3,5‑dichlorophenyl acetate is hydrolyzed to regenerate the phenol and produce acetic acid, commonly done by refluxing in aqueous HCl or NaOH (pH 1‑14) in water/ethanol.

Mitsunobu esterification; converts nicotinic acid to its methyl ester using methanol. Key transformation is activation of the carboxylic triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate to form an alkoxyphosphonium intermediate, which is displaced by methanol giving methyl nicotinate and producing triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazinedicarboxylate. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF (or dioxane) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; inert atmosphere; stoichiometric reagents; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (Grignard addition) to a phosphorus halide; forms diphenylchlorophosphine from phosphorus trichloride and phenylmagnesium bromide. Phenyl groups replace two chloride atoms, generating Ph₂PCl and MgCl₂ by‑products. Typical conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at −78 °C to 0 °C under inert gas; addition of Grignard reagent dropwise; quenched with aqueous NH₄Cl.

Acylation of an aromatic amine (nucleophilic acyl substitution); 4‑nitroaniline reacts with acetyl chloride to give 4‑nitroacetanilide and HCl. The amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing chloride. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine; pyridine or a base is often used to absorb the liberated HCl.

Benzylic free‑radical chlorination; toluene reacts with chlorine under UV light or heat to replace a benzylic hydrogen with chlorine, forming benzyl chloride and HCl. Key step is homolytic cleavage of Cl₂ to generate Cl· radicals that abstract benzylic H·. Typical conditions: UV irradiation (or thermal initiation) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or in the gas phase; ambient to elevated temperature.

Redox (oxidative chlorination) reaction; chlorine gas oxidizes vanadium(III) oxide to vanadium(IV) chloride, with concurrent reduction of Cl₂ to chloride incorporated in VCl₄ and liberation of O₂; typically carried out in the gas phase at 300–500 °C under a flow of dry Cl₂ in a sealed or quartz tube; no solvent, inert reaction vessel.

Hydrolysis of chlorosulfonyl isocyanate; water adds to the electrophilic carbon of the –N=C=O group, yielding chlorosulfonamide (ClSO₂NH₂) and releasing CO₂. Reaction proceeds readily at room temperature or with gentle heating; aqueous medium; can be neutral or slightly basic to accelerate.

Carbothermic reduction/chlorination; carbon reduces uranium(IV) chloride to metallic uranium while being chlorinated to carbon tetrachloride; high‑temperature (≈800–1000 °C) solid‑state reaction in a graphite or steel crucible under an inert (argon) atmosphere; no solvent, product gases (CCl₄) are condensed and uranium metal is retrieved as a solid.

Acylation of α‑methylbenzylamine with acetyl chloride to give the corresponding N‑acetyl amide. The primary amine attacks the carbonyl of acetyl chloride, forming N‑(1‑phenylpropan‑2‑yl)acetamide and HCl. The reaction is performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, in the presence of a base (triethylamine, pyridine, or NaHCO₃) to neutralize the HCl. Inert atmosphere is optional. The product can serve as a protected amine or as an intermediate.

Condacylhydrazide formation); purpose is synthesis of phenylacetylhydrazide; phenylacetic acid reacts with hydrazine, eliminating water to give the hydrazide; generally carried out in refluxing ethanol or methanol, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl); no special catalyst required.

Reductive hydrogenation; solid Ni2O3 is reduced by H2 gas to metallic nickel while water vapor is formed. Conducted at elevated temperature (300‑500 °C) under a flow of dry hydrogen; solid–gas reaction, no solvent.

Thermal decomposition (acid‑base decomposition); purpose is release of ammonia and formation of boric acid; ammonium borate decomposes on heating to give NH3, H2O, and B(OH)3; performed by gradual heating in a dry container, often in the open air; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed cleavage of an alkyl ether (SN2 substitution); 1‑methoxyoctane reacts with hydrogen chloride to afford 1‑chlorooctane and methanol. HCl protonates the ether oxygen, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbon attached to the –OCH₃ group; chloride attacks the primary carbon, displacing methanol. Typically performed by refluxing the ether with excess gaseous or aqueous HCl (conc. 6 M) in a non‑coordinating solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or without solvent; the products are isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Ester reduction with LiAlH4; purpose is conversion of methyl eicosanoate to the corresponding primary alcohol (1‑eicosanol); LiAlH4 reduces the ester carbonyl, producing eicosanol and methanol; reaction is carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere; work‑up with aqueous acid or water.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) ion‑exchange reaction in aqueous solution; barium metaborate reacts with ammonium chloride to exchange cations, forming soluble ammonium metaborate and barium chloride. Performed in water at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst is needed.

Electrophilic nitrosation; purpose is preparation of N‑nitrosomorpholine; morpholine reacts with nitrosonium perchlorate (NO⁺ ClO₄⁻) to give the N‑nitroso product and perchloric acid; typically performed at 0‑5 °C in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); purpose is isolation of insoluble barium oxalate; aqueous potassium oxalate reacts with aqueous barium chloride, exchanging ions to form precipitated BaC2O4 and soluble KCl; carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation in water between ammonium oxalate and thorium chloride; purpose: preparation of thorium oxalate; key transformation: ion exchange yielding precipitated Th(C2O4)2 and soluble NH4Cl; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient to slightly elevated temperature, stirring, no catalyst; product collected by filtration.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (Fischer esterification); the carboxyl group of nicotinic acid reacts with the primary hydroxyl of 2‑butoxyethanol to form the corresponding 2‑butoxyethyl ester, releasing water. Conducted on the solid acid montmorillonite K10 as a heterogeneous catalyst, typically at 80–120 °C under solvent‑free or minimal solvent conditions; the clay provides both acidity and a high surface area.

Sulfur insertion to form a higher‑order polysulfide; elemental sulfur adds across the S–S bond of dipropyl disulfide, yielding dipropyl trisulfide. Usually performed by heating the disulfide with a stoichiometric excess of powdered sulfur (1 equiv) at 100–150 °C in an inert solvent such as carbon disulfide or toluene, without additional catalyst.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of a saturated alkane to a terminal olefin; undecane loses two hydrogen atoms to generate 1‑undecene. Typical conditions involve a metal oxide or supported transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃, Pt‑Zn, or Ga₂O₃) at 300–500 °C under a flow of inert gas; the reaction is endothermic and often carried out in a fixed‑bed reactor.

Base‑catalyzed ester cleavage (saponification). NaOH attacks the carbonyl of methyl 2‑chloroacetate, forming the sodium salt of 2‑chloroacetate and releasing methanol. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at ambient temperature to reflux, often in a water/ethanol mixture.

Aqueous double‑displacement/acid‑base metathesis; aluminum chloride reacts with the citrate anion of potassium citrate, exchanging counter‑ions to produce aluminum citrate (a soluble metal‑organic complex) and potassium chloride as a by‑product. Conducted in water at ambient to mild heating (20–60 °C) with stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); benzoic acid donates a proton to potassium bicarbonate, forming potassium benzoate while releasing carbon dioxide and water. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; the evolution of CO₂ drives the reaction to completion.

Hydrolysis of a Si–H bond; methylsilane reacts with water to give methylsilanol and hydrogen gas; usually performed in aqueous or mixed organic–aqueous medium; may be acid- or base‑catalyzed (e.g., dilute HCl or NaOH) to accelerate Si–H cleavage; ambient temperature.

Hydrolysis of arsenic pentafluoride; purpose is to convert a non‑aqueous Lewis acid into soluble arsenic acid and HF; key transformation: AsF5 + 4 H2O → H3AsO4 + 5 HF; typical conditions: vigorous stirring in excess water at ambient temperature; solvent: water, no catalyst required.

Sodium borohydride reduction of an aldehyde; purpose is to reduce the formyl group of 5‑formyluracil to a primary alcohol; key transformation: C=O (aldehyde) → CH2OH; typical conditions: NaBH4 (1–2 equiv) in methanol, ethanol, or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, reaction complete within minutes to an hour; no additional catalyst.

Carbothermic reduction of gallium sesquioxide; purpose is to obtain metallic gallium from its oxide; key transformation: Ga2O3 + 3 C → 2 Ga + 3 CO; typical conditions: high temperature (≥1000 °C) in a furnace under inert or reducing atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Acid-catalyzed hydration (electrophilic addition) of propadiene (allene) to give 2‑propanol; Markovnikov addition of water across the C=C bonds; typically performed in aqueous sulfuric or phosphoric acid at reflux.

Jones oxidation of a primary alcohol; purpose is to oxidize 3,3‑dimethyl‑1‑butanol to the corresponding carboxylic acid; key transformation: primary alcohol → carboxylic acid (CH2OH → COOH); typical conditions: CrO3 (1.5 equiv) in aqueous H2SO4 (Jones reagent) added to the substrate dissolved in dry acetone, temperature 0 °C to 25 °C, reaction time 30 min–2 h; catalyst: chromium(VI) species.

Base‑catalyzed amide saponification; L‑theanine reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to produce the sodium salt of L‑glutamate and free ethylamine. Conducted in 0.5–2 M NaOH solution at 50‑80 °C for 1–4 h. Water is the medium; NaOH acts as both stoichiometric reagent and catalyst.

Acid‑carbonate neutralization; purpose is to neutralize acetic acid and generate a salt while evolving CO2; key transformation: 2 CH3COOH + K2CO3 → 2 CH3COOK + H2O + CO2; typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, gentle stirring; solvent: water, no catalyst.

Acetylation of carnitine with acetic anhydride; purpose is to install an acetyl group on the hydroxyl of carnitine forming acetyl‑carnitine; key transformation: –OH + (CH3CO)2O → –OCOCH3 + CH3COOH; typical conditions: carnitine (1 equiv) treated with acetic anhydride (1.2 equiv) in pyridine or another tertiary amine base, 0 °C to 25 °C for 1–2 h; solvent/catalyst: pyridine acts as solvent and base.

Direct chlorination (oxidation) of trichlorosilane; converts the Si–H bond to Si–Cl, yielding silicon tetrachloride and hydrogen chloride; typically carried out in the gas phase at 200‑300 °C under anhydrous conditions in a sealed tube or flow reactor, sometimes with metal chloride catalysts, no solvent required.

Oxidation reaction: alkaline potassium permanganate oxidizes 1‑indanone to 1,3‑indandione, converting the single ketone to a 1,3‑diketone and reducing Mn(VII) to MnO2 precipitate; typically performed in aqueous NaOH solution at moderate to reflux temperatures, with KMnO4 as both oxidant and catalyst.

Solid‑state high‑temperature synthesis: sodium carbonate reacts with zirconium dioxide to form sodium zirconate (Na2ZrO3) while releasing CO2 gas; requires heating the powdered reactants to 900‑1100 °C in a furnace under inert or air atmosphere, with no solvent or catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization/dissolution: concentrated nitric acid protonates and dissolves potassium aluminate, generating aqueous potassium nitrate and aluminum nitrate with water as by‑product; carried out in dilute aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating, often with stirring, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (hydroxide–acid reaction). Formic acid neutralizes magnesium hydroxide to give magnesium formate and water. Usually carried out in water or aqueous methanol under mild heating (30–60 °C) to ensure complete dissolution of the solid Mg(OH)₂. No catalyst required.

Direct combination (binary intermetallic synthesis): elemental cadmium and antimony are fused to produce cadmium antimonide (CdSb); performed by mixing the metals and heating above their melting points (≈900 °C) in an inert atmosphere or vacuum to prevent oxidation, without solvent or catalyst.

Fischer esterification: acetic acid reacts with the hydroxyl group of propylene glycol monomethyl ether to yield propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate and water; typically catalyzed by a strong acid such as H2SO4, refluxed in a non‑aqueous solvent (e.g., toluene or benzene) with removal of water to drive the equilibrium.

Hydrolysis and neutralization: aqueous sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes methylphosphonyl difluoride, replacing the fluorides with hydroxyls to form methylphosphonic acid, which is immediately neutralized to sodium methylphosphonate; the reaction proceeds at low to moderate temperature (0‑25 °C) in water, producing sodium fluoride as a by‑product; no additional catalyst required.

N‑methylation of the secondary nitrogen in Nordazepam; nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a nitrogen atom with methyl iodide to give Diazepam and HI. Typically carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO with a mild base (e.g., K2CO3 or NaH) at 50–80 °C under inert atmosphere.

Transesterification between methyl propionate and 2‑ethyl‑1‑butanol; forms 2‑ethylbutyl propanoate and methanol; useful for exchanging alkoxy groups without using strong acids; catalyzed by acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (NaOCH₃, K₂CO₃); carried out under reflux (≈80 °C) in excess alcohol or a solvent such as toluene; methanol is removed to drive equilibrium.

Radical recombination reaction; a nitrate radical (NO3•) combines with nitrogen dioxide (NO2) to give dinitrogen pentoxide (N2O5); occurs in the gas phase, especially at low temperatures during nighttime atmospheric conditions; no solvent or catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of phosphoryl fluoride (POF₃) with water; a nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus leading to cleavage of a P–F bond, producing hydrogen fluoride and difluorophosphoric acid (H₂PO₃F). Usually performed in aqueous medium at room temperature to mild heating; no special catalyst required, but neutral or slightly basic conditions help control HF evolution.

Esterification of phthalic anhydride with isoheptyl alcohol; Fischer esterification of the anhydride to give the diisoheptyl phthalate and water. Conducted under reflux in an inert, non‑polar solvent (toluene or xylene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) and removal of water (Dean–Stark apparatus) to drive the reaction to completion.

Direct amidation of ‑aminopropanoic acid (alanine) with ammonia; condensation of the carboxyl group with NH₃ to afford 2‑aminopropanamide and water. Typically performed at elevated temperature (150–200 °C) under reduced pressure or in a sealed tube, sometimes using a dehydrating agent (e.g., P₂O₅) or a catalytic amount of a coupling reagent to improve yield.

Oxidation ofodobenzene to iodobenzene diacetate (PhI(OAc)₂) using m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) in the presence of acetic acid; the peracid is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid while transferring acetate to the iodine(III) center. Reaction is run in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acid to promote the oxidation.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 4‑bromobiphenyl with phenylboronic acid to form p‑terphenyl; palladium‑catalyzed aryl‑aryl bond formation. Typical conditions use Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(dppf) (1–5 mol %), a base like K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, a mixed aqueous/organic solvent (toluene/ethanol or dioxane/water), and heating at 80–100 °C under nitrogen.

Oxidation of homovanillyl alcohol to homovanillic acid with aqueous potassium permanganate; primary aromatic alcohol is converted to the corresponding carboxylic acid; reaction conducted in aqueous medium, often at 0 °C to 25 °C, with KMnO₄ added portionwise; manganese dioxide precipitates as a brown solid, water is formed as a by‑product.

Esterification (Fischer esterification) of salicylic acid with benzyl alcohol catalyzed by sulfuric acid, producing benzyl salicylate and water; typically carried out under reflux in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or benzene with water removal (Dean‑Stark apparatus).

Fischer esterification; converts 3‑pentanol and acetic acid into the ester 3‑pentyl acetate; acid‑catalyzed dehydration; typically reflux in excess acetic acid with catalytic H2SO4, water removed to drive equilibrium.

Electrophilic α‑halogenation of a ketone using N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS). Purpose: install a chlorine atom at the carbonyl α‑position for further functionalization. Key transformation: the enol (or pyridine‑generated enolate) of acetophenone attacks the N‑Cl bond of NCS, transferring Cl to the α‑carbon and releasing succinimide; pyridine scavenges the generated HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; pyridine is used as base. No additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenolysis) of dodecanol to dodecane using molecular hydrogen and a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney nickel, Pd/C, or Pt) under pressure; water is formed as the by‑product; common solvents include ethanol or cyclohexane, temperature 50‑150 °C.

Oxidative N‑demethylation of 4‑methoxy‑N‑methyl‑aniline using peracetic acid generated in situ from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide; yields 4‑methoxyaniline, formaldehyde, and water; usually performed at 0‑25 °C in aqueous acetic acid without a metal catalyst.

Base‑mediated neutralization/hydrolysis of vanadium(V) oxide in aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium orthovanadate and water; conducted in water at ambient to elevated temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Radical halogen exchange where chlorine oxidizes iodide in iodopentafluoroethane to elemental iodine while substituting chlorine for iodine, producing perfluoroethyl chloride; typically initiated by UV light or heat in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or benzene.

Reductive amination of 3‑aminopropanal with dimethylamine using sodium cyanoborohydride, forming N,N‑dimethyl‑1,3‑propanediamine via imine formation and reduction; performed in methanol or dichloromethane at pH 5‑6, ambient temperature.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; forms a C(sp2)‑C(sp2) bond between phenylboronic acid and 4‑chloroimidazole to give 4‑phenylimidazole (KCl is generated from the base); typically catalyzed by Pd(0) complexes (e.g., PdPh3)4 or PdCl2(dppf)) with a base such as K2CO3; performed in mixed aqueous/organic solvents (toluene, dioxane or ethanol/water) at 80‑100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed lactone hydrolysis; water attacks the carbonyl of δ‑valerolactone opening the ring to yield 5‑hydroxyhexanoic acid; commonly carried out in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (NaOH) at reflux, followed by acidification to isolate the hydroxy acid; solvent is water or aqueous ethanol.

Acid hydrolysis of aluminum nitride; nitrogen is protonated to ammonia while aluminum forms aluminum sulfate. Used to generate NH₃ and dissolve Al as a sulfate salt. Typically performed in aqueous dilute H₂SO₄ at ambient to reflux temperature; no catalyst required.

Reductive amination (Schiff‑base reduction); benzaldehyde condenses with piperidine to form an imine which is reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to give N‑benzylpiperidine; typically performed in methanol or ethanol with a weak acid buffer (e.g., AcOH) at 0 °C to rt; NaBH3CN is the selective reducing agent.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis (saponification) of an acid chloride; regenerates 2‑propylpentanoic acid from its chloride and forms NaCl; NaOH in aqueous solution attacks the acid chloride carbonyl, producing the carboxylate which is then acidified; typically performed in a mixed solvent system (e.g., THF/H₂O) at 0 °C to reflux, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the free acid.

Hydrolysis of a phosphonate ester; methoxyphosphonoyloxymethane reacts with water, cleaving the P‑O‑CH₃ bonds to give methylphosphonic acid and methanol; typically carried out in aqueous solution, optionally under mild acid or base catalysis, at room temperature to moderate heating.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; preparation of insoluble zinc hydroxide. Aqueous zinc nitrate is mixed with aqueous sodium hydroxide at room temperature, forming a white precipitate of Zn(OH)₂ while sodium nitrate remains in solution. Stirring is sufficient; no catalyst needed.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between elemental bromine and tellurium tetraiodide; bromine replaces iodine on tellurium, producing tellurium tetrabromide and elemental iodine; usually carried out in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at room temperature or slight heating; no catalyst required.

Swern oxidation; dimethyl sulfoxide activated by oxalyl chloride at –78 °C forms a chlorosulfonium intermediate that reacts with 1‑cyclopropylethanol; subsequent addition of triethylamine deprotonates the alkoxysulfonium to give 1‑cyclopropylethanone, with dimethyl sulfide and CO/CO2 as by‑products; solvent is typically dry dichloromethane; reaction kept cold to avoid side reactions.

Metal‑amide generation (deprotonation of a secondary amine); n‑butyllithium deprotonates diisopropylamine in the presence of LiCl to afford lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) and butane gas; conducted in dry THF at –78 °C under nitrogen; LiCl is added to improve solubility and the stability of the LDA base.

Acid–base deprotonation of a tertiary propargylic alcohol with sodium metal; purpose is to generate the corresponding sodium alkoxide for use as a nucleophile or base. Sodium metal inserts into the O–H bond, releasing H₂ gas and forming sodium 2‑methyl‑but‑3‑yn‑2‑olate. Typical conditions are anhydrous, inert atmosphere, low temperature (0 °C to rt) in dry ether or THF as solvent.
Hydrolysis of 3‑azidopropyl acetate to 3‑azidopropanol and acetic acid; simple aqueous hydrolysis, often heated; neutral conditions, water as solvent.

Protonolysis (salt metathesis) of zinc dimethyldithiocarbamate with aqueous hydrochloric acid; purpose is to liberate the free dithiocarbamic acid and convert the zinc salt to soluble zinc chloride. The acid protonates the dithiocarbamate ligand, yielding dimethyl dithiocarbamic acid and ZnCl₂. Conducted in aqueous HCl at ambient temperature; water serves as solvent.

Chlorination of isoamyl alcohol by phosphorus trichloride; a substitution reaction that converts the alcohol to isoamyl chloride while reducing PCl₃ to phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃). Three equivalents of isoamyl alcohol react with one PCl₃, producing three equivalents of isoamyl chloride. The reaction is usually performed neat or in excess isoamyl alcohol as solvent, under reflux (50–80 °C) with a nitrogen atmosphere, no additional catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2). Sodium methoxide acts as nucleophile and attacks allyl bromide, substituting bromide to give allyl methyl ether and sodium bromide. Typically carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or neat methanol, at ambient or slightly elevated temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed ketal formation (protecting the carbonyl of ethyl acetoacetate) using ethylene glycol. Trifluoroacetic acid protonates the carbonyl, enabling nucleophilic attack by ethylene glycol and subsequent loss of water to give the ethylene glycol ketal of ethyl acetoacetate. The reaction is carried out under reflux in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or benzene, often with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water; catalytic amounts of TFA (5–10 mol %) are employed.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of 3‑chloropropionitrile to 3‑hydroxypropionitrile; water acts as nucleophile, displacing chloride and forming HCl as by‑product. Typically performed in aqueous medium with heatingreflux) and may be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed to accelerate the SN1/SN2 pathway. Commonly carried out in ethanol/water mixtures or pure water with a catalytic amount of HCl or NaOH followed by neutralization.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction between aluminum bromide (a Lewis acid) and potassium hydroxide (a strong base); results in formation of insoluble aluminum hydroxide precipitate and soluble potassium bromide. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; vigorous stirring promotes complete conversion. No special catalysts are required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) methylation of a primary amine; purpose is to install a methyl group on the nitrogen of tryptamine to afford N‑methyltryptamine. The lone pair on the amine attacks the methyl carbon of dimethyl sulfate, displacing methyl hydrogen sulfate. Typically conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, acetone or acetonitrile with a base (pyridine, NaOH or K₂CO₃) at 0 – 25 °C to control exotherm; stoichiometric dimethyl sulfate is used, no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; purpose is the synthesis of the local anesthetic quinocaine (dimethocaine) by forming an ester linkage between p‑aminobenzoic acid and 2‑diethylaminoethanol. The carboxyl group of the acid reacts with the alcohol hydroxyl to give the ester and water. Conducted with catalytic concentrated H₂SO₄, excess 2‑diethylaminoethanol, reflux (80 ‑ 120 °C) in an azeotropically drying solvent such as toluene or xylene; water is removed by Dean–Stark or by azeotropic distillation.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation using formic acid as the hydrogen donor; purpose is the reduction of veratraldehyde to veratryl alcohol. Formic acid decomposes to CO₂ while delivering two hydrogen atoms that reduce the aldehyde carbonyl to a primary alcohol. Conducted in an alcoholic or aqueous medium (ethanol, methanol, or water) at 50 ‑ 100 °C in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni; reaction is performed under an inert atmosphere, no additional solvents beyond the reaction medium are required.

Carbothermic solid‑state redox (reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon); purpose is to produce magnetite (Fe₃O₄) and carbon monoxide, a step common in metallurgical processes. Carbon reduces Fe₂O₃, being oxidized to CO while Fe₂O₃ is partially reduced to the mixed‑valence Fe(II,III) oxide. Requires high temperature (≈ 1000 ‑ 1300 °C) in a furnace or blast furnace; reactants are mixed as fine powders, no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) O‑methylation; the hydroxyl group of benzoin attacks methyl iodide to form O‑methyl benzoin and iodide ion; performed in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, or DMSO) with a mild base such as potassium carbonate or sodium hydride at reflux or room temperature; reaction proceeds cleanly to give the methyl ether.

Acid‑base salt metathesis; purpose is to protonate thiocyanate ion to give thiocyanic acid (HSCN) while forming potassium chloride. Proton transfer from HCl to SCN⁻ produces HSCN; K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give KCl. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, typically with dilute HCl; no catalyst or special solvent beyond water is required.

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange) in aqueous solution; magnesium acetate reacts with gluconic acid to transfer the magnesium cation to the gluconate anion, liberating acetic acid. Usually performed in water with gentle heating; acetic acid can be removed by evaporation. No catalyst required.

Redox reduction of the triphenylmethane dye malachite green to its leuco (colorless) form using Fe(II) as the reducing agent in acidic medium. Hydrochloric acid provides the acidic environment; FeSO₄ supplies Fe²⁺ which donates electrons to the dye. Conducted in aqueous solution or slightly elevated temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of 2‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol to give the alkene α‑methylstyrene. Protonation of the hydroxyl group forms a good leaving group, followed by carbocation formation and loss of a β‑hydrogen to afford the alkene; water is the only by‑product. Typical conditions: catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid (10–20 mol %) in refluxing toluene or dry benzene, often with a Dean–Stark trap to remove water and shift the equilibrium.

Phosphine‑mediated deoxygenation (Staudinger-type reduction) of an N‑oxide. Triphenylphosphine attacks the N‑oxide of 1‑methyl‑1‑oxidopyrrolidin‑1‑ium, yielding the corresponding amine (1‑methylpyrrolidine) and triphenylphosphine oxide as the oxidized by‑product. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as THF or CH₂Cl₂ at room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (SN2) of 1‑chloro‑2‑fluoroethane with hydrogen bromide to give 1‑bromo‑2‑fluoroethane; nucleophilic substitution of chlorine by bromide. Typically refluxed in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, using gaseous or aqueous HBr; generates HCl as by‑product.

Esterification via in‑situ formation of an acid chloride. Thionyl chloride converts cinnamic acid to cinnamoyl chloride with evolution of SO₂ and HCl; the freshly generated acid chloride then reacts with benzyl alcohol to give benzyl cinnamate. Reaction usually performed in dry dichloromethane or chloroform, often with pyridine or triethylamine as an HCl scavenger, at 0 °C to room temperature. No additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange in aqueous solution; ammonium fluoride reacts with lithium hexafluorosilicate to produce ammonium hexafluorosilicate and lithium fluoride. The reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring; the insoluble LiF can be filtered off and the (NH₄)₂SiF₆ crystallized from the filtrate. No catalyst required.

Strong oxidative cleavage of a 1,3‑diol to a dicarboxylic acid. Potassium permanganate oxidizes 1,3‑propanediol under aqueous, often alkaline, conditions, yielding malonic acid, water, and manganese dioxide precipitate. Typically heated under reflux with excess KMnO₄; the reaction mixture is later acidified to isolate the product. No additional catalyst.

Halogen exchange (SN1 nucleophilic substitution) on a tertiary benzylic chloride; triphenylmethyl chloride reacts with hydrogen bromide to give triphenylmethyl bromide and HCl. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone or dichloromethane) at reflux; excess HBr drives the exchange; no catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous zinc nitrate reacts with ammonium hydroxide to give zinc hydroxide precipitate and ammonium nitrate in solution; conducted in water at ambient temperature, often with stirring; no catalyst.

Chlorite oxidation (Pinnick oxidation) of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. NaClO2 oxidizes 2,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde to 2,4‑dihydroxybenzoic acid in aqueous buffer (phosphate, pH 4–5) at 0 °C to rt, often with a chlorine‑dioxide scavenger such as 2‑methyl‑2‑butene. No metal catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization; two equivalents of citric acid are deprotonated by three equivalents of calcium hydroxide to afford the tricalcium salt of citric acid (tricalcium citrate) and water. Conducted in aqueous solution with stirring and gentle heating to dissolve the solids; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of an acid chloride with ammonia; isobutyryl chloride is attacked by ammonia to form isobutyramide and HCl. Usually carried out at 0 °C to 25 °C in anhydrous solvent such as THF or dichloromethane, using gaseous or aqueous NH₃ to capture the generated HCl; a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) may be added as acid scavenger.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification converts the ethyl ester into its sodium carboxylate and releases ethanol; key step is nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the carbonyl carbon, cleavage of the C–O bond; typically carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at ambient temperature or under gentle reflux; solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst required.

Acidic hydrolysis of a calcium citrate salt; excess aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates the tricalcium citrate, releasing citric acid and forming soluble calcium chloride. Reaction is performed in aqueous HCl solution with heating (50–80 °C) to promote dissolution; no special catalyst required.

Electrophilic α‑chlorination (radical halogenation) of chloroacetyl chloride; chlorine adds to the α‑carbon of the acyl chloride, producing dichloroacetyl chloride and releasing HCl; usually initiated by UV light or a radical initiator at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; HCl gas is removed or trapped during the reaction.

Dehydrohalogenation (elimination) of DDT to DDE; p,p'-Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane loses HCl to form the conjugated alkene p,p'-Dichlorodiphenyldichloroethylene. Achieved by heating or treating with a base (e.g., NaOH or K₂CO₃) in a polar aprotic solvent (ethanol or acetone); the reaction proceeds via an E2 mechanism and is often used to assess environmental degradation of DDT.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction); converts the carbonyl group of cyclohexanone to a secondary alcohol (cyclohexanol); key transformation C=O → C‑OH; typically performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with Pd/C as catalyst in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to moderate heat.

Amide coupling using propylphosphonic anhydride (T3P); forms the diethylamide (diethylpropion) from 2‑phenylpropanoic acid and diethylamine; activation of the carboxylic acid by T3P followed by nucleophilic attack of the amine; usually carried out in dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often with a base (e.g., DIPEA) to scavenge generated acid.

Nucleophilic substitution at silicon (organosilicon synthesis); phenyl lithium replaces one chloride of SiCl₄ to give phenyltrichlorosilane and LiCl; typical conditions: low temperature (−78 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base dissolution of silica; HF attacks SiO₂ forming fluoro‑silicate species which are neutralized by Ba(OH)₂ to give barium hexafluorosilicate; reaction proceeds in aqueous HF solution, often at ambient to slightly elevated temperature, with careful control of acidity and metal ion stoichiometry.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of phenyl hydrogen sulfate; NaOH hydrolyzes the sulfate ester to phenol while forming sodium sulfate and water; generally performed in aqueous NaOH solution with heating (reflux) to ensure complete conversion.

Electrophilic addition of bromine to vinyl chloride; vicinal dibromination across the C=C bond yields 1,2-dibromo-1-chloroethane. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 2‑chloroacetamide by ammonia; chloride is displaced to yield glycinamide (2‑aminoacetamide) and HCl; conducted in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia solution, often at mild heating to promote substitution.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromoacetate by aqueous ammonia; purpose is to synthesize the amino ester ethyl 2‑aminoacetate; key transformation replaces the bromide with an –NH2 group yielding the ester and ammonium bromide; typical conditions use excess aqueous NH3, reflux or room temperature, water as solvent, no additional catalyst.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous AgNO3 replaces chloride ions of CrCl3·6H2O, yielding a white AgCl precipitate, soluble Cr(NO3)3 and water; carried out in water at room temperature, no catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis/precipitation) reaction between oxalic acid and copper(II) sulfate; purpose is to prepare insoluble copper(II) oxalate; key transformation swaps anions to give copper(II) oxalate precipitate and sulfuric acid in solution; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no special catalyst required.

Hydrohalogenation of hept‑2‑ene with hydrogen chloride gas. Markovnikov addition gives 2‑chloroheptane as the major product. Reaction is performed by bubbling HCl into a solution of the alkene in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at 0 °C to room temperature. No additional catalyst is required.

Triphosgene‑mediated conversion of chloromethanol to chloromethyl chloroformate (phosgene‑equivalent reaction); purpose is to generate the chloroformate reagent while releasing HCl; key transformation involves nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on triphosgene producing three equivalents of chloromethyl chloroformate and three equivalents of HCl; carried out in dry dichloromethane (or similar apro solvent) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, often with a base such as pyridine to scavenge HCl.

In‑situ peracid epoxidation (Prileschajew oxidation) of vinylcyclohexene using sodium hypochlorite and acetic acid; purpose is to convert the alkene to its epoxide (vinyl cyclohexene dioxide); key transformation involves formation of peracetic acid from NaOCl + HOAc which transfers an oxygen atom to the double bond; typical conditions are aqueous NaOCl, acetic acid, 0–5 °C, a biphasic mixture with an organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂), producing water and NaCl as by‑products.

Hydrolysis of an aryl isocyanate (acidic or basic aqueous work‑up); water adds across the N=C=O group, forming a carbamic acid intermediate that spontaneously decarboxylates to give 3,4‑dichloroaniline and CO₂; typically performed by stirring the isocyanate in a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF or acetone) at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; pH may be adjusted with dilute acid or base to accelerate the reaction.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) between chromium(III) nitrate and ammonium chloride; purpose is to exchange nitrate and chloride ions; key transformation yields chromium(III) chloride and ammonium nitrate in solution; carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature, no catalyst needed.

Alkylation esterification of methacrylic acid with methyl iodide in the presence of triethylamine; purpose is to form the ester methyl methacrylate; key transformation deprotonates the acid to a carboxylate which attacks MeI (SN2) giving the ester and triethylammonium iodide; performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, with TEA as base, at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere if desired.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis). Purpose: liberate free‑base lidocaine from its HCl salt. Key transformation: proton transfer from lidocaine·HCl to OH⁻ forming water and NaCl while the lidocaine molecule becomes neutral. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often followed by extraction into an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane). No catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Purpose: isolate insoluble cadmium oxalate. Key transformation: exchange of Na⁺ and Cd²⁺ ions, producing soluble NaCl and sparingly soluble CdC₂O₄ which precipitates. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at room temperature. Common solvent: water; no catalyst.

Redox (single‑displacement) reaction. Purpose: reduce ferric (Fe³⁺) to ferrous (Fe²⁺) while oxidizing aluminum to Al³⁺. Key transformation: Al metal donates electrons to Fe³⁺, forming iron(II) sulfate and aluminum sulfate. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (sulfate solution), moderate heating (50‑80 °C). No catalyst needed.

Condensation (imine formation) between formaldehyde and methylamine under acidic conditions. Purpose: synthesize N‑methylmethanimine (a Schiff base). Key transformation: nucleophilic addition of methylamine to the carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde, followed by loss of water to give the C=N bond. Typical conditions: dilute HCl as catalyst, temperature 0‑25 °C to avoid polymerisation, solvent such as aqueous methanol or ethanol. No additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis / decarboxylative hydrogenation of 2‑chloropropionic acid. Purpose: remove the carboxyl group to afford 2‑chloropropane. Key transformation: hydrogen addition to the carbonyl, followed by release of CO₂ and replacement of the carboxyl group with hydrogen. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % wt) catalyst, solvent like ethanol or THF, temperature 50‑100 °C. No other reagents.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification. Purpose: convert diethyl terephthalate to dimethyl terephthalate. Key transformation: exchange of ethoxy groups for methoxy groups; NaOCH₃ deprotonates methanol to generate methoxide, which attacks the ester carbonyl, releasing ethanol. Typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol, catalytic amount of sodium methoxide (0.5‑5 mol %), removal of ethanol to drive equilibrium. No additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1); purpose: form cyclopentene from cyclopentanol. Protonation of the alcohol by conc. H₂SO₄ creates a good leaving group, water departs to give a carbocation, and loss of a β‑hydrogen yields the alkene. Conditions: conc. H₂SO₄, heating to 140–180 °C, often in a sealed tube or reflux setup.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide; water reacts with beryllium iodide to generate beryllium hydroxide precipitate and regenerate hydroiodic acid; carried out in aqueous medium, typically at room temperature; no catalyst.

Solid‑state intermetallic formation. Direct reaction of elemental manganese with silicon to produce manganese silicide (e.g., MnSi, Mn5Si3). Conducted by heating a mixture of Mn and Si powders at 1000–1300 °C under argon or vacuum to prevent oxidation; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange anions to obtain soluble manganese nitrate and ammonium tungstate, often for preparing tungstate solutions. Key transformation: NH₄⁺ swaps with Mn²⁺ forming Mn(NO₃)₂ (aq) and (NH₄)₂WO₄ (aq). Typical conditions: dissolve reagents in water, stir at room temperature or gently heat (≤50 °C); filtration if precipitate forms. No catalyst needed.

Combustion (oxidative combustion). Nonane reacts with excess O₂ under ignition (≈500 °C) in the gas phase, fully oxidizing all carbon to CO₂ and hydrogen to H₂O, releasing heat. No solvent; reaction proceeds in open air or a furnace flame.

Acylation of an aromatic amine (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose is to synthesize 1‑naphthylacetamide (protective group or target amide). Key transformation: acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the amine, yielding the amide and one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: performed neat or in pyridine/dichloromethane at 0 °C to reflux; pyridine acts as base/solvent. No metal catalyst required.

Double replacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; copper(II) sulfate reacts with ammonium thiocyanate, exchanging anions to produce copper(II) thiocyanate (often a colored precipitate) and ammonium sulfate in solution. The mixture is typically heated to improve solubility and then allowed to cool so that Cu(SCN)₂ precipitates, which is collected by filtration.

Acid‑base neutralization with precipitation; purpose is to convert ferrous citrate to soluble sodium citrate while precipitating iron(II) hydroxide. Key transformation: OH⁻ deprotonates citrate to sodium citrate and combines with Fe²⁺ to give Fe(OH)₂ solid; water is formed. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, excess NaOH added dropwise, temperature kept 0–25 °C to control Fe(OH)₂ precipitation. No catalyst.

Urea formation via carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) coupling; type: condensation (CDImediated) reaction to a bis‑urea. Purpose is to synthesize 1,3‑bis[3-(dimethylamino)propyl]urea as a ligand or polymer precursor. Key transformation: CDI activates one amine to an imidazolyl carbamate intermediate, which reacts with a second amine, releasing two imidazole molecules and forming the urea linkage. Typical conditions: anhydrous organic solvent (THF, DMF, DCM), inert atmosphere (N₂), 20‑50 °C. No additional catalyst.

Oxidative rearrangement (aryl migration) converting a flavanone to an isoflavone; purpose is to obtain the biologically active isoflavone daidzein from liquiritigenin. Key transformation: migration of the B‑ring from C‑2 to C‑3 with concomitant oxidation, generating the isoflavone skeleton. Typical chemical method: oxidation with DDQ or MnO₂ in CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN at 0 °C to rt; alternatively enzymatic conversion using isoflavone synthase and NADPH. No metal catalyst required for the chemical version.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of basic aluminum acetate; purpose is to produce aluminum oxide and release acetic acid, often for material preparation. Key transformation: upon heating, acetate groups decompose, yielding Al₂O₃ solid and volatilized acetic acid. Typical conditions: heat solid to 350‑500 °C in a furnace or muffle oven, in air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of ethane. Ethane is converted to ethylene and hydrogen by removal of hydrogen atoms, usually over a metal oxide catalyst such as Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃ or Pt‑based catalysts. Reaction temperatures are 600–700 °C under a flow of inert gas; the feed is dry ethane, and the catalyst provides the activation energy.

Oxidative roasting: solid‑state oxidation of lead telluride by oxygen to give lead(II) oxide and tellurium dioxide. Purpose is conversion of a metal chalcogenide to its oxides. Key transformation: O₂ inserts into Pb–Te bonds forming PbO and TeO₂.
