Typically carried out at high temperature (400‑800 °C) in a furnace under a flow of air or pure O₂; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acylation (amide formation) of dicyclohexylamine with acetyl bromide. Purpose is synthesis of N,N‑dicyclohexylacetamide. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the amine on the acyl bromide, displacement of bromide to give the amide and HBr. Usually performed at 0‑20 °C in an aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or THF, with a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize HBr.

N‑bromination of acetamide under basic conditions (haloamination). Purpose is preparation of N‑bromoacetamide. Key transformation: Br₂ reacts with NaOH to form hypobromite, which brominates the amide nitrogen, yielding N‑bromoacetamide, NaBr and water. Conducted in aqueous NaOH at 0‑5 °C; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

SN2 alkylation of thioacetate; sodium thioacetate provides the nucleophilic CH3COS− anion which attacks methyl iodide to give methyl thioacetate and NaI; purpose: preparation of thioesters; key transformation: substitution of I by thioacetate group on a primary carbon; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, mild heating (40‑60 °C) if needed; NaI precipitates in some solvents; no catalyst required.

Metathesis (acid‑base neutralization) between lactic acid and cadmium nitrate. Purpose is formation of cadmium dilactate salt and release of nitric acid. Key transformation: exchange of anions, Cd²⁺ combines with lactate anions while nitrate ions pair with protons to give HNO₃. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2). Rubidium ethoxide attacks ethyl bromide to give diethyl ether and rubidium bromide. Reaction carried out in dry ethanol or THF at reflux, moisture excluded, no catalyst required.

Reductive hydrogenation (metal halide reduction); reduces hafnium(IV) iodide to metallic hafnium while producing hydrogen iodide; method for preparing pure hafnium metal; conducted at 500–800 °C under a flow of dry H2 (often in quartz tube); no solvent, may use a carrier gas such as Ar.

Metallothermic reduction of phosphorus pentachloride by magnesium. Purpose is production of elemental white phosphorus. Key transformation: Mg reduces PCl₅, removing chlorine as MgCl₂ and yielding P₄. Carried out in a high‑temperature furnace (≈600‑800 °C) under an inert atmosphere (argon); solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Fluorination/halogen exchange of terbium(III) bromide with elemental fluorine. Purpose is synthesis of terbium tetrafluoride and liberation of bromine, also oxidizing Tb³⁺ to Tb⁴⁺. Key transformation: F₂ replaces Br⁻ ligands and oxidizes the metal, producing TbF₄ and Br₂ gas. Conducted at elevated temperature (200‑400 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible reactor, often with an inert gas diluent; no solvent or catalyst.

Fischer esterification; 2‑methoxyacetic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid to give ethyl 2‑methoxyacetate and water; reflux in excess ethanol (or azeotropic removal of water) for several hours; acid catalyst 5–10 % v/v H₂SO₄, typically under reflux at 78 °C.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); sodium hydroxide attacks methyl propionate, cleaving the ester bond to yield methanol and the sodium salt of propionic acid (sodium propionate). Reaction is conducted in aqueous NaOH, typically at reflux (≈80‑100 °C) for several hours until complete conversion. No additional catalyst is needed; water–ethanol mixtures are common solvents to dissolve both reactants.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Acetyl chloride reacts with cis‑11‑octadecenol to form cis‑vaccenyl acetate and hydrochloric acid. The reaction is typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, using a base like pyridine or triethylamine to trap the liberated HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Hydrolysis (acid formation) of rhenium(VII) oxide; water reacts with Re2O7 to generate perrhenic acid (HReO4). The reaction proceeds readily when Re2O7 is added to aqueous solution, often at room temperature or with gentle heating. No catalyst is required; the solvent is water, and the product is obtained as an acidic solution.

Reductive conversion of a nitro group to an amine (dithionite reduction). 4‑Bromo‑nitrobenzene is treated with sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) in the presence of excess aqueous NaOH. The conditions are usually 50–80 °C in water, allowing the nitro group to be reduced to the corresponding aniline while the bromine substituent remains untouched. Water is produced and sodium sulfite is formed as a by‑product.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Aqueous solutions of oxalic acid and gadolinium sulfate are mixed, causing the exchange of anions to give insoluble gadolinium oxalate, which precipitates out, and soluble sulfuric acid remains in solution. The reaction is carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; gentle heating can improve precipitation. No catalyst is required.

Halide exchange (metathesis) in the solid‑state or dry medium. Titanium(III) chloride reacts with three equivalents of potassium fluoride to afford titanium(III) fluoride and three equivalents of potassium chloride. Because both products are moisture‑sensitive, the reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, often in a polar aprotic solvent such as molten KF/AlF₃ eutectic or dry acetonitrile, and heated to 150–200 °C to promote complete exchange. No additional catalyst is needed.

Metal‑halogen exchange followed by borylation to afford an arylboronic acid. n‑Butyllithium performs lithium‑halogen exchange on 4‑tert‑butylbromobenzene at –78 °C in dry THF, generating the aryl lithium species, which is then trapped with trimethyl borate. After aqueous work‑up (often with dilute HCl), 4‑tert‑butylphenylboronic acid is obtained. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere, dry THF, low temperature for the lithiation step, then warming to room temperature for borate addition and hydrolysis.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation. Salicylic acid is sulfonated with oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) to introduce a sulfonic acid group onto the aromatic ring, yielding sulfosalicylic acid. The reaction is conducted neat or in concentrated sulfuric acid at 80–150 °C, with careful temperature control to avoid over‑sulfonation. Water is generated as a by‑product; the sulfonated product is isolated after cooling and neutralization. No external catalyst is required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); chlorine gas adds to the activated aromatic ring of 4‑methylaniline, giving ortho‑chloro product and HCl; typically performed in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂) at 0 – 25 °C with a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃ to generate the electrophilic Cl⁺.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; aqueous barium chloride reacts with ammonium sodium phosphate to exchange cations, forming insoluble barium phosphate which precipitates, while sodium chloride and ammonium chloride remain in solution; carried out in water at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed); the acetate ester of 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol is cleaved by water to give acetic acid and dimethylaminoethanol; usually performed in aqueous HCl (reflux) or NaOH (reflux) followed by acid work‑up, using a polar protic solvent such as ethanol/water mixture.

Electrophilic fluorination using N‑fluorobenzenesulfonimide (NFSI); NFSI transfers an electrophilic fluorine atom to imidazole, affording 2‑fluoro‑1H‑imidazole while the sulfonimide fragment is released as benzenesulfonamide; reactions are run in dry organic solvents (e.g., MeCN or CH₂Cl₂) at 0 – 25 °C, often with a mild base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) to deprotonate the heterocycle.

Acid‑base metalation (generation of a strong, non‑nucleophilic base); sec‑butyllithium abstracts a proton from diisopropylamine, producing lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) and volatile butane gas; carried out under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF at –78 °C to –40 °C to prevent side reactions.

Formation of a Grignard reagent (organomagnesium halide) from ethyl bromide and magnesium; purpose is to generate ethylmagnesium bromide for carbon‑carbon bond formation. Mg inserts into the C–Br bond. Reaction performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen or argon, often initiated by a few drops of iodine or a small amount of alkyl halide, at ambient temperature or gentle reflux.

Acid‑base neutralization; hydrazine reacts with sulfuric acid to form hydrazinium sulfate salt and water; the process is performed in aqueous solution at low temperature (0 – 5 °C) to control exotherm, with no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of methyl 2‑hydroxyacetate; purpose is to obtain the sodium salt of glycolic acid (sodium glycolate). The ester is cleaved by hydroxide, yielding methanol and glycolate anion which is immediately neutralized by Na⁺ to give sodium glycolate. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at ambient temperature or gentle heating (30–60 °C); reaction proceeds rapidly and is often done in a water/ethanol mixture for better solubility. No additional catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to generate perchloric acid and precipitate insoluble silver chloride. Key transformation: exchange of chloride and perchlorate ions producing HClO4 (aq) and AgCl (solid). Typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special catalyst required. Simple stirring and filtration isolate AgCl.
Base‑catalyzed saponification of 3‑azidopropyl acetate; NaOH attacks the carbonyl, yielding 3‑azidopropanol and sodium acetate; performed in aqueous NaOH at ambient or reflux temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an isocyanate; converts 2‑chloroethyl isocyanate to the corresponding amine while releasing carbon dioxide. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the electrophilic carbon of the –N=C=O group, forming a carbamic acid intermediate that decarboxylates to give 2‑chloroethylamine and CO2 gas. Conducted in water (often with mild acid or base, e.g., NaOH or HCl) at ambient to gentle reflux temperatures (20–80 °C). No additional catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; converts primary alkyl chloride to primary alcohol; Cl is replaced by OH to give 1‑dodecanol and NaCl; usually performed with aqueous or ethanolic NaOH (1–2 equiv) at reflux (≈100 °C); polar protic solvent (water/ethanol) under basic conditions, no catalyst.

Reductive dechlorination (hydrogen reduction) of titanium trichloride; hydrogen gas reduces TiCl3 to TiCl2 with concomitant formation of hydrogen chloride. Key transformation: H2 donates electrons to Ti(III), reducing it to Ti(II) and generating HCl as a by‑product. Performed in the gas phase or sealed tube at elevated temperature (typically 200–300 °C) under a flow of H2; inert atmosphere (e.g., N2) may be used. No catalyst other than the metal halide itself.

Acid‑base neutralization; nitrous acid reacts with rubidium hydroxide to form rubidium nitrite and water. Key transformation: proton transfer from HNO2 to OH−, yielding H2O and Rb+NO2−. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring until complete neutralization. No catalyst required.

Hydrolysis (saponification) reaction. Purpose: Converts ester to carboxylate salt (sodium propionate) and alcohol (pentanol). Key transformations: Ester bond broken upon base treatment. Conditions: Requires aqueous NaOH, typically heated. General application: Laboratory-scale ester hydrolysis for carboxylate salts.

Non‑enzymatic Maillard-type glycation (advanced glycation end‑product formation); L‑arginine reacts with the dicarbonyl compound 3‑deoxyglucosone to form the fluorescent adduct argpyrimidine. Key transformation: nucleophilic addition of the guanidino group of arginine to the carbonyl carbons of 3‑deoxyglucosone followed by cyclization and oxidation to give the heterocyclic argpyrimidine. Typically occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.4) and temperature (≈37 °C) over hours to days; no external catalyst, though oxidative conditions can accelerate formation.

Acid–base neutralization of a carboxylate salt with hydrobromic acid. Potassium 2‑methylpropanoate is protonated by HBr to afford 2‑methylpropanoic acid, while potassium bromide remains in solution. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation; potassium thioacetate (CH3COS−K+) attacks iodomethane, displacing iodide to give S‑methyl thioacetate and potassium iodide. Key transformation: backside attack of the sulfur nucleophile on the methyl carbon, forming a new C–S bond. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, acetone, or DMSO, often at 0 °C to room temperature; stirring under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation. No additional catalyst required.

Transmetalation (alkyl/halide exchange) between indium trichloride and trimethylaluminum to afford trimethylindium and aluminum trichloride; employed for the preparation of volatile Me₃In in organometallic chemistry. Conducted under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at low to ambient temperature (0–25 °C) in dry, non‑coordinating solvents such as toluene, hexane, or petroleum ether; no external catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion (thermal oxidation) of lutetium nitride with molecular oxygen to give lutetium oxide and nitrogen gas; a combustion‑type reaction used to obtain the stable oxide from the nitride. Performed at elevated temperatures (typically >600 °C) in a flowing O₂ or air stream; no solvent, catalyst, or additive is needed.

Conversion of a nitrile to an amidine (benzamidine) via thionyl chloride activation followed by reaction with aqueous ammonia; a thionyl‑chloride‑mediated amidination. Reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, initially cooling the mixture of benzonitrile and SOCl₂ (0 °C) then adding aqueous NH₃; the mixture is warmed to reflux, generating HCl, H₂O and SO₂ as gaseous by‑products. No additional catalyst is required.

Oxidation of DL‑cysteine to DL‑cysteic acid using sodium periodate; a periodate‑mediated oxidation of thiol group to thefonic acid functionality. Conducted in aqueous medium (often buffered near neutral pH) at 0–25 °C; sodium periodate is used in stoichiometric excess (3 equiv) and no catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic addition of a deprotonated acetylene (acetylide) toone, known as alkynylation; potassium hydroxide deprotonates acetylene to generate the acetylide ion, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetone, forming 2‑methyl‑3‑butyn‑2‑ol after protonation. The reaction is carried out in an alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) or liquid ammonia, at low to moderate temperature (0 °C to 25 °C) under inert atmosphere to avoid acetylene oxidation. Potassium hydroxide serves both as base and catalyst.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; converts the primary alkyl bromide to a thioether (mercaptoethyl acetate); H2S acts as nucleophile displacing Br‑; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at reflux; HBr formed is often neutralized with a base.

Esterification of an acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose: synthesize ethyl 2‑chloropropanoate; key transformation: ethanol attacks the carbonyl carbon of 2‑chloropropanoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the ethyl ester and HCl; typical conditions: reflux ethanol in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃) to neutralize the liberated HCl; reaction proceeds at room temperature to reflux; solvent is ethanol (also reactant).

Sulfonylation (formation of an alkyl tosylate) of 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol with p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride in the presence of pyridine, which acts as both base and nucleophilic catalyst, yielding 2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl p‑toluenesulfonate and pyridinium chloride. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in pyridine (often used as solvent and base); the reaction is typically quenched with water and extracted. No external catalyst beyond pyridine is needed.

Intramolecular lactonization (dehydrative cyclization). Beta‑hydroxypropionic acid cyclizes to the four‑membered β‑propiolactone with loss of one molecule of water. Typically performed by heating the acid neat or in a high‑boiling aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene) in the presence of a strong dehydrating agent such as phosphorus pentoxide or acetic anhydride at 180–250 °C. No catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds via intramolecular attack of the carboxylate on the β‑hydroxyl carbon.

Double displacement (halide exchange) metathesis; used to prepare gallium(III) fluoride by exchanging chloride for fluoride ions. Key transformation: GaCl3 + KF → GaF3 (sparingly soluble) + KCl. Typically performed in aqueous solution or molten salts, often heated to promote precipitation of GaF3; water or polar organic solvents (e.g., ethanol) can be used; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl mesylate. Potassium thiocyanate supplies SCN⁻ which displaces the methanesulfonate group of ethyl methanesulfonate to give ethyl thiocyanate and potassium methanesulfonate. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO or acetonitrile) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, usually under nitrogen. No additional catalyst is needed.

Pinner‑type conversion of a nitrile to an amidine (benzamidine hydrochloride). Benzonitrile reacts with aqueous ammonia in the presence of gaseous hydrogen chloride (or concentrated HCl solution) in ethanol. The acid protonates the nitrile, forming an imidate that is attacked by ammonia, followed by proton transfers to afford the amidine hydrochloride salt. Reaction is refluxed in ethanol for several hours; the HCl serves both as catalyst and to generate the hydrochloride salt of benzamidine.

Metathesis/halide exchange (acid‑base double displacement). Aqueous hydrofluoric acid reacts with cerium(III) chloride to replace chloride ligands with fluoride, producing cerium(III) fluoride precipitate and three equivalents of hydrochloric acid. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the insoluble CeF₃ is isolated by filtration. No catalyst is required.

Chlorination an alcohol using phosphorus pentachloride. 2‑Ethoxyethanol is treated with PCl₅, which converts the primary hydroxyl group to a chloride, yielding 2‑chloroethyl ethyl ether, phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and hydrogen chloride as by‑products. The reaction is performed in an anhydrous, non‑protic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to room temperature. No additional catalyst is needed.

Metal‑catalyzed carboxylation of an aryl bromide with CO₂; a palladium or copper catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄ or CuI) under CO₂ pressure (1–5 atm) and a base such as Cs₂CO₃ or NaOtBu in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) yields the aryl carboxylic acid, converting the C–Br bond into a C–CO₂H group.

Reductive amination via the Leuckart‑Wallach reaction. 4‑Methylphenylacetone is heated with ammonium formate, which acts as both ammonia source and reducing agent. The ketone is converted to 4‑methylphenethylamine with release of carbon dioxide and water (the latter from formic acid decomposition). Reaction is conducted in a sealed tube or high‑pressure vessel at 150–200 °C, often without added solvent or using a small amount of formic acid as medium. No external catalyst is required.
Solid‑state synthesis (direct combination) of cerium nitride; nitrogen gas reacts with metallic cerium at high temperature (≈800‑1100 °C) under a nitrogen atmosphere to give CeN, no solvent required.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of trimethylsilyl benzoate with 1‑butanol; purpose is to generate n‑butyl benzoate and trimethylsilanol; the butanol oxygen nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl, displacing the trimethylsilyl group; typical conditions involve refluxing the silyl ester in excess 1‑butanol, optionally with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., imidazole); 1‑butanol acts as both reagent and solvent.
Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; NiSO₄ solution mixed with Mg(OH)₂ suspension forms insoluble Ni(OH)₂ precipitate and soluble MgSO₄, typically at room temperature in water.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone; dimethyl sulfide is oxidized by O₂ to dimethyl sulfone, usually in the presence of a transition‑metal (e.g., CuCl₂, Co‑Mn oxides) in an organic solvent such as acetonitrile or MeCN at elevated temperature (80‑150 °C) and O₂ pressure.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl 2‑nitroacetate to nitroacetic acid and methanol; performed in aqueous NaOH at 60‑80 °C followed by acid work‑up, or under aqueous HCl reflux; no special catalyst needed.

Thermal polymerization/condensation of cyanamide to cyamelide (polycyanamide). Heating neat cyanamide at 150–200 °C drives intermolecular condensation with loss of ammonia, forming the polymeric cyclic trimer/oligomer cyamelide. No solvent or catalyst is needed; the reaction is typically performed under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Single displacement redox (metal exchange). Zinc metal reduces Cu(II) in copper(II) iodide to metallic copper while being oxidized to Zn²⁺, forming zinc iodide. Typically performed in a dry or inert‐solvent medium (e.g., THF) at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

SN2 amination; purpose: production of primary allylamine; key transformation: ammonia attacks the allylic carbon, displacing iodide and forming allylamine with HI as by‑product; typical conditions: excess aqueous or liquid NH₃, 0–25 °C (often in ethanol); HI neutralized by a base such as NaOH if needed.
Jones oxidation of a secondary benzylic alcohol; indan‑1‑ol is oxidized to 1H‑inden‑1‑one using CrO₃/H₂SO₄ (Jones reagent) in acetone, typically at 0‑25 °C, generating a ketone and Cr³⁺ by‑products.
Aqueous ion‑exchange (double‑displacement) metathesis; BaCl₂ reacts with NaSCN in water to give soluble Ba(SCN)₂ and NaCl, carried out at room temperature, no precipitation or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution/organometallic formation; MeLi attacks SnCl₄, substituting four Cl⁻ for Me groups to afford tetramethyltin (Me₄Sn) and LiCl; performed in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of a tertiary phosphine by a peracid; triphenylphosphine (PIII) is converted to triphenylphosphine oxide (PV) while meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid is reduced to meta‑chlorobenzoic acid. Typically run in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric m‑CPBA, no catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl acetate with rubidium hydroxide; the ester bond is cleaved to give ethanol and rubidium acetate. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solution under reflux with excess RbOH.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of a thio. Purpose: convert S‑phenyl ethanethioate to thiophenol under basic conditions, generating sodium acetate as the by‑product. Key transformation: NaOH attacks the carbonyl, forming PhSH (after subsequent acidification) and NaOAc. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–3 h; after completion, the mixture is acidified (e.g., with HCl) to liberate thiophenol. Solvent: water/ethanol mixture.

Electrophilic α‑chlorination of 2‑butanone under acidic conditions; the enol form attacks chlorine, installing a chlorine atom at the α‑position to afford 3‑chloro‑2‑butanone. Usually carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as chloroform or CCl₄ with aqueous HCl at 0–5 °C to limit over‑chlorination.

Acid‑base metathesis between lithium carbonate and hydrazine sulfate; carbonate neutralizes the acidic hydrazine salt, releasing CO₂ gas, water, free hydrazine, and forming lithium sulfate in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; no special catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) between sodium sulfite and cadmium chloride in water; insoluble cadmium sulfite precipitates while sodium chloride remains dissolved. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; the solid cadmium sulfite is filtered off.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of carbonyl sulfide. Purpose: convert OCS to hydrogen sulfide and carbon monoxide. Key transformation: OCS + H₂ → H₂S + CO. Typical conditions: gas‑phase reactor, metal catalyst such as Cu, Ni, or Pd, temperature 200–400 °C, hydrogen pressure 1–10 atm, inert carrier gas (N₂) as needed.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of a phosphate ester; NaOH attacks the phosphorus of trimethyl phosphate, cleaving one P‑O‑CH3 bond to give methanol and the sodium salt of dimethyl phosphate; usually performed in aqueous NaOH at reflux (50‑100 °C); water is the solvent.

Appel‑type halogenation of an aldehyde; triphenylphosphine reacts with iodine to generate a phosphonium iodide which transfers iodide to formaldehyde, producing diiodomethane and triphenylphosphine oxide; mild conditions (0 °C to rt) in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

Synthesis of saccharin (Miller or saccharin route); phthalic anhydride condenses with ammonium sulfamate in the presence of NaOH, forming a cyclic imide that decarboxylates to give sodium sacchar while releasing NH₃, CO₂ and water; typically carried out in aqueous alkaline medium at 80‑120 °C; water is the solvent.

Halogen (Finkelstein) SN2 substitution; sodium bromide displaces the chloride of 4‑chlorobutyronitrile to afford 4‑bromobutyronitrile, with precipitation of NaCl driving the reaction; performed in dry acetone (or another polar aprotic solvent) at reflux; no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; converts a primary alkyl bromide to a primary amine; purpose is preparation of 3‑pentylamine; key transformation is replacement of Br by –NH2 and formation of NH4+Br– in water; typically performed by heating 3‑bromopentane with aqueous NH3 (excess) under reflux; no special solvent needed, aqueous medium; product isolated by extraction, aqueous layer contains ammonium bromide.

Thermal decomposition of a metal nitrate; heating solid samarium nitrate drives off gases to samarium oxide solid, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen; usually conducted in a furnace or muffle tube under controlled heating (≈300‑400 °C); no solvent; no catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) between two soluble salts; calcium nitrate reacts with ammonium chloride to exchange cations and anions, yielding soluble ammonium nitrate calcium chloride; carried out in water at ambient temperature; no special reagents or conditions needed.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of phenethyl acetate with aqueous NaOH, yielding phenethyl alcohol and sodium acetate. The hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release acetate ion and the alcohol. Performed in aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) with heating (reflux) for 1–3 h; a co‑solvent like ethanol or THF can improve miscibility.

LiAlH₄ reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; isobutyric acid is reduced to isobutanol, with concurrent formation of lithium hydroxide and aluminum hydroxide as inorganic by‑products; performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C then reflux LiAlH₄ is the hydride source.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type) reaction; converts trimethylsilyl chloride to trimethylsilyl fluoride, a fluorinating/silyl transfer reagent; nucleophilic substitution of Cl by F⁻; typically in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Reductive amination; synthesis of bis(2‑pyridylmethyl)amine, a chelating ligand; condensation of 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde with ammonia (from ammonium acetate) followed by reduction with sodium triacetoxyborohydride; carried out in dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; NaBH(OAc)₃ serves as the mild reducing agent, no additional catalyst.

Azo coupling (electrophilic aromatic substitution); formation of 1‑(phenylazo)-2‑naphthol, an azo dye; phenyl diazonium chloride couples to activated 2‑naphthol under mildly basic acetate buffer; performed at –5 °C in a mixture of acetonitrile/water; pH controlled by acetate buffer, no external catalyst.

Acid dissolution and gas evolution. Bismuth(III) sulfide is treated with aqueous hydroiodic acid, producing soluble bismuth triiodide and liberating hydrogen sulfide gas. Reaction performed by stirring Bi2S3 in concentrated HI, often with gentle heating.

Transesterification; exchange of methyl esters in dimethyl succinate for ethyl groups to give diethyl succinate, with methanol as by‑product; usually acid‑catalyzed (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or base‑catalyzed; reflux in ethanol, often with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove methanol; ethanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Solid‑state oxide synthesis (high‑temperature ceramic reaction); preparation of lead germanate (PbGeO₃) material; powdered lead(II) oxide and germanium dioxide are intimately mixed and heated to 1000–1300 °C in a furnace, sometimes with a flux; proceeds in the solid state, no solvent or catalyst.

Complete combustion; oxidation of 2,4‑dimethyloctane to carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat; requires an ignition source and excess O₂, occurs at high temperature in a flame; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic addition/condensation of aniline with isothiocyanic acid to form phenylthiourea; a thiourea formation reaction performed in ethanol or water at ambient temperature, typically catalyst‑free, sometimes aided by a slight acid or base; key step is attack of the amine nitrogen on the electrophilic carbon of the isothiocyanate followed by proton transfer.

Condensation of ortho‑phenylenediamine with 4‑bromobenzaldehyde under microwave irradiation in ethanol to give parbendazole, a benzimidazole; reaction type is benzimidazole synthesis via imine formation and cyclization of o‑phenylenediamine with an aldehyde, followed by oxidative aromatization; usually carried out at 100‑150 °C for a few minutes, often with catalytic acetic acid or HCl; solvent is ethanol (or methanol).

Direct fluorination; synthesis of gadolinium(III) fluoride; Gd metal is oxidized to Gd³⁺ while fluorine is reduced to fluoride, producing GdF₃; the metal is exposed to dry F₂ gas at 300–500 °C under anhydrous conditions; no additional reagents are required.

Corey‑Chaykovsky epoxidation of benzaldehyde using trimethylsulfoxonium iodide and sodium hydride to afford styrene oxide; sodium hydride deprotonates the sulfoxonium salt to generate a dimethylsulfonium ylide which transfers a carbonyl oxygen to the aldehyde; typical conditions: NaH (1 eq) added to trimethylsulfoxonium iodide in THF or DMSO at 0 °C, then benzaldehyde added and the mixture warmed to rt; by‑products are dimethyl sulfide, sodium iodide and hydrogen gas; solvent is an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMSO.

Catalytic hydrogenation of phenylacetylene with molecular hydrogen to produce ethylbenzene, a full reduction of the alkyne to the corresponding alkane; reaction type is catalytic hydrogenation; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, palladium on carbon (10 wt %) or Raney Ni as catalyst, ethanol (or methanol/ethyl acetate) as solvent, temperature from ambient to 50 °C; purpose is conversion of the C≡C bond to a saturated C‑C bond.

Acid‑base neutralization of zinc carbonate with propanoic acid; purpose is preparation of zinc propanoate salt. Key transformation: carbonate anion reacts with protons, forming zinc propanoate, CO₂, and H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient or mildly elevated temperature to evolve CO₂; stirring until gas evolution ceases. No catalyst required; water serves as solvent.

Oxidation of 2‑hexanol with chromium(VI) oxide in sulfuric acid to give 2‑hexanone; a Jones oxidation (chromic acid oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone); commonly performed with CrO₃ or Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O in aqueous H₂SO₄, often using acetone as co‑solvent, at 0 °C to room temperature; solvent system is acetone/water with sulfuric acid.

Lithiation followed by carboxylation (direct CO₂ insertion). n‑Butyllithium deprotonates 5‑methylisoxazole at the C‑3 position to generate an organolithium intermediate, which captures CO₂ to afford the corresponding carboxylate; acidic work‑up furnishes 3‑carboxy‑5‑methylisoxazole and protonates the remaining n‑BuLi to give n‑butane. Performed at –78 °C to 0 °C in anhydrous THF under inert atmosphere; CO₂ gas is bubbled in; quench with aqueous acid.

Acid–base neutralization (hydroxide with acid). Beryllium hydroxide reacts with phosphoric acid to afford beryllium hydrogen phosphate and water. Carried out in water at ambient temperature; the hydroxide is added to dilute H3PO4 under stirring, yielding the salt without need for additional reagents.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous ammonia provides OH⁻ that reacts with holmium(III) chloride to precipitate insoluble holmium(III) hydroxide while forming soluble ammonium chloride; carried out at room temperature in an aqueous solution of NH₃, often with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride with hydroxide; hydrolyses the chloride to the corresponding primary alcohol. 1‑chloro‑2‑methylbutane reacts with aqueous NaOH (often as aqueous ethanol) at reflux to give 2‑methylbutan‑1‑ol and NaCl. No catalyst required; polar protic solvent (water/ethanol) facilitates the SN2 pathway.

Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride; nucleophilic acyl substitution where trichloroacetyl chloride reacts with aqueous NaOH to give trichloroacetic acid and NaCl; performed in water or aqueous NaOH at 0 °C → room temperature, no added catalyst.

Radical chlorination of a saturated alkane; UV light or heat initiates Cl₂ cleavage, chlorine radicals abstract hydrogen from heptane and recombine to form 2‑chloroheptane and HCl; typical conditions: neat heptane or inert solvent (e.g., CCl₄), Cl₂ gas, UV lamp or heating (~120 °C).

Acid‑base neutralization forming a metal acetate; acetic acid protonates chromium(III) hydroxide, producing water and soluble chromium(III) acetate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol; lithium aluminium hydride delivers hydride to the carbonyl of 3‑pentanone, affording 3‑pentanol after aqueous work‑up; performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C → reflux under nitrogen, quenched with water or dilute acid.
Thermal decomposition (dehydration) of barium hydroxide; heating solid Ba(OH)₂ (~400‑500 °C) gives BaO solid and water vapor, no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration); concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates the two hydroxyl groups of 2‑butene‑1,4‑diol, promoting loss of water and formation of the cyclic ether 2,5‑dihydrofuran; typically heated to 80–120 °C, often using the diol as solvent, water removed by azeotropic distillation.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether synthesis) using a less reactive chloride. 1‑chlorobutane reacts with methoxide ion to give 1‑methoxybutane and sodium chloride. Requires higher temperature or a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO); sodium methoxide provides the nucleophile.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of selenophene; Cl₂, activated by a Lewis acid such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃, attacks the 2‑position of the selenophene ring, displacing a proton to give 2‑chloroselenophene and HCl; carried out in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C → room temperature under anhydrous conditions.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to exchange anions and form an insoluble cobalt(II) iodate product. Key transformation: Co^2 pairs with IO3‑ to give Co(IO3)2, while Na^+ pairs with NO3‑ to give NaNO3. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration/esterification of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural with ethanol to afford ethyl levulinate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O. Reaction converts the alde and hydroxymethyl groups into a carbonyl‑derived ester. Conducted at 150‑200 °C in excess phosphoric acid (10‑30 wt %); ethanol serves both reactant and solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis/precipitation) reaction; purpose is to replace the iodide with tetrafluoroborate and to obtain insoluble silver iodide; key transformation: lithium iodide reacts with silver tetrafluoroborate to form lithium tetrafluoroborate in solution and a dark precipitate of silver iodide; performed in water or a suitable polar solvent at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Condensation (Mannich‑type) cyclization forming a 2,3‑dihydro‑1,4‑benzoxazine from formaldehyde and 2‑(aminomethyl)phenol with loss of water. Involves formation of a Schiff‑base intermediate that cyclizes to the heterocycle. Usually carried out in an alcohol solvent (methanol or ethanol) at reflux (60‑80 °C) under mild acidic or neutral conditions; catalyst optional.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a thioacetate ester to generate the corresponding thiol and acetic acid. attacks the carbonyl of butyl thioacetate, cleaving the C‑S bond. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl or H₂SO₄, reflux (80‑100 °C) for 1‑3 h; solvent can be a mixture of water and a miscible organic (e.g., ethanol). No special catalyst beyond the acid.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation forming chromium(III) oxalate from sodium oxalate and chromium(III) sulfate. The reaction swaps counter‑ions, yielding an insoluble Cr₂(C₂O₄)₃ precipitate and soluble Na₂SO₄. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water as solvent; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 1‑decanol to 1‑decene with elimination of water (E1 mechanism). Typically uses concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ at 150‑180 °C; sometimes performed with a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water to drive the equilibrium. No special solvent needed; the alcohol itself can act as the reaction medium.

Reductive amination; converts the aldehyde 2,2-dimethylpropanal to the primary amine 2,2-dimethylpropylamine using ammonia as the nitrogen source and NaBH3CN as a mild hydride donor. The reaction proceeds via formation of an imine (or iminium ion) which is reduced in situ. Typically performed in methanol or ethanol solvent at 0 °C to room temperature under mildly acidic conditions (pH ≈ 5–6) to keep NaBH3CN stable.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; elemental iron and sulfur react to form iron(II) sulfide (FeS). The process is a solid‑state synthesis that requires intimate mixing of fine powders and heating to high temperature (≈ 500 °C) under an inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen or argon) to prevent oxidation. No solvent or catalyst is needed.

Acid–base/neutralization reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with calcium silicate (CaSiO₃) to give calcium sulfate, silica, and water. The silicate is protonated and decomposes, releasing SiO₂ as a solid. Commonly carried out by suspending calcium silicate in aqueous H₂SO₄ and heating (often 80–120 °C) with stirring. The reaction medium is water; no additional catalyst is required.

Reductive amination (hydrogenation) of a carbonyl; acetone reacts with ammonia to form an imine that is hydrogenated over Raney nickel to give isopropylamine and water. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 30–50 bar, temperature 100–150 °C, in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) with Raney Ni as the heterogeneous catalyst.

N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution, SN2) of theophylline with 5‑chloro‑2‑pentanone to afford pentoxifylline, with liberation of HCl. Theophylline acts as a nucleophile at the N7 position, displacing chloride. Typical conditions use a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, gentle heating (30–70 °C), and an inert atmosphere. The reaction is employed in the pharmaceutical synthesis of the vasodilator drug pentoxifylline.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) halogen exchange (fluorination). Potassium fluoride provides fluoride ion that displaces iodide in ethyl iodide to form ethyl fluoride and potassium iodide. Reaction polar such as DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile, often with 18‑crown‑6 to increase KF solubility; heated to 80–120 °C to achieve reasonable rates.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage with hydrogen iodide. Purpose: deprotect benzyl methyl ether or generate benzyl iodide. Key transformation: protonation of the ether oxygen followed by nucleophilic attack of I⁻; the benzylic carbon is displaced as benzyl iodide, and the methyl fragment leaves as methanol (which can be protonated further to methyl iodide under excess HI). Typical conditions: reflux in concentrated (48 %) aqueous HI, 80–100 °C, for 1–2 h. No additional solvent required, though aqueous HI can be diluted with a small amount of THF for better mixing.

Acid‑base solid‑gas reaction; preparation of lead(II) sulfate; sulfur trioxide reacts with lead(II) oxide to afford lead(II) sulfate; performed at 200‑300 °C under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Azo‑coupling (electrophilic substitution) of acetylacetone with phenyl diazonium chloride yielding 3‑phenylazoacetylacetone and HCl. The acetylacetone enol form attacks the diazonium electrophile, forming the azo bond. Conducted in a cold (0–5 °C) aqueous alkaline medium (NaOH or Na₂CO₃) to generate the enolate, followed by acidification after coupling. Solvent is a mixture of water and a miscible organic co‑solvent (e.g., ethanol); the reaction proceeds at ambient temperature and does not require additional catalysts.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; aqueous ammonia provides hydroxide ions that precipitate cadmium hydroxide while forming soluble ammonium nitrate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst required.

Acetylation of 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol using acetic anhydride to produce 2‑(dimethylamino)ethyl acetate and acetic acid; usually conducted neat or in a solvent like dichloromethane at room temperature or gentle reflux; a base (pyridine or triethylamine) may be added to neutralize the generated acetic acid.

Acid- or base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis of isoamyl acetate; water cleaves the ester bond to give isoamyl alcohol and acetic acid; typically performed in aqueous acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (NaOH) under reflux, followed by acid work‑up if base is used; solvent is water or water/organic mixture; catalyst is the acid or base.

Base‑catalyzed acylation (esterification) of ethylene glycol monoethyl ether with acetic anhydride; pyridine acts as nucleophilic base and solvent, scavenging the generated acetic acid and yielding 2‑ethoxyethyl acetate; performed at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, usually neat pyridine or pyridine solution; byproduct is acetic acid.

Metathesis precipitation reaction between sodium sulfide and antimony trichloride; sulfide ions replace chloride to form insoluble antimony trisulfide precipitate while sodium chloride remains in solution; carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Knoevenagel condensation / cyclocondensation to 4‑hydroxycoumarin; used to build the coumarin core. Malonic acid reacts with salicylaldehyde forming a β‑oxo‑acid which cyclizes onto the ortho‑phenolic OH and decarboxylates, releasing CO₂ and H₂O. Typical conditions: reflux in pyridine or acetic anhydride with a catalytic base (piperidine, pyridine) for 2–6 h. Solvent/catalyst: pyridine, acetic anhydride, occasionally ethanol as solvent and a base catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution at silicon to give an ethoxytrimethylsilane (silyl ether formation). Trimethylsilyl chloride is attacked by ethoxide ion, displacing chloride as NaCl and forming EtO–SiMe₃. Conducted in dry aprotic solvent (THF, DMF) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; acid‑base neutralization of Cr³⁺ and OH⁻. Chromium(III) sulfate reacts with aqueous NH₄OH, hydroxide precipitates insoluble Cr(OH)₃ while ammonium sulfate remains in solution. Performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special reagents required.

High‑temperature thermolysis/chalcogenide synthesis of MoSe₂ nanomaterial. Mo(CO)₆ decomposes in oleylamine; trioctylphosphine selenide supplies Se, generating MoSe₂, while CO gas is liberated and trioctylphosphine is oxidized to trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO). Reaction carried out under N₂ at 250–300 °C in oleylamine (or similar long‑chain amine) as solvent and surfactant.

Acid‑base formation of sodium zincate; ZnO reacts with NaOEt and water to give Na₂ZnO₂ (sodium zincate) and ethanol. Typically performed in refluxing ethanol/water mixtures with NaOEt in excess; the ZnO dissolves as the zincate salt and ethanol is released. No additional catalyst required.

Metal‑acid reduction of duroquinone to 2,5‑di‑tert‑butylhydroquinone. Zn dust in glacial acetic acid supplies electrons, reducing the quinone double bond to the hydroquinone while acetic acid serves as proton source. Reaction proceeds at reflux (≈80 °C) under stirring; by‑product is Zn²⁺ salts (Zn(OAc)₂). No further catalyst is needed.

Oxidation (peracid oxidation) of a sulfoxide to a sulfone; peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to methyl phenyl sulfoxide, forming methyl phenyl sulfone and acetic acid. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; stoichiometric peracid, no additional catalyst required.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde; purpose: form a secondary alcohol; key transformation: nucleophilic addition of methylmagnesium bromide to the carbonyl carbon of 2‑methoxyacetaldehyde, giving after protonation 1‑methoxy‑2‑propanol; typical conditions: dry THF or Et2O under N2, MeMgBr (1 M in ether) added dropwise to a chilled (0 °C) solution of the aldehyde, then stirred to rt; aqueous NH4Cl work‑up to destroy excess Grignard.

Nitrosation of guanidine using nitrosyl sulfuric acid to give N‑nitrosoguanidine and water. The nitrosonium ion generated from the acid attacks a guanidine nitrogen, forming the N‑nitroso product. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium, usually 0–5 °C to limit side reactions; no catalyst needed.

Conversion of trichloroacetic acid to trichloroacetyl chloride with oxalyl chloride, releasing CO, CO₂ and HCl gases. This is an acid‑chloride formation (acyl chloride synthesis). Performed in a dry non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform) under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to rt; excess oxalyl chloride is vented as gas.

Formation of isopropyl lithium from isopropyl bromide and lithium metal (metal‑halogen exchange). Reaction carried out in dry ethereal solvent (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen or argon, at –78 °C to 0 °C to avoid side reactions; lithium is activated and LiBr precipitates, no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of vinylidene chloride to 1,1‑dichloroethane. Hydrogen adds across the C=C bond in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Raney, or PtO₂) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, under 1–5 atm H₂ at 25–50 °C; the reaction selectively reduces the alkene while leaving the chloro substituents intact.

Gattermann–Koch formylation of anthracene at the 9‑position to give 9‑anthracenecarboxaldehyde. CO and HCl generate a formyl electrophile in the presence of AlCl₃ (≈1 eq) and CuCl (≈0.1 eq) under anhydrous conditions, typically in dry CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂, at 0–25 °C and CO pressure of 1–2 atm. This electrophilic aromatic substitution installs a formyl group onto anthracene.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of an acyl chloride with a phenoxide ion; the phenoxide attacks the carbonyl of acetyl chloride to give phenyl acetate while chloride is displaced as potassium chloride. Typically performed at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often in the presence of a mild base (pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize generated HCl.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) halide‑acetate exchange; silver acetate reacts with indium(III) chloride, precipitating insoluble silver chloride and forming soluble indium(III) acetate. Conducted in aqueous or polar organic medium (e.g., acetone or water) at ambient temperature; the reaction drives to completion by removal of AgCl precipitate.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification of nitric acid (generated in situ from potassium nitrate and sulfuric acid) with methanol to afford methyl nitrate; water and potassium bisulfate are by‑products. The mixture is kept cold (0‑5 °C) to control the highly exothermic nitration, using excess methanol as solvent and concentrated H₂SO₄ as catalyst; the reaction is usually performed under anhydrous conditions to prevent hydrolysis.

Oxidative cleavage of ethylene glycol by metaperiodic acid; HIO4 cleaves the 1,2‑diol to generate formaldehyde (often two equivalents) while the periodate is reduced to iodic acid; conducted in water or a water‑acetone mixture at 0 °C to rt; no additional catalyst required.

Formation of an amide by nucleophilic acyl substitution of phenylacetyl chloride with 4‑methoxyaniline; the amine attacks the acyl chloride, displacing chloride and giving N‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)-2‑phenylacetamide. Carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge HCl.

Nucleophilic addition/condensation; used to synthesize hydroxyurea, an anticancer and antimalarial agent; hydroxylamine nitrogen attacks the electrophilic carbon of the cyanate ion forming N‑hydroxycarbamimidic acid which rearranges to hydroxyurea while sodium hydroxide is released; typically carried out in aqueous or methanol solution at 0–50 °C under neutral to slightly basic conditions; no special catalyst required, base may be added to keep pH mild.

SN2 alkylation (C‑alkylation) of barbituric acid; employed to produce the sedative barbiturate barbital (5,5‑diethylbarbit acid deprotonates barbituric acid to give the enolate which attacks ethyl iodide, displacing iodide and forming the diethyl product; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO (or ethanol) under reflux (80–120 °C); potassium carbonate acts as the base and iodide is the leaving group.

Salt metathesis (ligand exchange) between palladium(II) acetate and hydrobromic acid; converts Pd–OAc bonds to Pd–Br bonds while generating acetic acid. Typically performed in aqueous or polar protic solvent (e.g., water or methanol) at ambient temperature; no catalyst required. Used to prepare palladium(II) bromide from the acetate salt.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive hydrogenation of aldehyde); hydrogen gas over Pd/C reduces 2‑methoxybenzaldehyde to 2‑methoxybenzyl alcohol; usually run in ethanol or ethyl acetate under H₂ pressure (1–3 atm) at room temperature or mild heating.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a primary alkyl bromide; 3‑phenylpropyl bromide reacts with water (often aqueous NaOH or refluxing ethanol/water) to afford 3‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol and hydrobromic acid; conditions usually involve reflux for 1‑2 h followed by acidic work‑up.

Acid‑catalyzed peroxide formation (ene oxidation) of α‑terpinene with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of trifluoroacetic acid; yields the endoperoxide ascaridole and water. Conducted at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; TFA acts as both proton source and hydrogen‑bonding catalyst. Purpose is to produce a biologically active cyclic peroxide.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification between 4‑tert‑butylphenol and ethyl salicylate, producing p‑tert‑butylphenyl salicylate and ethanol. Commonly performed under reflux an excess of phenol or in a high‑boiling solvent (toluene, xylene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., p‑TsOH or sulfuric acid); removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium. Employed to synthesize phenolic salicylate esters.

Redox halogenation of chromium(II) sulfide with bromine; bromine oxidizes sulfide to elemental sulfur while forming chromium(II) bromide. Typically carried out under anhydrous conditions in an inert organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, chloroform) at room temperature or mild heating. Serves as a method to generate metal bromides and recover elemental sulfur.

Transesterification of methyl carbonocyanate with ethanol – methyl carbonocyanate reacts with excess ethanol to give ethyl carbonocyanate and methanol; conducted under reflux in ethanol using an acid catalyst (p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a mild base (NaOEt).

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of 2‑chloropentane with water to give 2‑pentanol and hydrochloric acid. Usually performed under reflux in aqueous acid or base (e.g., dilute HCl or NaOH) to accelerate the SN1 (secondary carbocation) or SN2 pathway, respectively; temperatures of 80‑100 °C are common. Used to convert alkyl halides to corresponding alcohols.

Type: amide to amidine conversion via imidoyl chloride intermediate. Purpose: synthesis of benzamidine (often isolated as its hydrochloride salt). Key transformation: benzamide reacts with phosphorus oxychloride to form a benzamidoyl chloride, which is then attacked by aqueous ammonia to give benzamidine; work‑up with HCl furnishes benzamidine·HCl. Typical conditions: POCl₃ added dropwise to dry benzamide under inert atmosphere, temperature 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful addition of excess aqueous NH₃ (or NH₄OH) at 0–25 °C; the reaction mixture is then acidified with HCl. Common solvent/catalyst: POCl₃ acts as both reagent and solvent; no external catalyst required.

Type: acid‑base neutralization / salt formation (metathesis). Purpose: preparation of potassium acetate from acetic acid. Key transformation: two equivalents of acetic acid donate protons to carbonate anion of potassium carbonate, yielding two equivalents of potassium acetate and carbonic acid, which rapidly decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, stirring until gas evolution ceases. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst needed.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a quinone to a hydroquinone). Purpose: production of tert‑butylhydroquinone from the corresponding quinone. Key transformation: the C=O double bonds of tert‑butylbenzoquinone are reduced to C–OH groups, converting the quinone ring into a hydroquinone ring. Typical conditions: hydrogen gas at 1–5 atm, room temperature to 50 °C, in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as 10 % Pd/C, Pt/C or Raney nickel; solvent commonly ethanol, methanol or acetic acid. No additional reagents required.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) amination of alkyl bromides. Purpose: synthesis of bis(2‑aminoethyl) ether from bis(2‑bromoethyl) ether. Key transformation: each bromoethyl group undergoes displacement by ammonia to give an aminoethyl group, generating two equivalents of NH₄Br as by‑product. Typical conditions: excess aqueous or gaseous NH₃ (often 10–20 equiv), reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, reaction time several hours to overnight. The mixture is then neutralized or filtered to remove solid NH₄Br.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: ion exchange to form insoluble silver carbonate and soluble potassium sulfate. Key transformation: carbonate anion exchanges with sulfate anion, producing Ag₂CO₃ as a pale yellow precipitate and K₂SO₄ remaining in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of K₂CO₃ and Ag₂SO₄ mixed at room temperature, vigorous stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed. No catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Type: oxidation of an amino acid side chain (hydroxylation). Purpose: conversion of L‑histidine to 2‑oxohistidine, a model for oxidative protein damage. Key transformation: hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the imidazole ring of histidine, introducing a carbonyl group at the C‑2 position to give 2‑oxohistidine; water is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH near neutral (6–8), mild excess of H₂O₂ (1.5–2 equiv), temperature 0–25 °C; reaction may be accelerated by trace transition‑metal catalysts (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺) or by using a buffered system. No organic solvent is required.

Thermal or catalytic cracking of 3,3-dimethylpentane to give ethane and 2‑methyl‑2‑butene; purpose is to produce lighter alkanes and olefins. Key transformation is C–C bond scission producing a small alkane and a branched alkene. Typical conditions: 500–800 °C under inert atmosphere, often over solid acid zeolite; no solvent required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of benzyl methanesulfonate by ammonia, yielding benzylamine and methanesulfonic acid. Used to prepare a primary aromatic amine. The methanesulfonate group is displaced by NH₃. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., methanol, water) at ambient to 50 °C; excess NH₃ is used; no catalyst needed.

Redox (oxidative) reaction of chlorine with sodium hydrosulfide forming hydrogen chloride, sodium chloride and elemental sulfur. Chlorine is reduced to Cl⁻ while HS⁻ is oxidized to S⁰, with proton release. Performed in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C to control rate; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (partial reduction) of nitrobenzene to phenylhydroxylamine; purpose: generate N‑hydroxy aniline intermediate; nitro group (–NO2) is reduced to N‑hydroxy (–NHOH) with water as by‑product; typically carried out under 1–5 atm H2 using Raney Ni, Pd/C or Pt catalyst in ethanol or methanol at 0–25 °C.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between potassium sulfate and bismuth nitrate yielding potassium nitrate and bismuth sulfate. Purpose is ion exchange; bismuth sulfate may precipitate. Reaction is carried out in aqueous solution with stirring at room temperature; the solid product is filtered; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base exchange between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydrogen difluoride to give sodium chloride and hydrofluoric acid. Proton transfer from HCl to the fluoride anion produces HF. Conducted in aqueous medium, often with excess HCl, at low to moderate temperature; no catalyst required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction: aqueous chlorine oxidizes sulfite ion to sulfate while being reduced to chloride, which protonates to give hydrochloric acid. Purpose is conversion of sulfite to sulfate and generation of HCl. Key transformation: SO3^2‑ → SO4^2‑ and Cl2 → 2 Cl⁻ + 2 H⁺ (forming HCl). Typical conditions: dilute aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no external catalyst required. Common solvent: water.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; replacement of benzylic bromide by fluoride to give benzyl fluoride. Typically carried out with TBAF as a soluble fluoride source in an aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at room temperature or mild heating; the by‑product is tetrabutylammonium bromide.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic hydroxymethylation (a Mannich‑type addition) of uracil at C‑5 using formaldehyde in dilute HCl. Purpose is to introduce a hydroxymethyl substituent to form 5‑(hydroxymethyl)uracil. Key transformation: formaldehyde is protonated to a hydroxymethyl cation which attacks the C‑5 of uracil, followed by loss of a proton to give the product and water. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (≈.1–1 M HCl), room temperature to gentle heating (30–50 °C). Solvent: water (often the reaction mixture itself).

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an ether; used to remove benzyl protecting groups. The benzylic C–O bond of benzyl ethyl ether is cleaved over Pd/C under H₂ pressure, converting the benzylic carbon to toluene and releasing ethanol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd on carbon (0.1–0.5 eq), solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate or methanol, temperature from room temperature to reflux (25–80 °C).

Fischer esterification: acid‑catalyzed condensation of 1‑pentanol with acetic acid to afford pentyl acetate and water. Purpose is synthesis of an ester. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the protonated carbonyl of acetic acid, followed by elimination of water. Typical conditions: reflux in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst) to drive equilibrium; removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark trap) improves yield. Common solvent: excess acetic acid or an inert solvent such as toluene when a Dean‑Stark apparatus is used.

Oxidative cyclization to form 2‑mercaptobenzothiazole from carbon disulfide, 2‑aminobenzenethiol, hydrogen peroxide and KOH. Purpose is construction of the benzothiazole heterocycle. Key transformation: KOH deprotonates the thiol and amine, CS2 inserts to give a dithiocarbamate intermediate, which is oxidized by H2O2 and cyclizes to the thiazole ring, releasing water. Typical conditions: aqueous basic medium, temperature 0–25 °C for addition, then gentle reflux (≈50–80 °C) for cyclization. Catalyst: KOH (base); hydrogen peroxide acts as oxidant. Solvent: water or mixed water/ethanol.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling (peptide‑bond formation): Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl group of glycine to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate, which reacts with ammonia to give glycinamide; the by‑product is dicyclohexylurea. Purpose is synthesis of a simple amide. Key transformation: conversion of –COOH to –CONH2 via DCC activation. Typical conditions: anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, DMF), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N2) to avoid side reactions. No additional catalyst needed; DCC itself drives the reaction.

Double nucleophilic substitution (alkaline hydrolysis) of 1,7‑dichloroheptane with sodium hydroxide to yield 1,7‑heptanediol and sodium chloride. Purpose is conversion of a dihaloalkane to the corresponding diol. Key transformation: each chloride is displaced by hydroxide via SN2 mechanism, forming two C–O bonds and releasing Cl⁻. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (excess), reflux (≈80–100 °C) for several hours. Solvent: water or a water/ethanol mixture.

Reaction type: organometallic salt metathesis/alkylation. Purpose: preparation of pentamethylantimony, a valuable organo‑antimony reagent. Key transformation: five methyl groups from methylmagnesium bromide are transferred to SbCl5, forming SbMe5 and generating MgBr2 and MgCl2 as by‑products. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), low to ambient temperature; addition of Grignard reagent to a solution of SbCl5 with stirring.

N‑oxide formation (oxidation) of pyridazine; purpose is to install an N‑oxide functionality yielding 1‑oxidopyridazin‑1‑ium. Key transformation: pyridazine nitrogen is oxidized to the N‑oxide cation. Typical conditions: peracetic acid (≈30 % in acetic acid) used neat or in a miscible solvent (acetic acid or dichloromethane), temperature 0–25 °C, often with a small amount of pyridine as a base to buffer the medium.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Purpose: synthesis of benzyl cyanide (phenylacetonitrile) from benzyl chloride. Key transformation: cyanide ion from lithium cyanide displaces chloride on the benzylic carbon, forming the nitrile and LiCl. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone; often heated to 50‑80 °C; inert atmosphere not required but may be used to avoid moisture.

Reaction type: amide formation via acyl substitution (acylation of an amine). Purpose: introduction of a chloroacetyl group onto β‑alanine to give N‑(2‑chloroacetyl)‑β‑alanine. Key transformation: the amino group attacks the carbonyl carbon of 2‑chloroacetyl chloride, releasing chloride as HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HCl; temperature 0 °C to room temperature; inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Reaction type: double displacement (salt metathesis). Purpose: preparation of magnesium tetrafluoroborate, a Lewis‑acidic salt used as a catalyst or electrolyte. Key transformation: exchange of anions between LiBF4 and MgCl2, producing Mg(BF4)2 and LiCl. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic solution (water or ethanol), stirring at ambient temperature; after reaction, removal of LiCl by filtration or evaporation; drying of Mg(BF4)2 under reduced pressure.

Halogenolysis/oxidative cleavage; converts a trialkylborane to boron trichloride and an alkyl chloride. The B–C bonds are broken, forming BCl3 and RCl (ethyl chloride). Typically performed with stoichiometric Cl2 in a dry inert solvent such as diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; radical initiation may be assisted by light or mild heating.

Reaction type: solid‑gas redox reaction. Purpose: oxidation of FeO to Fe2O3 with concomitant reduction of NO2 to NO; historically used for nitric oxide generation. Key transformation: Fe(II) is oxidized to Fe(III) while NO2 is reduced; overall stoichiometry yields Fe2O3 and NO. Typical conditions: high temperature (300‑600 °C) in a furnace or heated tube; solid FeO mixed with a flow of NO2 gas; reaction carried out in the gas phase with continuous removal of NO product.

Reaction type: strong hydride reduction of an ester. Purpose: conversion of isoamyl acetate to the corresponding primary alcohols (ethanol from the acetyl fragment and isoamyl alcohol from the alkoxy fragment). Key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide intermediate that collapses to give the two alcohols after work‑up. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen or argon; addition of LiAlH4 at 0 °C followed by reflux; quench with careful addition of water, then acidic work‑up to isolate ethanol and isoamyl alcohol.

Electrochemical oxidation (anodic oxidation); purpose is to convert a secondary alcohol to a ketone while generating hydrogen gas; key transformation is oxidation of the –CH(OH)– group to a carbonyl (2‑methyl‑3‑pentanone) with loss of two electrons and proton release; typical conditions involve an alkaline aqueous solution (e.g., 0.1 M KOH), platinum anode, controlled current or potential at ambient temperature; solvent is water/alkaline medium, platinum electrode serves as catalyst.

Intramolecular dehydration of pentanedioic (glutaric) acid to form its cyclic anhydride, oxane‑2,6‑dione (glutaric anhydride). The reaction is a condensation (anhydride formation) that eliminates one molecule of water. Commonly performed by heating the diacid neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (toluene, xylene) with a Dean‑Stark trap, or using strong dehydrating agents such as phosphorus pentoxide or acetic anhydride; no catalyst is generally required.

Acid–base metathesis (salt‑acid reaction); purpose is to liberate free oxalic acid from its insoluble strontium salt; key transformation is protonation of the oxalate anion by HCl, forming oxalic acid and exchanging Sr²⁺ for Cl⁻ to give soluble SrCl₂; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; common solvent is water, no special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of alkyl chloride, SN2 or SN1 depending on substrate); purpose is to replace the chloro substituent with a hydroxyl group to give the corresponding alcohol; key transformation is attack of water (or OH⁻) on the 2‑chloroethyl carbon, displacing Cl⁻ and forming 2‑hydroxyethyl methyl sulfide with release of HCl; typically carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol medium, often heated gently (50‑80 °C); no additional catalyst required, though a weak base can be added to scavenge HCl.

Phosphorylation (nucleophilic substitution of a phosphorochloridothioate); purpose is to synthesize the organophosphate insecticide Dioxathion; key transformation is attack of the phenolic oxygen of 3‑methyl‑4‑nitrophenol on the phosphorus atom of O,O‑diethyl phosphorochloridothioate, displacing chloride ion and forming a phosphorothioate ester; reactions are run under anhydrous conditions, typically in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, at 0 °C to room temperature; a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) is added to neutralize the generated HCl.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; purpose: preparation of lead(II) formate as a precipitate; key transformation: exchange of anions between ammonium formate and lead(II) nitrate to give lead(II) formate (sparingly soluble) and ammonium nitrate (soluble); typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; common solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Alkylation via SN2 using a strong base; purpose is to install a butyl group onto the nitrogen of 1‑deoxynojirimycin, yielding N‑butyl‑1‑deoxynojirimycin; key transformation is deprotonation of the amine by sodium hydride to generate a nucleophilic nitrogen anion, followed by backside attack on n‑butyl bromide with displacement of Br⁻; typical conditions employ an anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, under inert atmosphere (N₂), at 0 °C to reflux; NaH acts as base and generates H₂ gas, no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2 of a primary bromide); purpose is to convert 1‑bromodecane into the corresponding primary alcohol; key transformation is attack of hydroxide ion on the carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br⁻ and forming 1‑decanol; performed with aqueous or alcoholic KOH, often in ethanol/water mixture, heated under reflux (80‑100 °C) to drive the reaction; solvent is ethanol/water, KOH provides the nucleophile, no metal catalyst is needed.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation of an alkoxide); converts potassium methoxide and methyl iodide into dimethyl ether while forming potassium iodide; performed in an anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF at 0 °C to reflux; no additional catalyst is required.

Esterification via carbodiimide activation; DCC converts acetic acid to an O‑acyl‑urea intermediate which reacts with hexan‑2‑ol to give hexan‑2‑yl acetate, producing dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP; inert atmosphere recommended.

Oxidation of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide; peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to amitriptyline, affording amitriptylin‑N‑oxide and acetic acid. Conducted in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0‑25 °C, controlling temperature to avoid over‑oxidation; the reaction is generally rapid and stoichiometric.

Conversion of vicinal diols to dibromides using phosphorus tribromide; each hydroxyl group of octane‑1,2‑diol is replaced by bromine, yielding 1,2‑dibromo‑octane and generating phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃) as the acid by‑product. Carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or CH₂Cl₂ at 0‑rt, often with excess PBr₃ to drive completion.

Redox oxidation of sodium ascorbate by molecular oxygen; ascorbate is oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid while O₂ is reduced to hydrogen peroxide. Occurs in aqueous solution, typically near neutral pH, and can be accelerated by metal ions (e.g., Cu²⁺) or mild base; the reaction is relevant in biological systems and in catalytic H₂O₂ generation.

Alkylation (nucleophilic substitution); ethylenediamine acts as a nucleophile toward methyl p‑toluenesulfonate, yielding N,N′‑dimethylethylenediamine and p‑toluenesulfonic acid; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, often under reflux; no external base is required as the sulfonate itself serves as the leaving group.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of aromatic imidazole to saturated 2‑imidazoline. H₂ gas is passed over Pd/C in an alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at 1–5 atm and 25–80 °C. The Pd surface delivers hydrogen to the C=N bonds, converting the five‑membered heterocycle to the corresponding imidazoline.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; purpose is introduction of a nitro group onto 3‑methylphenol; key transformation is substitution of a hydrogen ortho/para to the activating hydroxyl group, giving 3‑methyl‑4‑nitrophenol and water; carried out by adding concentrated HNO₃ to concentrated H₂SO₄ (nitrating mixture) at 0–50 °C (often 30 °C) with the phenol dissolved in the acid mixture itself; no external solvent or catalyst is needed.

N‑Methylation via SN2 alkylation; DL‑amphetamine is deprotonated by potassium carbonate and reacts with methyl iodide to afford DL‑methamphetamine and potassium iodide; standard conditions include reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, inert atmosphere, and excess base to drive the reaction to completion.

Chromic‑acid oxidation; ethanol is oxidized by potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid to acetaldehyde, with concomitant reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) sulfate and formation of potassium sulfate and water; performed in aqueous medium, typically heated under reflux; the reaction is carried out under strongly acidic conditions (conc. H₂SO₄) to generate the active chromic acid oxidant.

Type: metathesis/acid–base neutralization. Purpose: preparation of potassium tetrafluoroborate and liberation of ammonia gas. Key transformation: exchange of cations between ammonium tetrafluoroborate and potassium hydroxide (NH4BF4 + KOH → KBF4 + NH3 + H2O). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring to ensure complete exchange; reaction may be done in an ice bath to control exotherm. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation; aniline reacts with oleum (fuming H₂SO₄) to install a sulfonic acid group para to the amino substituent, producing sulfanilic acid and water; the reaction is conducted at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) in the liquid oleum medium, often followed by careful quench with ice water and neutralization to isolate the sulfonated product.

Oxidation of secondary alcohol (Dess‑Martin periodinane); 1,1,1‑trichloro‑2‑propanol is oxidized to the corresponding ketone, 1,1,1‑trichloropropan‑2‑one, using Dess‑Martin periodinane as the oxidant; typical conditions involve stirring the substrate with a stoichiometric amount of DMP in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; by‑products are acetic acid and 2‑iodobenzoic acid, which are removed during work‑up.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of a tertiary amine to a quaternary ammonium salt; purpose is synthesis of tetramethylammonium iodide, a common phase‑transfer catalyst; key transformation is attack of trimethylamine on methyl iodide displacing iodide; usually conducted in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile, acetone or dichloromethane at ambient temperature or gentle reflux; no catalyst required.

Acid–base salt metathesis; converts calcium acetate to calcium chloride while liberating acetic acid; the acetate ion is exchanged for chloride from HCl, yielding CaCl2 and CH3COOH; usually done in aqueous solution, sometimes with gentle heating to drive the reaction to completion; no catalyst needed.

Disproportionation/hydrolysis of nitrogen dioxide in water forming nitric acid and nitrous acid; used to generate HNO₃/HNO₂, performed in aqueous medium typically at 0‑30 °C to limit further oxidation, no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); nicotinic acid reacts with ammonium hydroxide to give the ammonium salt of nicotinic acid; the carboxyl proton is transferred to NH₄⁺ producing ammonium nicotinate and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Carbamylation (addition of amine to isocyanic acid) forming a carbamic acid; nucleophilic attack of dimethylamine on the electrophilic carbon of isocyanic acid yields dimethylcarbamic acid; typically performed in a polar solvent (e.g., water or methanol) at 0 °C to room temperature, no catalyst required.

N‑Methylation (alkylation) of a secondary amine; methyl iodide reacts with the amine in the presence of potassium carbonate base, which deprotonates the amine to enable SN2 attack, giving 2,5‑dimethoxy‑N‑methylamphetamine and KI; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone at ambient temperature.

Selective reduction of a thioester to aldehyde (hydride reduction); DIBAL‑H delivers a hydride to the carbonyl of benzyl thioacetate, producing benzaldehyde and benzyl mercaptan; performed in dry ether or THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere, then quenched with aqueous work‑up.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange in aqueous solution; mixing solutions of magnesium sulfate and sodium bromide results in formation of sodium sulfate and magnesium bromide; carried out at room temperature in water, no special reagents.

Precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction; aqueous potassium sulfate and barium nitrate exchange ions to give insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble potassium nitrate; performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; solid BaSO₄ is filtered off.

Fischer esterification/condensation of phthalic anhydride with two alcohols; p‑toluenesulfonic acid catalyzes the reaction of phthalic anhydride with benzyl alcohol and n‑butanol to form butyl benzyl phthalate (mixed di‑ester) and water; reflux in an inert solvent (e.g., toluene) with Dean‑Stark removal of water, typically 80‑120 °C.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis). Proton transfer from trifluoromethanesulfonic acid to acetate anion forms acetic acid and lithium triflate. Typically performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid–base / double displacement reaction in aqueous solution. Calcium hydrogen phosphate reacts with dissolved CO₂ and water, yielding phosphoric acid and precipitating calcium carbonate. Conducted in water under atmospheric or modest CO₂ pressure, often at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis precipitation reaction in aqueous medium. Thallium(I) chloride exchanges anions with ammonium carbonate to give thallium carbonate (often precipitated) and ammonium chloride in solution. Performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Benzene is acylated by butyryl chloride in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl₃, producing butyrophenone (phenyl‑butan‑one) and HCl as a by‑product. Reaction carried out under anhydrous conditions in solvents like dichloromethane, carbon disulfide or nitrobenzene, typically at 0 °C to reflux.
NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone; fluoroacetone is reduced to the secondary alcohol 1‑fluoropropan‑2‑ol, generating sodium borate as by‑product. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification. tert‑Butyl alcohol attacks ethyl formate, exchanging the alkoxy groups to afford tert‑butyl formate and ethanol. Requires a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and reflux in a solvent such as toluene or xylene; removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium.
