High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (calcination). Silica reacts with calcium hydroxide at temperatures around 1300–1500 °C to form dicalcium silicate (Ca₂SiO₄) with release of water. Conducted in a dry kiln atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Double‑replacement/acid‑base metathesis between ammonium sulfite and calcium hydroxide; calcium sulfite precipitates, ammonia gas is liberated and water formed; carried out in aqueous medium at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, insoluble CaSO₃ filtered off.

Esterification using a carboxylic‑anhydride; ethanol attacks the carbonyl of hexanoic anhydride yielding ethyl hexanoate and the remaining hexanoic acid; usually run neat or in a non‑protic solvent with catalytic pyridine or DMAP, gentle heating (reflux) to drive equilibrium.

Free‑radical chlorination of acetyl chloride at the methyl group; chlorine gas under UV light or a radical initiator replaces a hydrogen to give chloroacetyl chloride and HCl; performed in an inert solvent such as CCl₄ or dichloromethane at low temperature, with light or AIBN as initiator.

Acid‑base neutralization to form the hydrochloride salt of mepivacaine; the basic amine of mepivacaine accepts a proton from HCl, yielding mepivacaine·HCl; typically done in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution at room temperature, followed by crystallisation or drying.

Redox oxidation of chloride by permanganate; purpose is generation of chlorine gas; KMnO4 oxidizes Cl⁻ to Cl2 while Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(II); products are KCl and MnCl2 in aqueous solution; performed in aqueous HCl, usually at 0–5 °C to control vigorous Cl2 evolution, water is the solvent.

Diazo methylation (methyl ester formation) using diazomethane; the diazomethane adds a methyl group to the carboxylate, releasing N2 and giving methyl 2,2-dimethylpropanoate; carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no added catalyst needed, careful handling due to explosivity.

Catalytic hydrogenation of pyrrole to pyrrolidine; H₂ gas over palladium on carbon reduces the aromatic ring, fully saturating it to give pyrrolidine; carried out in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol) under 1–3 atm H₂ at ambient to 50 °C, using Pd/C as catalyst.

Solid‑state redox reduction of plutonium hexafluoride with carbon. Purpose: convert volatile PuF6 to less volatile PuF4 and generate CF4 gas. Key transformation: carbon reduces Pu(VI) to Pu(IV) while being fluorinated to carbon tetrafluoride. Typical conditions: high temperature (≈700–900 °C) in a sealed nickel or graphite vessel under inert atmosphere; reagents mixed intimately as solids. No solvent, no additional catalyst.

Acid–base double‑displacement (salt metathesis) reaction. Potassium hydroxide reacts with ammonium chloride to yield potassium chloride, aqueous ammonia (which escapes as gas), and water. Typically carried out by heating a solid mixture or by mixing aqueous solutions, the evolution of NH3 drives the reaction forward. No catalyst; water is the solvent when using solutions, and gentle heating is employed for the solid route.

Acid‑base complexation (metal chelation) of catechol with zinc oxide. Purpose: preparation of zinc catecholate chelate. Key transformation: deprotonation of the two phenolic OH groups of benzene‑1,2‑diol by ZnO to form Zn(oxinate) and release water. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or water at 80–120 °C; solid ZnO added to a solution of catechol. No extra catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalysed halogen exchange converting 3‑iodopyridine to 3‑bromopyridine. Purpose: synthesize aryl bromide from the corresponding aryl iodide. Key transformation: oxidative addition of Pd(0) into the C–I bond, ligand exchange with bromide (from NaBr), and reductive elimination to give C–Br. Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), PPh₃ as ligand, NaBr (1–2 equiv), solvent DMF or 1,4‑dioxane, 80–120 °C under nitrogen, reaction time 2–12 h.

Selective reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H). Purpose: obtain 3‑methylbutanal from methyl 3‑methylbutanoate. Key transformation: DIBAL‑H delivers a hydride to the carbonyl, forming an alkoxy‑aluminium intermediate that, on work‑up, yields the aldehyde and methanol. Typical conditions: dry THF, –78 °C to 0 °C, 1 equiv DIBAL‑H, inert atmosphere, quench with methanol or aqueous Rochelle’s salt after 30 min–1 h.

Acidic redox oxidation of iodide by bromate (halogen generation). Purpose: generate iodine in situ. Key transformation: bromate (BrO₃⁻) oxidizes I⁻ to I₂ while being reduced to Br⁻; sulfuric acid provides the acidic medium and forms potassium sulfate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, 3 equiv H₂SO₄, 6 equiv KI, 1 equiv KBrO₃, temperature 20–60 °C, stirring; no catalyst required.

Selective monobromination of 2,2′‑bithiophene using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) to give 5‑bromo‑2,2′‑bithiophene; electrophilic substitution mediated by NBS provides controlled bromine delivery; typically run in CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to room temperature, sometimes with a catalytic amount of light or radical initiator; succinimide is generated as by‑product.

Carbamate synthesis via alcohol‑urea exchange. Purpose: produce propyl carbamate and release ammonia. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of 1‑propanol on the carbonyl carbon of urea, displacing ammonia and forming propyl carbamate. Typical conditions: excess urea, 1‑propanol heated to 150–200 °C under reduced pressure to remove NH₃, usually in a sealed reactor; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: convert oxalic acid to lithium oxalate, a water‑soluble salt. Key transformation: proton transfer from oxalic acid to lithium hydroxide forming water and lithium oxalate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric amounts, ambient temperature, gentle stirring. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion; sodium chlorite in the presence of hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the hydroxymethyl group of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural to second aldehyde, giving 2,5‑furandicarboxaldehyde. Reaction is performed in aqueous medium, pH ≈ 3–4, at 0–25 °C, with stoichiometric NaClO₂ and catalytic H₂O₂, sometimes buffered with acetate.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of thionyl chloride. Purpose: quench excess thionyl chloride and generate gaseous HCl and SO₂. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on thionyl chloride, releasing two equivalents of HCl and one equivalent of SO₂. Typical conditions: addition of thionyl chloride to water at 0–25 °C under vigorous stirring; gases evolve. Solvent: water; no catalyst.

Oxidation of diallyl sulfide to diallyl sulfone using potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone). Purpose: convert a thioether to the corresponding sulfone. Key transformation: two‑electron oxidation of the sulfur atom, adding two oxygens to give the sulfone. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer or acetone‑water mixture, ambient temperature to 40 °C, slight excess of Oxone (2 eq), pH ~6–7. Oxidant: potassium peroxymonosulfate; no additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of calcium iodate. Purpose: generate insoluble calcium iodate and soluble ammonium chloride. Key transformation: exchange of cations between ammonium iodate and calcium chloride, precipitating Ca(IO₃)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions mixed at room temperature with stirring; precipitate filtered and washed. Solvent: water; no catalyst.

Skeletal isomerization of 3‑methylnonane to 2‑methylnonane. Purpose: move the methyl substituent to a more stable position. Key transformation: migration of a carbon fragment on the chain, effecting a methyl‑shift. Typical conditions: high temperature (300–500 °C) in the gas phase over a solid acid catalyst such as HZSM‑5 or other zeolite; catalyst provides acidic sites for carbocation rearrangement. No reagents; catalyst only.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed methanolysis (transesterification); the ester reacts with methanol to exchange the alkoxy group, producing methyl hexanoate and hexanol; common conditions use methanol with a catalytic amount of NaOMe or NaOH (5‑10 mol %) at 50‑80 °C, or acidic catalysts such as sulfuric acid (1‑2 mol %) under reflux; solvent is usually excess methanol.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) / acid‑base exchange; conversion of a primary alkyl sulfonate to the corresponding amine. Ammonia acts as nucleophile, displacing the methanesulfonate anion to give octyl amine and methanesulfonic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia (e.g., ethanol/water) at reflux temperatures (50‑80 °C); no added catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1/E2) of a primary alcohol to an alkene. Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates 2,3‑dimethyl‑1‑pentanol, enabling loss of water and formation of 2‑methyl‑1‑pentene. Typical conditions: excess conc. H₂SO₄, heating to 150‑170 °C; the acid acts both as solvent and catalyst. No additional reagents are needed.

Double displacement precipitation with gas evolution; purpose is to precipitate copper(II) sulfide and produce K2SO4 while releasing H2S. Aqueous KHS is mixed with aqueous CuSO4, leading to formation of insoluble CuS precipitate, soluble K2SO4, and H2S gas. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Neutralization of cyanamide hydrochloride with sodium hydroxide; the strong base deprotonates the HCl salt, producing cyanamide, sodium chloride and water. Performed in aqueous solution, often at 0–25 °C, with stoichiometric NaOH; the cyanamide can be isolated by evaporation or precipitation after removal of salts.

Halogen exchange/fluorination of chlorosulfonic acid to give chlorosulfonyl fluoride; purpose is to prepare a sulfonyl‑fluoride electrophile; key transformation replaces the OH of ClSO3H with F, producing ClSO2F and water; typically performed at 0‑50 °C using excess hydrogen fluoride (often as 48 % aqueous HF or HF‑pyridine) in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or a fluorinated solvent, under sealed PTFE conditions; no additional catalyst is required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in acidic solution; sulfite is oxidized to sulfate while chromate (Cr(VI)) is reduced to Cr(III) chloride. Serves as a quantitative redox titration (e.g., dichromate‑sulfite standardization). Performed in aqueous medium with excess HCl, usually at ambient temperature; stirring is sufficient, no external catalyst required.

Type: reduction of nitrile to primary amine. Purpose: synthesis of 2‑ethylhexylamine from the corresponding nitrile. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the nitrile carbon, reducing it through an imine intermediate to the primary amine, with formation of Al‑containing by‑products. Typical conditions: dry ether or THF solvent, reaction initiated at 0 °C under inert atmosphere, then stirred at reflux (≈65 °C) for 2–4 h; work‑up with careful quench (water then dilute acid). Common solvent: dry THF or diethyl ether; reducing agent: LiAlH₄ (no additional catalyst).

Redox oxidation (direct synthesis) of a metal halide. Metallic gold is oxidized by liquid bromine to give gold(III) bromide, AuBr3. The reaction requires elevated temperature (usually 200–300 °C) or bromine vapor in a sealed tube because gold is inert at room temperature. No solvent is needed; the bromine acts as both oxidant and halide source. The product is a dark solid that sublimes on heating.

Condensation/cyclodehydration forming a benzothiazole heterocycle; 2‑aminothiophenol reacts with benzaldehyde to give 2‑phenylbenzothiazole and water via imine formation followed by intramolecular cyclization. Conducted by refluxing in ethanol or acetic acid, often without added catalyst; sometimes a mild oxidant (e.g., I2) is used to promote cyclization.

Electrophilic demethylation of an aryl methyl ether using boron tribromide. BBr₃, a strong Lewis acid, cleaves the C–O bond of 3‑chloroanisole, yielding 3‑chlorophenol and methyl bromide as the by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, typically at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; reaction is quenched with water after completion.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination (multiple substitution) catalyzed by FeBr₃. FeBr₃ activates Br₂ to generate Br⁺, allowing successive bromination of benzene until all six positions are substituted, affording hexabromobenzene. Reaction is run with excess Br₂ in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at reflux or ambient temperature; FeBr₃ is used in catalytic amounts (≈5 mol %).

Metal reduction / preparation of a nickel‑boride catalyst. Sodium borohydride reduces Ni(II) acetate to a nickel boride solid (Ni₂B or NiB) while evolving hydrogen gas; sodium acetate remains in solution. Typically performed in ethanol or a water/ethanol mixture at 0‑25 °C under inert gas (N₂ or Ar) to prevent oxidation; no additional catalyst is required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of 2-(chloromethyl)pyridine with excess ammonia, forming bis(2‑pyridylmethyl)amine (a tertiary amine) and ammonium chloride; typically carried out in anhydrous ethanol or methanol under reflux, with excess NH₃ serving as nucleophile and base, followed by removal of solvent and washing to eliminate NH₄Cl.
Double displacement (metathesis); precipitation of lead telluride via ion exchange; aqueous solution at room temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

Dealkylation (N‑demethylation) using iodotrimethylsilane; Me₃SiI silylates the nitrogen, generating a good leaving group and transferring the methyl as methyl iod, leaving norfluoxetine (primary amine). Conducted in dry dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere.

Chemical reduction of sodium tetrachloroaurate(III) with sodium borohydride in water, producing metallic gold, sodium chloride, sodium borate (or borate salts), and hydrogen gas. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at 0–25 °C (ice bath) to moderate gas evolution; the reaction proceeds via electron transfer from BH₄⁻ to Au(III); no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed oxidation of thymol with hydrogen peroxide to thymoquinone (a para‑quinone); the phenolic ring is oxidized, generating water as the only by‑product; performed in aqueous H₂O₂ with a strong acid (e.g., 1–2 M H₂SO₄) at 25–60 °C, often in a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (acetone or acetonitrile).

Conjugate (1,4) reduction of coumarin with sodium borohydride, delivering hydride to the α,β‑unsaturated lactone to afford dihydrocoumarin (3,4‑dihydro‑2H‑chromen‑2‑one); conducted in methanol or a methanol‑water mixture from 0 °C to rt, then quenched with dilute acid.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction: sodium metaborate exchanges ions with calcium hydroxide to give calcium metaborate (sparingly soluble) and sodium hydroxide. Performed in aqueous solution with stirring at room temperature; no catalyst.

ATP‑dependent phosphorylation of L‑serine (kinase reaction); installs a phosphate on the side‑chain hydroxyl to give O‑phospho‑L‑serine. Key transformation: transfer of the γ‑phosphate of ATP to the serine hydroxyl, producing ADP and a phospho‑ester. Conditions: catalyzed by serine kinases (e.g., phosphoserine kinase) in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8), requiring Mg²⁺ or Mn²⁺ as a cofactor, typically at 30–37 °C. No organic solvent; enzyme and metal ion are the catalysts.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: aqueous ytterbium trichloride reacts with potassium carbonate, exchanging the anions to give insoluble ytterbium carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium chloride. Usually performed in water with mild heating to improve completion; the solid YbCO₃ is filtered off.

One‑pot Knoevenagel condensation/cyclization of salicylaldehyde with ethyl acetoacetate to produce chromone; base (piperidine, pyridine, or NaOH) catalyzes condensation of the aldehyde with the β‑keto ester, followed by intramolecular O‑alkylation and dehydration to assemble the 4‑H‑chromen‑4‑one ring, usually refluxed in ethanol or propionic acid and isolated after acidic work‑up.

Reductive dehalogenation; metal reduction of a vicinal dibromide to the corresponding alkane. Zinc dust serves as the reducing metal, acetic acts both as solvent and proton source. The reaction removes two bromine atoms from 1,2‑dibromooctane, yielding octane, zinc bromide precipitate, and regenerates acetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux of zinc dust in glacial acetic acid under inert atmosphere (nitrogen or argon); reaction time varies from 1–12 h depending on scale. No additional catalyst needed.

Reduction; LiAlH₄ reduces the carboxylic acid group of 2‑chlorobenzoic acid to a primary alcohol, yielding 2‑chlorobenzyl alcohol. Conducted in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; excess LiAlH₄ is quenched with water or dilute acid.

Direct combination oxidation; synthesis of gold(III) chloride; elemental gold is oxidized from Au(0) to Au(III) while chlorine is reduced to chloride; carried out by passing dry Cl₂ gas over gold metal at 200–300 °C in a dry, inert atmosphere; no solvent, the product is collected as a solid.

Condensation (oxime formation). Hydroxylamine condenses with cyclohexanone to give N‑cyclohexylidenehydroxylamine (cyclohexanone oxime) and water. Typically performed in ethanol or pyridine at room temperature to reflux; catalytic amounts of acid (p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base can accelerate the reaction, and removal of water (e.g., molecular sieves) drives the equilibrium toward product. No metal catalyst is required.

Transesterification of 4‑methylphenyl acetate with methanol, producing methyl acetate and 4‑methylphenol. Catalyzed by acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (NaOMe), heated under reflux in methanol; excess methanol shifts equilibrium toward products.

Gas‑phase redox exchange between chlorine and oxygen difluoride forming chlorine monofluoride and molecular oxygen; 2 Cl₂ + 2 O F₂ → O₂ + 4 ClF proceeds exothermically at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert carrier gas and is employed in specialized fluorination chemistry.

Reaction type: oxygen atom transfer / reduction (silane reduces phosphine oxide). Purpose: generate trimethylphosphine ligand and silicon tetrachloride from trichlorosilane. Key transformation: HSiCl3 donates chlorine to phosphorus oxide, releasing HCl and converting SiCl3‑H to SiCl4 while reducing Me3P=O to Me3P. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere, reflux in anhydrous non‑polar solvent (toluene, THF) or neat, often at 80‑120 °C. No external catalyst required; stoichiometric amounts of reagents are used.

Hydride reduction of 3‑chlorooxolane with lithium aluminum hydride; LiAlH4 reduces the C–Cl bond to C–H, converting the substrate to tetrahydrofuran; typically performed in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) under reflux under nitrogen; lithium chloride and aluminum hydroxide form on work‑up.

Reaction type: electrophilic addition (halogenation of an alkene). Purpose: install vicinal bromine atoms on the α,β‑unsaturated ester to obtain a dibromo ester intermediate. Key transformation: Br2 adds across the carbon‑carbon double bond of ethyl acrylate to give ethyl 2,3‑dibromopropionate (anti addition). Typical conditions: dilute solution of ethyl acrylate in carbon‑tetrachloride or dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, protected from light to avoid radical side reactions. No catalyst needed.

Reaction type: base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: convert the methyl ester to the free carboxylic acid (3‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)propionic acid). Key transformation: hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of the methyl ester, yielding a carboxylate salt and methanol; subsequent acid work‑up protonates the carboxylate to give the acid. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv), reflux 1–3 h, then acidify with dilute HCl. Solvent often water‑ethanol mixture.

Type: Nucleophilic ring‑opening of a sultone (sulfonate ester). Purpose: Synthesize the open‑chain sulfonic acid (tramiprosate) from the cyclic precursor. Key transformation: Ammonia attacks the electrophilic carbon of 1,3‑propanesultone, cleaving the C–O bond and opening the five‑membered ring to give 3‑aminopropanesulfonic acid (tramiprosate). Typical conditions: Stirring 1,3‑propanesultone with excess aqueous or gaseous NH₃ at ambient temperature or mild heating (25–60 °C) for several hours. No catalyst required; solvent can be water or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., MeCN) if liquid NH₃ is used.

Reaction type: nucleophilic addition of hydroxide to carbon disulfide forming a thiocarbonate salt. Purpose: synthesize potassium thiocarbonate, a precursor for xanthates and other sulfur‑containing reagents. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks CS2, generating the trithiocarbonate anion which pairs with K⁺; water is released. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (excess), ambient to slightly elevated temperature (20‑60 °C). Reaction is usually carried out in water; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to exchange the methyl ester for an ethyl ester. Methyl 3‑methylbutanoate reacts with excess ethanol, producing ethyl 3‑methylbutanoate and methanol. Typical conditions: reflux with a catalytic amount of NaOEt or K₂CO₃ in ethanol; removal of methanol shifts equilibrium toward product. Solvent is ethanol; catalyst is a mild base.

Reaction type: carbonylation / hydroesterification (acid‑catalyzed carbonylation of an olefin). Purpose: industrial production of methyl methacrylate (MMA). Key transformation: isobutylene undergoes insertion of CO and subsequent methanolysis to form the methyl ester of methacrylic acid, releasing water. Typical conditions: high pressure CO (30–60 bar), temperature 150‑200 °C, catalyst such as acidic zeolite (e.g., sulfated ZrO₂) or a palladium‑phosphine complex with an acid co‑catalyst. Solvent often methanol itself; water is a coproduct.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) forming a carbon‑selenium bond. Purpose: synthesize diethyl selenide from ethyl iodide. Key transformation: Se²⁻ (from Na₂Se) attacks the primary carbon of ethyl iodide, displacing I⁻; a second equivalent of ethyl iodide reacts with the intermediate to give R‑Se‑R and two equivalents of NaI. Typical conditions: dry aprotic polar solvent (DMF, DMSO), inert atmosphere, reflux or moderate heating (50‑80 °C). Sodium selenide is usually prepared in situ from elemental selenium and sodium metal or NaBH₄. No additional catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction used to prepare a metal carboxylate (cupric stearate). Copper(II) chloride reacts with potassium stearate in aqueous solution, usually under gentle heating and stirring, to exchange anions and precipitate the insoluble copper(II) stearate while forming soluble potassium chloride. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, reflux or heating to 60‑80 °C, followed by filtration and washing of the solid.

Electrophilic halogenation (iodination) of 2′‑deoxyuridine using N‑iodosuccinimide (NIS) as the iodine source. The reaction installs an iodine atom at the 5‑position of the uracil base to give the antiviral nucleoside analog idoxuridine, with succinimide formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous DMF or acetonitrile, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, and protection from light; no additional catalyst required.

LiAlH₄ reduction of benzophenone to diphenylmethanol; strong hydride donor reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol; executed in dry ether (Et₂O or THF) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful quench with water or dilute acid.

Acid‑catalyzed Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (condensation) of 3‑nitrophenol with acetone in the presence of hydrochloric acid to afford 3,3′‑dinitrobisphenol A and water. The reaction proceeds via protonation of acetone to generate a carbocation which attacks the activated aromatic ring of the phenol, followed by deprotonation. Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent, excess HCl (often 6 M), temperature 60‑80 °C, and vigorous stirring; the product precipitates on cooling.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in strongly acidic solution where dichromate(VI) oxidizes hydrazine (from hydrazine sulfate) to nitrogen gas while being reduced to chromium(III). Sulfuric acid provides the acidic medium and supplies sulfate ions for the final salts. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O and hydrazine sulfate, 5 equiv. H₂SO₄, heating to reflux; the evolved N₂ gas is collected, and the mixture is cooled to crystallize Na₂SO₄ and Cr₂(SO₄)₃.

Synthesis (halogenation); direct combination of elemental antimony with chlorine gas to form antimony trichloride (SbCl3). Typically performed by passing dry Cl2 over powdered Sb at 250‑300 °C in a sealed tube or flow reactor; gas‑phase reaction, no solvent, no catalyst required.

Aminolysis of carbonate; purpose is formation of phenyl carbamate (urethane) from ethyl phenyl carbonate; key transformation is ammonia attacking the carbonyl, displacing ethoxy to give phenyl carbamate and ethanol; typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃ at 50‑100 °C, often in ethanol or THF as solvent; may be run under pressure when using gaseous ammonia.

Single‑displacement redox reaction where metallic cobalt reduces mercuric chloride to elemental mercury while cobalt itself is oxidized to cobalt(II) chloride. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution or molten salt to allow ion exchange. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at elevated temperature (≈80‑100 °C) or in a sealed tube with inert atmosphere; the mercury separates as a liquid layer, and the cobalt(II) chloride remains dissolved.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification; purpose is to prepare a monoglyceride surfactant. The hydroxyl group of glycerol attacks the carbonyl of lauric acid in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄, forming the ester bond of glyceryl monolaurate and releasing water. Typically performed by heating the mixture (reflux) to 120‑150 °C, often with the fatty acid in excess as solvent; water is removed by azeotropic distillation. No additional catalyst beyond the strong acid is required.

High‑temperature metallothermic reduction; used to obtain metallic thorium from its dioxide. Lithium metal reduces ThO₂, yielding elemental thorium and lithium oxide. The reaction is carried out in a sealed, inert‑atmosphere vessel (argon) at 800‑1000 °C. No solvent is used; the molten lithium serves both reductant and reaction medium.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); conversion of the zwitterionic N,N‑dimethylglycine to its sodium salt. NaOH deprotonates the carboxylic acid group, producing sodium N,N‑dimethylglycinate and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; excess NaOH may be employed to drive completion. No special catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement/metathesis precipitation of cerium(III) nitrate with oxalic acid to give cerium(III) oxalate solid and nitric acid in solution. Used to obtain cerium oxalate as a precursor. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at low to moderate temperature to avoid oxalate decomposition; stirring and subsequent filtration; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an azide ion on an alkyl hydrogen sulfate; generates ethyl azide. Sodium azide supplies N₃⁻, which displaces the hydrogen sulfate leaving group on the ethyl sulfate. The reaction is usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to room temperature, and may be heated mildly (30‑50 °C) to improve yield. No additional catalyst is needed; the by‑product is sodium hydrogen sulfate.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ammonia on a primary bromide; produces 1‑amino‑2‑butanone. Ammonia attacks the carbon bearing the bromine, displacing Br⁻ as HBr and forming the corresponding amino‑ketone. The reaction is typically run in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia solution at 0‑25 °C to suppress elimination, sometimes under reflux for less reactive substrates. No catalyst is required; the generated HBr is neutralized by excess ammonia or removed by gas evolution.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition (oxy‑acetylation) of an alkene with acetic anhydride; yields 2‑pentyl acetate and acetic acid. The double bond of 2‑pentene attacks the carbonyl of acetic anhydride in the presence of a strong Lewis or Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, BF₃·OEt₂), forming a carbocation that is trapped by the acetate moiety, giving the acetate ester. The reaction is carried out at 0‑50 °C in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; the generated acetic acid is a co‑product. No additional catalyst beyond the acid promoter is required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Tetrafluoroboric acid reacts with potassium bicarbonate in aqueous solution, exchanging protons for potassium. The key transformation is conversion of HBF4 and KHCO3 into potassium tetrafluoroborate (KBF4) while carbonic acid is generated, which decomposes to CO2 and H2O. Typical conditions are ambient temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Mannich condensation (amine alkylation of a phenol). Phenol, formaldehyde and ammonia undergo a three‑component condensation to install an aminomethyl group ortho/para to the phenolic oxygen, yielding 2‑(aminomethyl)phenol and water. The reaction is usually performed in an aqueous or alcoholic medium at 0–50 °C, often under slightly acidic or neutral conditions; no metal catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a α‑keto acid). Pyruvic acid is reduced by H2 in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt‑O₂, converting the keto group to a secondary alcohol and giving lactic acid. Conditions typically involve 1–5 atm H₂, temperatures from room temperature to 80 °C, in water or an alcohol solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation (phenol–aldehyde coupling). Two equivalents of 2,6‑dimethylphenol condense with an aldehyde (commonly formaldehyde) in the presence of the solid acid Montmorillonite K10 to give 4,4′‑methylenebis(2,6‑dimethylphenol). The reaction proceeds at 80–120 °C, often solvent‑free or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene; the clay provides the catalytic acidic sites.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange (salt formation). Salicylic acid reacts with potassium acetate in aqueous solution, swapping the acidic proton for potassium. The products are potassium salicylate and acetic acid. Heating may be applied to drive off volatile acetic acid; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization; reaction of selenium trioxide (SeO₃) with potassium hydroxide to give potassium selenate (K₂SeO₄) and water. SeO₃ acts as the anhydride of selenic acid; addition of aqueous KOH converts it to the salt. Performed in aqueous medium at ambient or mildly elevated temperature, using stoichiometric KOH; the product precipitates or remains dissolved depending on concentration.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) of a tertiary bromide with hydroxide; purpose is to synthesize a tertiary alcohol. Key transformation: departure of bromide to form a tertiary carbocation, capture by OH⁻ to give 3‑ethylpentan‑3‑ol, with NaBr as by‑product. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (≈80 °C) or at 60–70 °C; polar protic solvent (water or water/ethanol) favours substitution over elimination.

Tishchenko disproportionation (aldehyde dimerization to ester and alcohol). Acetaldehyde, in the presence of aluminum ethoxide (Al(OEt)₃) as a Lewis‑acid/alkoxide catalyst, undergoes intermolecular redox coupling: two aldehyde molecules are converted into ethyl acetate (the ester) and ethanol (the alcohol). The reaction is typically performed neat or in a non‑protic solvent at 80–150 °C under inert atmosphere; the aluminum alkoxide is the essential catalyst.

Acid–base precipitation (double displacement); purpose is to precipitate silver as insoluble AgCl for removal of silver ions; key transformation: Ag2O + 2 HCl → 2 AgCl (s) + H2O; typical condition: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; common solvent: water.

Self‑propagating combustion (fuel‑oxidizer) synthesis using citric acid as fuel and metal nitrates as oxidizers; purpose is to prepare a mixed nickel‑titanium oxide (NiTiO3) material; key transformation: citric acid + Ti(OiPr)4 + Ni(NO3)2 decompose, releasing CO2, H2O, NO2 and leaving NiTiO3 solid; typical condition: solid‑state mixture heated to 300–500 °C in air until the combustion wave passes, followed by calcination; no solvent is required, though a small amount of water may be used to homogenize the precursor.

Transcarbamoylation (carbamate formation); the nucleophilic amine (benzylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of tert‑butyl (4‑nitrophenyl) carbonate, displacing 4‑nitrophenol and forming benzyl carbamate. The tert‑butyl group leaves as tert‑butanol or remains bound to the carbonate intermediate, but the overall stoichiometry produces the phenol and carbamate. Common conditions: mild temperature (0 °C to room temperature), organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, optionally a weak base (e.g., triethylamine) to scavenge the liberated acid. Reaction proceeds without metal catalyst.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of an alkene with reductive work‑up; purpose is to fragment 3‑methyl‑1‑butene into carbonyl compounds; key transformation: C=C bond is cleaved to give formaldehyde + 3‑methylbutanal; typical condition: O3 bubbled through dry CH2Cl2 (or MeCN) at –78 °C, then reductive quench with dimethyl sulfide (or Zn/AcOH); common solvent: dichloromethane, low temperature required.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro group (Sn/HCl reduction); purpose is to convert 4‑nitrophenylarsonic acid to the corresponding aniline derivative for further functionalization; key transformation: 4‑nitrophenylarsonic acid + Sn + 2 HCl → 4‑aminophenylarsonic acid + SnCl2 + H2O; typical condition: aqueous HCl solution with tin filings, heated under reflux or gentle heating; solvent: water/HCl mixture.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation – Aqueous silver nitrate reacts with solid potassium chloride to precipitate insoluble silver chloride (AgCl) while forming soluble potassium nitrate (KNO3). The reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; vigorous stirring aids mixing. No catalyst is needed, and the formation of the white AgCl precipitate is often used as an analytical test for chloride ions.

Reductive amination. Purpose: Converts ketone and amine into an alkylated amine (mephentermine). Key transformation: Ketone carbon reduced to CH2N(CH3)2. Conditions: Dimethylamine, sodium cyanoborohydride (NaCNBH3), mildly acidic pH. Solvent: Methanol/water mixture.

Nucleophilic substitution (halide exchange) to generate a silyl isothiocyanate; purpose is to prepare trimethylsilyl isothiocyanate as a versatile reagent; key transformation: (CH3)3SiCl + NaSCN → (CH3)3SiNCS + NaCl; typical condition: dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or THF at ambient temperature, inert atmosphere, stirring for several hours; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of a primary alkyl bromide; purpose is to obtain the saturated alkane octane; key transformation: H₂ adds across the C–Br bond, releasing HBr; performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with Pd/C or Pd(OH)₂ (Pearlman’s catalyst) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to 50 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed cleavage (protonolysis) of tetramethylsilane to form trimethylsilyl triflate, a silylating reagent, and methane; usually carried out at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane under nitrogen, with triflic acid acting as both reactant and catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed); converts methyl (E)-but‑2‑enoate to trans‑2‑butenoic acid and methanol; key C–O bond cleavage of the ester; typically performed in water or aqueous ethanol with HCl, H₂SO₄ or NaOH at reflux; solvents: water, MeOH, sometimes THF; catalyst: acid or base.

Oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis) of 1‑decene producing formaldehyde (from the terminal carbon) and nonanal; performed at –78 °C to 0 °C in CH₂Cl₂ or MeOH, followed by a reductive work‑up (Zn/AcOH) or oxidative work‑up (H₂O₂) to isolate the aldehydes.

Acid‑base neutralization (proton transfer); sodium ethoxide deprotonates sulfuric acid, forming ethanol and sodium bisulfate. Usually performed in aqueous solution at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control the exotherm; no catalyst required.

Metathesis/acid–base exchange; hydrochloric acid protonates acetate ion of cadmium acetate, yielding cadmium chloride and acetic acid; carried out in water at room temperature or slight heating, aqueous solution as solvent, no catalyst.

Metathesis/precipitation double‑displacement; sulfide anion from sodium sulfide replaces bromide in gold(I) bromide to form insoluble gold(I) sulfide (Au₂S) and sodium bromide in solution. Typically carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous–organic media (e.g., water or ethanol‑water) at ambient temperature, often under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of sulfide. The gold sulfide precipitates and is isolated by filtration; no catalyst required.

O‑methylation of honokiol phenol using methyl triflate in the presence of DIPEA base, yielding 4‑O‑methylhonokiol; carried out in dry aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; DIPEA scavenges the triflic acid by‑product.

Acid‑base exchange between hydrochloric acid and potassium picrate producing picric acid and potassium chloride; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; simple neutralisation, no catalyst needed.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde (nucleophilic addition); purpose is carbon–carbon bond formation to give a secondary alcohol; phenylmagnesium bromide adds the phenyl nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon of 2,2‑dimethylpropanal forming an alkoxide that is protonated to 2,2‑dimethyl‑1‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol; performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by aqueous NH₄Cl work‑up; no additional catalyst.

Direct combination (synthesis) of iron metal with chlorine gas to give iron(II) chloride; typically conducted by passing dry Cl₂ over iron at 200–300 °C in a quartz tube or sealed reactor; no solvent, inert atmosphere used to avoid higher oxidation states.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); purpose is to install a chloro substituent onto benzene. Key transformation: generation of the electrophilic chlorosulfonyl cation from sulfuryl chloride and AlCl3, which attacks the aromatic ring forming chlorobenzene while releasing HCl and SO2. Typical conditions: anhydrous, dilute mixture in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, AlCl3 (1–2 equiv) added, temperature 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose is to convert selenous acid to a water‑soluble selenite salt while generating bicarbonate. Key transformation: proton transfer from H2SeO3 to carbonate, yielding monosodium selenite (NaHSeO3) and sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3). Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent beyond water, mild stirring, often under atmospheric pressure.

Dehydrative chlorination of a dicarboxylic acid; purpose is to prepare the corresponding di‑acid chloride (terephthaloyl chloride) for polymer or polyamide synthesis. Key transformation: each –COOH group is converted to –COCl, producing POCl3 and HCl as gaseous by‑products. Typical conditions: anhydrous environment, excess PCl5 (1.5–2 equiv per –COOH), solvent such as dry chloroform or dichloromethane, temperature initially 0 °C then warmed to reflux (≈ 40–50 °C), inert atmosphere.

Redox (fluorination) reaction; purpose is to reduce xenon difluoride to elemental xenon while oxidizing iron to iron(II) fluoride. Key transformation: XeF2 acts as a fluorine donor, delivering two fluoride ions to Fe to form FeF2 and releasing Xe gas. Usually performed in anhydrous hydrogen fluoride or liquid HF as solvent, at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere to control the highly reactive fluorinating species.

Carbothermal reduction (solid‑state synthesis) of tungsten carbide; tungsten dioxide mixed with carbon powder and heated to 1400–1600 °C in an inert (argon) or vacuum atmosphere; carbon reduces WO₂, providing carbon to form WC while CO gas evolves; purpose is production of WC ceramic; no solvent, carbon acts as reductant and carbon source.

Thermal decomposition (solid‑state redox) of sodium nitrate to sodium nitrite with release of oxygen gas (2 NaNO₃ → 2 NaNO₂ + O₂). Employed for preparation of sodium nitrite or oxygen generation. Performed by heating solid NaNO₃ to 400–500 °C in a furnace, often under inert atmosphere; no solvent; catalyst generally not required, though metal surfaces can aid.

Peracid formation (peroxyacylation); purpose is to generate peracetic acid, a strong oxidizing agent, from hydrogen peroxide and acetic anhydride. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of H2O2 on the carbonyl of Ac2O, yielding peracetic acid and one equivalent of acetic acid. Conducted neat or in a minimal amount of inert solvent, temperature 0 °C to 25 °C, often with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H2SO4) to speed up the reaction, and careful temperature control due to exotherm.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to convert ethylparaben to the more water‑soluble methylparaben. Key transformation: methanol attacks the carbonyl of the ethyl ester, displacing ethanol and forming methylparaben. Typical conditions: excess methanol, catalytic sulfuric acid (0.1–1 mol % relative to substrate), reflux (≈ 65 °C) for several hours, inert atmosphere optional, solvent is methanol itself.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone using a peracid; purpose is to increase the oxidation state of sulfur; key transformation: conversion of diethyl sulfide (R‑S‑R) to diethyl sulfone (R‑SO₂‑R) with m‑chloroperbenzoic acid delivering two oxygen atoms; typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, using ~2 equivalents of m‑CPBA under inert atmosphere; by‑product is m‑chlorobenzoic acid.

Acid–carbonate reaction; used to convert calcium carbonate into a soluble calcium tellurate salt while releasing CO₂. Calcium carbonate reacts with aqueous telluric acid (H₆TeO₆) to form calcium tellurate (CaTeO₄), carbon dioxide gas and water. Typically carried out in water at ambient temperature or with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base (precipitation) reaction: Aluminum ethoxide reacts with phosphoric acid; protonation of the ethoxide gives ethanol, and the resulting Al³⁺ combines with PO₄³⁻ to give insoluble aluminum phosphate (AlPO₄) as a precipitate. Typically carried out in water at room temperature with stoichiometric acid; the product is filtered and washed; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution of iodosilane with n‑butyllithium to form n‑butylsilane; purpose is to generate an alkylsilane via organolithium chemistry. Key transformation: R₃Si–I + n‑BuLi → R₃Si‑Bu + LiI. Conducted in dry ether or THF at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric n‑BuLi is added dropwise; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst; the by‑product lithium iodide remains dissolved or precipitates.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation) of phosphine; converts 4 PH₃ into P₄ (white phosphorus) and 6 H₂; performed at high temperature (≈500 °C) often over metal surfaces (e.g., Cu); no solvent required.

TEMPO‑catalyzed oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using sodium hypochlorite (bleach). The reaction converts 3‑hydroxymethylpyridine to 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde with catalytic TEMPO and stoichiometric NaOCl, producing water and NaCl as by‑products. Conducted in a biphasic water/volatile organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, buffered (pH 8–9), and often includes a small amount of NaBr to accelerate the oxidation.

Redox oxidation of molybdenum(II) chloride by molecular oxygen producing molybdenum dioxide and chlorine gas. The overall process is a gas‑phase oxidation where O₂ serves as oxidant and Cl⁻ is liberated as Cl₂. Usually requires elevated temperature (≈300–500 °C) in a flow reactor under dry conditions; no solvent is employed.

Electrophilic addition of bromine to cyclohexene; anti‑addition gives trans‑1,2‑dibromocyclohexane via a bromonium ion that is opened by bromide attack from the opposite face. Typical procedure: dissolve cyclohexene in carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, cool to 0 °C, add 1 equiv Br2 dropwise until the bromine color disappears. Reaction is performed in the dark or under amber light; no catalyst required.

LiAlH₄ reduction of a difluoro‑substituted amide to the corresponding primary amine. Lithium aluminum hydride transfers hydride to the carbonyl of 2,2‑difluoroacetamide, yielding 2,2‑difluoroethylamine after work‑up. Performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, with careful quenching of excess hydride using aqueous acid.

Ozonolysis of the vinyl side chain of 2‑vinylpyridine. O₃ adds across the C=C bond, and reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH) cleaves the ozonide to give formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde from the carbon attached to the ring. The reaction is carried out in a non‑protic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ at –78 °C under an O₃ atmosphere, followed by low‑temperature reduction.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann‑type aryl amination (C–N coupling). Dimethylamine is coupled with bromobenzene in the presence of CuI (catalyst), 1,10‑phenanthroline (ligand), and potassium carbonate (base) to afford N,N‑dimethylaniline, with KBr as a by‑product. Typical conditions use DMF or DMSO as solvent, heating to 110–130 °C under nitrogen, and stirring for several hours.

Direct fluorination (redox) of zinc phosphide with elemental fluorine. Purpose: convert the phosphide into metal fluoride and volatile phosphorus pentafluoride. Key transformation: zinc phosphide reacts with fluorine gas to give zinc fluoride and PF Conditions: dry F₂ gas passed over solid zinc phosphide at 0–25 °C (often under an inert atmosphere). No solvent; reaction is highly exothermic and must be tightly controlled.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction between sodium bicarbonate and calcium hydroxide; purpose is to generate insoluble calcium carbonate and sodium hydroxide. Key transformation: NaHCO3 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3(s) + NaOH + H2O. Conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, stirring; water serves as solvent, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) hydrolysis of benzyl chloride; purpose is to convert a primary alkyl chloride to the corresponding primary alcohol. Water (often as aqueous ethanol) attacks the benzylic carbocation formed after chloride loss, yielding benzyl alcohol and HCl. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous ethanol or water with a base (e.g., NaOH or Na2CO3) to neutralize the generated HCl; common solvent is ethanol/water mixture.

Selective chemical reduction of oxcarbazepine with sodium borohydride; purpose is to reduce the ketone/lactam carbonyl to the secondary alcohol giving licarbazepine (the hydroxyl analogue). The key transformation is NaBH4 delivering a hydride to the carbonyl carbon, converting C=O to C‑OH. Typical conditions: dissolve oxcarbazepine in dry THF or methanol, add NaBH4 at 0 °C, then stir at room temperature for 1–2 h; reaction is usually performed under nitrogen. No additional catalyst is required.

Oxidation of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; purpose is to increase oxidation state of the aldehyde carbon from –1 to +3. The aldehyde is oxidized to 4‑ethylbenzoic acid while KMnO4 is reduced to MnO2 (or Mn2+ in acidic work‑up). Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or K2CO3), warm (50–80 °C) stirring; after completion the mixture is acidified (HCl) to precipitate the acid. Common solvent is water; sometimes a mixed water/acetone system is used.

Acidic (or basic) hydrolysis of the amide bond in hippuric acid (benzoyl‑glycine) to give benzoic acid and glycine; purpose is cleavage of the peptide‑like linkage. The key transformation is nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon of the amide, followed by breakdown to the free acid and amine. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous hydrochloric acid (6 M) for several hours, or alternatively reflux in 1 M NaOH followed by acidification to isolate benzoic acid. Solvent is water; the reaction may be carried out in a sealed tube for high temperature.

Esterification of creatine’s carboxyl group via activation with thionyl chloride to form the methyl ester; purpose is to convert the acid functionality into a more lipophilic ester. Thionyl chloride reacts with the carboxylic acid to give an acyl chloride intermediate, which is immediately captured by methanol, producing creatine methyl ester and releasing gaseous HCl and SO2. Typical conditions: add excess thionyl chloride to a solution of creatine in dry methanol at 0 °C, then stir at room temperature for 1–2 h under nitrogen; gases evolve and are vented through a trap. No additional catalyst is needed; dry, inert atmosphere is important.

Acid‑base neutralization between selenous acid (H2SeO3) and sodium bicarbonate; purpose is to generate the monosodium selenite salt while evolving carbon dioxide. The key transformation is deprotonation of H2SeO3 by HCO3⁻ to give NaHSeO3, CO2, and H2O; the transient carbonic acid formed from CO2 and water rapidly decomposes to CO2 + H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring until gas evolution ceases. Solvent is water; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of alkyl bromide; 1,2‑dibromohexane is treated with aqueous NaOH (often heated under reflux) to replace bromides with hydroxyl groups, producing 1,2‑hexanediol, NaBr and water; basic aqueous medium, temperature 80–100 °C.

Base‑promoted Hofmann elimination; sodium hydroxide dehydrohalogenates sodium chloroacetate to give the unsaturated carboxylate sodium acrylate, with formation of sodium chloride and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH, 60–100 °C, often performed in water or dilute aqueous solution.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); sulfuric acid protonates cesium bromide, liberating hydrogen bromide gas and generating cesium bisulfate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to evolve HBr; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑base salt metathesis (double displacement). Ammonium trifluoroacetate exchanges its cation with sodium bicarbonate in aqueous solution, producing sodium trifluoroacetate and ammonium bicarbonate. Usually performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required. Useful for preparing buffers or converting salts.

Formation of a chloroformate protecting reagent; 9‑fluorenylmethanol attacks phosgene to give 9‑fluorenylmethyl chloroformate while pyridine scavenges the generated HCl, forming pyridinium chloride. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; pyridine acts as the base.

Metathesis (halide exchange) reaction; three equivalents of sodium fluoride replace chloride ligands of titanium(III) chloride, yielding titanium(III) fluoride and sodium chloride. Performed in dry, polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF) or by solid‑state grinding, often at elevated temperature (50–100 °C); no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalysed ether cleavage (hydrolysis). Protonation of the ether oxygen followed by heterolytic C–O bond cleavage gives the more substituted alcohol (2‑butanol) and the corresponding alkyl halide (chloroethane) from the ethoxy fragment. Typically performed by heating the ether in excess concentrated aqueous HCl, often refluxing; water serves as solvent and the reaction proceeds via an SN1‑type mechanism.

Oxidative fluorination (redox gas‑phase reaction). Tungsten metal is oxidized from 0 to +6 while nitrogen trifluoride serves as both fluorine donor and oxidant, being reduced to nitrogen gas. The key transformation is W → WF₆ and NF₃ → N₂. Typical conditions are high temperature (400–600 °C) in a sealed reactor under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Reaction type: Isotopic exchange. Key transformations involve proton-deuteron exchange between deuterium oxide (D2O) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH), forming sodium deuteroxide (NaOD) and water. Occurs under standard temperature and pressure; no solvent or catalyst required.

Metathesis (acid–salt exchange) in aqueous solution. Acetic acid protonates the oxalate ion of iron(II) oxalate, liberating oxalic acid and forming ferrous acetate by coordination of AcO⁻ to Fe²⁺. The reaction proceeds at room temperature to gentle reflux, often in water or mixed water/ethanol. No catalyst is needed.

Direct combination (hydrogenation) of titanium metal with hydrogen gas to form titanium dihydride. Typically performed at elevated temperature (300‑400 °C) under H₂ pressure (several atm) in a sealed tube or furnace; no solvent, inert atmosphere optional.

Periodate oxidation (vicinal diol cleavage). Sodium periodate oxidatively cleaves the 1,2‑diol of thymine glycol, yielding formaldehyde from the cleaved carbon and converting the remaining fragment into 5‑formyluracil, with water as a by‑product. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 5–7) at 0 °C to room temperature; stoichiometric NaIO₄ is used, no catalyst required.

Alpha‑bromination of a ketone (halogenation); tetrabutylammonium tribromide, a solid source of Br2, is added to acetophenone in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature; the tribromide releases Br⁺ which brominates the enol form of acetophenone, giving α‑bromoacetophenone and tetrabutylammonium bromide as by‑product; mild conditions, no external catalyst.

Sulfur transfer (reagent synthesis). Phosphorus pentasulfide transfers sulfur atoms to 1,1'-carbonyldiimidazole, converting the carbonyl groups into thiocarbonyls to give 1,1'-thiocarbonyldiimidazole while generating phosphorus pentoxide as a by‑product. Usually performed under nitrogen in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dry THF or toluene, with reflux; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base deprotonation (salt formation) with gas evolution. Sodium hydride abstracts the acidic proton of trifluoroacetic acid, releasing hydrogen gas and forming sodium trifluoroacetate. The reaction is carried out in dry aprotic solvents (e.g., THF, DMF) at 0 °C to ambient temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aromatic system. 2‑Aminonaphthalene is partially reduced over palladium on carbon in ethanol under a hydrogen atmosphere (1–5 atm) at ambient moderate temperature, saturating of the naphthalene double bonds to afford 2‑amino‑1,2‑dihydronaphthalene. Ethanol acts as both solvent and hydrogen‑transfer medium; the Pd/C catalyst enables heterogenous H₂ activation.

Nucleophilic substitution (halide exchange) at silicon; a Grignard reagent attacks triethylbromosilane to replace the bromide with a phenyl group, forming triethylphenylsilane and MgBr2. Typically performed in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of a terminal alkyne (Kucherov reaction); HgSO4/H2SO4 mediates addition of water across the C≡C bond of ethyl pent‑4‑ynoate, yielding the corresponding β‑keto ester, ethyl 4‑oxopentanoate. Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid, refluxing; mercury(II) sulfate acts as the catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (sulfonamide formation); n‑Butylamine attacks benzenesulfonyl chloride, displacing chloride which is scavenged by triethylamine, affording N‑butylbenzenesulfonamide. Carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen.

Redox reaction; iodide ions are oxidized to elemental iodine by dichromate in strongly acidic medium (HCl), while dichromate is reduced to Cr(III) chloride. Typically performed in aqueous solution with concentrated HCl, ambient temperature; no special solvent beyond water.

Oxidative conversion of sulfide to sulfone (ozonolysis); thioanisole reacts with ozone to give methyl phenyl sulfone as the major product. Conducted in dry dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C, with a reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide or zinc/acetic acid) to remove excess ozone.

Reduction of a nitroxyl radical; TEMPO is reduced by sodium borohydride to the corresponding hydroxylamine (TEMPO‑H), generating sodium borate as by‑product. Performed in methanol or THF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation‑complexation reaction; cobalt(II) is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to cobalt(III) while the diethyldithiocarbamate anion coordinates to form a Co(III) dithiocarbamate complex; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often in the presence of a mild base; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation reaction; aqueous sodium ferrocyanide reacts with calcium chloride to exchange cations, forming sparingly soluble calcium ferrocyanide which precipitates, while sodium chloride remains in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water, often with stirring; the solid is filtered and washed.

Sulfidation/precipitation; cadmium oxide reacts with hydrogen sulfide gas to form cadmium sulfide and water; typically performed by bubbling H₂S through an aqueous suspension of CdO at 80‑100 °C or by heating the solid mixture; no catalyst, CdS precipitates.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between manganese carbonate and ammonium oxalate producing manganese(II) oxalate and ammonium carbonate; performed in water with stirring at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide using sodium hypochlorite under mildly acidic (acetic acid) conditions; usually conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic medium at 0–25 °C; NaOCl acts as the oxidant, no metal catalyst required.

Nitration/esterification of benzyl alcohol to benzyl nitrate using lead(II) nitrate and hydrochloric acid; proceeds via substitution of the hydroxyl group by nitrate; typically refluxed in aqueous medium or a polar organic solvent; lead nitrate provides the nitrate source, no additional catalyst.

Halogenation (substitution) of glycerol to 1,2,3‑trichloropropane using phosphorus pentachloride; all three hydroxyl groups are replaced by chloride atoms; carried out anhydrous in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, under inert atmosphere at 0–25 °C; PCl₅ is the reagent, no catalyst.

Hydroformylation (oxo process) of 2‑methyl‑1‑butene with synthesis gas (CO/H₂) to give the aldehyde 3‑methylpentanal. Uses a homogeneous catalyst such as Rh(acac)(CO)₂ with phosphine ligands (or a cobalt carbonyl system) at 80–120 °C and 1–10 MPa syngas; solvent commonly toluene or dioxane.

Alcoholysis (methanolysis) of an ester; nucleophilic attack of methanol on cyclopropyl benzoate displaces the cyclopropoxy group, forming methyl benzoate and cyclopropanol; can be catalyzed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or a base (e.g., NaOMe) and is usually run under reflux in methanol as solvent.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Methyl chloride generates a methyl carbocation in the presence of anhydrous aluminum chloride, which attacks phenol ortho and para to the hydroxyl group. Repeated substitution yields 2,4,6‑trimphenol (mesitol) and liberates HCl. Reaction is carried out under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to reflux in non‑protic solvents such as carbon disulfide, dichloromethane, or nitrobenzene, with AlCl₃ as Lewis acid catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization of sodium thiophosphate with hydrochloric acid, producing sodium chloride and thiophosphoric acid; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring, no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis/acid‑base reaction where nitric acid protonates potassium periodate, yielding potassium nitrate and metaperiodic acid (HIO4); typically carried out in water at mild temperature, no special catalyst.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of 2,5‑dichloronitrobenzene to 2,5‑dichloroaniline; key transformation is NO2 → NH2 while preserving chloro substituents; conducted under inert atmosphere in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether), usually at 0‑80 °C, followed by careful aqueous quench.

Thermal or acid‑catalyzed retro‑aldol decomposition of diacetone alcohol to give two molecules of acetone; induced by heating (≈150‑200 °C) or by adding a small amount of mineral acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (NaOH) in aqueous medium.

Nucleophilic substitution (metal‑halogen exchange) of tin tetraiodide with methyl lithium to form tetramethyltin and lithium iodide; performed at low temperature (−78 °C) in anhydrous THF under nitrogen or argon, LiI precipitates as by‑product.
double displacement reaction; purpose: produce copper(II) oxalate precipitate; transformation: oxalate and acetate ion exchange; aqueous solution at ambient conditions; no catalyst

Acid‑base neutralization of picric acid with potassium hydroxide to afford potassium picrate and water; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, may require cooling due to exotherm, no catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (halide to nitrite) used to prepare alkyl nitrites; silver nitrite provides NO2⁻ which replaces the chloride, precipitating AgCl. Conducted in dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or ether) under reflux or gentle heating, inert atmosphere optional, no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a C–Cl bond; Pd/C under hydrogen reduces 1,1,1‑trichloroethane to 1,1‑dichloroethane while generating HCl. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–80 °C, often neat substrate or in a solvent such as ethanol; palladium on carbon serves as the catalyst.

Hydrolysis of organosilane; Si–OCH₃ bond cleaved to form a silanol (methylsilanol) and methanol; water attacks the silicon center, often acid- or base‑catalyzed; typically performed at ambient temperature in aqueous or mixed aqueous/alcoholic solvent; catalyst may be a dilute acid or base.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (amination) of 2‑chlorobiphenyl with ammonia to give 2‑aminobiphenyl; typically performed with excess NH₃ (gas or aqueous) at high temperature (200‑300 °C) or under Cu‑ or Pd‑catalyzed conditions in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF, ethanol). By‑product HCl is neutralized or removed.

Hydrolysis/acid‑base dissociation of ammonium dihydrogen phosphate in water; the salt ionizes to give phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) and free ammonia (NH₃); occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature without added catalyst.

Reductive conversion of nitrobenzene to phenylhydrazine hydrochloride (Béchamp‑type reduction); Zn dust in acidic medium (HCl with NH₄Cl) reduces the nitro group to –NHNH₂, which is isolated as its HCl salt. Carried out in aqueous HCl/ethanol, reflux 60–80 °C; Zn acts as the reducing agent, NH₄Cl buffers the solution.

Epoxidation of pent‑2‑ene using peracetic acid (Prilezhaev reaction); forms 2,3‑epoxypentane with acetic acid as by‑product; typically conducted in dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C, peracetic acid generated in situ from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide; no metal catalyst required; CH₂Cl₂ is the common solvent.

Halogen exchange redox reaction; iodide ion reduces the bromine cation of pyridinium tribromide to bromide, being oxidized to elemental iodine, while pyridinium bromide and potassium bromide are formed. Usually performed at room temperature in a polar solvent such as acetonitrile or water; no external catalyst needed.

Acid chloride synthesis employing oxalyl chloride. Purpose: convert 2‑methylbenzoic acid into its acid chloride. Key transformation: COOH → COCl with release of CO, CO₂, and HCl gases. Typical conditions: oxalyl chloride added to the acid in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C followed by stirring at room temperature; a trace of DMF may be used to initiate the reaction; inert atmosphere and efficient removal of gaseous by‑products are advisable.

Solid‑state double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction; carbonate exchanges with hydroxide, precipitating calcium carbonate and forming soluble rubidium hydroxide. Typically carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of Rb₂CO₃ and Ca(OH)₂, heating to 50–80 °C to promote CaCO₃ precipitation; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base (hydrolysis) reaction; the basic oxide La₂O₃ reacts with water to form the hydroxide La(OH)₃. Usually performed by stirring La₂O₃ in deionized water at room temperature or with gentle heating; aqueous medium, no catalyst required; the precipitated hydroxide is filtered and washed.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amidation; used to convert a carboxylic acid into a Weinreb amide. The dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates benzoic acid, which then reacts with methoxyamine to give N‑methoxybenzamide while dicyclohexylurea precipitates. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane under nitrogen, stoichiometric DCC, no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic addition of HCl (hydrohalogenation); purpose is to install a chlorine atom onto the norbornene double bond, yielding mainly 2‑chloronorbornane (Markovnikov product). The reaction proceeds by protonation of the alkene followed by nucleophilic attack of chloride. Usually performed by bubbling HCl gas or using aqueous HCl in an inert solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; Lewis acids (e.g., ZnCl₂) can be added to accelerate the reaction.

Acid‑base deprotonation / salt formation; sodium hydride abstracts the acidic proton of the carboxyl group of glycine, generating sodium glycinate and releasing hydrogen gas. Usually carried out in a dry aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF under nitrogen at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Strong reduction of a carboxylic acid anhydride: lithium aluminum hydride reduces propionic anhydride to the corresponding primary alcohol, 1‑propanol (both acyl units are reduced, giving two equivalents of propanol). Conducted in an aprotic ether such as dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen, with careful quenching of excess LiAlH₄.

LiAlH₄ reduction of a sulfoxide to a sulfide; lithium aluminium hydride reduces the sulfoxide function of omeprazole to give omeprazole sulfide. Conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether) or THF, often at reflux or 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; excess LiAlH₄ is quenched carefully with water or dilute acid.
Salt‑metathesis ligand exchange: TaCl₅ + LiNMe₂ → Ta(NMe₂)₅ + LiCl; carried out in anhydrous ether or THF at 0 °C to rt under N₂/Ar; no catalyst, LiCl precipitates.

Halogen‑lithium exchange (organolithium) metalation; n‑butyllithium exchanges bromine atoms for lithium on 1,2‑dibromobenzene, producing 1,2‑dilithiobenzene (and n‑butyl bromide). Performed at –78 °C in dry THF under nitrogen; the dilithiated intermediate is typically trapped immediately with an electrophile.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction; purpose is synthesis of nitriles. Chlorine atom in 1-chloropropane is replaced by cyanide ion (CN⁻). Typically requires polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMSO, DMF) to solubilize sodium cyanide and facilitate reaction. Reaction conditions often involve heating to enhance reactivity.

Acid‑base neutralization; sulfuric acid protonates ammonium hydroxide, forming ammonium sulfate and water. Reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of methanol to formaldehyde using copper(II) oxide. Methanol is passed over heated CuO (≈400–500 °C); the copper oxide abstracts hydrogen from methanol, being reduced to metallic Cu while methanol is oxidized to formaldehyde and water. The reaction is gas‑phase catalyst‑driven, and typically performed in a flow reactor under inert carrier gas.

Salt formation from metal oxide and acid anhydride; trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride reacts with copper(II) oxide, transferring triflate groups to copper to give copper(II) triflate and water. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; the copper(II) triflate is isolated as a solid.

Acid‑base (salt‑metathesis) reaction; proton transfer from nitric acid to ammonium nitrite forms ammonium nitrate and nitrous acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to avoid decomposition of HNO₂; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic addition of dimethyl phosphite (P–H) to trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral), a Pudovik‑type phosphite addition, giving the α‑hydroxy phosphonate trichlorfon. Typically run in anhydrous solvent such as THF or CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to room temperature, using a mild base catalyst (triethylamine or pyridine) to deprotonate the phosphite; no metal catalyst is needed.

Straightforward acid‑base neutralization; acetic acid reacts with rubidium hydroxide to afford rubidium acetate and water. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring until complete dissolution; no additional reagents or solvents beyond water.

Strong reduction of an ester to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride (LAH). Methyl heptadecanoate is treated with LAH (1–2 equiv) in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; the reaction is quenched carefully with water followed by dilute acid to give 1‑heptadecanol. No extra catalyst; inert atmosphere (N₂) is common.

Catalytic hydrogenation of the pyridine ring to a saturated piperidine ring while retaining the 4‑benzyl substituent, yielding 4‑benzylpiperidine. Performed under H₂ pressure (50–100 atm) with a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a protic solvent (ethanol or methanol) at 25–80 °C for several hours; work‑up involves filtration of the catalyst and solvent removal.

Strong reduction with lithium aluminium hydride (ester → primary alcohol); purpose: convert methyl phenylacetate to phenethyl alcohol; key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, reducing the ester first to an aldehyde then to the primary alcohol; the methoxy group is liberated as methanol upon aqueous work‑up; typical conditions: dry THF or diethyl ether, 0 °C to reflux under N₂, 2 equiv LiAlH₄, quench with aqueous NaOH or water at 0 °C; no catalyst required.

Leuckart‑Wallach reductive amination (transfer hydrogenation); converts vanillin to vanillylamine using ammonium formate as both nitrogen source and hydrogen donor. The mixture is heated to 140–180 °C in a sealed tube or high‑boiling solvent (often methanol or formic acid) where formate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂, reducing the in‑situ‑formed imine to the amine and generating water as a by‑product.

N‑methylation via SN2 substitution – 4‑aminophenol acts as a nucleophile, deprotonated by NaOH, and attacks the methyl group of methyl p‑toluenesulfonate (methyl tosylate). The reaction replaces the tosylate leaving group with an N‑methyl group, producing N‑methyl‑4‑aminophenol and sodium p‑toluenesulfonate. Typically carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., water/acetone) at 0 °C to ambient temperature under basic conditions; no special catalyst is required.

Organolithium alkylation (SN2) of bromomethane with methyllithium; methyl lithium attacks CH3Br to form ethane and lithium bromide. Performed at low temperature (‑78 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere to prevent protonation of the organolithium reagent.

Halide exchange metathesis between chromium(II) chloride and ammonium fluoride; fluoride replaces chloride to give chromium(II) fluoride and ammonium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at room temperature or with gentle heating; excess NH4F drives the reaction to completion.

Electrophilic addition of bromine to propene; anti‑addition yields racemic 1,2‑dibromopropane (CH3‑CHBr‑CH2Br). Mechanism identical to that for ethylene, involving a bromonium ion intermediate. Conducted at 0 °C–room temperature in CCl4, CH2Cl2, or CHCl3, with 1 equiv Br2 added slowly in the dark or under low‑light conditions to avoid side reactions.

Double‑displacement precipitation of silver azide with potassium chloride; silver ion exchanges with potassium, precipitating insoluble AgCl while forming soluble potassium azide. Carried out in water at ambient temperature; AgCl is removed by filtration.

Sandmeyer bromination: the 4‑nitrobenzenediazonium chloride is treated with copper(I) bromide (CuBr) under similar low‑temperature aqueous acidic conditions to give 4‑bromonitrobenzene and nitrogen gas; another Sandmeyer halogenation where CuBr acts as the halide source and catalyst; typical solvent is aqueous HCl, temperature 0‑25 °C.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of antimony and selenium to form antimony(III) selenide (Sb₂Se₃). Purpose is preparation of the semiconductor chalcogenide. Key transformation: 2 Sb + 3 Se → Sb₂Se₃. Typical conditions: sealed tube or inert‑gas furnace, heating at 400–600 °C for several hours. No solvent or catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation of iron(III) hydroxide and calcium sulfate; calcium hydroxide provides OH⁻ to precipitate Fe(OH)3, while sulfate from iron(III) sulfate reacts with calcium to form sparingly soluble CaSO4. Conducted in aqueous solution with stirring at room temperature; solids are filtered off.

Redox oxidation; purpose is to oxidize Cr(III) to Cr(VI) producing chromium(VI) oxide (CrO3). Key transformation: Cr2O3 is oxidized while H2O2 is reduced to water in acidic medium. Typical conditions: aqueous hydrogen peroxide (30 %); concentrated H2SO4; temperature 0 °C to reflux; reaction performed under stirring. No special catalyst beyond the Cr(III) oxide itself; water is the only solvent.

Acetylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol; purpose is to protect or derivatize citronellol as its acetate ester. Key transformation: the hydroxyl group of citronellol attacks acetic anhydride, forming citronellyl acetate and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; often catalyzed by a base such as pyridine, DMAP, or a tertiary amine. Common solvents: dichloromethane, chloroform, or neat acetic anhydride. Reaction proceeds within 1–2 h.

Oxidation (combustion) of a metal sulfide; converts Sn(II) in SnS to Sn(IV) oxide and oxidizes sulfide to SO₂; carried out by heating the solid mixture in air or oxygen at 400‑600 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of ferrous carbonate; when heated to 350–500 °C in a furnace, the carbonate breaks down to iron(II) oxide (FeO) and carbon dioxide. Usually performed in an inert or reducing atmosphere to prevent oxidation; no solvent or catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (solid‑state oxidation‑reduction) of silver tellurite; purpose is to generate tellurium dioxide and silver oxide. Key transformation: Ag2TeO3 (or AgTeO3) breaks down upon heating, yielding TeO2 (solid) and Ag2O (solid). Typical conditions: heating the solid to 300–500 °C in a furnace or muffle oven under air or inert atmosphere. No solvent; reaction is performed in a crucible.

Acetylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol; purpose is to convert 3‑pentanol into its acetate ester for protection or fragrance synthesis. Key transformation: 3‑pentanol attacks acetic anhydride, forming 3‑pentyl acetate and one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature; catalytic base (pyridine, DMAP) often employed. Solvent options include dichloromethane, toluene, or the reaction can be run neat with excess acetic anhydride. Reaction time 30 min–2 h.

Sulfurization of an isocyanate to an isothiocyanate; purpose is to replace the carbonyl oxygen with sulfur, producing methyl isothiocyanate, a valuable intermediate in agrochemical synthesis. Key transformation: methyl isocyanate reacts with elemental sulfur, inserting S to give the N=C=S functional group. Typical conditions: refluxing sulfur (or sulfur dissolved in carbon disulfide, CS2) with methyl isocyanate; temperature 80–120 °C; inert atmosphere (N2). Solvent: carbon disulfide, toluene, or neat sulfur melt. Reaction proceeds 1–4 h.

Epoxide ring‑opening N‑alkylation of guanine – Sodium hydroxide deprotonates guanine, generating a nucleophilic nitrogen that attacks ethylene oxide. Ring opening installs a 2‑hydroxyethyl side chain at the N9 position, yielding acyclovir (9‑(2hydroxyethoxy)guanine). Conducted in aqueous NaOH at low temperature (0‑5 °C) followed by neutralization; no catalyst is required.

Oxidation of a secondary benzylic alcohol with Jones reagent (CrO3 in acetone); purpose is to convert the alcohol to the corresponding ketone. Key transformation: oxidation of 1‑(4‑methylphenyl)ethanol to 4‑methylacetophenone (4‑methylphenylacetone), reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III). Typical conditions: Jones reagent (prepared from CrO3 and H2SO4) added to a solution of the alcohol in acetone at 0 °C to rt; reaction quenched with isopropanol or methanol after completion.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) reaction; converts oxalyl dichloride to oxalyl difluoride, a useful fluorinating reagent. Key transformation: replacement of two Cl atoms by F atoms using ammonium hydrogen fluoride (NH4HF2). Typically performed under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to room temperature in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; the generated HCl is scavenged by the ammonium salt. No metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) on silicon; generates trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN), a versatile cyanide source. Cyanide ion from tetrabutylammonium cyanide displaces chloride on trimethylsilyl chloride. Reaction is usually carried out in dry acetonitrile or THF at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often under nitrogen. No additional catalyst needed; the tetrabutylammonium chloride by‑product precipitates.

Reductive hydrogenation; cadmium oxide is reduced by hydrogen gas to metallic cadmium and water; requires high temperature (≈500‑700 °C) in a flow of H₂, usually in a tubular furnace; solid‑gas reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Williamson ether/ester synthesis (alkylation of a carboxylate); forms butyl benzoate from potassium benzoate and n‑butyl chloride. The benzoate anion performs an S_N2 attack on the primary alkyl halide, displacing chloride. Conducted in refluxing acetone (or DMF) with the potassium salt in suspension; the insoluble potassium chloride precipitates, driving the reaction forward. No catalyst required.

Condensation of ammonia with cyanuric acid – Ammonia substitutes for one –OH of cyanuric acid (1,3,5‑triazine‑2,4,6‑triol), forming ammelide (6‑amino‑1,3,5‑triazine‑2,4‑diol) and releasing. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution, often under reflux (~100 °C) with excess NH₃; no additional catalyst is needed.

Metal‑catalyzed carbene insertion (C–H functionalization); ethyl diazoacetate thermally or photochemically loses N₂ to generate a metal‑carbene (commonly Rh(II) or Cu(I)) which inserts into a cyclohexane C–H bond, yielding ethyl 2‑cyclohexylacetate. Typical conditions: catalytic Rh₂(OAc)₄ (1–2 mol %) in dichloromethane or toluene at room temperature under nitrogen; nitrogen gas is released as the only by‑product.

Radical dimerization; two trifluoromethyl radicals couple to form perfluoroethane (C₂F₆).
