Typically performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to reflux, using 1–2 equiv LAH, followed by careful aqueous work‑up.

Direct fluorination; gas‑phase halogenation of cyanogen (CN)2 with F2 to afford cyanogen fluoride (FCN); purpose is to synthesize the monofluoro nitrile; key transformation is cleavage of the N≡C–C≡N bond and addition of fluorine to each carbon; typically carried out in a stainless‑steel flow reactor at low temperature (0–25 °C) under dry inert atmosphere; no solvent, fluorine gas as reagent, nickel or Monel alloy reactor walls.

0 Acid–base/complexation reaction; preparation of the square‑planar Pt(II) complex potassium tetrachloroplatinate(II). Platinum(II) oxide is dissolved in aqueous hydrochloric acid in the presence of excess potassium chloride; heating promotes dissolution and complex formation, yielding K2[PtCl4] and water. Typical conditions: reflux in water/HCl, no additional catalyst, inert atmosphere optional.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive conversion) of phenoxyacetaldehyde to phenoxyethanol; purpose is to obtain the primary alcohol from the aldehyde; key transformation is addition of two hydrogen atoms to the carbonyl to form an –CH2OH group; typical conditions: H2 gas (1–5 atm) over 5 % Pd/C or Raney Ni in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C; reaction conducted under inert atmosphere.

Hydrolysis of formyl cyanide (HCOCN) to formic acid and hydrogen cyanide; type is aqueous acid‑catalyzed (or base‑catalyzed) acyl‑cyanide hydrolysis; purpose is cleavage of the C≡N bond to release HCN; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon followed by proton transfers; usually carried out in water with a dilute acid (e.g., 0.1 M HCl) at 40–80 °C; aqueous medium, no special catalyst needed but acid accelerates the reaction.

Nucleophilic substitutionamination) of phenylphosphorus dichloride (C6H5PCl2) with ammonia to give phenylphosphorodiamidate (C6H5P(NH2)2) and HCl; purpose is preparation of a phosphorodiamidate ligand; key steps are replacement of the two P–Cl bonds by P–NH2 groups; reaction is typically performed in anhydrous ether or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, using excess gaseous or aqueous NH3; HCl generated is removed by gas‑flow or trapped in a base.

Double‑replacement precipitation (metathesis) of oxalic acid with cadmium nitrate to afford insoluble cadmium oxalate precipitate and nitric acid in solution; purpose is isolation of cadmium oxalate; key transformation is exchange of the Cd²⁺ cation with H⁺, forming CdC2O4·2H2O solid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring until precipitation is complete; water is the solvent, no catalyst required; the filtrate contains diluted HNO3.

Acid‑base reaction (metal‑alcohol deprotonation). Sodium metal reduces 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol to its sodium alkoxide, releasing H₂ gas. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, often at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration. Concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ nitrates anthranilic acid preferentially at the 5‑position to give 5‑nitroanthranilic acid, with water as the by‑product. Reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C initially, then warmed to 50–80 °C; mixed acid serves as both nitrating agent and solvent.

Acid‑base neutralisation. Oxalic acid reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide to afford ammonium oxalate and water. The process is performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with stoichiometric amounts and gentle stirring.

Ester aminolysis (transamidation). Aniline attacks methyl acetoacetate, displacing methanol and forming acetoacetanilide (a β‑keto‑amide). The reaction is usually refluxed in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or xylenes, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid or base to accelerate methanol removal.

Reduction of a cyclic disulfide; sodium borohydride selectively reduces the disulfide bond of lipoic acid to give the dithiol dihydrolipoic acid; by‑product is sodium metaborate. Typical conditions: NaBH4 (1–2 equiv) in methanol or aqueous ethanol at 0 °C to rt, mild stirring.

Alcoholysis of a metal halide (alkoxide formation). Titanium tetrachloride reacts with four equivalents of 1‑butanol to give titanium tetrabutoxide and four equivalents of HCl gas. Performed anhydrously in a dry non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen, with the liberated HCl removed or trapped.

Type: Lewis acid‑base adduct formation (gas‑phase addition). Purpose: synthesis of ammonia borane, a solid hydrogen‑storage material. Key transformation: diborane (B2H6) reacts with ammonia (NH3) to give the adduct NH3·BH3 (ammonia borane). Typical conditions: excess gaseous NH3 passed over B2H6 at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert solvent such as dry THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); aqueous NaOH cleaves cyclopropyl benzoate to give cyclopropanol and sodium benzoate; usually conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol) under reflux; no special catalyst required.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation of a diene. Purpose: saturation of 1,3‑pentadiene to the corresponding alkane (pentane). Key transformation: addition of H2 across both C=C bonds of 1,3‑pentadiene to yield pentane. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, 5–10 % Pd/C, PtO2 or Raney Ni as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–80 °C, inert atmosphere optional.

Type: Salt metathesis (double displacement) in aqueous medium. Purpose: preparation of aluminum formate, often as a precursor for materials or coordination complexes. Key transformation: exchange of Br⁻ from AlBr3 with formate anion from potassium formate to give Al(HCOO)3 and KBr. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient temperature or mild heating (≤50 °C); insoluble Al(HCOO)3 precipitates, filtrated and washed; no special catalyst required.

This is a gas‑solid/solution precipitation (acid‑base) reaction in which calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) reacts with carbon dioxide to precipitate calcium carbonate and water. The key step is neutralization of CO₂ by the hydroxide, forming the insoluble carbonate. It is carried out by bubbling CO₂ through an aqueous suspension of Ca(OH)₂ at ambient temperature (20–30 °C) or slightly elevated temperature to improve kinetics. The reaction proceeds in water; no additional solvents or catalysts are required.

Type: Base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination). Purpose: conversion of 1,1,1‑trichloroethane to the alkene 1,1‑dichloroethene. Key transformation: NaOH abstracts a proton and eliminates a chloride ion, forming water, NaCl, and the C=C product. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux temperature (≈80‑100 °C) for 1–2 h, often in ethanol/water mixture; no additional catalyst needed.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of alcohols with phosphorus tribromide. Purpose: synthesis of primary alkyl bromides (1‑nonyl bromide) from the corresponding primary alcohols. Key transformation: PBr3 converts the –OH group of 1‑nonanol to –Br, generating phosphorous acid (H3PO3) as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry diethyl ether or THF, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, addition of PBr3 dropwise under nitrogen; reaction proceeds in 1–2 h.

Type: N‑alkylation (SN2) of a heterocycle using a methyl halide. Purpose: preparation of 1‑methyl‑beta‑carboline, a methylated indole‑derived heterocycle. Key transformation: the nitrogen of beta‑carboline attacks methyl iodide, displacing I⁻; triethylamine scavenges the generated HI, forming triethylammonium iodide. Typical conditions: aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, 1–4 equiv of Et3N, reaction time 2–12 h.

Thermal decomposition of monoethanolamine formate; heating the formate salt causes decarboxylation and reduction, releasing carbon dioxide, regenerating free monoethanolamine and producing hydrogen gas. Typical conditions are dry heating at 150‑200 °C under an inert atmosphere; no catalyst is required and common solvents are avoided.

Reaction type: electrophilic addition (halogenation of alkene). Purpose: add bromine across the double bond. Key transformation: 1‑pentene adds Br₂ across the C=C to afford 1,2‑dibromopentane via a bromonium‑ion intermediate. Typical conditions: room temperature, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or CH₂Cl₂, performed in dark or amber glass to avoid radical side reactions.

Wurtz coupling (aryl‑aryl coupling) of chlorobenzene using metallic sodium. Dry, aprotic ether (e.g., dry diethyl ether or THF) is used under anhydrous conditions; sodium metal is added and the mixture is refluxed, effecting radical‑mediated coupling to give biphenyl and sodium chloride as by‑product. Reaction requires excess sodium and exclusion of moisture.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of fluorene using acetyl nitrate (AcONO₂) as the nitrating agent; the nitronium equivalent attacks the 2‑position of fluorene, producing 2‑nitrofluorene while acetic acid is liberated. The reaction is performed at 0‑5 °C in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or glacial acetic acid, and the mixture is quenched with water after completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl chloride with nitrite ion provided by tetrabutylammonium nitrite; the nitrite displaces chloride to give benzyl nitrite, while tetrabutylammonium chloride is formed. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or DMF) and may be aided by phase‑transfer conditions; no additional catalyst is required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation between sodium oxalate and silver acetate; the exchange of cations yields insoluble silver oxalate as a precipitate and sodium acetate remains in solution. The reaction is carried out in aqueous medium (or aqueous‑ethanol) at room temperature with stirring; the solid silver oxalate is filtered and washed.

Hydrolysis of a metal peroxide; strontium peroxide reacts with water to produce soluble strontium hydroxide and hydrogen peroxide; performed in aqueous solution, mild heating may be used; no catalyst.

Chlorination of a phosphoric ester with thionyl chloride; the hydroxyl group of O,O‑diethyl hydrogen phosphate is replaced by chlorine to give O,O‑diethyl chlorophosphate, with evolution of SO₂ and HCl; performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine, often with pyridine as a base, under reflux and inert atmosphere.

Hydrolysis of a tertiary amide; purpose is to convert N,N‑dimethylhexanamide into the corresponding carboxylic acid and release dimethylamine. Key transformation: cleavage of the C(=O)‑NMe2 bond with water, forming hexanoic acid and dimethylamine (which is protonated under acidic work‑up). Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 1–6 M HCl) or aqueous base (NaOH) for several hours, followed by acidification if basic conditions were used. Common solvent: water or aqueous ethanol; catalyst: mineral acid or alkali.

Jones oxidation (chromic acid oxidation) of an aldehyde; purpose is oxidation of 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde to 4‑methoxybenzoic acid; key transformation is oxidation of the aldehyde carbonyl to a carboxylic acid using the CrO3/H2SO4 reagent; performed in acetone at 0 °C initially, then allowed to warm to room temperature; reaction is quenched with a small amount of isopropanol or methanol; no extra catalyst beyond the chromic acid reagent.

Carbamate (Boc) protection of terbutaline using tert‑butyl chloroformate in the presence of pyridine; pyridine acts as a base and nucleophilic catalyst, capturing the generated HCl to form pyridinium chloride while the tert‑butoxycarbonyl group is transferred to the amine of terbutaline, giving the prodrug bambuterol. Typical conditions are 0 °C to rt in dry pyridine (or pyridine/CH₂Cl₂ mixture), with the reaction monitored until completion and then worked up by aqueous extraction.

General type: Acid-base reaction. Purpose: Production of indium phosphate and water. Key transformation: Protonation of hydroxide ions by phosphoric acid, forming water, while indium cations react with phosphate anions. Conditions: Typically room temperature, aqueous solution. No specific catalyst required.

General type: Redox reaction. Purpose: Synthesis of hydrogen bromide and lithium bromide. Key transformation: Oxidation of lithium hydride (hydrogen loss) and reduction of bromine (electron gain). Conditions: Likely conducted with dry reagents at elevated temperatures. Common solvent: Inert atmosphere (no explicit solvent noted).

General type: Double displacement (precipitation) reaction. Purpose: Formation of insoluble cadmium hydroxide. Key transformation: Exchange of cations between potassium hydroxide and cadmium sulfate, yielding potassium sulfate and cadmium hydroxide. Conditions: Aqueous solution at room temperature. Common solvent: Water.

Oxidative chlorination/disproportionation in alkaline medium to generate perchlorate. A mixture of sodium hydroxide and sodium chlorate is treated with chlorine gas (often bubbled through the solution) at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C). Chlorine oxidizes chlorate to perchlorate while being reduced to chloride, producing water, NaCl and NaClO4. Common solvent: aqueous solution; reaction performed under stirring and controlled addition of Cl2.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between two soluble salts. Aqueous solutions of NaCN and CaCl2 are mixed at ambient temperature; calcium cyanide precipitates (or remains soluble depending on concentration) while sodium chloride stays in solution. No catalyst required; reaction proceeds readily under standard laboratory conditions.

General type: Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction). Purpose: Conversion of nitrile to amine. Key transformation: Selective hydrogenation of the cyano group in ethyl cyanoacetate to form an amino group. Conditions: Hydrogen gas under mild pressure, Raney nickel catalyst. Common solvent: Ethanol (common aliphatic ester-compatible solvent).

Alkylation (N‑methylation) of ethylenediamine with dimethyl sulfate; purpose is to introduce a methyl group on each nitrogen to give N,N′‑dimethylethylenediamine. Key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the amine nitrogen on the methyl sulfonate, generating methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile, often with an inorganic base (e.g., Na₂CO₃ or K₂CO₃) to neutralize the acid formed.

Oxidative roasting (combustion) of iron(II) sulfide with oxygen; purpose is to convert sulfide to sulfur dioxide while oxidizing iron to the oxide Fe₂O₃. Key transformation is simultaneous oxidation of S²⁻ to SO₂ and Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺. Conducted at high temperature (400–800 °C) in an air or O₂ stream; no solvent is used. The solid mixture is heated in a furnace under an oxygen‑rich atmosphere.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride (Markovnikov addition) – HCl adds across the double bond of 1‑methylcyclohexene to give 1‑chloro‑1‑methylcyclohexane; reaction proceeds in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄ at 0 °C to rt; the proton adds to the less substituted carbon, generating the more stable carbocation intermediate that captures chloride.

Metathesis/precipitation; copper(II) sulfate reacts with rubidium azide to give copper(II) azide precipitate and rubidium sulfate; key transformation: 2 RbN3 + CuSO4 → Cu(N3)2↓ + Rb2SO4; performed in aqueous medium, often at 0–5 °C with careful stirring; copper(II) azide is explosive, so reaction is done behind a blast shield.

Redox/metathesis reaction; analogous to (0) but using copper(II) acetate; Cu(OAc)2 in aqueous solution reacts with KI, precipitating CuI, forming I2 and potassium acetate; performed at ambient temperature in water; no additional reagents or catalyst needed.
Redox reaction; bromine oxidizes selenide to elemental selenium; bromide produced as byproduct; aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkene using aqueous potassium permanganate; purpose is to convert the propenyl side chain of 2,4,5‑trimethoxy‑1‑propenylbenzene into a carboxylic acid, yielding 2,4,5‑trimethoxybenzoic acid. The key step is KMnO₄‑mediated addition of oxygen across the C=C bond followed by oxidative fragmentation to the acid. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or KOH), temperature 50–80 °C, with excess KMnO₄; reaction is quenched with acid work‑up. Water is the solvent.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkene (Lemieux–Johnson oxidation). (E)-oct‑2‑ene is first dihydroxylated by catalytic OsO₄, then the vicinal diol is cleaved by stoichiometric NaIO₄ to give acetaldehyde and hexanal. Reaction is performed in a biphasic mixture such as t‑BuOH/H₂O or acetone/H₂O, at 0 – 25 °C; OsO₄ (0.1–1 mol %) acts as catalyst, NaIO₄ as oxidant.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction forming thulium(III) oxalate; thulium(III) nitrate solution is mixed with oxalic acid, insoluble Th₂(C₂O₄)₃ precipitates and nitric acid remains in solution; performed in water at ambient temperature or mild heating, stirring, no catalyst.

Oxidation of a thiol to a disulfide using hydrogen peroxide; purpose is to couple two ethanethiol molecules into diethyl disulfide. The key transformation is peroxide‑mediated oxidation of the sulfhydryl groups, forming an S–S bond and generating water. Usually performed at 0–25 °C in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane, THF, or ethanol, often with a mild base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to buffer the solution and minimize over‑oxidation.

Iodination of praseodymium arsenide; solid‑state halogen exchange where iodine oxidizes PrAs to praseodymium(III) iodide and arsenic triiodide. Conducted by heating the mixture under iodine vapor (≈300°C); inert atmosphere may be used, no solvent needed.

Conversion of a primary amine to an isothiocyanate using thiophosgene; purpose is synthesis of ethyl isothiocyanate. The key transformation involves nucleophilic attack of ethylamine on thiophosgene, displacing chloride and forming the N=C=S functionality while releasing two equivalents of HCl. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, typically in the presence of a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 4‑iodophenol with 4‑nitrophenylboronic acid; purpose is formation of the biaryl 4‑(4‑nitrophenyl)phenol. Key transformation is palladium‑catalyzed to mediate transmetallation and reductive elimination, coupling the aryl iodide and aryl boronate. Standard conditions employ Pd(OAc)₂ (0.5–5 mol %), triphenylphosphine as ligand, K₂CO₃ as base, and a mixed solvent system (e.g., toluene/water, dioxane/water, or DMF/water) at 80–100 °C under nitrogen or argon. By‑products are water, KI, and Pd⁰ (the latter regenerated in the catalytic cycle).

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂). Purpose: generate the reactive 3,4‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride for subsequent acylation or coupling reactions. Key transformation: replacement of the –OH of the carboxyl group by Cl, with loss of SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: 1.2–2 equiv SOCl₂, dry dichloromethane (or chlorobenzene) as solvent, 0 °C to rt; a catalytic amount of DMF (0.1 equiv) or pyridine can be added to accelerate formation of the Vilsmeier intermediate. Reaction is usually refluxed for 30 min to 1 h; excess SOCl₂ is removed under reduced pressure.

Reductive oxidation of carbon dioxide by a highly electropositive alkali metal. Metallic caesium reacts vigorously with CO2 (typically at elevated temperature, 200–400 °C) under an inert atmosphere, reducing CO2 to CO and forming caesium oxide (Cs2O). The reaction is conducted in a sealed tube or flow reactor to manage the exothermicity and avoid ignition; no solvent or catalyst is used.
Metal hydride reduction of bromine; NaH serves as a reducing agent, yielding hydrogen gas and sodium bromide; typically performed in dry ether or THF at 0 °C rt under inert atmosphere.

Acylation reaction where ethane-1,2-diamine reacts with acetic anhydride to form N-(2-aminoethyl)acetamide and acetic acid. Key transformation involves converting one amine group to an amide. Common conditions include mild heating in a solvent like THF or pyridine, which can also act as a catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis: sodium propoxide attacks ethyl bromide to give propyl ethyl ether (1‑ethoxypropane). Key transformation: an SN2 displacement of Br⁻ by the propoxide ion, forming an ether and NaBr. Usually performed in dry ethanol or THF under reflux with stoichiometric NaOPr, under anhydrous conditions to avoid protonation of the alkoxide.

Transfer hydrogenation of quinoline to tetrahydroquinoline using ammonium formate as a hydrogen donor over Pd/C; reduces the aromatic heterocycle by four electrons; usually run in EtOH or MeOH at 80–100 °C in a sealed tube.

Acid‑catalyzed ether formation (SN1) between tert‑butyl alcohol and tert‑butyl chloride producing di‑tert‑butyl ether and HCl; common conditions use concentrated H₂SO₄ or HCl catalyst, heated to 70–90 °C, solvent often absent or a non‑polar solvent such as toluene.

Oxidation (combustion) of ammonia; used for nitrogen removal or N2 production in emission control. Key transformation: NH3 is oxidized to N2 while water is formed. Typically carried out in the gas phase at high temperature (600–900 °C) over metal catalysts such as platinum, copper or nickel; no solvent required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction between sodium carbonate and calcium lactate, driven by the precipitation of calcium carbonate as an insoluble solid. Occurs in aqueous solution, with no catalyst required. Purpose includes calcium carbonate isolation from lactate salts.

Oxidation of a vicinal diol to a quinone using periodate; sodium periodate oxidatively converts the 1,2‑dihydroxynaphthalene (a catechol‑type system) into 1,2‑naphthoquinone. Typical conditions: aqueous NaIO₄ (often 0.1–0.2 M) in a water/acetone or water/t‑butanol mixture, 0 °C to room temperature, 1–2 h reaction time. No catalyst required; work‑up by extraction and purification of the quinone.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis of a sulfonyl chloride to the corresponding sulfonate salt; benzenesulfon chloride reacts with aqueous NaOH to give sodium benzenesulfonate, NaCl and water. Conducted in aqueous solution (often 1–2 M NaOH) at 0 °C to reflux for 0.5–2 h. The reaction is a nucleophilic substitution (S_N2 at sulfur) and proceeds without additional reagents; the product is isolated by acidification or ion‑exchange.

N‑Oxidation of pyridine with aacid; peroxytrifluoroacetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to pyridine, affording pyridine N‑oxide and trifluoroacetic acid as by‑product. Peracid is added dropwise to a solution of pyridine (1 M) in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt; the mixture is stirred 1–3 h. The reaction is an electrophilic oxidation; work‑up involves aqueous wash to remove TFA and extraction of the N‑.

Epoxidation of an allylic alcohol (Prilezhaev reaction) using peracetic acid; the alkene of allyl alcohol is converted to the epoxide glycidol while peracetic acid is reduced to acetic acid. Typical procedure: generate peracetic acid in situ (acetic acid/H₂O₂) or add commercial peracetic acid to a solution of allyl alcohol in dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, 1–4 h. The reaction is an oxygen‑transfer oxidation; the crude mixture is washed to remove excess acetic acid and the epoxide is purified by distillation or chromatography.

Catalytic hydrogenation of fluorobenzene to fluorocyclohexane; the aromatic ring is fully reduced while the fluorine substituent is retained. Performed under high pressure H₂ (30–50 atm) with a metal catalyst such as/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, at 50–100 °C for several hours. The reaction is a heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenation; after completion the catalyst is filtered and the product is isolated by distillation or extraction.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling of phenylboronic acid with 2‑chloro‑1H‑imidazole to give 2‑phenyl‑1H‑imidazole; base K₂CO₃ and a Pd complex (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄) in a water/ethanol or dioxane mixture at 80–100 °C; KCl is the inorganic by‑product.

Decarboxylation; used to remove the carboxyl group from 3‑hydroxybenzoic acid, producing phenol and CO₂; key transformation is loss of CO₂ from the aromatic ring; typically performed by heating the acid alone or with copper oxide/copper powder at 300‑400 °C (solid‑phase, no solvent) or in the presence of sodium hydroxide in a high‑boiling solvent.

Base‑catalyzed carbonate formation (transesterification of CO2 with methanol). Purpose: preparation of sodium methyl carbonate, a useful organic carbonate. Key transformation: CO₂ + CH₃OH + NaOH → NaOCO₂CH₃ + H₂O. Typical conditions: methanol solvent, NaOH as base, temperature 0–80 °C, CO₂ pressure 1–30 bar. No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition of a Grignard reagent to an acyl anhydride; the ethyl–MgBr adds to one carbonyl, giving a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give acetic acid and 2‑butanone while forming MgBr2. Performed under anhydrous ether (e.g., THF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; no external catalyst besides the Grignard reagent.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts acylation) coupled with intramolecular lactonization to afford the xanthene dye fluorescein. Aluminum chloride acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst, typically in a non‑protic solvent such as nitrobenzene or CS₂, heated under reflux to promote condensation of resorcinol with phthalic anhydride.

Double SN2 substitution of 1,1‑dibromopentane with the sodium diphenylphosphide anion generated in situ from diphenylphosphine and NaH. The reaction installs two diphenylphosphino groups on the carbon chain, releasing H₂ and NaBr. Conducted in dry THF or DMF under nitrogen, usually at 0 °C to rt; no additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation; silver nitrate exchanges its anion with calcium cyanide to form insoluble silver cyanide precipitate and soluble calcium nitrate. Commonly used as a qualitative test for cyanide or to isolate AgCN. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water as solvent; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a benzylic (chloromethyl) C–Cl bond. Hydrogen gas over Pd/C reduces chloromethylcyclopropane to cyclopropylmethane, producing HCl as a by‑product. Carried out in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at 1–5 atm H₂ and room temperature to 50 °C.

Thermal decarboxylation (soda‑lime type). Heating cinnamic acid with sodium carbonate at 250‑300 °C in the solid state eliminates CO₂ and forms styrene; no solvent, used to convert a cinnamic acid derivative to the corresponding alkene.

Condensation (esterification) of two molecules of methacrylic acid with the diol triethylene glycol to give the di‑acrylate monomer and water. Typically acid‑catalyzed (e.g., p‑TsOH) or using a coupling reagent (DCC) under reflux in toluene or xylene with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Acid‑catalyzed redox (halogen displacement) where bromate oxidizes iodide to molecular iodine in aqueous HCl. Results in formation of I₂, water, NaCl and KBr. Conducted at room temperature in aqueous solution; no special catalyst required.

Sodium borohydride reduction of the carbonyl group in 1‑methoxypropan‑2‑one to give 1‑methoxypropan‑2‑ol; typically performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, with NaBH₄ added portionwise, leaving the methoxy substituent unchanged.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of cyclohexyl bromide by methanethiolate to give methyl cyclohexyl sulfide; purpose is thioether synthesis; key transformation is deprotonation of methanethiol (using NaH, K2CO3, or triethylamine) to generate the thiolate, which attacks the primary carbon displacing bromide and releasing HBr (neutralized by the base); common conditions employ a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0–50 °C; no metal catalyst needed.

Type: Oxidation of a vicinal diol to a diketone. Purpose: Convert adjacent secondary alcohols into carbonyl groups, generating 1,2-cyclopentanedione. Key transformation: Each C‑OH group is oxidized to C=O with loss of two hydrogens, producing water as by‑product. Typical conditions: Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in anhydrous dichloromethane, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂). Common solvents/catalysts: Dry CH₂Cl₂, occasionally a buffering base such as pyridine.

Benzylic radical bromination; diphenylmethane undergoes bromination at the benzylic carbon with Br₂ under UV light or heat, yielding bromodiphenylmethane and HBr; usually carried out in carbon tetrachloride or chloroform as solvent at room temperature or mild heating.

N‑alkylation/cyclization of a nucleobase (nucleophilic substitution); the nitrogen atoms of adenine attack the electrophilic carbon of chloroacetaldehyde, displacing chloride and forming a –CH2‑CH2‑ bridge that yields 1,N6‑ethanoadenine. Reaction is carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium (e.g., methanol/water) at mild temperature (0–50 °C) often with a slight excess of chloroacetaldehyde; pH adjusted to keep adenine nucleophilic.

Reduction of an aromatic aldehyde to a primary alcohol using sodium borohydride; selective for the C=O while the nitro group remains untouched; NaBH4 (1–2 equiv) in methanol or ethanol (0 °C to rt); yields 4‑nitrobenzyl alcohol.

Oxidative chlorination of dimethylsilane using sulfuryl chloride; the Si–H bond is converted to a Si–Cl bond, producing dimethylchlorosilane while SO₂ and HCl evolve as gaseous by‑products. Usually carried out neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to reflux, without additional catalyst.

Redox oxidation; elemental tellurium is oxidized in alkaline medium by molecular oxygen to produce sodium tellurite and water; performed in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution, often at 60‑80 °C with air or O₂ bubbling, no special catalyst needed.

Reductive amination of an aldehyde; indole‑3‑acetaldehyde reacts with methylamine to give an imine intermediate, which is reduced by NaBH₃CN to N‑methyltryptamine, releasing water. Typical conditions: methanol solvent, pH adjusted to 6‑8 with a weak acid (e.g., acetic acid), temperature 0‑25 °C; reaction proceeds in 1‑2 h and is quenched with dilute acid before work‑up.

Redox (electron‑transfer) reaction: Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ by oxidation of sodium ascorbate to dehydroascorbic acid, while NaCl is formed from the chloride counter‑ions. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often used in Fenton‑type systems; no additional reagents needed.

Oxime formation (condensation) of acetaldehyde with hydroxylamine; nucleophilic addition of hydroxylamine to the carbonyl followed by dehydration gives acetaldoxime. Typically carried out in ethanol or aqueous ethanol (1–2 M), pH 4–6, 0–25 °C; acid (acetic acid) may be added to promote dehydration.

Acid–base double‑displacement (metathesis) producing lutetium phosphate precipitate and liberating acetic acid. Lutetium(III) acetate reacts with phosphoric acid in aqueous medium, often heated to reflux to drive off the volatile acetic acid; the lutetium phosphate precipitates and is isolated by filtration.

Prodrug activation (ester hydrolysis) of famciclovir to the active antiviral penciclovir. In vivo the conversion occurs enzymatically by hepatic esterases; in vitro it can be mimicked by acidic hydrolysis (e.g., 0.1 M HCl, 60 °C, 1–2 h). No special catalyst beyond the enzyme or acid is required.

Chlorination (acyl chloride formation) of isobutyric acid with phosphorus trichloride; each acid reacts with PCl₃ to give isobutyryl chloride and phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃) as by‑product. Conducted under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, under nitrogen atmosphere; reaction temperature 60–80 °C; excess PCl₃ ensures complete conversion.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of isopropylboronic acid with bromobenzene in the presence of potassium carbonate. The bromide is replaced by the isopropyl group to give isopropylbenzene (cumene), with KBr and boric acid as inorganic by‑products. Common solvents: dioxane/H₂O or THF/H₂O, reflux under nitrogen; catalyst such as Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(dppf).

Acid‑catalyzed cyclization (intramolecular Friedel‑Crafts alkylation). Purpose: converts cannabigerolic acid (CBGA) into the cannabinoid acid cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Key transformation: protonation of the olefinic side chain followed by electrophilic aromatic substitution onto the resorcinol ring, forming the new heterocyclic ring and eliminating a water molecule. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic HCl (1–3 M), reflux or gentle heating (50‑80 °C) for 1–2 h; common solvent methanol, ethanol or a water/acetone mixture; no additional catalyst required.

One‑pot multicomponent condensation (Schiff‑base formation and cyclization) to synthesize 1,10‑phenanthroline. Purpose: builds a bidentate nitrogen chelating ligand from o‑phenylenediamine, formaldehyde and glyoxal. Key transformations: formation of two imine (‑C=N‑) linkages with the diamine, followed by oxidative cyclization and loss of water to give the fused phenanthroline ring system. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or acetic acid with ammonium acetate as a buffer (0.5–1 equiv), reaction time 3–6 h; no metal catalyst required.

Acid dissolution / salt formation; palladium(II) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrobromic acid, the oxide is protonated and converted to soluble PdBr₂, releasing water; performed in aqueous HBr (1–6 M) with gentle heating (≤80 °C) and stirring.

Hydrolysis of gallium(III) chloride; aqueous precipitation reaction. GaCl3 is dissolved in water, where it reacts with water to form insoluble gallium(III) hydroxide precipitate and liberates HCl into the solution. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature; stirring accelerates precipitation. No additional reagents needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of nitro groups to amines. Purpose: reduces 2,4‑dinitrotoluene to 2,4‑diaminotoluene, an intermediate for dyes and polymers. Key transformation: each nitro group (‑NO₂) is hydrogenated to an amine (‑NH₂) with release of water. Typical conditions: hydrogen pressure 1–5 atm, 5–10 % Pd/C (10–20 wt % of substrate), solvent ethanol or methanol, temperature 25‑50 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Acid–metal hydride reaction (hydrogen evolution). Purpose: generates hydrogen gas and a soluble metal chloride. Key transformation: protonation of rubidium hydride (RbH) by HCl to give H₂ and rubidium chloride (RbCl). Typical conditions: aqueous or dilute HCl (1 M), ambient temperature, vigorous gas evolution; often performed in an inert‑gas‑free beaker with stirring.

Hydrolysis (acid‑base) of a metal amide; lithium amide reacts with water to give lithium hydroxide and ammonia gas. The reaction converts the strong base into a more soluble hydroxide while liberating NH3. Usually performed at room temperature in aqueous solution; no catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of ammonium aluminum sulfate (ammonium alum). Purpose: yields basic inorganic products and releases gaseous by‑products. Key transformation: heating causes breakdown of the double salt to ammonia (NH₃), water (H₂O), sulfur trioxide (SO₃) gas and solid aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃). Typical conditions: strong heating above 300 °C in a dry furnace, no solvent; decomposition proceeds in the solid state under a flowing inert or air atmosphere.

Metathesis/acid‑salt reaction of trisodium hexafluoroaluminate with hydrochloric acid. Purpose: converts the fluoro‑aluminate complex into aluminum fluoride and liberates hydrofluoric acid. Key transformation: exchange of Na⁺ for H⁺; the hexafluoroaluminate anion [AlF₆]³⁻ is protonated to AlF₃ (solid) while NaCl forms in solution and HF is released. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (3 equiv) at room temperature or mild heating (30‑60 °C) to improve solubility; stirring until effervescence (HF evolution) subsides.

Direct combination (synthesis) of elemental indium with iodine, a redox halogenation that yields indium(III) iodide; carried out by heating indium metal with excess I₂ in a sealed evacuated tube or under inert atmosphere at 200–300 °C; no solvent needed.

Halogen exchange redox reaction; fluorine, the most electronegative halogen, oxidizes chloride ion to chlorine gas while forming potassium fluoride. carried out in the gas phase at elevated temperature (150‑300 °C) under anhydrous conditions; no solvent required, inert atmosphere often used.

Metal carbonyl formation via reduction; carbon monoxide reduces chromium(VI) oxide to chromium(0), yielding chromium hexacarbonyl and carbon dioxide as by‑product. Conducted in a sealed high‑pressure reactor with CO pressure of 50‑200 atm at 150‑250 °C; usually solvent‑free gas‑phase reaction.

Direct combination (synthesis) redox reaction; oxidizes elemental gold to Au(I) while reducing iodine to iodide, forming gold(I) iodide; requires heating of solid gold with iodine vapour or in dry inert solvent (e.g., dry acetonitrile) at 200‑300 °C; no catalyst.

α‑Bination of an ester (electrophilic halogenation); bromine substitutes a hydrogen on the difluoroacetate α‑carbon, producing ethyl bromodifluoroacetate and hydrogen bromide. Performed in an inert non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt; reaction may be quenched with a base to absorb HBr.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 substitution); sodium methoxide attacks cyclohexyl chloride, displacing chloride to give cyclohexyl methyl ether and sodium chloride. Typically run in dry polar aprotic solvents (THF, DMF, DMSO) under reflux or at 60‑80 °C; inert atmosphere prevents moisture.

Acid‑base deprotonation to generate a strong, non‑nucleophilic base (lithium diisopropylamide, LDA); n‑butyllithium abstracts a proton from N,N‑diisopropylamine, forming butane gas and LDA as the lithium salt. Conducted at –78 °C to –20 °C in dry THF under nitrogen or argon; LDA is used immediately in subsequent reactions.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of thiophene; acetic anhydride supplies the acetyl group, activated by FeCl₃ (Lewis acid), to afford 2‑acetylthiophene with loss of acetic acid. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; FeCl₃ is used in catalytic amounts (5‑20 mol %).

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange); used to prepare soluble zinc triflate, a non‑nucleophilic Lewis acid; Zn(NO3)2 reacts with two equivalents of CF3SO3H giving Zn(CF3SO3)2 and HNO3; typically carried out in anhydrous polar organic solvent (e.g., MeCN or CH2Cl2) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); provides insoluble cadmium carbonate for removal of Cd2+ from solution; Na2CO3 + CdSO4 → CdCO3↓ + Na2SO4; performed in aqueous solution, ambient temperature with stirring; simple filtration isolates the precipitate; no catalyst needed.

Direct oxidation (combustion) of manganese metal; forms manganese(II) oxide, a basic oxide used in ceramics and catalysis; 2 Mn + O2 → 2 MnO; carried out by heating manganese metal in a flow of O2 or air at 600–800 °C; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of 1,3‑propane sultone by a primary amine (amination); yields sulfonic‑acid‑functionalized amine used as a zwitterionic buffer or intermediate; cyclohexyl + 1,3‑propane‑sultone → 2‑(cyclohexylamino)ethanesulfonic acid; usually performed in an aprotic polar solvent (e.g., MeCN, DMF) at 0 °C to rt, often under nitrogen; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization; gallium(III) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to form gallium(III) chloride (GaCl3) and water; performed by adding Ga2O3 to hot (≈60 °C) concentrated HCl (6–12 M) with stirring; water/HCl solution as solvent, no catalyst.

High‑temperature chlorination of a metal oxide; converts Y2O3 to yttrium chloride while liberating O2, useful for preparing YCl3 as a synthesis precursor; 6 Cl2 + 2 Y2O3 → 4 YCl3 + 3 O2; conducted in a furnace at 400–600 °C under a stream of dry Cl2 gas; solid‑state reaction, no solvent, inert‑gas handling required.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide (acid‑base reaction); generates indium(III) hydroxide precipitate and hydroiodic acid; InI3 + 3 H2O → In(OH)3↓ + 3 HI; performed in aqueous media at room temperature, often under stirring; the insoluble In(OH)3 is filtered off; no catalyst needed.

Redox (hydride) reaction of sodium aluminum hydride with iodine; analogous to the bromine reaction, NaAlH4 reduces I2 to iodide, forming aluminum iodide and releasing H2 gas. Conducted in dry ether or THF, often at 0 °C to avoid rapid gas evolution. No catalyst needed; useful for preparing aluminum iodide and hydrogen gas.

Condensation of carbonyl chloride (phosgene) with imidazole to form 1,1'‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) and hydrogen chloride; reaction proceeds in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl; purpose is to generate the coupling reagent CDI.

Oxidative cyclization; peracetic acid oxidizes the thiol‑amine pair of 2‑aminobenzenethiol to form the heterocycle 1,2‑benzisothiazol‑3(2H)‑one while being reduced to acetic acid. Typical conditions: solution in glacial acetic acid or dichloromethane, 0–25 °C, slow addition of peracid, inert atmosphere.

Solid‑state redox (thermite‑type) reaction; Cr(VI) oxide is reduced to Cr₂O₃ and metallic copper is oxidized to CuO. Usually performed by heating a finely mixed powder blend at 600–800 °C in a crucible under air; no solvent or catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; ammonium nitrate and magnesium oxalate exchange ions to give soluble ammonium oxalate and magnesium nitrate. Conduct by dissolving both salts in water, stirring at ambient temperature; products can be isolated by selective crystallization or evaporation.

High‑temperature nitridation; converts gallium(III) oxide to gallium nitride while releasing water vapor; Ga₂O₃ + 2 NH₃ → 2 GaN + 3 H₂O; performed in a flowing NH₃ atmosphere at 800–1000 °C (often in a tube furnace); solid‑state reaction, no solvent; sometimes a slight excess of NH₃ is used to drive the reaction forward.

Electrophilic halogen addition to an alkene; Cl₂ adds across the C=C bond of 1‑chloro‑3,3,3‑trifluoropropene to afford 1,1,2‑trichloro‑3,3,3‑trifluoropropane. Typically carried out in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, with light excluded to suppress radical pathways.

Fluorination/acid‑exchange reaction; antimony(V) oxide reacts with hydrofluoric acid to replace oxide ligands with fluorine, producing volatile antimony pentafluoride (SbF5) and water. Usually conducted with excess anhydrous HF (often in a PTFE or glass‑lined vessel) at ambient to moderate temperature; the HF acts as both reactant and solvent. No additional catalyst is required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 substitution); NaOEt deprotonates 2,4‑dichlorophenol to the phenoxide, which attacks chloroacetic acid to form sodium 2,4‑dichlorophenoxyacetate. Reaction run in dry ethanol or THF under reflux for several hours; ethanol and NaCl are generated as by‑products.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis); triethylamine abstracts the proton from pyridin‑4‑ylmethanol hydrochloride, yielding free pyridin‑4‑ylmethanol and triethylammonium chloride. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Esterification via acyl fluoride substitution; purpose is to prepare methyl 2,2‑difluoroacetate. Key transformation: the fluorine‑substituted acyl fluoride reacts with methanol, the alkoxy oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing fluoride as HF and forming the ester. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) is added to scavenge the generated HF and drive the reaction to completion.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using chromic acid (Jones oxidation). Purpose is conversion of cyclopentanol into cyclopentanone. Key transformation: sodium dichromate is protonated by concentrated H₂SO₄ to generate the active oxidizing species Cr₂O₇²⁻/H₂CrO₄, which oxidizes the alcohol via a two‑electron transfer, yielding the ketone and reducing chromium to Cr³⁺. Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid, typically under reflux (≈80 °C) with vigorous stirring; no organic solvent is required.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt displacement). Purpose is to liberate oxalic acid from its lead salt. Key transformation: lead(II) oxalate reacts with aqueous HCl; the oxalate anion is protonated to give free oxalic acid, while lead(II) pairs with chloride to form soluble lead(II) chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete dissolution.

Reductive decomposition of a metal peroxide. Purpose is to convert strontium peroxide to the corresponding oxide while generating water. Key transformation: hydrogen gas reduces the peroxide O–O bond, producing water and leaving SrO. Requires elevated temperature (typically 300–500 °C) and a flow of H₂ gas over solid SrO₂; the reaction is carried out in a quartz tube or high‑temperature furnace under an inert carrier gas.

Base‑promoted E2 dehydrohalogenation; purpose is to eliminate HBr and form the alkene 1‑phenylpropene; key transformation is abstraction of a β‑hydrogen by potassium tert‑butoxide with simultaneous departure of bromide, producing the double bond; typical conditions: strong, non‑nucleophilic base (KOtBu) in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMSO, often at reflux or 60–80 °C; no additional catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) fluorination of a primary alcohol; pyridinium fluoride acts as a source of fluoride that replaces the hydroxyl group of benzyl alcohol, yielding benzyl fluoride and water. Typically done in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to 25 °C; pyridine hydrofluoride is used in excess; no additional catalyst.

Thermal decarboxylation of a cyclic carbonate (pyrolytic decomposition). Purpose is to generate propylene oxide and CO₂ from propylene carbonate. Key transformation: the five‑membered cyclic carbonate undergoes ring opening and loss of CO₂, forming the epoxide. Conducted at 300–450 °C, often under reduced pressure; heterogeneous catalysts such as zeolites (e.g., H‑Y) or metal oxides (e.g., Al₂O₃) can lower the required temperature and improve yield. No solvent is used in the gas‑phase process.

N‑alkylation of a diamine (nucleophilic substitution, SN2). Purpose is to introduce methyl groups onto both nitrogen atoms of ethylenediamine, yielding N,N′‑dimethylethylenediamine. Key transformation: each nitrogen lone pair attacks a methyl iodide molecule, displacing iodide and forming a new N‑C bond; HI is produced as a by‑product. Typically carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF at 0 °C to reflux, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., NaHCO₃, K₂CO₃, or triethylamine) present to neutralize the generated HI and drive the reaction to completion.

Acid‑base metathesis (double displacement) used to convert lutetium(III) acetate to lutetium(III) nitrate; nitric acid protonates acetate releasing acetic acid and exchanges the anion; typically performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating or reflux; no catalyst required; water serves as solvent.

Allylic oxidation with selenium dioxide; converts the alkene cyclohexene to the allylic alcohol cyclohex‑2‑en‑1‑ol while reducing SeO₂ to elemental selenium. Usually performed under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as 1,4‑dioxane or tert‑butanol/water (80‑120 °C). No additional catalyst is needed, though catalytic variants may use a co‑oxidant to regenerate SeO₂.

Reductive amination of 3‑chlorobenzaldehyde with piperazine using sodium cyanoborohydride; the aldehyde condenses with one nitrogen of piperazine to form an imine which is reduced in situ to give 1‑(3‑chlorophenyl)piperazine; carried out in methanol or ethanol often with a weak acid (e.g., acetic acid) to promote imine formation; temperature 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH3CN provides hydride reduction; no metal catalyst.

Buchwald‑Hart amination of ortho‑difluorobenzene with ammonia to afford 2‑fluoroaniline; Pd(OAc)₂ with tri‑tert‑butylphosphine ligand and Cs₂CO₃ base in a polar aprotic solvent (toluene, dioxane) at 100–120 °C under nitrogen.

Oxidation of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural to 2,5‑furandicarboxaldehyde using manganese dioxide; MnO2 oxidizes the primary alcohol (CH2OH) to the aldehyde (CHO) while leaving the existing aldehyde unchanged; typically carried out at ambient to 50 °C in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone; MnO2 is used in stoichiometric excess as a heterogeneous oxidant; no additional catalyst required; solid MnO2 removed during work‑up.

Acid‑catalyzed formation of ethyl orthoformate from ethanol and formaldehyde; catalytic HCl protonates formaldehyde enabling successive addition of three equivalents of ethanol with loss of water to give HC(OCH2CH3)3; performed in excess ethanol which also acts as solvent; water removed by azeotropic distillation or Dean‑Stark trap; reflux temperature; no catalyst beyond HCl.

Conversion of 1‑naphthol to 1‑chloronaphthalene using thionyl chloride in pyridine; thionyl chloride activates the phenolic OH to a chlorosulfite intermediate that collapses to the aryl chloride, releasing HCl and SO2 gases; pyridine serves as solvent and HCl scavenger; reaction refluxed (≈110 °C) under anhydrous conditions with excess SOCl2; no metal catalyst required.

Condensation (hydrazone formation) of a carbonyl compound with hydrazine hydrochloride; converts the aldehyde carbonyl into a benzaldehyde hydrazone; used for carbonyl protection or as a precursor to Wolff‑Kishner reduction; typically performed in ethanol or acetic acid under reflux with catalytic acid, generating ammonium chloride as by‑product.

Acid–base displacement using nitric acid; purpose is to generate perrhenic acid from potassium perrhenate while producing potassium nitrate. The H⁺ from HNO₃ protonates ReO₄⁻, and K⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻. Conducted in aqueous solution, often under reflux to ensure complete conversion; no catalyst needed.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis/reduction to synthesize samarium antimonide; metallic antimony reacts with samarium trichloride in the presence of calcium reductant, producing SmSb and calcium chloride; carried out in an inert atmosphere (argon) at 600–800 °C in a sealed tube; no solvent, solid reagents only.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; nitrous acid generated in situ (NaNO₂ + HCl) reacts with N‑methylcyclohexylamine to give the N‑nitroso derivative and water; employed to prepare nitrosamines; performed in cold aqueous acidic solution (0–5 °C) to control side reactions.

Acid–peroxide hydrolysis; used to generate hydrogen peroxide while forming an insoluble sulfate salt; peroxide anion is protonated to H2O2 and Ca2+ pairs with SO4^2‑; performed in aqueous solution with dilute H2SO4, temperature kept below ~40 °C to limit H2O2 decomposition; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Electrophilic demethylation of a methoxy ether using boron tribromide; BBr₃ cleaves the 3‑methoxy group of codeine to afford morphine (phenolic hydroxyl) and boron‑bromide by‑products; carried out in dry dichloromethane under inert atmosphere, typically at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed to room temperature; BBr₃ acts as both reagent and Lewis acid catalyst.

Reduction of ketone to secondary alcohol. Lithium aluminum hydride serves as a hydride donor to convert the ketone (1-methoxypropan-2-one) to the corresponding alcohol (1-methoxypropan-2-ol). Requires anhydrous ether solvents (e.g., THF, diethyl ether) and controlled temperature (0–25°C).

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a secondary alkyl bromide; water attacks 2‑bromopropane to replace Br with OH, yielding isopropanol and HBr (or Br⁻ in basic media); generally performed by refluxing the bromide in aqueous solution or using dilute NaOH, often under heating; solvent is water or water/alcohol mixture.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; silver nitrate reacts with cadmium phosphate to exchange anions, forming insoluble silver phosphate precipitate and soluble cadmium nitrate; carried out in water at ambient temperature; the solid silver phosphate can be filtered off, leaving a clear cadmium nitrate solution.

Nucleophilic amidation → cyclic imide formation. Ammonia attacks a carbonyl of succinic anhydride, opening the ring; intramolecular condensation then closes to give succinim with loss of water. Conducted in refluxing aqueous NH₃ or in liquid ammonia/ethanol (1–2 M NH₃) at 80–100 °C; sometimes a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaOH) is used to neutralize generated acid. Purpose: prepare the cyclic imide from the anhydride.

Thermal decomposition/disproportionation of sodium tetrasulfide; purpose is to convert the polysulfide into sulfide and elemental sulfur. Key transformation: Na2S4 → Na2S + 3 S (solid). Typically carried out by heating an aqueous or alcoholic solution of Na2S4 at 50–100 °C under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required; common solvent water or ethanol.

DCC‑mediated Steglich esterification; purpose is to form a methyl ester from a carboxylic acid. Key transformation: butyric acid + MeOH → methyl butyrate with formation of dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; DCC acts as coupling agent; no additional catalyst needed.

SN2 O‑alkylation (methylation) of dihydroartemisinin; purpose is synthesis of the antimalarial artemether. Key transformation: the phenolic/alcoholic OH of dihydroartemisinin is methylated by methyl p‑toluenesulfonate in the presence of potassium carbonate, giving artemether and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. Reaction performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetone, DMF or THF, refluxing (50–80 °C) under inert atmosphere; base K2CO3 serves to deprotonate the alcohol; no metal catalyst required.

N‑alkylation of a primary amine (SN2); methyl iodide alkylates the nitrogen of 2‑aminoindane to give N‑methyl‑2‑aminoindane, with HI as a by‑product. Typically carried out in an aprotic polar solvent (acetone, DMF, or MeCN) in the presence of a base (triethylamine, NaHCO3, or Na2CO3) to neutralise HI. Reaction temperature is kept low to moderate (0–25 °C) to avoid over‑alkylation.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 4‑methylbenzyl alcohol to give 4‑methylstyrene; performed with concentrated H₂SO₄ or phosphoric acid at 140–180 °C, water is removed to drive the equilibrium toward the alkene.

Strong reduction of aromatic carboxylic acid; lithium aluminium hydride (LAH) reduces the carboxyl group of 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzoic acid to the benzylic alcohol, 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzyl alcohol. Performed under inert atmosphere in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C then reflux; excess LAH is quenched cautiously with water then dilute acid.

Phosphorus oxychloride‑mediated amidation of salicylic acid; purpose is preparation of salicylamide. Key transformation: salicylic acid is converted to its acid chloride by POCl3, which then reacts with ammonia to give salicylamide, releasing three equivalents of HCl and forming phosphoric acid as by‑product. Conducted at 0–5 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; POCl3 acts as the activating/dehydrating agent; no external catalyst needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is ion exchange and isolation of insoluble barium sulfate. Key transformation: Ba(NO3)2 + Tl2SO4 → BaSO4(s) + 2 TlNO3(aq). Both salts are dissolved in water, mixed at ambient temperature, and the BaSO4 precipitate is filtered off. No catalyst or special solvent beyond water is required.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration of N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)urea to 2‑oxazolidinone; purpose is construction of a five‑membered heterocycle. Key transformation: loss of water to form the cyclic carbamate (oxazolidinone). Commonly achieved by treating the urea with phosgene, triphosgene, or carbonyldiimidazole in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often in the presence of a base such as triethylamine to capture HCl. The activating carbonyl reagent serves as the cyclization promoter; no additional metal catalyst is needed.

Peroxide oxidation of sulfite; purpose: rapid conversion of SrSO₃ to SrSO₄; key transformation: SO₃²⁻ + H₂O₂ → SO₄²⁻ + H₂O; conditions: aqueous solution, add H₂O₂ (≈30 % or dilute) at 20–60 °C, pH neutral to slightly acidic; solvent: water.

Acid‑base salt hydrolysis; used to liberate hydrazine from its acetate salt. Proton transfer from the acetate anion to the hydrazinium cation yields neutral hydrazine and acetic acid. Typically performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating (80‑120 °C) to drive off acetic acid; no catalyst required; solvent is water or dilute aqueous ethanol.

Redox reduction of a metal salt; employed to recover platinum metal from chloroplatinic acid. Hydrogen gas reduces Pt(IV) in H₂PtCl₆ to elemental Pt⁰ while chloride ions are protonated to HCl. Conducted in aqueous solution under reflux with excess H₂ (sometimes under pressure). No additional catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation); synthesizes ethyl salicylate from salicylic acid and ethanol. The carboxylic acid reacts with ethanol, losing water to form the ester. Catalyzed by solid acidic aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) or by mineral acid; reflux in excess ethanol with Al₂O₃, removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) improves yield. Solvent: ethanol (used as both reactant and solvent).

Hydration/crystallization of anhydrous nickel(II) bromide from water to give the hexahydrate; typically achieved by dissolving NiBr2 in water and allowing slow evaporation or cooling to precipitate NiBr2·6H2O.

Hydrolysis of a carbamate (prodrug activation); converts Racecadotril to the active inhibitor thiorphan. Water attacks the ethoxycarbonyl group, cleaving it to give thiorphan and ethanol. Occurs in aqueous medium at physiological pH (~7‑8) and temperature (≈37 °C), often mediated by amidase enzymes; chemical hydrolysis can be accelerated with mild acid or base. Solvent: water.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange in solution; swaps aluminum and magnesium between sulfate and citrate anions to give magnesium sulfate and aluminum citrate. Performed in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient temperature; pH may be adjusted to maintain solubility. No catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

2-chlorobenzamide + bromine + sodium hydroxide → 2-chloroaniline + sodium carbonate + sodium bromide + water  
Type: Hofmann (or Bayer) rearrangement. Purpose: one‑carbon loss conversion of an amide into a primary amine. Key transformation: bromination of the amide nitrogen to form an N‑bromoamide, followed by base‑induced migration of the R group from carbonyl carbon to nitrogen, expelling CO₂. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (5–10 % w/v) with Br₂ added at 0 °C, then the mixture warmed to reflux (≈80 °C) for 1–2 h. Reaction performed in water; no additional solvent needed.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative cross‑coupling (carbonylation) to form an ester; converts bromobenzene, CO, and ethanol to ethyl benzoate while generating HBr. Involves oxidative addition of Pd⁰ to the aryl bromide, CO insertion, and ethanolysis to release the ester. Typical conditions: CO pressure 1–5 atm, Pd catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄), base such as triethylamine or Na₂CO₃, solvent like DMF or toluene, temperature 80–120 °C. No additional catalyst beyond the palladium complex.

Enzyme‑catalyzed methyl‑transfer (betaine‑homocysteine S‑methyltransferase); trimethylglycine (betaine) donates a methyl group to L‑homocysteine, forming L‑methionine and N,N‑dimethylglycine; reaction occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.4) and temperature (37 °C); requires the BHMT enzyme and often Zn²⁺ as cofactor.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration (double nitration); purpose to introduce a second nitro group ortho to the methoxy substituent, converting p‑nitroanisole to 2,4‑dinitroanisole. Key transformation: generation of the nitronium ion (NO2⁺) from fuming HNO3/H2SO4 and attack on the aromatic ring; second nitro adds at the 2‑position. Typical conditions: mix p‑nitroanisole with concentrated H2SO4 and fuming HNO3, keep temperature 0‑5 °C then allow to warm to 20‑30 °C. Solvent: concentrated H2SO4 (acts as both solvent and catalyst).

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); purpose to convert sparingly soluble Rh(III) hydroxide to soluble Rh(III) nitrate. Key transformation: proton transfer from HNO3 to OH⁻ on rhodium, yielding water and Rh(NO3)3. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stoichiometric amounts of concentrated nitric acid added to a suspension of Rh(OH)3. Solvent: water.

Esterification (acylation) of an alcohol with an acyl chloride; converts the secondary alcohol to its acetate ester while generating hydrogen chloride. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Thermal decarboxylation of malonic acid; purpose to generate a one‑carbon shorter carboxylic acid. Key transformation: loss of one carboxyl group as CO2, converting malonic acid to acetic acid. Typical conditions: heating malonic acid neat or in high‑boiling solvent (e.g., xylene) at 200‑250 °C, sometimes with a copper catalyst. No special solvent required; reaction often performed under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of epichlorohydrin (chlorooxirane) to glycerol; purpose to open the strained epoxide ring and replace the chloride with hydroxyl groups. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the epoxide, formation of a glycol intermediate, displacement of chloride as HCl, yielding 1,2,3‑propanetriol. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 10 % H2SO4) or aqueous base followed by acid work‑up; temperature 80‑100 °C. Solvent: water or mixture of water and an organic co‑solvent (e.g., acetone). Catalyst: mineral acid or base.

Redox/acid‑base reaction forming disodium telluride; purpose to generate the telluride anion and release hydrogen gas. Key transformation: Na metal reduces H2Te, each Na donates an electron, forming Na⁺ and H· which combine to H2, while Te²⁻ pairs with two Na⁺ to give Na2Te. Typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free environment (argon) at 0‑20 °C, using dry ether or THF as solvent; Na added slowly to a solution of H2Te gas or liquid. No additional catalyst needed.

Aminolysis of ethyl acetate (nucleophilic acyl substitution) to give acetamide; purpose to synthesize a primary amide from an ester. Key transformation: ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon, tetrahedral intermediate collapses, expelling ethanol and forming acetamide. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH3, reflux 60‑80 °C for several hours; removal of ethanol by azeotropic distillation or nitrogen sweep. Solvent: usually ethanol or water; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium formate; used as a convenient source of gaseous ammonia, carbon dioxide and hydrogen for reduction or gas‑generation applications. Upon heating (≈120‑200 °C) the solid breaks down to NH₃, CO₂ and H₂, typically in the absence of solvent or under a flow of inert gas.

Oxidative combustion of boron phosphide in oxygen to give boron oxide and phosphorus pentoxide; demonstrates the instability of BP in air and can be used for analytical conversion; the reaction oxidizes B‑P bonds to B2O3 and P2O5; generally occurs rapidly at temperatures above 400 °C when BP is exposed to air or O2 flow; no solvent or catalyst required.

Condensation (aminoalkylation) – Ammonia reacts with formaldehyde in aqueous solution (0–50 °C, pH ≈ 8–10) to give tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane (TRIS) with loss of water; the reaction proceeds via stepwise addition of hydroxymethyl groups to the amine.

Halide metathesis (double displacement) converting antimony(III) chloride to antimony(III) fluoride. Ammonium fluoride supplies fluoride ion, displacing chloride and forming ammonium chloride as a by‑product. Usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the insoluble SbF₃ precipitates and is isolated by filtration.

General type: halogen oxidation (redox) and sulfide displacement. Purpose: conversion of cadmium sulfide to cadmium chloride and elemental sulfur. Key transformation: CdS + Cl₂ → CdCl₂ + S. Typical conditions: dry chlorine gas passed over solid CdS at 200‑400 °C in a furnace or tubular reactor; reaction is exothermic and may be carried out under flowing inert gas to remove sulfur vapor. Common medium: solid‑gas; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of 1‑propanol to propanal with potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid. Under acidic conditions (dilute H₂SO₄) and low temperature (0‑25 °C) the dichromate ion oxidizes the primary alcohol to the aldehyde, stopping before further oxidation to the acid. The reaction is usually carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑acetone medium, and water is produced as a by‑product.

The reaction is a reduction reaction. Its purpose is to convert the amide group of salicylamide into an amino group. Key transformation involves the reduction of the amide (CONH₂) into an amine (NH₂), yielding 2-aminophenol. Lithium aluminum hydride serves as a strong hydride donor reagent, typically used in aprotic solvents such as THF or diethyl ether under anhydrous conditions followed by controlled hydrolysis.
Hydrolysis reaction; N,N-diisopropylurea undergoes nucleophilic attack by water, cleaving N-C bonds to produce isopropylamine and CO₂. Typically occurs in aqueous or acidic conditions with heat.

Ligand exchange (metathesis) between sodium cyanide and gold(I) bromide, producing gold(I) cyanide and sodium bromide. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, the cyanide ion replaces bromide on Au⁺, and the resulting AuCN precipitates (or remains soluble depending on concentration), while NaBr stays in solution. This reaction is used to prepare gold cyanide salts for further processing.

Alpha‑halogenation of a ketone (bromination); NaOBr generates enolate of acetone which is brominated at the α‑position to give bromoacetone and NaOH. Typical conditions: aqueous sodium hypobromite at 0–5 °C, pH ~9, water as solvent; reaction proceeds quickly without additional catalyst.

Nitro‑group reduction (reductive amination) using tin(II) chloride; SnCl₂ in acidic aqueous medium reduces p‑nitrobenzenesulfonic acid to the corresponding amine, sulfanilic acid, with concomitant oxidation of Sn²⁺ to Sn⁴⁺ (SnCl₄) and formation of water. Conducted under reflux in a mixture of water and concentrated HCl or ethanol; SnCl₂ serves as both reagent and catalyst.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate; upon strong heating the orange solid decomposes explosively to nitrogen gas, solid chromium(III) oxide (green) and water vapor. Reaction is carried out by heating the solid in a crucible or on a porcelain dish; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Acid‑base metathesis (double displacement) between phosphoric acid and calcium propionate; the strong acid protonates the propionate anion liberating propionic acid, while calcium combines with phosphate to form calcium phosphateitate. Performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off the volatile propionic acid; no special catalyst required.
LiAlH₄ reduction of an ester; tert‑butyl heptanoate is reduced to 1‑heptanol while tert‑butyl alcohol is formed as a by‑product; performed in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux.

Oxidative conversion of a phenol to a quinone; 2,5‑dichlorophenol is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide in acetic acid to give 2,5‑dichloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone. The reaction is an electrophilic oxidation, commonly carried out at 0–25 °C in glacial acetic acid; catalytic amounts of transition‑metal ions (e.g., Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺) or peracid formation can accelerate the process.

Redox decomposition of diborane by nitric acid; HNO₃ oxidizes B₂H₆ to boric acid while itself is reduced to nitrogen dioxide and water. Usually conducted in cold, dilute nitric acid (0–5 °C) to control vigorous gas evolution; reaction mixture is aqueous, no external catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation (formation of Prussian‑blue type complex); ammonium hexacyanoferrate(II) reacts with iron(III) chloride in aqueous solution to produce ferric hexacyanoferrate(II) (Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃) and ammonium chloride. Reaction carried out at room temperature in water; mixing of the two solutions causes immediate precipitation of the deep‑blue ferric ferrocyanide complex, while NH₄Cl remains soluble.

Oxidative coupling; MnO₂ oxidizes phenylhydrazine to azobenzene while being reduced to MnO (Mn(II) oxide). Usually performed in an organic solvent such as ethanol, acetic acid or dichloromethane at 50‑80 °C with excess MnO₂. Purpose is preparation of the azo compound.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous lead(II) nitrate reacts with sodium formate to produce lead(II) formate (sparingly soluble) and sodium nitrate. Reaction: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2 NaHCOO → Pb(HCOO)₂↓ + 2 NaNO₃. Performed in aqueous medium at room temperature; solid lead formate is filtered off, no catalyst needed.

Oxidation (redox) of a telluride to tellurite; purpose is to convert Te²⁻ to Te⁴⁺. Disodium telluride reacts with molecular oxygen (or air) in aqueous alkaline solution to give sodium tellurite (Na₂TeO₃). Performed at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring and O₂ bubbling; no catalyst required.

Acylation (esterification) of Etilefrine with pivalic anhydride; the phenolic hydroxyl of Etilefrine attacks the anhydride, forming Etilefrine pivalate and releasing pivalic acid. Standard conditions employ an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, a base (e.g., pyridine or DMAP) to scavenge the acid, and temperatures from 0 °C to room temperature.

This is an acetylation reaction, a type of nucleophilic substitution. The hydroxyl group of 1-phenylethanol reacts with acetic anhydride to form an acetoxy ester. The reaction typically proceeds under mild acidic or basic conditions, often using pyridine or sulfuric acid as a catalyst. Common solvents include dichloromethane or acetic acid.

This is an acid-base reaction forming a hydrochloride salt. Phenothiazine acts as a base, accepting a proton from hydrochloric acid. The reaction is typically carried out in aqueous solution or in a solvent like ethanol to facilitate salt formation.

Condensation of tert‑butyl isocyanate with ammonium carbonate to give tert‑butylurea with simultaneous release of carbon dioxide and water; performed in aqueous or alcoholic medium under mild heating (reflux), no additional catalyst needed.

This double displacement reaction between lanthanum(III) nitrate and oxalic acid synthesizes lanthanum oxalate, an insoluble solid. Key transformations include nitrate and oxalate ion exchange, producing lanthanum oxalate precipitate and nitric acid. The reaction occurs in aqueous solution, often under heating to enhance dissolution of oxalic acid. Water is the solvent, and no catalysts are needed.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction. Hydroxylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon adjacent to the iodide in iodoacetic acid, displacing iodide. The reaction is conducted in aqueous or ethanol solution, often under mild heating.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbonate synthesis) – Potassium ethoxide (generated in anhydrous ethanol) attacks ethyl chloroformate,placing chloride to give diethyl; reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, using dry ethanol or THF as solvent, and the only by‑product is KCl.

Electrolytic decomposition of molten cadmium chloride (molten‑salt electrolysis); at the cathode Cd²⁺ is reduced to cadmium metal, while at the anode Cl⁻ is oxidized to chlorine gas. Performed at temperatures ≥600 °C to keep CdCl₂ molten, using inert electrodes (graphite or steel) in a sealed cell or under an inert gas atmosphere.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acyl azide synthesis); preparation of 4‑fluorobenzoyl azide from the acid chloride. Performed by treating the acid chloride with sodium azide (1.2–2 equiv) in dry DMF or a mixed aqueous/organic solvent at 0 °C to rt. The azide ion displaces chloride, yielding the acyl azide and NaCl; low temperature helps prevent premature Curtius rearrangement.

This is a reductive amination reaction. Ammonia and 2-pyridinecarboxaldehyde form imines, which are reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to produce bis(2-pyridylmethyl)amine. The reaction is conducted in aqueous or methanol solution, often under mildly acidic conditions.

Wittig olefination of 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde with methylenetriphenylphosphorane to give the α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde 2‑nitrocinnamaldehyde; triphenylphosphine oxide is formed as by‑product. Performed under anhydrous conditions in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) between ammonium chromate and cadmium chloride forming insoluble cadmium chromate and ammonium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no additional reagents needed.

Enolate alkylation of 2‑cyclohexen‑1‑one: LDA generates the kinetic enolate in dry THF at –78 °C, which is then methylated with methyl iodide to afford 2‑methyl‑2‑cyclohexen‑1‑one. Reaction is performed under inert atmosphere, quenched with water; no catalyst.

Multi‑component condensation/cyclization (heterocycle formation) – Formamide, methyl chloroacetate, and 2‑amino‑5‑chlorobenzophenone are combined in ethanol with sodium ethoxide as base; the mixture is refluxed, allowing amidation of the formamide, ester‑amine displacement, and intramolecular cyclization to afford the triazolo‑benzodiazepine core of estazolam; the reaction proceeds under reflux (≈78 °C) and is typically purified by crystallization.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of 2-(2‑hydroxyethoxy)ethyl acetate with water to give diethylene glycol and acetic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous acidic (e.g., dilute HCl) or basic medium, heated to reflux; solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Double displacement reaction; prepares mercuric dithiocyanate from ammonium thiocyanate and mercury(II) fluoride; key transformation: HgF2 + 2 NH4SCN → Hg(SCN)2 + 2 NH4F; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; solvent water; no catalyst.

Reduction of acid chloride (hydride reduction) – Heptanoyl chloride is reduced by lithium aluminium hydride in anhydrous diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; LiAlH4 donates hydride to the carbonyl carbon, generating the primary alcohol 1‑heptanol after aqueous work‑up, with evolution of H2 gas and formation of Al(OH)3.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ester; reduces the C=C double bond while leaving the carbonyl intact. Purpose: obtain saturated ethyl butanoate. Key transformation: ethyl trans‑2‑butenoate + H2 → ethyl butanoate. Typical conditions: H2 pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 wt %) as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate or methanol, temperature 20–50 °C, stirring until uptake ceases.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of phenethyl bromide by acetate ion to form phenethyl acetate; used to synthesize fragrance ester; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF with sodium acetate, reflux heating, and removal of NaBr precipitate.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (saponification) of N‑[3‑(4‑aminobutylamino)propyl]acetamide; yields spermidine and sodium acetate; carried out with aqueous NaOH, often heated under reflux, optionally in water or mixed water‑methanol solvent.

Iron(III)‑catalyzed oxidation of catechol using tert‑butyl hydroperoxide as oxidant; converts catechol to 1,2‑benzoquinone while reducing TBHP to tert‑butyl alcohol; reaction run in aqueous or mixed organic solvent at ambient to moderate temperature, Fe(III) sulfate as catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 4,4‑dinitrobiphenyl to benzidine (4,4′‑diaminobiphenyl); reduces two nitro groups to amines; performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt‑O₂, in ethanol or methanol at 50‑100 °C.

Catalytic hydrogenation of carbon dioxide to formic acid; CO₂ is reduced by H₂ in the presence of a homogeneous metal complex (e.g., Ru, Ir, or Mn pincer catalysts) or heterogeneous metal catalyst; reactions usually conducted under elevated pressure (10‑50 bar) and temperatures of 50‑120 °C in aqueous or mixed solvent, often with a base to generate formate.

Halogenation of propargyl alcohol with phosphorus tribromide to give propargyl bromide; a typical Appel‑type conversion of primary alcohols to bromides; carried out at 0‑25 °C in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with PBr₃ added dropwise, yielding phosphorous acid as by‑product.

Alcoholysis (metal alkoxide formation); used to prepare titanium(IV) isopropoxide for sol‑gel or polymerization; replaces Ti–Cl bonds with Ti–O‑iPr bonds, releasing HCl; typically performed under anhydrous conditions by adding excess isopropanol to TiCl4 at 0 °C to reflux, often in a dry inert atmosphere; no additional solvent required or the reaction is run neat.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts bromination); brominates anisole preferentially at the para position to give bromoanisole while generating HBr; AlBr3 acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst activating Br2; carried out in anhydrous non‑protic solvents such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; reaction is quenched with water to remove residual AlBr3.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of a chloro‑adenine with fluoride. 2‑Chloro‑adenine is mixed with excess potassium fluoride in dimethyl sulfoxide and heated to 80–120 °C under an inert atmosphere. Fluoride displaces chloride at the 2‑position, producing 2‑fluoroadenine and potassium chloride. DMSO acts as a polar aprotic solvent that solvates KF and facilitates the SNAr pathway.

High‑temperature solid‑state oxide synthesis; combines WO3 and Li2O to yield lithium tungstate (Li2WO4) through a direct oxide‑oxide reaction; usually performed by grinding the powders together and heating in a furnace at 800–1000 °C for several hours in air or inert gas; no solvent; sometimes a flux (e.g., Na2CO3) is added to promote sintering.

O‑alkylation (SN2 methylation) of phenolic hydroxyl groups in a flavonoid; purpose is to convert quercetin’s phenols to methoxy groups, increasing lipophilicity and altering biological activity. Silver oxide acts as a mild base and precipitates AgI, driving the reaction forward. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF) under reflux; methyl iodide as methyl donor; reaction proceeds until AgI precipitates, then work‑up isolates the tetramethoxyflavone.
